title: Total knee arthroplasty, post-operative day 2
setting: Orthopedic ward of an acute care hospital
client_profile: Mr. Harpreet Gill is a 71-year-old retired bus driver, two days after a left cemented total knee arthroplasty for osteoarthritis. He lives with his wife in a two-storey home with six entry steps. History: hypertension, type 2 diabetes, body mass index 33 kg/m2. Medications: ramipril, metformin, acetaminophen, a low-molecular-weight heparin injection once daily, and an opioid as needed. Today at rest: blood pressure 138/84 mmHg, heart rate 104 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20, temperature 37.6 degrees C, oxygen saturation 93 percent on room air (95 percent yesterday). Pain is 7 out of 10 with movement. Left knee active flexion 50 degrees, extension lag 10 degrees, dressing dry. Left calf is 3 cm larger than the right at mid-calf, warm and tender to light palpation. He reports he walked to the bathroom twice with the nurse.
clinical_scenario: Mr. Gill is anxious to go home on day 3 because his wife has a medical appointment he does not want her to attend alone. The surgeon's pathway lists discharge once he can walk 30 metres and climb stairs. Mr. Gill asks you to write that he met the goals. His daughter, who lives in another province, phones the ward and asks you to tell her everything about his condition and says her father does not like to worry people. The nurse is busy with an admission and the surgical resident is in the operating room until the afternoon.

questions.prompt: Describe how you interpret the findings from your initial assessment today and what you decide to do first. Explain which findings you consider most important and why.

checklist.point: Identifies the unilateral calf swelling, warmth and tenderness as the priority finding rather than the limited knee flexion.
Links the swelling to the post-operative risk of venous thromboembolism given surgery, obesity, age and reduced mobility.
Notes the new tachycardia, lower oxygen saturation and low-grade temperature as a possible sign of a pulmonary complication or other deterioration.
Recognizes that knee flexion of 50 degrees and pain of 7 out of 10 are expected on day 2 and are secondary.
States that mobilization and calf-loading exercise are held until a physician has assessed him.
Plans to recheck vital signs and ask about chest pain, dyspnea, cough and light-headedness.
Describes communicating findings promptly and clearly to the nurse and the surgical team using a structured format.
Mentions comparing both calves with a tape measure at a consistent landmark and documenting the values.

questions.model_answer:
My first impression is that the most important finding today is not the knee range, it is the left calf together with the change in his vital signs. Let me take it in order.

On the knee, 50 degrees of flexion with a ten degree extension lag and pain of 7 out of 10 on day 2 after a cemented replacement is about what I would expect. That is a rehabilitation problem I can work on, but it is not what worries me.

What worries me is that the left calf is 3 centimetres bigger than the right, warm and tender, and he has other findings that moved the wrong way since yesterday. His heart rate is 104, his oxygen saturation has dropped from 95 to 93 percent on room air, and his temperature is slightly raised. He has several risk factors for a blood clot: recent major lower limb surgery, age, a body mass index of 33, diabetes and limited mobility, even though he is on a daily anticoagulant injection. Prophylaxis lowers risk but does not remove it. A one-sided swollen, tender calf could be a deep vein thrombosis, and a faster heart rate with falling saturation raises the possibility that a clot has already travelled to the lungs. Other causes such as a hematoma, cellulitis or normal post-operative swelling are possible, but I cannot sort that out with my hands, and I should treat the dangerous explanation first.

So first, I would stop and not walk him or load the leg, and I would not massage the calf or do vigorous ankle pumps. I would keep him comfortable in bed with the leg supported. Then I would ask about chest pain, shortness of breath, cough, and light-headedness, and I would repeat his pulse, respiratory rate and oxygen saturation myself. I would measure both calves at the same distance below the tibial tuberosity and record the numbers.

Next, I would not wait for the resident to finish in the operating room. I would go directly to the nurse in charge, explain it is urgent, and give a short structured report: the patient, the surgery, my findings with the numbers, what I have held, and what I am asking for, which is a physician assessment now and a decision about imaging. If his breathing worsens or he has chest pain, I would call for the rapid response team.

Only after he has been medically cleared would I return to the usual plan of walking, knee flexion, extension work and stair practice. I would document the time, findings, who I told and their response.

scale.4: Names the calf and vital sign changes as the priority, explains the clot risk with case facts, holds mobilization, escalates urgently with a clear message, and places knee range as secondary.
scale.3: Recognizes the calf finding and escalates, but explains the risk factors or the vital sign link only briefly, or does not state what is held.
scale.2: Lists several findings and plans knee rehabilitation while mentioning the calf only in passing, or reports it without a clear reason.
scale.1: Proceeds with walking and stairs, attributes the calf to normal swelling, or does not notify anyone.

questions.prompt: Mr. Gill tells you he feels fine, wants to walk the hallway so the discharge goals can be signed off, and asks you to hold off mentioning the leg. How do you respond and what do you do next?

checklist.point: Acknowledges his worry about his wife and his wish to go home before addressing the safety concern.
Explains in plain language why walking is paused today, including the possible risk to his health.
Refuses to agree to withhold the finding from the team and explains that sharing it is part of keeping him safe.
Checks his understanding and invites questions using teach-back.
Offers safe alternatives while waiting, such as positioning, comfort measures and reassurance.
Presents discharge as a goal that depends on the medical assessment, without promising or ruling out day 3.
Respects his right to make decisions after he has been informed and documents the discussion.
Explores practical solutions for his wife's appointment, such as asking about family, social work or transport.

questions.model_answer:
I would start by listening to what is behind his request, because I think it comes from caring about his wife. I would say something like, you are clearly worried about being there for your wife, and I want to help you get home as soon as it is safe.

Then I would be honest about why I am not going to walk him today. I would sit at his level and use plain words: the leg I examined is more swollen and tender than the other side, and your heart rate and oxygen level have changed since yesterday. After a knee replacement, that can mean a blood clot in the leg. If we walk on it, there is a small chance the clot could move to the lungs, which is serious. I would say I am not sure that is what it is, but I am not willing to take that chance, and the doctors need to check it.

He asked me not to mention the leg. I cannot agree to that and I would tell him why, kindly and directly. My role is to keep him safe, and the people who can test for a clot need to know what I found. Sharing it with his care team is part of his care, and it does not mean he will not go home. I would tell him I will be the one to explain to the nurse and the team, and that he will hear the results.

I would check what he understood by asking him to tell me in his own words what we are waiting for and why walking is paused. I would answer questions and watch for fear. People often hide symptoms when they are afraid of staying longer, so I would also ask him directly about chest pain, breathlessness or light-headedness, and tell him to press the call bell right away if any of those start.

While we wait, I would help him find a comfortable position with the leg supported, and I would give him simple things he can do, such as breathing exercises and gentle upper body movement, nothing that loads or squeezes the calf.

About discharge, I would not promise or rule out tomorrow. I would say it depends on what the doctors find, and that I will work with him on a plan either way. I would also ask whether the social worker could help with options for his wife's appointment, like a relative, a ride service or a hospital escort, so that worry is not driving his decisions.

If, once informed, he still wants to go ahead, he has the right to decide, but I would involve the nurse and physician before anything happens, and I would document what I told him, his answer and who I informed.

scale.4: Responds with empathy, explains the risk plainly, declines to withhold information and says why, checks understanding, offers interim options and addresses his actual worry.
scale.3: Explains and declines to withhold, but is brief on empathy, teach-back or his underlying concern.
scale.2: Delays walking but is vague on why, or goes along partly with his request without telling the team.
scale.1: Agrees to keep the finding private or walks him to avoid conflict.

questions.prompt: Mr. Gill's daughter phones and asks you to tell her everything about his condition and not to mention it to him. Describe how you handle the call and the documentation expectations for this day.

checklist.point: Identifies that personal health information may only be shared with consent from the client or an authorized substitute decision-maker.
Does not disclose clinical details to the daughter without his permission, and does not confirm findings by phone.
Offers to ask Mr. Gill if he would like her to be updated and by whom.
Declines to keep information from the client about his own care.
Notes that capacity is presumed, and that nothing suggests he lacks it.
Redirects her to the nurse or most responsible physician for general inquiries within the facility's privacy policy.
Documents the phone call, what was and was not shared, and the clinical findings with times and the person notified.
References provincial health privacy legislation and the regulator's standards on confidentiality and records.

questions.model_answer:
I would handle this call by protecting his privacy while staying kind to his daughter, who is far away and afraid.

First, my duty. Under provincial health privacy legislation and my regulator's standards, I can share a client's personal health information only with his consent, or with a substitute decision-maker if he cannot decide. Nothing I have seen suggests Mr. Gill lacks capacity, and capacity is presumed. He is alert and gave clear instructions today. So his daughter does not have an automatic right to details, even though she is family and even though she is clearly worried.

Second, how I would say it. I would be warm and brief: I can hear how concerned you are, and I am glad you called. I am not able to share details of your father's care without his permission, but I will ask him whether he wants you to be updated and how. I would not confirm or deny any findings, and I would not say whether he is doing well or poorly, because even that is health information. If the facility has a process for a code or a designated contact, I would check if his chart lists her. I would point her to the nurse in charge or the physician for any general information the hospital policy allows.

Third, the part about not telling him. I cannot agree to hide things from Mr. Gill about his own care. He has the right to know his findings and make decisions. If I agreed, I would be working for the daughter instead of the client, and I would damage his trust. I would tell her that politely and then speak to him. I would ask him: your daughter called and wants to know how you are. Would you like her to know, and who should speak to her? If he agrees, I would note that consent, including what he allows me to share. If he says no, I respect that.

Fourth, documentation. Today my note should show the assessment findings with numbers: heart rate, saturation, temperature, the calf measurements for both sides, his symptoms. It should record that I held mobilization, who I told and when, what the response was, and what he said to me. I would also write that his daughter phoned, what I did and did not disclose, and that I will follow up on his consent. I would date and time each entry, and keep it factual, not interpretive.

If I felt unsure about the policy, I would consult the privacy officer or my manager.

scale.4: Cites consent and capacity, withholds details kindly, refuses secrecy from the client, obtains his wishes, and describes precise documentation.
scale.3: Protects privacy and informs the client but is brief on capacity, redirection or documentation detail.
scale.2: Declines the call but without explaining the consent principle, or documents only vaguely.
scale.1: Discloses clinical details to the daughter or agrees to hide information from the client.

safety_or_ethics_point: The buried issue is the unilateral calf swelling with tachycardia and falling oxygen saturation, a possible clot, while the client pushes for discharge goals. A competent candidate holds mobilization, escalates urgently, and does not agree to hide findings. The daughter's call also tests consent and confidentiality.
common_errors: Candidates focus on knee range of motion and stairs and mention the calf late or not at all. Others tell the daughter the findings because she is family, or agree to the client's request to stay quiet, to be kind.
examiner_notes: A pass finds the calf and vital sign picture first, holds activity, escalates with numbers and a clear request, and protects consent. A fail treats this as a routine day 2 knee rehabilitation case.

title: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, pulmonary rehabilitation intake
setting: Hospital-based outpatient pulmonary rehabilitation program
client_profile: Mr. Daniel Beaulieu is a 69-year-old retired welder, referred by his respirologist after a hospital admission eight weeks ago. Diagnosis: severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, post-bronchodilator FEV1 38 percent predicted. Former smoker, 45 pack-years, quit 3 years ago. Medications: long-acting inhaled bronchodilator and an inhaled corticosteroid combination, and a short-acting rescue inhaler. He has home oxygen prescribed at 2 L/min for exertion but says he leaves it at home. Today at rest on room air: oxygen saturation 92 percent, heart rate 88, blood pressure 132/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 22. Six-minute walk test: 230 metres, stopped twice, lowest saturation 85 percent, peak dyspnea 7 out of 10 on the modified Borg scale. Chronic cough, usually clear sputum. Reports he avoids stairs, stopped his weekly card game, and feels short of breath dressing. Quadriceps strength is reduced bilaterally.
clinical_scenario: Mr. Beaulieu lives alone in a small town 55 kilometres away and drives himself to the program. He tells you the oxygen tank is embarrassing and that he would rather be breathless than be seen with it. At intake he mentions that for the last three days he has been coughing up thicker, yellowish sputum and has felt more tired, but says it is nothing new because winters are always bad. The program runs two supervised sessions per week for eight weeks. He tells you he skips some inhaler doses because the cost adds up each month.

questions.prompt: Outline the exercise and education plan you would propose for Mr. Beaulieu's rehabilitation, and explain how you would set the intensity, progress it and measure whether it is working.

checklist.point: Sets goals with the client that relate to his valued activities such as dressing, stairs and the card game.
Plans combined aerobic training, such as walking or cycling, and lower and upper limb resistance training.
Sets intensity using symptoms and the Borg scale (for example dyspnea of 3 to 4 out of 10), supported by the walk test result, rather than a standard heart rate formula alone.
Plans interval training for a client who stops frequently, with progressive lengthening of work periods.
Includes supplemental oxygen during exercise to keep saturation at or above the target set by the team, and discusses its benefit.
Includes breathing strategies such as pursed-lip breathing and energy conservation in the plan.
Specifies outcome measures to repeat, such as six-minute walk distance, dyspnea scale and a validated quality of life questionnaire, and states reassessment timing.
Describes a progression rule and a plan for a home program and maintenance after the eight weeks.
Recognizes that the plan should start only after recent symptom changes are assessed.

questions.model_answer:
I would build the plan around what Mr. Beaulieu wants to be able to do, and I would start by agreeing on two or three goals with him: dressing without stopping, climbing a flight of stairs, and getting back to his card game. Those become the yardsticks.

The core is supervised exercise, two sessions a week, supported by a home program on non-program days. I would combine aerobic work with strength training. For aerobic work, walking on the treadmill or cycling. Because he stopped twice in six minutes and his dyspnea hit 7 out of 10, continuous exercise will not work at first, so I would use intervals: for example three minutes of work and two of rest, repeated to a total of about 20 minutes. I would set intensity by symptoms, aiming for a Borg dyspnea rating of 3 to 4 out of 10, and use his walk test speed as a starting reference, because heart rate formulas are unreliable in chronic obstructive disease. As he improves, I would first lengthen work intervals, then shorten rests, then raise speed or resistance, once he reports the effort as easier at the same load.

For strength, his quadriceps are weak, so I would use leg press or sit-to-stand work and upper limb exercises for the muscles used in dressing, two sets of 8 to 12 repetitions, progressing when he can complete the last repetitions at a Borg of 3 or less. Teaching pursed-lip breathing, a paced breathing rhythm and energy conservation for dressing would be part of every session.

His walk test showed a fall to 85 percent. Exercise desaturation is the reason oxygen was prescribed, so I would discuss using his portable oxygen during training, explain how it lets him train longer, and agree with the respirologist on a saturation target to keep during exercise, for example staying above about 88 to 90 percent, monitored with a finger oximeter. I would also make it more acceptable with a smaller carrier or a discreet bag. I would also cover self-management: inhaler technique, an action plan for flare-ups, and sputum clearance.

Outcome measures: I would repeat the six-minute walk at the end of the eight weeks, with the minimal important change of about 30 metres in mind, with Borg ratings and a quality of life questionnaire. After week 8, I would link him to a community maintenance exercise program, give him a written home program to continue, and recheck the six-minute walk at about 3 months to confirm he has kept his gains.

Before he starts, though, I would deal with the recent change he mentioned: three days of thicker, yellow sputum and more fatigue. I would not begin the exercise plan until that has been looked at. That is why my first session would be assessment and communication, not training.

scale.4: Gives a structured plan linked to his goals with intervals, symptom-based intensity, progression rules, oxygen use, measures and timing, and holds the start until recent symptoms are addressed.
scale.3: Gives a sound exercise plan with intensity and measures, but is brief on progression, oxygen or the recent change in sputum.
scale.2: Lists generic exercises and education without intensity, progression or measures.
scale.1: Prescribes high-intensity exercise by age-predicted heart rate or starts training without addressing his symptoms.

questions.prompt: Mr. Beaulieu says the sputum is nothing new and that he wants to start exercising today. Explain how you decide whether it is safe to proceed and how you would work with his views about the oxygen.

checklist.point: Recognizes the three-day change in sputum colour, volume and fatigue as a possible exacerbation or infection that needs medical review before exercise.
Screens further: temperature, resting vital signs, increased dyspnea, change in sputum volume, chest pain, confusion, ankle swelling.
Holds the exercise session today and arranges same-day contact with the respirologist or family physician.
Explains the reasoning to the client in plain words and respects his goals while declining to proceed.
Gives clear return precautions and what to do if breathing worsens, including calling emergency services.
Explores why he avoids oxygen and addresses embarrassment without dismissing it.
Explains the safety reason for oxygen during exertion and agrees on a saturation target set with the medical team.
Uses shared decision-making, offering options he can accept, and documents his choices.

questions.model_answer:
I would answer this by deciding about safety before deciding about exercise.

What he calls nothing new is, to me, the most important thing he has told me. Three days of thicker yellowish sputum and more tiredness in a man with severe obstructive disease and a recent admission could be the start of an exacerbation or a chest infection. The risk of exercising during one is that his oxygen could fall further, his breathing could get much worse, and he could end up in hospital again. So I would not start training today until a physician has reviewed him.

Here is how I would do it. First, I would gather more facts: take his temperature, repeat his pulse, respiratory rate and resting oxygen saturation, and listen to how he speaks, whether he completes sentences. I would ask whether the sputum amount has increased, whether he is more breathless than usual at rest, whether he has chest pain, a fever or chills, new ankle swelling, drowsiness or confusion, and whether he has used his rescue inhaler more. If any red flags are present, such as saturation well below his baseline, difficulty speaking, chest pain or confusion, I would arrange urgent medical care now and, if severe, call for emergency help.

Second, I would call his respirologist's office or the family physician the same day, with his symptoms and numbers, and ask for an assessment. He can then restart the program when cleared.

Third, I would explain this respectfully. I would say that I understand he wants to get going and that his effort matters to me, and that I want him exercising as soon as it is safe. Exercise during a chest infection can make things worse, and the team can treat this early, which often keeps people out of the hospital. I would give him a written action plan: when to call, and to call emergency services for severe breathlessness, chest pain or confusion.

About oxygen, I would not argue. I would ask what bothers him about it and whether it is how it looks or how it feels. I would explain that his level drops to 85 percent on walking, and that the tank allows his muscles and heart to work with more oxygen so he can train longer. We could look at lighter portable systems and agree on a saturation target with the medical team. If he declines, I would explain the risks, respect that it is his decision, document it, and tell the doctor.

scale.4: Identifies the possible exacerbation, screens, holds exercise, arranges medical review, gives safety advice, and engages with the oxygen concern using shared decision-making.
scale.3: Holds exercise and refers, but is brief on screening, return precautions or the oxygen discussion.
scale.2: Recognizes some concern but allows a light session or does not arrange medical contact.
scale.1: Proceeds with training or accepts that the sputum change is nothing new.

questions.prompt: Mr. Beaulieu then tells you he has been skipping inhaler doses because of cost, and asks you not to mention it to his doctor. Discuss your professional responsibilities and what you do.

checklist.point: Recognizes that undisclosed non-adherence affects his safety and the physician's treatment decisions.
Explores the reasons and the details without judgment, including which medications and how often.
Explains that you cannot promise to keep safety-relevant information from the treating team and asks for his consent to share.
Discusses confidentiality and the limits, and the use of consent for sharing within the circle of care.
Stays within scope: does not advise changing, stopping or substituting medications.
Connects him with options such as the pharmacist, provincial drug benefit programs or a social worker.
Documents the disclosure, the consent discussion and the communication with the team.
Reflects on equity and cultural safety, noting that cost is a barrier to care.

questions.model_answer:
My responsibility here sits between two duties: respecting his confidence and keeping him safe. I would handle it by being open with him from the start.

I would first thank him for telling me, because it takes trust to say that, and I would ask without judgment: which inhalers are you skipping, how often, and what would make it easier? I want to understand whether he is skipping the long-acting medication he takes every day or only the rescue inhaler, because that changes the risk. I would also ask how long this has been going on, since it may be connected to the hospital admission and to how breathless he is now.

Then I would be honest about what I can promise. I cannot agree to hide this from his doctor. Taking his medications as prescribed affects his breathing, his risk of more flare-ups, and how his doctor reads his progress. If the respirologist thinks his medication is working while it is not, they may increase doses or add treatments that he does not need, which is unsafe. So I would say that I would like to share this with his health care team, because it affects his care, and I would ask for his permission. Within the circle of care, sharing relevant information for his treatment is appropriate with his agreement, and I would explain that. I would also tell him I would present it as a cost problem to be solved, not as a failure on his part.

I would stay within my scope. I would not tell him to change a dose, take less, or swap products. That is for his physician or pharmacist. What I can do is help him get to the right person. I could suggest he talk to his pharmacist about lower-cost options or generics, ask about provincial or private drug coverage and assistance programs, and I could refer him to the program's social worker. I would offer to make the call with him.

Afterwards I would document what he told me, the discussion of consent, what I shared, with whom and when, and the referrals I made. I would also keep in mind that cost barriers like this one affect many clients, and that I should raise it with the team so others get support too. If he still refuses consent, I would explain the risk again, respect his right to decide, and consult my regulator's guidance or my supervisor about next steps.

scale.4: Balances confidentiality and safety, explores reasons, asks for consent to share, stays in scope, offers practical cost resources and documents clearly.
scale.3: Seeks consent and refers appropriately, but is brief on scope, documentation or exploring his reasons.
scale.2: Offers support for the cost issue but does not address sharing with the team, or promises secrecy in part.
scale.1: Agrees to keep it secret or advises him to change his medication.

safety_or_ethics_point: The buried issue is a three-day change in sputum and fatigue in a client with severe disease and a recent admission, a possible exacerbation, which the client dismisses. A competent candidate holds exercise, screens, and arranges same-day medical review. The medication cost disclosure tests consent and scope.
common_errors: Candidates write a complete exercise prescription and never address the recent symptoms, or accept his view that winters are always bad. Others promise confidentiality about the skipped doses or advise him how to adjust his inhalers.
examiner_notes: A pass writes a client-centred plan, then pauses it for the symptom change and arranges medical review. A fail prescribes training without screening, or oversteps scope on medications.

title: Shin pain in a university distance runner
setting: Varsity athletics clinic at a university
client_profile: Aaliyah Okafor is a 20-year-old third-year student and middle-distance runner. For five weeks she has had pain on the inner border of the left shin, now present when walking to class and at night. She increased weekly mileage from 50 to 85 km over the autumn and added hill sessions. Previous right foot stress fracture at age 17. Menstrual periods: none for 5 months. Body mass index 17.6 kg/m2. She reports eating little before morning training and skipping meals on race days. Examination: focal tenderness over the distal third of the posteromedial tibia about 2 cm long, pain with single-leg hop (6 out of 10), pain on tibial percussion, normal knee and ankle range, mild pes planus, calf strength 18 single-leg heel raises on the right and 12 on the left limited by shin pain. Vitals are normal at rest, resting heart rate 48.
clinical_scenario: The national championships are in six weeks and she is the team's best chance at a medal. Her coach has told her to just tape it and keep running, and later emails the clinic asking for a full report and a return date. Aaliyah asks you not to tell the coach about her periods or her eating because she is afraid of losing her scholarship place. The clinic is busy, with a long waiting list, and the athletic therapist offers to supervise her cross-training while you see other clients.

questions.prompt: Describe your clinical impression based on the history and examination, what other conditions you considered, and what further steps you would take in your assessment.

checklist.point: Forms a working impression of a bone stress injury of the tibia based on focal tenderness, pain with hopping, percussion pain, night pain and a training load increase.
Distinguishes it from medial tibial stress syndrome, which is typically diffuse over a longer length of the tibial border, and from exertional compartment syndrome, tendinopathy and referred pain.
Recognizes the history of a previous stress fracture, absent menses for 5 months, low body mass index and restricted eating as risk factors.
Raises relative energy deficiency in sport or low energy availability as a likely contributor.
Plans referral to a physician for imaging, most often magnetic resonance imaging, and for bone health, hormonal and nutritional evaluation.
Notes that radiographs are often negative early and do not rule out a bone stress injury.
Evaluates training load, footwear, running surface and biomechanics as contributing factors.
Considers screening for associated concerns such as mood, disordered eating behaviours and pain in other sites, and uses sensitive questions.

questions.model_answer:
Let me reason from the findings to an impression.

My leading impression is a bone stress injury of the left distal tibia, ranging from a stress reaction to an early stress fracture. What points that way: she has focal tenderness over a small area, about 2 centimetres, rather than a long stretch of the shin. She has pain on hopping and on percussion of the bone, she has night pain, and the pain began after a sharp rise in mileage from 50 to 85 kilometres with added hills. Pain at night and pain on walking suggest the bone is no longer coping with ordinary loads.

I considered other causes. Medial tibial stress syndrome is the main alternative. It usually gives more diffuse pain along a longer stretch of the inner border, often over 5 centimetres, tends to ease as she warms up, and does not usually hurt on hopping or at night. Exertional compartment syndrome would bring tightness and cramping during running that settles with rest. Tibialis posterior or soleus tendinopathy would be tender over the tendon rather than the bone. Referred pain from the back is unlikely with normal knee and ankle range. Because tenderness is focal and provoked by hopping, I rank bone injury first. The mild pes planus and calf weakness are contributing factors, not the explanation.

The feature that changes my approach most is the context. She had a stress fracture at 17, she has had no periods for five months, her body mass index is 17.6, she eats little before training, and her resting heart rate is 48. Together this suggests low energy availability, meaning her intake does not cover what she spends on training, with effects on bone. I would raise relative energy deficiency in sport as a likely contributing cause, and I would say it as a possibility to be confirmed, not a diagnosis I make.

For next steps, I would refer her to a sport physician the same week for imaging, usually magnetic resonance imaging, since plain films are often normal early. I would also request assessment of bone health, menstrual disturbance, labs and nutrition, and involve a dietitian. I would not make her run or hop-test again.

My own assessment would continue with gentle questions in private: how she is eating, her mood, her sleep, and other sore sites. I would review her training log, shoes, surfaces and running form, and measure her strength and hip control, because those shape the plan once the bone is protected.

scale.4: Gives a reasoned impression of bone stress injury with differentiating features, links the history to low energy availability, and plans imaging, medical referral and contributing-factor review.
scale.3: Reaches the correct impression and refers, but differential reasoning or the link to energy availability is brief.
scale.2: Lists possible diagnoses without ranking or reasoning, or treats it as shin splints without considering risk factors.
scale.1: Concludes shin splints and plans to continue running, or ignores the menstrual and nutritional history.

questions.prompt: Aaliyah tells you she is afraid of losing her scholarship place and asks you to let her keep training. How do you respond, and what do you recommend about her activity in the meantime?

checklist.point: Acknowledges her fear and her goals and starts from a supportive, non-judgmental stance.
Recommends stopping running and impact loading until imaging and medical assessment, and explains the risk of a complete fracture.
Offers a plan for maintaining fitness with non-impact cross-training that is pain-free, such as pool or cycling if tolerated.
Addresses low energy availability sensitively and explains why it matters for bone healing.
Gives a rough, honest explanation of recovery timeframes, without promising a championship return.
Involves her in decisions and uses open questions and shared goal-setting.
Asks about her mood, safety and coping, and provides resources if she is distressed.
Explains warning signs that need urgent care, such as sudden severe pain or inability to bear weight.

questions.model_answer:
I would begin by acknowledging how much this means to her. I would say, I can see how hard you have worked and how scary it is to think about losing your place. I want to help you get through this season in the best way, and still have a career at the end of it.

Then I would be honest about my recommendation. Based on what I found, I think the bone in your shin is under more stress than it can cope with, and running or hopping on it risks turning a stress injury into a full break. A full fracture can mean surgery and many months out, which would hurt her more than a few weeks of rest. So I recommend she stop running and any jumping or impact work now, until the scan and physician visit are done. Because walking already hurts and she has night pain, I would advise protected weight bearing with crutches until imaging and physician review, keep walking to the minimum needed, and show her how to use the crutches safely.

She will not lose all her fitness. With the athletic therapist, we can plan non-impact work such as deep-water running or cycling, as long as it causes no shin pain, and upper body and core strength. I would add hip and calf work that does not hurt. I would ask her what she can commit to, and let her help choose the plan, so it is her plan and not mine.

Because I think her body may be short of energy, I would raise it gently. I would explain that bone repairs itself only when there is enough fuel, and that missed periods and low weight make bone injuries more likely and slower to heal. I would say I would like a dietitian and doctor to help, and that this is common in athletes and nothing to be ashamed of. I would ask her how she feels about it.

About timing, I would say bone injuries like this usually take weeks to months, depending on the scan, so I cannot promise she will compete in six weeks, and I will not guess until we know more. I would check how she is coping, how she is sleeping and whether she has support, and tell her about the student health and counselling services.

Finally, I would give clear warning signs: if she gets sudden severe pain, cannot put weight on the leg, or has new swelling, she should go to the emergency department.

scale.4: Responds with empathy, recommends stopping impact loading with clear reasons, offers realistic cross-training, raises energy availability gently, is honest about timing and gives warning signs.
scale.3: Recommends rest and cross-training with reasons, but is brief on energy availability, timing or warning signs.
scale.2: Allows modified running or gives reassurance without a clear risk explanation.
scale.1: Permits continued training to protect the scholarship or dismisses her concerns.

questions.prompt: The coach emails asking for a full report and a return date, and the athletic therapist offers to supervise her cross-training. Discuss how you manage the records, communication and workload in this situation.

checklist.point: Does not release health information to the coach without the athlete's informed consent, and limits it to what she agrees to share.
Offers a function-based summary to the coach, such as activity restrictions, if she consents, without diagnosis or menstrual and nutrition details.
Declines to give a firm return date before imaging and medical assessment.
Documents assessment, recommendations, consent discussion and communications accurately and on time.
Delegates supervised exercise to the athletic therapist or a physiotherapist assistant only with a written, specific plan, clear limits and a way to contact you.
Retains responsibility for assessment, plan and progression and arranges regular reassessment.
Schedules follow-up and balances her appointment times with the clinic's wait list without compromising safety.
Addresses pressure from the coach professionally, and uses a team approach with the physician and dietitian.

questions.model_answer:
There are three parts here: records and privacy, who does what, and how I run my own schedule.

First, the coach. The coach is not part of Aaliyah's circle of care, and the clinic holds her personal health information. So I would not send a report. I would speak to Aaliyah first and ask what she is comfortable with the coach knowing. If she consents, I would give a short, function-based note and not a clinical file. For example: she has an injury to the lower leg that needs medical imaging; she must not run or do impact training until cleared; she can do the following cross-training; and we will update when we know more. I would not mention her periods, her eating, her weight or any suspected diagnosis, because those are not the coach's to know and she has told me about them in confidence. I would record her consent and exactly what I agreed to share, and I would reply to the coach in writing, copying nothing else. On the return date, I would say plainly that I cannot give one until the imaging and medical review are complete, and that I will provide updates with her consent. If the coach pressures me to allow training, I would stay polite and firm, explain that my recommendation is based on safety, and, if needed, involve the sport physician or clinic manager.

Second, delegation. The athletic therapist can supervise her cross-training, but I remain responsible for the assessment, the plan and progression. I would give a written plan: the exact exercises, the limit of pain-free effort, equipment, durations, and what to stop and report, for example any shin pain or night pain. I would explain it in person and check understanding, give them a way to reach me the same day, and ask them to record each session. I would review her myself every one to two weeks, and not hand over any decision about loading or return to running.

Third, workload and time. I would book a recheck soon after the imaging results, and book regular follow-up visits instead of leaving it open. With a long waiting list, I would still protect enough time for her visit, because the complexity of this case needs it, and I would ask the team about triage support rather than shortening safety steps.

I would document everything the same day: findings, advice, referrals, consent, communications and the delegation plan.

scale.4: Protects consent and limits disclosure to function, refuses a premature date, documents, delegates with a written plan while keeping responsibility, and manages scheduling and pressure professionally.
scale.3: Addresses consent and delegation sensibly but is brief on documentation, limits or scheduling.
scale.2: Shares broad information or delegates with little structure.
scale.1: Sends the full report or return date to the coach without consent, or hands over her management entirely.

safety_or_ethics_point: The buried issue is low energy availability (absent periods, low body mass index, restricted eating, prior stress fracture) behind a bone stress injury, with coach pressure to keep training and a request for a full report. A competent candidate stops impact loading, refers medically, protects her confidence and shares only what she consents to.
common_errors: Candidates diagnose shin splints and advise relative rest while keeping running, or ignore the menstrual and nutritional history. Others send the coach the full report or give a return date to the national championships.
examiner_notes: A pass identifies bone stress injury and energy deficiency, stops impact loading, refers, and handles consent and delegation correctly. A fail treats it as overuse and complies with the coach.

title: Systemic lupus erythematosus with joint pain and a hot knee
setting: Hospital outpatient musculoskeletal clinic
client_profile: Mei-Ling Zhao is a 34-year-old elementary school teacher with systemic lupus erythematosus diagnosed 6 years ago. She is referred for hand, wrist and knee pain and fatigue that limit marking papers and standing in the classroom. Medications: hydroxychloroquine, prednisone 10 mg daily, and mycophenolate. Last rheumatology note, 3 months ago, reported low disease activity. Today: symmetrical morning stiffness of hands about 45 minutes, mild swelling of both wrists, fatigue 7 out of 10, grip strength reduced bilaterally. The right knee has been hot, swollen and painful for 2 days with an effusion, active flexion limited to 70 degrees, and pain even at rest. Temperature 38.2 degrees C, heart rate 98, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg. She says she has had chills last night. The left knee and hips are normal.
clinical_scenario: Mei-Ling asks for a program to build strength and endurance because she wants to return to full-time teaching, and she wants to start tomorrow. She says she does not want to bother her rheumatologist because the next appointment is in 6 weeks. The clinic owner has asked all physiotherapists to add a paid ten-session group conditioning package to each plan and to schedule half-hour appointments. A physiotherapist assistant is available at the clinic to supervise exercise.

questions.prompt: Describe the plan of care you would develop for Mei-Ling, including how you would decide the timing and priority of what you do first, and how the plan would change over time.

checklist.point: Identifies the hot, swollen, painful knee with fever and chills in an immunosuppressed client as needing urgent medical assessment before any exercise program.
Holds the exercise program and manual treatment to the knee until medical clearance.
Distinguishes the knee finding from the expected polyarthralgia and fatigue of lupus, which are secondary today.
Plans, once cleared, graded aerobic and resistance exercise adapted to fatigue, with pacing and avoidance of flares.
Includes joint protection, hand therapy strategies, splinting options and workplace adaptations for teaching.
Includes sun protection and skin considerations for outdoor exercise, and infection and medication awareness.
Specifies outcome measures such as pain, fatigue scale, grip strength and a function questionnaire, and reassessment timing.
Describes monitoring for disease flare and triggers to modify, pause or refer.

questions.model_answer:
The way I decide what comes first is by sorting what is urgent from what is important, and today those two things are not the same.

What is most urgent is her right knee. A hot, swollen, very painful knee with pain at rest, limited motion, a temperature of 38.2 and chills, in someone taking prednisone and mycophenolate, which suppress her immune system, must be treated as a possible joint infection until proven otherwise. Her lupus could also be flaring, or it could be another cause, and I cannot tell which from the bedside. A septic joint can damage cartilage within days and can become life-threatening. So the first step in my plan is not exercise. It is to stop, check her vitals again, and arrange an urgent medical assessment today, through the emergency department or the rheumatologist on call, with my findings communicated clearly. I would not wait six weeks for her scheduled visit, and I would not start any exercise or manual therapy on that knee.

Once she has been assessed and it is safe, the longer-term plan follows. Her stiffness, wrist swelling and fatigue are typical of lupus and are my second priority. The plan would have these parts. One, an exercise program built gradually: aerobic work like walking or cycling at a low to moderate effort, starting with short bouts of 10 minutes with rests, and resistance training for the legs, trunk and shoulders, increasing slowly. I would use a rate of perceived exertion to set the level, and a rule that if she feels worse the next day, we step back. Two, pacing and energy conservation strategies that fit teaching: planned rest, sitting for some tasks, and sharing marking. Three, joint protection and hand strategies, such as wrist splints at night if the rheumatologist agrees, larger-handled pens, and gentle range work. Four, sun protection when she exercises outdoors, because ultraviolet light can trigger flares.

For outcomes, I would repeat her pain and fatigue ratings, grip strength, and a function questionnaire every few weeks, and track the days she works.

The plan would change with her disease activity. If she has a flare, I would reduce intensity and focus on gentle movement. If her labs or symptoms change, I would adjust with the rheumatologist. I would set goals with her for returning to full-time teaching in steps.

scale.4: Prioritizes the possible joint infection and holds exercise with urgent referral, then outlines a staged, fatigue-aware plan with measures and flare-based adjustments.
scale.3: Recognizes the knee and refers, but the longer-term plan or reassessment is general.
scale.2: Writes a reasonable lupus exercise plan and mentions the knee without urgency.
scale.1: Starts a strengthening program that includes the knee or treats the fever as unrelated.

questions.prompt: Mei-Ling says she does not want to bother her rheumatologist and would rather start the program tomorrow. How do you approach this conversation, and what do you do before she leaves the clinic?

checklist.point: Explains that the combination of fever and a hot swollen knee while on immune-suppressing medication needs same-day medical care.
Does not diagnose, but states the concern about infection plainly and in everyday language.
Arranges or facilitates the contact, for example phoning the rheumatologist or sending her to emergency with a written summary.
Advises her not to drive herself if unwell and arranges safe transport.
Acknowledges her wish to return to work and her reluctance to bother others and reframes urgency as protecting her goals.
Provides clear instructions on red flag symptoms and where to go.
Respects her autonomy to decide after she understands the risk and documents the discussion and her response.
Confirms her understanding with teach-back and follows up the same day.

questions.model_answer:
I would start by saying I understand. Mei-Ling has worked hard to manage her disease, she wants her classroom life back, and she does not like to be a burden. I would tell her that taking this seriously is part of reaching her goal, and that the people at her rheumatology office would rather hear from her today than see her sicker later.

Then I would explain, in plain words, what I found and why it worries me. Your right knee is hot, swollen and very sore even at rest, you have a fever of 38.2 and you had chills last night. Your medications keep your immune system quieter, which is good for lupus but makes infections easier to get and harder to spot. A joint can become infected quickly, and if that is what this is, it needs treatment soon to protect it. It might turn out to be a lupus flare or something less serious, but I cannot tell the difference by examining it, and tests are needed today. I would say I am not diagnosing, I am saying this should not wait six weeks.

Before she leaves, I would act, not just advise. I would phone the rheumatology office, tell them it is urgent, and ask what they want done. If I cannot reach them promptly, I would send her to the emergency department today with a written note: her medications, my findings and numbers, and the time the fever began. I would suggest she does not drive herself with a fever and a painful leg, and I would help her arrange a ride, a family member or a taxi. I would give her the red flags, to call emergency services for worsening pain, a higher fever, confusion, shortness of breath, chest pain or shaking chills.

I would check understanding by asking her to say back what she will do next and when. If after hearing all this she still declines, she has the right to decide, and I would not force her. I would make sure she knows the risks, offer the options again, tell her to call me if she changes her mind, and document everything: findings, my explanation, her words, what I arranged, and who I told. I would call her later that day or the next morning to follow up. No exercise starts tomorrow, and I would tell her I will restart the program once she has been checked.

scale.4: Explains the infection concern plainly, takes concrete action to secure same-day care, addresses her reluctance, gives red flags, respects autonomy and documents.
scale.3: Advises same-day care with a good explanation, but does not arrange contact or follow up.
scale.2: Suggests she mention it at her next appointment, or advises a general call without urgency.
scale.1: Agrees to start the program or reassures her it is likely a flare.

questions.prompt: The clinic owner wants every plan to include the paid ten-session group conditioning package and half-hour appointments. Discuss how you manage your practice, billing and use of the assistant in Mei-Ling's case.

checklist.point: States that recommendations and fees must be based on the client's clinical needs and not on clinic revenue targets.
Declines to apply the group package to Mei-Ling until she is medically cleared and the plan is appropriate for her, and explains the conflict of interest.
Provides clear fee information and obtains informed consent before any service, including alternatives and the right to decline.
Determines appointment length from the complexity of the case, and requests longer slots for the assessment and communication needed.
Delegates supervised exercise to the assistant only once an individualized plan exists, with specific parameters, a stop rule and reassessment by the physiotherapist.
Retains responsibility for assessment, interpretation, progression and the decision to modify the plan.
Documents the assessment, the referral, the consent and the rationale for plan choices promptly.
Raises the concern with the owner or the regulator's guidance if the policy conflicts with professional obligations.

questions.model_answer:
My answer is that my obligations to Mei-Ling come first, and I will manage the business requests inside that.

On the package and billing. I am accountable to my regulator for recommending care that is in the client's interest. A ten-session paid group program is a reasonable option for some people, but it is not appropriate for Mei-Ling today, because she needs a medical assessment for a possible joint infection, and because she has a complex condition that needs an individual plan first. If I added it just because the clinic asks, I would have a conflict of interest between her needs and the clinic's income. I would tell the owner, politely, that I will offer it to clients when it is clinically indicated and not as a default, and I would explain that my professional standards require this. When it is appropriate later, I would give Mei-Ling clear information: what the package includes, the total cost, how it differs from individual sessions, what the alternatives are, and that she can say no without it changing the quality of her care. I would get her informed consent before she pays for anything, and I would not pressure her.

On appointment length. A half-hour is not enough for this case. She needs time for the full assessment, communication with her physician, and teaching. I would book longer visits for her and explain to the owner that the length reflects clinical complexity. If the clinic cannot accommodate me, I would document the limit and raise it with management, and I would not shorten safety steps.

On the assistant. Once Mei-Ling is cleared and I have designed the program, the assistant can supervise exercise sessions. I would give the assistant a written individual plan with the exercises, intensities, rest breaks, a clear stop rule such as unusual joint swelling, fever, new rash or high fatigue, and the way to reach me. I would explain it in person and confirm they understand. I would still do the reassessment and decide the progression, and I would review her regularly, since the assistant does not interpret findings or change the plan.

Finally, documentation. I would record the findings, the urgent referral, my reasoning, her consent for each service and fee, and the delegation instructions.

scale.4: Puts client need before revenue, declines the default package with reasons, ensures informed consent on fees, books suitable time, delegates with specific limits and keeps responsibility, and documents.
scale.3: Addresses conflict of interest and delegation but is brief on consent, appointment length or documentation.
scale.2: Complies partially with the policy or delegates generally without a plan.
scale.1: Adds the package without regard to clinical need or hands over the assessment and decisions to the assistant.

safety_or_ethics_point: The buried issue is a hot, swollen, painful knee with fever and chills in a client on prednisone and mycophenolate, a possible septic joint, hidden among typical lupus symptoms and a request to start exercise. Another issue is a clinic revenue policy that conflicts with clinical judgment.
common_errors: Candidates attribute the knee to a lupus flare and begin exercise planning, or advise her to mention it at the next appointment. Others add the group package to satisfy the owner and delegate the assessment to the assistant.
examiner_notes: A pass escalates the infection concern the same day, then outlines a staged lupus plan and manages the business pressure ethically. A fail writes a conditioning program around a hot, swollen knee with fever.

title: Persistent fatigue and exertional breathlessness after viral illness
setting: Community outpatient physiotherapy clinic
client_profile: Priya Nair is a 43-year-old project manager and mother of two. Eight months ago she had a respiratory viral illness managed at home. Since then she reports ongoing fatigue, breathlessness on stairs and light housework, brain fog and poor sleep. She used to run 5 km three times weekly. Two attempts to return to running made her feel worse for several days afterward, with headaches, aching and needing to lie down. No smoking. No other medical history. Seated at rest: heart rate 78, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, oxygen saturation 98 percent. After standing for 3 minutes: heart rate 112, blood pressure 112/70 mmHg, with light-headedness and a feeling of heart pounding. One-minute sit-to-stand: 17 repetitions, oxygen saturation lowest 96 percent, heart rate peak 128, dyspnea 4 out of 10. Chest auscultation is clear. A family physician's chest radiograph and basic blood tests 4 months ago were reported normal.
clinical_scenario: Priya's employer has asked for a return-to-work plan after a long period of reduced hours. Priya fears being seen as unreliable and wants a fitness program to get her to full capacity in a month. Her friend, who recovered after a similar illness, told her to push through with a graded walking program. Priya has not seen any physician for four months. The occupational health nurse at her workplace has offered to join a call.

questions.prompt: Outline the plan of care you would propose for Priya and explain how you would decide how much activity to prescribe and how you would adjust it.

checklist.point: Recognizes that her pattern of symptoms worsening after exertion, with delay, calls for a cautious energy-limited approach rather than a standard graded exercise progression.
Uses symptom-guided pacing within an energy envelope, with a baseline of activity she tolerates without next-day worsening.
Includes breathing retraining, positioning, and strategies for orthostatic symptoms such as gradual position changes, fluid and salt guidance per physician advice.
Plans to monitor heart rate, symptoms and recovery after activity, with a diary to identify triggers.
Sets small, agreed functional goals, such as stairs and household tasks, before aerobic fitness targets.
Includes sleep, cognitive load pacing and rest strategies as part of the plan.
Specifies outcome measures such as fatigue, dyspnea scale, function questionnaire and the sit-to-stand test and their reassessment timing.
Describes criteria to progress, hold or step back based on symptom response over 24 to 48 hours.

questions.model_answer:
I would shape the plan around what her body does after activity, because that tells me how much to prescribe.

The pattern in her story is important. Both times she tried to run, she felt worse for several days afterwards, with headaches, aching and needing to lie down. That delayed worsening after effort is a signal that her usual rule of building up fitness by pushing through does not apply right now. A standard graded exercise program, like her friend's advice, could set her back, so I would not use one. Instead I would use pacing: finding an amount of activity she can do without paying for it the next day or two, and staying inside that.

Step one is to find her baseline. I would ask her to keep a simple diary for two weeks of what she does, how she feels during and after, her fatigue and breathlessness, and her sleep. From this we would set a starting level, perhaps short household tasks and short walks, with rests planned before she is tired, not after. Her one-minute sit-to-stand, with a heart rate of 128 and dyspnea of 4, gives me a sense of what a short effort costs her.

Step two is the supportive strategies. For breathing: diaphragmatic and pursed-lip breathing, and positioning to ease breathlessness. For the light-headedness and rapid heart rate when she stands: change positions slowly, avoid standing still for long, use seated options for tasks, and ask her physician about fluids, salt and other medical measures. I would also teach her to protect her sleep and to pace mental effort as well as physical.

Step three is goals and measures. Her first goals are practical: climbing a flight of stairs, cooking a meal, and two half-days of work. Aerobic fitness comes later. I would track fatigue, breathlessness, a function questionnaire, and repeat the sit-to-stand every three to four weeks.

How I adjust: if she stays steady or improves over 24 to 48 hours after an increase, I add a small amount, around 10 percent. If symptoms flare, I hold, then step back to the last tolerated level. I would only consider gradual aerobic work much later, once she is stable and the physician is on board.

Before all of that, though, I would be talking to her physician, because some of her findings need a medical review.

scale.4: Recognizes the delayed worsening, uses pacing within an energy envelope with diary, supportive strategies, functional goals, measures and clear progress or step-back rules.
scale.3: Uses pacing and sensible strategies, but is brief on progression rules, measures or orthostatic management.
scale.2: Offers a generic graded exercise program with some caution.
scale.1: Prescribes progressive aerobic training to push through symptoms.

questions.prompt: Priya asks to start a walking and jogging program next week and says she is willing to push through the tiredness. How do you respond, and what safety steps do you take?

checklist.point: Recognizes the heart rate rise of about 34 beats per minute on standing with light-headedness and pounding as a finding needing medical evaluation.
Recommends medical review before increasing activity because she has not been seen in four months and has new orthostatic findings.
Explains why pushing through could worsen her symptoms, using her own experience of the two failed return attempts.
Screens for red flags such as chest pain, syncope, palpitations at rest, leg swelling, severe dyspnea or neurological symptoms.
Validates her frustration and her fear of being seen as unreliable.
Offers a safe starting alternative in the meantime, consistent with pacing.
Uses shared decision-making and respects her choice after informing her.
Gives clear instructions on symptoms that need urgent medical attention.

questions.model_answer:
I would start with understanding, because she is frustrated. I would say, you have been trying hard to get back to yourself, and it makes sense that you want a plan and a date. I want to help you move forward in a way that works.

Then I would explain, in her own experience, why I would not start jogging next week. She has told me that both times she tried to run, she was worse for several days. If she pushes through again, the likely result is another setback, not faster recovery. I would say that her body seems to need a different approach for now, and I will show her what it is.

There is a second reason, and it is about safety. When she stood for three minutes today, her heart rate went from 78 to 112, and she felt light-headed with her heart pounding. That is a large rise on standing. It may have a cause that her physician should look at, and I am not in a position to explain it. She has not seen a physician for four months and her symptoms are ongoing. So before we build up her activity, I would ask her to see her family physician in the next week or so, with a summary from me of today's findings, so that they can examine her, consider tests such as an electrocardiogram and further assessment, and tell us if there is anything that limits safe exercise.

I would also screen for red flags today: any chest pain, fainting or near-fainting, palpitations at rest, leg swelling, worsening breathlessness at rest, or new weakness or confusion. If she had any of these, I would send her for urgent care the same day. I would give her a short list of symptoms for which she should call emergency services.

In the meantime, I would offer something safe: short, paced activities inside her energy limit, breathing exercises, and slow position changes, with a diary. That way she is doing something active while we wait.

I would use shared decision-making. If she still wants to try jogging, I would explain the risks again, respect that it is her decision, and agree on a way to keep her safe. I would ask her to stop at the first sign of symptoms. I would document the discussion.

scale.4: Validates her, links the orthostatic findings and past setbacks to a clear recommendation for medical review before progression, screens for red flags, offers a safe alternative and respects autonomy.
scale.3: Recommends medical review and caution with reasoning, but does not screen red flags or offer an interim plan.
scale.2: Advises caution generally but allows a cautious jogging trial without medical review.
scale.1: Supports the walk-jog program or dismisses her heart rate response as deconditioning.

questions.prompt: Priya's employer wants a return-to-work plan and the occupational health nurse has offered to join a call. Describe how you would organize the collaboration, including who is involved, what is shared, and how roles are defined.

checklist.point: Obtains Priya's informed consent for any communication with the employer and the occupational health nurse, and agrees on what will be shared.
Shares functional information such as tolerances and recommended adjustments, and not diagnosis or detailed health information without consent.
Identifies the family physician as a key team member who provides medical clearance and direction, and communicates findings to them first.
Defines each person's role: physiotherapist for pacing and functional recommendations, physician for medical decisions, occupational health nurse and employer for workplace accommodation.
Proposes a gradual return-to-work schedule with flexible hours, rest breaks, remote options and review points, tied to her symptom response.
Involves Priya as an active participant who sets her own priorities and speaks for herself.
Sets timelines and a method for ongoing communication, and records the agreements.
Considers other supports, such as a mental health professional, occupational therapist or dietitian, if indicated.

questions.model_answer:
I would organize this around Priya, with her consent and her voice at the center, and I would be clear about who does what, what is shared, and when.

First, consent and content. Before any contact with her employer or the occupational health nurse, I would sit down with Priya and ask what she wants them to know. I would explain that I would share information about what she can and cannot do and what adjustments help, not her diagnosis or details of her health history, unless she chooses to share those. We would agree on this together, I would note her consent in writing, and I would invite her to be on the call so she can speak for herself.

Second, the team. The key person is her family physician, because I have findings that need medical review, and the return-to-work plan depends on what they find. So I would contact the physician first, with a summary of my assessment, including the heart rate response on standing, the pattern of delayed worsening, and my questions. The physician provides medical clearance, any tests or treatment and guidance about the safe level of activity. I would not send a return-to-work plan to the employer until I hear back or at least have told the physician what I plan to recommend.

Third, roles. My role as physiotherapist is to assess her tolerance, teach pacing, and give functional recommendations such as how long she can sit, stand or work before needing a rest, and how to build up. The physician's role is medical decisions. The occupational health nurse and employer are responsible for implementing accommodations and deciding the practical arrangements, like hours and tasks. I would say this clearly at the beginning of the call so that nobody is giving advice outside their role.

Fourth, the plan. I would suggest a gradual return, for example short days or half-days, with scheduled breaks, the option to work from home or sit for tasks, limited back-to-back meetings, and no pressure to increase until her symptoms are steady over a couple of weeks. We would set review dates, perhaps every two to four weeks, and agree to adjust it based on how she responds, not just on the calendar.

Finally, I would write down who agreed to do what and by when, share the summary with Priya first, and keep a record of all communications.

scale.4: Secures consent and limits content to function, brings in the physician first, defines roles, proposes a symptom-linked gradual plan with review points, and documents agreements.
scale.3: Covers consent, roles and a gradual plan, but is brief on the physician's role, timelines or documentation.
scale.2: Lists people to contact without clear roles or limits on information shared.
scale.1: Sends a detailed health report to the employer without consent or sets a fixed return date.

safety_or_ethics_point: The buried issue is a large heart rate rise with light-headedness on standing and a pattern of delayed worsening after exertion, in a client who has not been medically reviewed for four months and wants to push through. A competent candidate recommends medical review, uses pacing, and shares only functional information with the employer, with consent.
common_errors: Candidates prescribe a graded walking and jogging progression as in a deconditioning case, or ignore the heart rate response on standing. Others send diagnostic details to the employer without checking consent.
examiner_notes: A pass picks up the delayed worsening and the orthostatic finding, paces activity, involves the physician, and protects consent in the work plan. A fail treats this as simple deconditioning and pushes progressive exercise.

title: Pelvic girdle pain in the third trimester
setting: Community health centre physiotherapy clinic
client_profile: Simran Gill, 31, is a first-time mother at 28 weeks gestation. She works as a pharmacy cashier, standing most of her shift. For three weeks she has had deep aching over the pubic region and both buttocks, worse with rolling in bed, stairs, getting in and out of the car and standing on one leg. Pain is 6/10 at worst, 2/10 at rest. No back pain above the waist, no leg numbness, no bladder or bowel change. Her midwife reports a normal pregnancy. Objective: BP 112/68 mmHg, heart rate 84, gait wide-based with a reduced stride. Active hip abduction is limited by pain. Posterior pelvic pain provocation test and active straight leg raise are positive bilaterally, symphysis pubis palpation is tender, and lumbar movements are pain free. Pelvic girdle questionnaire score 48 of 100. Neurological screen of both legs is normal.
clinical_scenario: Simran moved to Canada eight months ago and speaks Punjabi at home with limited English. Her husband attends and answers most questions for her. She says she has not told her employer about the pain because she fears losing hours. She mentions that she flew back from visiting family overseas ten days ago, a long-haul trip of about sixteen hours, and that since then her left calf has felt tight at night. She would like a belt and a quick fix so she can keep working until her leave starts in six weeks.

questions.prompt: Based on the history and findings you have, explain your clinical impression of Simran's pain and how you arrived at it. Describe what else you would consider and how you would decide among those possibilities.

checklist.point: States a working impression of pregnancy-related pelvic girdle pain involving the sacroiliac joints and symphysis pubis
Links bilateral positive posterior pelvic pain provocation and active straight leg raise to pelvic girdle origin
Uses pain location, aggravating movements and pain free lumbar movement to argue against a primary lumbar source
Notes normal neurological screen makes radiculopathy or a cauda equina picture unlikely
Identifies that the calf tightness after long travel is a separate finding that must not be attributed to pelvic pain
Lists other differentials such as hip joint pathology, urinary tract infection or obstetric causes and how screening addresses them
Describes using the pelvic girdle questionnaire and pain scores as a baseline for reassessment
Explains that the pregnancy stage and normal midwife report support a musculoskeletal explanation
Proposes additional objective checks such as hip range and the lumbar and hip screen to complete the differential

questions.model_answer:
My impression is pregnancy-related pelvic girdle pain, with the sacroiliac joints and the symphysis pubis both involved. I am reaching that conclusion from four things. First, the location: deep ache over the pubic region and both buttocks, not above the waist. Second, the pattern: it gets worse with single leg loading tasks such as stairs, rolling and getting into a car, which are the movements that shear the pelvic joints. Third, the tests: the posterior pelvic pain provocation test and the active straight leg raise are both positive on both sides, and the symphysis is tender to palpation. Fourth, the lumbar spine moves freely and without pain, and her neurological screen is normal, so a lumbar or nerve root cause is much less likely. A questionnaire score of 48 out of 100 tells me the disability is moderate and gives me a number to compare against.

I would still keep other possibilities open. Hip joint pain is one, so I would check hip rotation range and the groin pain response to hip flexion and rotation. A urinary tract infection or an obstetric problem can refer pain to the pelvis, but she has no urinary symptoms and her midwife reports a normal pregnancy, so I would ask directly about fever, bleeding, fluid loss and fetal movement and refer back to the midwife if any of those are present.

The other finding I want to be careful with is not part of the pelvic picture at all. She told me her left calf has felt tight at night since a sixteen hour flight ten days ago. Pregnancy and long travel both raise the chance of a clot in the leg, and tightness is not explained by pelvic girdle pain. So my assessment would include a look and a measure of both calves, checking for swelling, warmth, colour change and tenderness along the deep veins, and I would treat the calf as a separate problem needing its own decision, not as a footnote.

To decide among the possibilities, I would combine the pattern of provocation tests, the absence of neurological signs and the response to a simple unloading position. If pelvic girdle pain is the whole story, the pain should reproduce with the pelvic tests, settle with support and rest, and not change with spinal movement. If the calf screen is concerning, that takes priority over everything else today.

scale.4: Names pelvic girdle pain with specific supporting findings, explains why lumbar, hip and neurological causes are less likely, and independently identifies the calf tightness after travel as a separate priority needing its own assessment.
scale.3: Gives the correct impression with sound supporting findings and some differentials but treats the calf only briefly or without linking travel and pregnancy to clot risk.
scale.2: Names the impression and lists tests but gives little reasoning, ignores differentials or overlooks the calf symptom.
scale.1: Attributes the calf tightness to the pelvic condition, proposes a wrong source such as disc herniation, or recommends treatment before any assessment of safety.

questions.prompt: While you are completing the assessment, Simran says her left calf also feels warm to the touch when she wakes. Describe how you would proceed in this session and what you would tell her. Include how you would involve her in decisions.

checklist.point: Recognizes possible deep vein thrombosis given pregnancy, recent long travel, unilateral tightness and warmth
Stops or withholds manual treatment, calf massage and exercise that load the leg
Arranges same day medical assessment, such as emergency department or her physician or midwife on the same day, rather than waiting for the next visit
Asks about chest pain, shortness of breath, cough or light-headedness and tells her to call emergency services if they occur
Measures and compares calf circumference and inspects for swelling, redness and tenderness without squeezing or deep palpation
Explains in plain language why this is being treated seriously and what will happen next
Uses a professional interpreter and offers a private conversation so she can decide with full understanding
Confirms she agrees with the plan and how she will get to the assessment safely, not driving herself if unwell
Gives the pelvic pain advice only after the safety step is settled

questions.model_answer:
I would stop what I am doing and change the plan for today. A warm, tight, one-sided calf in a woman at twenty-eight weeks, ten days after a sixteen hour flight, has to be treated as a possible deep vein thrombosis until someone with the right tools says otherwise. I cannot rule it in or out in a clinic, and the risk of waiting is a clot travelling to the lungs.

Here is what I would do in order. First, I would stop any treatment that loads or compresses the leg. That means no calf massage, no walking tests or exercise, and no strong palpation of the calf. Second, I would make a quick, gentle check: look for swelling, redness or a visible vein pattern, compare the circumference of both calves at the same landmark, and ask about tenderness. I would document the numbers so the physician has them. Third, I would ask directly about chest pain, breathlessness, a new cough, a racing heart or feeling faint. If any are present, I would call emergency services from the clinic, and keep her resting and not walking.

If she has none of those, I would still arrange a same day medical assessment, ideally by phone call to her physician or midwife, or send her to an emergency department where an ultrasound can be done today. I would not leave it for her next appointment. I would tell her not to drive herself, and ask her husband to take her.

For her decision making, I would book a professional interpreter, by phone or video, instead of relying on her husband, because this is a health message that must be exact. I would ask whether she would like to speak privately. I would explain in simple words: your leg may have a blood clot, pregnancy and long flights make this more likely, it is common to check for it, and the test is safe for the baby.
