Then I would use teach-back, asking her to tell me in her own words what the plan is and why. I would ask if the plan works for her and for her family, and answer her questions. The pelvic pain, the belt and the work conversation are important, but I would deal with them after the clot question is answered.

scale.4: Names the suspected clot with reasons, stops loading the leg, escalates to same day medical assessment, screens for pulmonary symptoms, and builds the decision with an interpreter and teach-back.
scale.3: Recognizes the risk and arranges medical review but is vague on timing, omits pulmonary symptom screening or the interpreter.
scale.2: Mentions a possible clot but proposes monitoring, delayed review or continues treatment of the pelvis in the same session.
scale.1: Dismisses the calf symptom, performs calf massage or stretching, or has the client wait until her next visit.

questions.prompt: Simran's husband keeps answering for her and she is quiet. Describe how you would communicate with both of them over the rest of this visit and the next ones so that she understands her care and her views are heard.

checklist.point: Books a qualified interpreter, in person or by phone or video, and explains why this is the standard rather than relying on family
Speaks to Simran directly, with eye contact, while the interpreter relays
Offers some time alone with her in a way that does not suggest suspicion of the husband
Uses short plain sentences, avoids jargon and explains pelvic pain with a simple model
Uses teach-back to confirm understanding of the plan and warning signs
Provides written or pictorial home advice in Punjabi where available
Respects cultural and family roles by inviting the husband to take part without answering for her
Asks her about work concerns and fears about hours so goals reflect her priorities
Documents the interpreter use and her consent decisions

questions.model_answer:
My aim is that Simran, not her husband, is the one who understands and decides, while treating him with respect. I would start by explaining to both of them, kindly, that I will use a professional interpreter at visits so that everything I say is exact and so that I do not make either of them carry that job. I would say that this is how I work with every client who prefers another language, which keeps it neutral and not about them. I would book the interpreter by phone or video for the rest of today and for every following visit.

When we speak, I would look at Simran and address her directly, using short sentences and no medical words. For example, instead of talking about a joint dysfunction I would say the two joints at the back and front of your pelvis are moving unevenly and are sore, and we can help them with support and the right exercises. I would pause often for interpretation and invite questions after each short piece.

I would invite her husband into the process as a support and not a substitute. I might say that he knows her best at home, so I would like his help with the plan, and then ask him to let Simran answer first and add anything after. If the moment feels right, and always with the interpreter, I would say that I like to spend a few minutes with each client on their own as routine for every patient. That also gives her a private chance to raise worries about work or about home that she may not mention in front of others.

I would use teach-back at the end of each section: please tell me, in your own words, what you will do if the leg gets worse, and what you will do for your pelvis at home. If she cannot, I explain again in a different way, and I take responsibility for the gap, not her. I would give written advice in Punjabi where it exists, or use clear pictures. I would also ask about her priorities, which she has hinted at: she is worried about her hours and about work. Her goals will then be stated in her words, such as being able to stand through a shift. I would document the interpreter's name or ID, her stated goals and her consent for each decision.

scale.4: Insists on a professional interpreter with a respectful rationale, speaks to the client directly, creates safe private space, uses plain language and teach-back, and builds goals from her own priorities.
scale.3: Uses an interpreter and plain language but misses private time, teach-back or her own goals.
scale.2: Relies on the husband to interpret or gives generic advice to communicate clearly without specific strategies.
scale.1: Continues to take answers from the husband only, uses jargon, or dismisses language support as unnecessary.

safety_or_ethics_point: The buried issue is the unilateral calf tightness and warmth after a long flight in the third trimester, a possible deep vein thrombosis that the pelvic pain presentation distracts from. A competent candidate separates it from the musculoskeletal picture, stops leg loading and massage, screens for pulmonary symptoms, and arranges same day medical assessment with an interpreter.
common_errors: Candidates attribute the calf symptoms to pregnancy or referred pelvic pain and move on to treating the pelvis. Others identify the clot concern but forget the interpreter, treat the husband as the decision maker, or offer an exercise program or pelvic belt before safety is resolved.
examiner_notes: A passing candidate gives a clear pelvic girdle impression with reasoning, then recognizes the calf finding as the priority in question 2 and acts the same day. A fail misses the calf issue or leaves communication to the husband. Strong answers link each action to this client's language, pregnancy stage and work worries.

title: Repeated falls in a resident with mild dementia
setting: Long-term care home, interprofessional team meeting and unit
client_profile: Mr. Lucien Tremblay, 79, has lived in a long-term care home for ten months. He has mild Alzheimer type dementia, hypertension, mild osteoarthritis of both knees and a previous right hip fracture repaired six years ago. He was a retired machinist. He has fallen four times in eight weeks, mostly in the late afternoon, three times while walking to the toilet alone. Medications include amlodipine, a recently increased dose of an antihypertensive, and a night time sedative started two months ago. Seated blood pressure is 138/80 mmHg, standing at one minute 112/66 mmHg with mild light-headedness. Montreal Cognitive Assessment 19 of 30. Timed Up and Go 21 seconds with a four wheeled walker, which he often leaves behind. Berg Balance Scale 38 of 56. Hearing is reduced and his glasses are frequently missing. He is continent but has urgency.
clinical_scenario: The care team is tired of falls and has asked for a plan. A personal support worker mentions that Mr. Tremblay's right forearm has a new bruise the shape of fingers and that the night nurse had been rough when helping him up. His daughter, who holds power of attorney for personal care, asks you to approve a lap belt and a bed alarm so he cannot get up alone. Mr. Tremblay says he only wants to be able to go to the toilet by himself, as he always has.

questions.prompt: Describe the plan of care you would develop with the team to reduce Mr. Tremblay's falls. Include the goals, the interventions you would choose and why, and how you would judge whether the plan is working.

checklist.point: Sets a client-centred goal such as safe independent toileting, in his own words
Identifies orthostatic blood pressure drop and recent medication changes as modifiable contributors and asks for a medication review by the physician or pharmacist
Plans a scheduled, prompted toileting routine timed to his late afternoon pattern and urgency
Specifies a balance, strength and gait program with dosage, such as supervised sessions several times a week with progression
Addresses the walker habit with cues, placement and a visible reminder rather than assuming he can recall instructions
Includes sensory and environmental changes such as glasses within reach, a hearing assessment, lighting and clear path to the bathroom
Names outcome measures such as fall frequency, Timed Up and Go and Berg score and sets review dates
Explains how to teach using short repeated steps and demonstration given his cognition
Defines triggers to reassess, such as new fall, injury or new symptoms

questions.model_answer:
I would build the plan around what Mr. Tremblay told me he wants: to get to the toilet by himself. So the goal is safe independent toileting, with fewer falls over the next three months, and I would write the goal in his words.

Next I would address the causes I found, in order of how changeable they are. The first is blood pressure. His standing pressure falls by about twenty-six points systolic, and he gets light-headed, which makes late day falls likely. His medications were changed recently and he also takes a night time sedative. I would ask the physician and the pharmacist to review his blood pressure medication and the sedative, and I would give them my measurements. I would also teach staff to have him sit on the edge of the bed for a minute before standing.

Second is the toileting pattern. Three of the four falls were on the way to the toilet, and he has urgency. I would set up a prompted toileting schedule that includes the late afternoon, with a staff member walking with him, and agree this with the nursing team so it is done reliably.

Third is the physical program. His Berg score of 38 and Timed Up and Go of 21 seconds show a real fall risk. I would run supervised sessions three times a week for about thirty minutes, focusing on sit to stand practice, standing balance with progression from wide to narrow base, and walking with the walker including turns. I would progress the difficulty every two weeks as he succeeds. Because of his dementia, I would use short demonstrations, the same words every time and repetition, instead of long explanations.

Fourth is the walker. He leaves it behind, so I would place it directly in front of his chair with a bright mark, ask staff to hand it to him each time, and add a simple sign at eye level.

Fifth is the environment and senses. I would ask that his glasses are within reach every day, that his hearing be assessed with hearing aids checked daily if he has them, that a night light lights the path to the bathroom, and that the route is clear.

To see whether it works, I would track falls each week, repeat Timed Up and Go and Berg in six weeks and in three months, and review sooner after any fall, injury or new confusion.

scale.4: Links each intervention to a finding, sets a client-centred goal, gives specific dosage and progression, addresses medication and orthostatic hypotension through the team, and defines outcome measures and review triggers.
scale.3: Offers a reasonable plan with exercise and environment changes but is general on dosage, medication review or measures.
scale.2: Lists generic fall prevention steps without linking to his findings or goal.
scale.1: Relies on restricting mobility or restraint, or ignores the orthostatic and medication contributors.

questions.prompt: His daughter asks you to approve a lap belt and a bed alarm. Explain how you would respond and what you would do to keep Mr. Tremblay safe while respecting his wishes.

checklist.point: Explains that restraints such as a lap belt raise risks of injury, agitation, pressure injury and loss of function and are a last resort
States that any restraint requires assessment, trial of less restrictive alternatives, consent and an order under the home's policy and applicable legislation

States that the daughter acts as substitute decision maker only if he is found incapable of this decision, so the team assesses his capacity for consenting to a restraint, and still seeks his views and assent
Acknowledges the daughter's fear and explains the plan to reduce falls differently
Proposes alternatives such as scheduled toileting, low bed, floor mats, proximity to nursing station and sensor alerts used without confinement

Notes that bed alarms have limited evidence for preventing falls and can be restrictive or distressing, so any sensor is a cautious staff alert only, never a confinement tool, and only if the team agrees
Plans supervised walking and sets who is responsible at high risk times
Arranges follow-up and review of any measure used

questions.model_answer:
I would start with the daughter's worry, because it is a loving one. I would say that I understand she is frightened that her father will be hurt, and that I share that goal. Then I would explain, in plain words, why I do not recommend a lap belt. A belt does not prevent falls. People with dementia often try to get out of them, which can cause worse injuries such as strangulation or falling from a greater height. They also cause agitation, weakness, skin breakdown and loss of the very walking ability he is trying to keep. In long-term care, a restraint is a last resort. It needs a full assessment, a documented trial of less restrictive options that did not work, an order from the right professional and consent from the person who can give it, following the home's policy and provincial legislation.

About consent, I would take his daughter's input seriously, but her role as substitute decision maker only applies if Mr. Tremblay is found incapable of this particular decision. His dementia is mild, so I would ask the team to assess whether he can understand and weigh a decision about a restraint, and I would not assume he cannot. Either way he still has a voice. He told me he wants to go to the toilet by himself, and I would explain his wish to her and ask if we can work toward it safely. I would also ask him, with simple words, how he feels about being held in a chair, and note his reaction.

I would then offer what we can do now. Scheduled toileting should reduce his need to get up alone. We can lower his bed, place floor mats where safe, move his room closer to the nursing station if possible, and make sure he has his walker, glasses and a night light. I would be honest that bed alarms have limited evidence for preventing falls, and they can startle or distress a resident with dementia. If the team uses a sensor at all, it is a short term alert for staff, never a way to keep him in bed, and only after checking policy and his reaction. Supervised walking at high risk times, like late afternoon, gives him independence with a person nearby.

I would agree on a review date, perhaps in two weeks, to talk about what is working. If another fall occurs, we meet earlier and consider the next less restrictive step, not a restraint first.

scale.4: Explains the harms of restraint, applies the last resort principle and legislative requirements, links the daughter's substitute decision maker role to his capacity for this decision while including the resident, and offers concrete alternatives with review.
scale.3: Declines restraint with reasons and offers alternatives but is vague on consent requirements or on involving the resident.
scale.2: Declines or approves the belt with weak reasoning or does not engage the daughter's concern.
scale.1: Approves a restraint without assessment or consent process, or dismisses the daughter's role.

questions.prompt: A support worker tells you about a finger-shaped bruise on Mr. Tremblay's forearm and says the night nurse was rough with him. Explain what you would do and what your professional obligations are in this situation.

checklist.point: Identifies the report as a possible case of resident abuse or neglect that must not be ignored
Follows legislated and facility reporting duties, informing the director of nursing or administrator promptly and not waiting to gather proof

States that in many provinces regulated health professionals and care staff have a personal duty to report suspected abuse to a named provincial authority, that details differ by province, and does not rely on the home to report
Examines and documents the bruise objectively with location, size, colour and a note of what was reported, without leading questions
Ensures immediate safety of Mr. Tremblay, such as medical assessment and asking that he not be alone with the staff member while the review is underway
Does not confront or accuse the night nurse and does not investigate alone
Maintains confidentiality and shares only with those who need to know
Considers alternative explanations such as bruising from a fall or from assisted transfers while still reporting
Informs the daughter and Mr. Tremblay in a manner consistent with policy and the review process

questions.model_answer:
I would treat this as a report of possible abuse, and I would act the same day. The finger-shaped bruise could have another cause, because he has fallen four times and is moved often, but the pattern and the comment about rough handling mean I cannot assume it is harmless, and it is not my job to decide the cause.

My first step is the resident's safety. I would see Mr. Tremblay, check how he is, and ask the nurse in charge to have the bruise assessed by a nurse or physician. I would look at the forearm and write down exactly what I see: the side of the arm, the size in centimetres, colour, any swelling, and the date and time. I would also record what the support worker told me in her own words, with her name, and not add my opinion. I would not ask Mr. Tremblay leading questions such as did someone hurt you. If he wishes to say something, I would listen calmly and write down his own words.

My second step is to report. In many provinces, regulated health professionals and care staff working in long-term care have a legal duty to report suspected abuse or neglect, and the exact duty differs by province, so I would confirm it. I would not wait for proof or for someone else to decide. I would go to the director of care or the administrator, as the policy directs, and tell them what I have been told and what I saw. The home has its own duties to begin a review. But where the duty applies it is mine personally, so I would follow the home's policy and my own regulator's standard, report directly and immediately to the named provincial authority, for example the Director under the long-term care legislation in Ontario, and not rely on the home to do it for me. I would note that I made both reports and ask how the review is being handled.

Third, I would be careful about fairness. I would not confront the night nurse, discuss it with other staff members or investigate on my own. I would keep it confidential. I would ask the management to arrange that Mr. Tremblay is not alone with that staff member until the review is complete.

Finally, I would make sure Mr. Tremblay's family are informed by the right people, following the home's process. I would document my actions and continue to treat him with respect.

scale.4: Recognizes and acts on suspected abuse the same day, reports internally and personally to the named provincial authority where the province requires it, following the home's policy and regulator's standard, documents objectively, protects the resident, and avoids confronting or investigating alone.
scale.3: Reports internally and documents but is vague on the personal legal duty to report to the authority, resident protection or process.
scale.2: Reports informally to a colleague or waits for more evidence before acting.
scale.1: Ignores the report, confronts the nurse, investigates alone or treats the bruise as a fall injury without reporting.

safety_or_ethics_point: The buried issue is the possible abuse suggested by the finger-shaped forearm bruise and the support worker's comment about rough handling. A competent candidate does not assume a fall explains it, protects the resident, documents objectively, and reports promptly through the facility and legislated channels without confronting or investigating alone.
common_errors: Candidates focus on the fall prevention plan and never address the bruise, or they decide the bruise is from a fall and do not report. Others approve the lap belt to appease the daughter, or confront the night nurse directly.
examiner_notes: A pass shows a plan tied to orthostatic blood pressure, toileting and a dosed exercise program, a firm explanation about restraint and consent, and a clear duty to report. A fail misses the abuse indicator or relies on restraint. Reasoning that keeps the resident's own wish central separates strong answers.

title: Persistent symptoms after concussion in a teenager
setting: Outpatient sports and concussion physiotherapy clinic
client_profile: Amara Okafor, 16, plays high school soccer. Six weeks ago she was struck in the head by a ball during a game and had a brief headache, dizziness and fogginess. She was told to rest, returned to school after one week and tried to return to practice at week three, when headaches and fatigue worsened. She now reports daily headaches rated 4/10 that rise to 7/10 by afternoon, light sensitivity, trouble concentrating in class, sleeping about five hours and feeling overwhelmed. Past history is migraine in her mother, no prior concussion. Objective: resting heart rate 78, BP 108/66 mmHg. Cervical flexion and extension are slightly limited with tenderness over the upper cervical muscles. Saccades and smooth pursuit provoke headache and dizziness. Vestibular ocular motor screening shows symptoms of 3 to 4 points above baseline on horizontal head movement. Symptom-limited treadmill test stops at 8 minutes at a heart rate of 150 with headache increase. Neurological screen and balance with eyes closed are normal.
clinical_scenario: Amara's father brought her and wants her cleared to play in a tournament in two weeks. Her teacher has asked for a letter with accommodations. Amara is quiet and gives short answers. She tells you privately, while her father is out of the room, that she sometimes thinks everyone would be better off if she just was not around, and asks you not to tell him. Her friends have stopped contacting her since she left the team.

questions.prompt: Explain your clinical impression of what is driving Amara's persistent symptoms, and describe which findings support it and which assessment or information you would still want.

checklist.point: States that symptoms beyond four weeks in an adolescent constitute persistent post-concussion symptoms and a multi-factor presentation
Identifies likely contributing subtypes such as cervicogenic, vestibular-ocular and exertional intolerance based on findings
Links limited and tender upper cervical findings to possible cervicogenic headache
Links provoked symptoms on saccades, pursuit and head movement to vestibular-ocular dysfunction
Uses the symptom-limited treadmill test result to show exercise intolerance and identify a symptom threshold of 150, with a starting dose at about 80 to 90 percent of it
Recognizes that sleep loss, stress and mood can maintain symptoms and screens for them
Mentions family history of migraine as a possible influence and that post-traumatic headache may have migraine features
Names further information needed, such as sleep and mood questionnaires, school workload, and screens for red flags

questions.model_answer:
My impression is persistent symptoms after a concussion, six weeks out, in a sixteen year old. In young people, symptoms past about four weeks are not a failure of rest. They usually come from several overlapping problems, and my job is to sort out which ones are present so treatment can target them.

The first I see is a cervical contribution. Her neck is stiff in flexion and extension and tender over the upper cervical muscles, and she has daily headaches that build through the afternoon, which fits a cervicogenic pattern, especially with posture and school work.

The second is a vestibular and ocular motor problem. Saccades and smooth pursuit bring on headache and dizziness, and horizontal head movement raised her symptoms by three to four points. That tells me her eyes and balance systems are not coping with movement and busy visual scenes, which explains why class and screens are so hard.

The third is exercise intolerance. On the symptom-limited treadmill test she stopped at eight minutes with a heart rate of 150 when her headache rose. That gives me a symptom threshold of 150, and I would start aerobic work at about 80 to 90 percent of it, roughly 120 to 135 beats per minute. It also shows she can exercise under control, which is encouraging. Her attempt at practice at week three, before anyone had set this threshold, likely overshot it.

Fourth, I see factors that maintain symptoms. She sleeps five hours, feels overwhelmed, has lost contact with friends and has a family history of migraine, which can make post-traumatic headache feel migraine-like. Mood, sleep and stress can all prolong symptoms, so I need to measure these and not assume it is only physical.

I would still want more information. I would use a symptom inventory and sleep and mood screens, ask about her school workload, her screen time and how she is coping, and confirm there are no red flags such as worsening headache, vomiting, new neurological signs or neck pain with arm symptoms. Her normal neurological screen and balance are reassuring, and I do not think she needs imaging at this point.

scale.4: Names a multi-factor persistent symptom picture with cervical, vestibular-ocular and exertional components tied to specific findings, includes mood, sleep and stress as maintaining factors, and identifies what further information is needed.
scale.3: Identifies two or more contributors with findings but gives limited reasoning on psychosocial factors or additional data.
scale.2: Lists tests or labels the condition as post-concussion syndrome without explaining which findings point to which problem.
scale.1: Recommends complete rest, attributes everything to one cause, or ignores the findings.

questions.prompt: During a private moment Amara tells you something that worries you and asks you to keep it from her father. Describe how you would respond and what you would do about it, while also addressing her father's request about the tournament.

checklist.point: Responds with calm, nonjudgmental listening and thanks her for telling you
Asks directly about thoughts of suicide, plan, intent and means in a caring way
Explains the limits of confidentiality: safety concerns cannot be kept secret
Arranges same day mental health support appropriate to risk, such as crisis line, physician, or emergency department if risk is imminent
Does not leave her alone if there is imminent risk and involves a parent or guardian in a collaborative way
Gives crisis resources such as a national suicide crisis helpline in Canada
Explains to her father that clearance to play is not decided today and that return to sport follows a staged plan based on her symptoms
Documents the conversation and actions

questions.model_answer:
What Amara said is the most important thing that happened in this visit, and I would treat it that way. I would stay with her, speak calmly and say thank you for trusting me with that. I would not rush to reassure her or change the subject.

I would ask her directly and kindly. Are you having thoughts of ending your life? Do you have a plan? Have you thought about how or when? Do you have access to anything you could use? Asking does not plant the idea, and the answers tell me how urgent this is. I would also ask whether she has felt this before and who she talks to.

She asked me not to tell her father. I would be honest. I would say, I understand why you asked, and I wish I could promise that, but when someone's safety is at risk I cannot keep it secret. I would say I want to do this with her, not behind her back, and ask how she would like her father to be told, whether by me with her in the room or by her with me beside her. That respects her voice while meeting my duty to keep her safe.

What I do next depends on risk. If she has a plan or intent, or says she cannot keep herself safe, I would not leave her alone. I would bring in her father right away, and arrange for her to be assessed in an emergency department today, calling emergency services if needed. If she has passive thoughts without a plan or intent, I would still tell her father together with her, arrange a same day or next day call with her physician or a mental health service, give her a Canadian crisis line number to call or text any time, and agree on a safety plan with her and her family, including limiting access to means at home. I would follow up with a phone call within a day.

For her father's question about the tournament, I would explain that the decision is not today, and that returning to sport is staged and symptom based. Her treadmill test shows we can start controlled aerobic exercise, but contact play comes much later. I would say her health, including her mood, comes first. I would document everything.

scale.4: Asks directly about suicide risk, is honest about confidentiality limits, matches the response to risk with same day mental health arrangements, involves the parent collaboratively, and handles the tournament question without pressure.
scale.3: Responds supportively and refers for mental health support but is vague on risk assessment, confidentiality limits or urgency.
scale.2: Offers reassurance, agrees to keep the secret, or recommends follow-up at the next routine visit.
scale.1: Ignores the statement, promises secrecy and does nothing, or clears her for play.

questions.prompt: Plan how you would communicate her recovery plan to Amara, her father and her school, so that each understands what to expect and what is needed. Describe the specific words and strategies you would use.

checklist.point: Speaks to Amara directly as the main partner in the plan and asks for her goals
Explains persistent symptoms in simple terms, normalizing that most youth recover and that rest alone is not the plan
Gives her father a clear explanation of why clearance for the tournament is not possible yet and the stages needed
Obtains Amara's consent for what is shared with school and shares only what is needed
Writes a school letter with practical accommodations such as reduced screen time, rest breaks, extended deadlines and no exams for a period
Uses teach-back and written summary for key points and warning signs
Acknowledges her emotions and social isolation and offers ways to reconnect with friends
Sets clear expectations for review and for when to contact the clinic

questions.model_answer:
I would talk to Amara first and most, because it is her recovery. I would start by asking what she most wants right now, perhaps to feel less tired, to get through class or to see her friends. That gives me the words to anchor the plan.

To explain the situation, I would say: after a concussion most teenagers recover, but some take longer because several systems, like your neck, your eyes and balance system, and your energy and sleep, are all a bit out of tune. The good news is that we found which ones, and each can be treated. I would be clear that complete rest is not the treatment. Gentle, planned activity is. Then I would give her something concrete: a walking or bike program at about 80 to 90 percent of the heart rate where her symptoms rose, around 120 to 135 beats per minute, with her pulse checked, plus neck and eye exercises that I would show her.

For her father, I would say that I understand he wants her back on the field, and I want that too. But the tournament is two weeks away and she is not ready for contact. I would explain that return to sport moves in steps: daily activity, then aerobic exercise, then sport specific drills, then non-contact practice, then full practice, then games, and she can only move up when her symptoms stay settled. I would tell him I will not be clearing her for the tournament, and offer to go through the steps with a chart so he can see the path.

For school, I would ask Amara what she wants her teachers to know. With her permission, I would write a short letter with practical needs only, not her diagnosis details or her mood: shorter work periods with breaks, reduced screen time, extra time on assignments, no tests for now, and a plan to review in two weeks. I would send it through her or her parent, as she prefers.

I would finish by asking her to tell me the plan back in her own words, give her a written summary, and tell her when to call, such as worsening headaches or new vomiting. I would also gently acknowledge that missing her team and friends is hard.

scale.4: Addresses Amara directly with a clear explanation and exercise plan, explains staged return to sport to the father without giving clearance, uses consent-based minimal school communication with specific accommodations, and checks understanding.
scale.3: Communicates clearly with the family and school but is limited on consent, teach-back or emotional acknowledgement.
scale.2: Gives general information, speaks mainly to the father, or shares more with the school than needed.
scale.1: Clears or implies clearance for the tournament, shares her disclosure without consent, or recommends only rest.

safety_or_ethics_point: The buried issue is Amara's private statement that others would be better off without her, which is a suicide risk disclosure. A competent candidate asks directly about plan and intent, explains that safety limits confidentiality, arranges same day mental health care matched to risk, and involves her family collaboratively.
common_errors: Candidates keep the secret to preserve trust, offer reassurance without asking about plan or intent, or focus entirely on the tournament and concussion plan. Others give clearance to play to satisfy the father.
examiner_notes: A pass identifies multiple contributors to persistent symptoms from the findings, responds to the disclosure with direct risk assessment and honest limits of confidentiality, and gives a staged return plan. A fail misses or minimizes the risk statement. Strong answers keep Amara involved in each decision.

title: Shoulder pain in a house painter
setting: Private outpatient physiotherapy clinic
client_profile: Marcus Beaulieu, 52, is a self-employed house painter who works with a small crew. For four months he has had right shoulder pain over the lateral upper arm, worse when painting overhead and reaching behind, and waking him at night when he lies on the right side. Pain is 5/10 on activity. No injury event. He smokes about a pack a day and has lost roughly 5 kg in three months, which he attributes to a busy summer. He also has mild tingling in the right ring and little fingers in the morning. Objective: active elevation 140 degrees with a painful arc between 70 and 110 degrees, external rotation strength 4/5 with pain, positive Hawkins-Kennedy and painful arc tests, negative drop arm test, normal cervical rotation, grip strength within normal limits. Shoulder Pain and Disability Index 54%. Pulse 72, BP 134/84 mmHg.
clinical_scenario: Marcus has applied to the provincial workplace safety board for his shoulder, and a case manager has asked for his clinical information. His crew supervisor on a large commercial contract phones the clinic and asks you to confirm he can return to ladder work next week. The clinic owner suggests prepaying a package of twelve sessions at a discount, saying it will help him commit.

questions.prompt: Explain your clinical impression of Marcus's shoulder problem and the reasoning behind it. Describe what other conditions you would consider and how you would decide among them.

checklist.point: States rotator cuff related shoulder pain as the likely musculoskeletal source
Supports the impression with overhead aggravation, painful arc, positive impingement-type tests and painful external rotation strength
Explains why a full thickness cuff tear is less likely, using the negative drop arm test and the ability to elevate, and what would change that view
Considers cervical radiculopathy, ulnar nerve entrapment and lower brachial plexus involvement (C8 to T1 pattern) as explanations for the ring and little finger tingling and how to test each
Identifies the combination of weight loss, heavy smoking, night pain and C8 to T1 tingling as a possible non-musculoskeletal cause such as an apical lung tumour that needs prompt medical screening
Lists further screening such as lung and general health review, Horner syndrome, hand intrinsic wasting, supraclavicular findings, cervical screen and neurological testing
Mentions other differentials such as acromioclavicular joint or biceps pathology and how to examine for them
Explains how response to treatment and reassessment will confirm or change the impression

questions.model_answer:
My leading impression is rotator cuff related shoulder pain, which means pain from the tendons and tissues under the shoulder arch, in a man who spends his days with his arms overhead. The supporting findings are the lateral upper arm pain, the pain between seventy and one hundred and ten degrees of elevation, the positive Hawkins-Kennedy test and the pain on resisted external rotation. Those match a loaded, overused cuff.

I have considered a full thickness tear. His drop arm test is negative and he can lift his arm to one hundred and forty degrees, so a large tear is less likely. If he had a sudden loss of strength, a lag sign or a clear weakness that does not improve, I would want imaging and a surgical opinion.

The tingling in the ring and little fingers is a separate clue that I would not ignore. His cervical rotation is normal, but I would test cervical range further, do a neurological exam for strength, reflexes and sensation, and check the ulnar nerve at the elbow, since a painter who grips a roller may irritate it, though that would not explain the weight loss. I would use a combined movement of neck and arm to see if the tingling reproduces. Tingling in the ring and little fingers follows a C8 to T1 pattern, so it may not be a separate problem. With the smoking, weight loss and night pain, it could be part of one red flag cluster, with the lower brachial plexus involved by a lesion at the lung apex. I would also look for Horner syndrome, such as a drooping eyelid, a small pupil and less sweating on that side, for wasting of the hand muscles and for fullness above the collarbone.

Now the part that concerns me most. He has lost about five kilograms over three months without trying, smokes a pack a day, and the pain wakes him at night. Taken separately each might be dismissed, but together they could mean something outside the shoulder, such as a lung apex tumour or another illness referring pain there. A musculoskeletal shoulder pain should change with position and movement. So I would ask more questions about cough, coughing blood, shortness of breath, fatigue, appetite, fever and night sweats, check for chest findings and hand muscle wasting, and arrange a prompt medical review with his physician rather than waiting.

I would examine the acromioclavicular joint and biceps tendon to complete the picture. I would confirm my impression by how he responds over a few weeks, and I would refer sooner if pain does not follow a mechanical pattern.

scale.4: Gives a reasoned cuff-related impression, differentiates tear, cervical and ulnar sources, and independently identifies the weight loss, smoking, night pain and C8 to T1 tingling as a pattern needing medical screening.
scale.3: Gives the correct impression and some differentials but treats the weight loss and smoking history only briefly or without a clear action.
scale.2: Names impingement and lists tests with limited reasoning and no consideration of non-musculoskeletal causes.
scale.1: Misses the red flags entirely or states a diagnosis without supporting findings.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would manage the safety concerns in this case, including what you would tell Marcus and how you would proceed with treatment in the meantime.

checklist.point: Tells Marcus plainly that some of his symptoms need a medical check to rule out a cause outside the shoulder
Arranges prompt referral to his physician with a written summary of findings and the specific concerns
Explains the reason without causing alarm or stating a diagnosis
Limits treatment to low risk, symptom-guided measures until the medical review, avoiding vigorous mobilization or loading that might mask changes
Asks about his readiness and willingness to follow up and addresses obstacles such as time, cost and fear
Gives advice on activity modification at work, such as limiting sustained overhead work and ladder use while pain and review are ongoing
Sets a follow-up time to confirm the medical visit occurred
Provides immediate advice on when to seek urgent care, such as coughing blood, severe breathlessness or sudden weakness

questions.model_answer:
I would be honest with Marcus, and calm. I would say that most of what I found fits a shoulder tendon problem, which is very treatable, but a few things you told me, the weight loss, the night pain and your smoking history, are the kind that I want a doctor to check. Most of the time these turn out to be something else, but it is not safe for me to assume that, and I would feel better if we ruled out a cause outside the shoulder first. I would not name a specific diagnosis because I cannot make one, and I would not frighten him.

I would then make it easy for him to act. I would write a clear letter to his physician, listing the shoulder findings, the five kilogram weight loss, the pack a day smoking, the night pain and the ring and little finger tingling, and ask for review this week. If he has no physician, I would help him find a walk-in clinic. I would ask what might get in the way, perhaps time away from work or fear of the result, and work out a plan with him, such as an early appointment or a phone visit. I would book a call or visit with him in a week to confirm it happened.

Until the medical review, I would use gentle, low risk treatment guided by his pain. That could include education, relative rest from sustained overhead work, pain-free range of motion and light isometric strengthening that does not provoke night pain. I would avoid aggressive mobilization or heavy loading, both because they might not be helpful and because I do not want to blur the picture before he is checked.

At work, I would suggest he avoid prolonged overhead painting and ladder work this week. I would explain that is for safety, since a painful arm on a ladder is a fall risk, not a judgment about his ability.

I would also give him clear warning signs: if he coughs up blood, becomes short of breath, has chest pain, sudden loss of strength in the arm or severe worsening pain, he should go to an emergency department.

scale.4: Explains the need for medical screening clearly and calmly, writes a specific referral with a follow-up, limits treatment to safe options, advises on ladder safety and gives urgent warning signs.
scale.3: Refers appropriately and modifies treatment but lacks detail on follow-up, warning signs or addressing barriers.
scale.2: Mentions a medical check vaguely or proceeds with full treatment alongside it.
scale.1: Does not refer, reassures that it is just the shoulder, or provides vigorous treatment before review.

questions.prompt: The workplace safety board case manager has requested his clinical information, his supervisor has phoned asking about ladder work, and the clinic owner has suggested a prepaid package. Explain how you would handle each of these requests, naming the professional obligations that apply.

checklist.point: Does not give information to the supervisor without Marcus's informed consent
Releases information to the workplace safety board only as required by the claim and legislation, limited to what is relevant, with Marcus informed
Provides objective, accurate and complete reports to the board, including functional restrictions without exaggeration
Raises the concern about the prepaid package as a potential conflict of interest and a risk to client autonomy
States that treatment plans and fees are based on his clinical needs and that he can pay per visit, with refund policies clear
Documents each request, consent and decision
Does not allow the clinic owner's financial interests to influence clinical decisions
Notes the duty to speak to the clinic owner or the regulator if pressure continues

questions.model_answer:
These are three different situations and each has its own rule, so I would take them one at a time.

First, the supervisor. A phone call from an employer asking about a worker's fitness for ladder work is a request for personal health information. Marcus is self-employed and the supervisor is on another company's contract, so he has no right to it. I would not confirm anything, not even that Marcus is a client. I would say that I cannot discuss any client without written consent, and I would suggest that Marcus speak to him himself. I would then tell Marcus about the call and ask what he wants shared. If he consents, I would share only the practical restriction, such as avoid sustained overhead work and ladders for now, not his diagnosis or history. I would record the call and his decision.

Second, the workplace safety board. Here the law and the claim give the board a legitimate need for relevant clinical information about the injury. I would confirm with Marcus that I am sending it, explain what it contains, and send only what relates to the claimed condition and his functional limits. I would not include unrelated health matters. My report would be accurate and objective: my findings, the measures I used, his restrictions and the expected course. I must not overstate or understate his limits to help or hurt the claim. Because I have asked for a medical review, I would state that clearly as part of my plan.

Third, the prepaid package. I see a conflict of interest. Marcus's needs may change after the medical review, and he may need fewer or different sessions, or none, while a prepayment ties him to a plan before I know that. Treatment recommendations must be based on clinical need. I would explain that to the owner respectfully, and ask that Marcus be offered the option to pay per visit, with a clear refund policy for unused sessions. If Marcus freely chooses a package after full information, that may be acceptable, but I would not suggest it now. If the owner continues to pressure me, I would document my concerns and consider seeking advice from my regulator, because my duty to the client comes before the clinic's income.

scale.4: Refuses to release information to the supervisor without consent, limits and informs the board report with objective content, identifies the prepayment conflict of interest and protects the client, and documents all actions.
scale.3: Handles consent and board report correctly but treats the prepaid package without identifying the conflict or the required safeguards.
scale.2: Shares some information with the supervisor or gives the board broad records without Marcus's input.
scale.1: Confirms fitness for ladder work to the supervisor, accepts the package without comment, or exaggerates restrictions for the claim.

safety_or_ethics_point: The buried issue is the combination of unexplained weight loss, heavy smoking and night pain with shoulder pain, which may indicate a serious non-musculoskeletal cause such as an upper lung tumour. A competent candidate recognizes the pattern, tells the client plainly, arranges prompt medical review, limits treatment and gives warning signs.
common_errors: Candidates diagnose rotator cuff impingement and plan a standard exercise program without addressing weight loss and smoking. Others disclose fitness information to the supervisor or accept the prepaid package without noting the conflict of interest.
examiner_notes: A pass explains the cuff-related impression, flags the red flag cluster and refers, and keeps third parties from clinical information without consent. A fail misses the cluster or breaches confidentiality. Strong answers separate the three requests and name the principle that governs each one.

title: Rheumatoid arthritis flare in a working parent
setting: Outpatient hospital physiotherapy department
client_profile: Nadia Rahimi, 45, is a married mother of three children aged 6, 9 and 13 and works part-time as a school office administrator. She has had seropositive rheumatoid arthritis for nine years, treated with methotrexate and a biologic agent by her rheumatologist. Over three weeks she has had a flare with morning stiffness lasting 90 minutes and swelling and pain in both wrists, the second to fourth metacarpophalangeal joints and both forefeet. Pain is 6/10 and fatigue is high. Disease Activity Score shows moderate activity per her rheumatologist's latest note. Objective: wrist extension 40 degrees on both sides, grip strength about 55 percent of expected for age, bilateral warm swollen MCP joints, tender forefeet, no deformity changes from last year. HAQ-DI 1.5 of 3. Her rheumatologist appointment is in three weeks. She also reports a new neck ache and, when she bends her neck forward, brief electric buzzing down both arms, which she has had for about two weeks.
clinical_scenario: Nadia wants to keep working and to keep up with her children's activities. She is worried about cost, since her extended health plan covers only a limited number of visits. She asks you for strong neck mobilizations because her neck feels stiff, and says her family physician told her to see a physiotherapist and an occupational therapist but she has not seen anyone else. Her husband works shifts and she has little help at home.

questions.prompt: Describe the physiotherapy plan of care you would put in place for Nadia's flare. Include goals, the main interventions with their dosage, how you would adapt to her flare, and how you would measure progress.

checklist.point: Sets client-centred goals around work, parenting tasks and fatigue management with timeframes
Plans joint protection education and activity pacing during the flare
Prescribes gentle pain-free range of motion for affected joints, avoiding forceful stretching of inflamed joints
Specifies low-load strengthening and low-impact aerobic activity with dosage and gradual progression as inflammation settles
Considers modalities such as heat or cold for symptom relief and hand or foot splints or footwear, in discussion with the team
Plans a flare action plan including when to rest, reduce load and contact the rheumatologist
Names outcome measures such as pain, grip strength, HAQ-DI, morning stiffness duration and participation goals
Plans efficient visit frequency within her coverage and a home program she can do with limited time
States clearly that the neck complaint is handled separately from this plan

questions.model_answer:
I would build this plan around what Nadia told me she wants: to keep working and to keep up with her children. My goals would be, over the next four weeks, to reduce her morning stiffness and pain, protect her joints during the flare, and have her manage her work tasks and school pickups with less fatigue. Over three months, I would aim to restore her grip strength toward her usual level and make sure she knows how to handle future flares.

During a flare, the main idea is protection with gentle movement. I would teach joint protection and pacing: spread tasks across the day, use larger joints to carry bags, use jar openers and tools that reduce grip force, and break up computer and filing work with short pauses. I would also teach her to plan rest ahead of busy periods, since fatigue is high.

For exercise, I would prescribe gentle, pain-free range of motion for her wrists, hands and feet, ten repetitions two or three times a day, held within comfortable range, and avoid forceful stretching of warm, swollen joints. I would add low-load isometric hand and forearm work and walking or stationary cycling for ten to fifteen minutes at a pace where she can still speak in sentences, increasing by a few minutes weekly as swelling and stiffness settle. If pain lasts more than two hours after exercise, she reduces the dose the next day.

For symptom relief, I would suggest warmth in the morning for stiffness, or cold for hot swollen joints, and discuss resting wrist splints at night with the occupational therapist. I would check her footwear and ask about podiatry for her forefeet.

I would give her a written flare plan: when to rest and reduce exercise, and when to call her rheumatologist, such as increasing swelling, fever or new joint pain. I would measure pain on a 0 to 10 scale, morning stiffness minutes, grip strength with a dynamometer, and HAQ-DI every four weeks, along with her own goal of completing work tasks.

Because her coverage is limited, I would see her every two weeks at first and then monthly, relying on a short home program she can do in about fifteen minutes. The neck complaint I would address separately, before I decide anything about her neck.

scale.4: Gives client-centred goals, flare-appropriate interventions with specific dosage and progression, joint protection and a flare plan, measurable outcomes and a plan that fits her coverage, and keeps the neck complaint separate.
scale.3: Provides a sound plan with appropriate exercises but is vague on dosage, flare adaptation or outcomes.
scale.2: Lists general exercises and modalities without adapting to the flare or her goals.
scale.1: Prescribes vigorous stretching or strengthening of inflamed joints, or ignores the flare.

questions.prompt: Nadia asks you for strong neck mobilizations because her neck feels stiff. Explain how you would respond, what you would assess and what you would do about her neck symptoms.

checklist.point: Recognizes that neck pain with electric sensations down both arms on flexion in long-standing RA may indicate cervical spine instability or cord involvement
Declines manual techniques and end-range cervical movement until instability has been medically excluded
Performs a screen of neurological function including strength, sensation, reflexes and signs of myelopathy without provoking symptoms
Arranges urgent communication with her rheumatologist or physician, not waiting three weeks, for assessment and imaging
Explains the reason to Nadia in clear terms and checks she understands
Advises avoiding forceful neck movements, and gives warning signs such as weakness, balance change, bladder or bowel changes needing emergency care
Provides interim safe advice for comfort such as supported posture, avoiding sustained neck flexion
Respects her request while sharing the decision and offering alternatives

questions.model_answer:
I would take her neck symptom very seriously and I would say no to strong neck mobilizations today. My reason is the combination she described: neck ache, and a buzzing, electric feeling down both arms when she bends her neck forward, in someone with nine years of rheumatoid arthritis. This disease can weaken the ligaments at the top of the neck and allow the vertebrae to move too much, which can press on the spinal cord. That electric sensation on flexion, which is a known sign of cord irritation, is not the same as a simple stiff neck. Strong mobilization or end-range movement could make it worse and cause serious harm.

I would explain this to Nadia honestly and without scaring her. I might say, I understand you want relief, but your symptoms mean I need your doctor to check the stability of your neck before anyone moves it. This is a safety step I take for people with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis, and it does not mean something terrible has happened.

I would gently assess what I can without provoking symptoms. I would test strength in her arms and legs, sensation in her hands, reflexes, and look for signs of cord involvement such as clumsy hands, trouble walking in a straight line, hyperreflexia or a positive Hoffmann sign. I would not move her neck to end range, apply any sustained flexion or perform manual techniques.

Then I would act now, not in three weeks. I would telephone her rheumatologist's office or her physician today, describe the symptoms and findings, and ask for urgent review and imaging of her cervical spine, usually flexion and extension views or MRI. I would send a written note with my findings. If she has any new weakness, trouble walking, loss of bladder or bowel control, or worsening arm symptoms, I would send her to the emergency department.

For now, I would give her safe comfort advice: keep her neck in a supported neutral position, avoid long periods looking down at her computer or phone, and avoid lifting heavy loads overhead. I would offer to continue treating her hands and wrists, and work with her on what she would like for the neck while we wait for the answer.

scale.4: Declines manual neck techniques with a clear rationale about RA cervical instability, screens neurological function safely, arranges urgent medical review and imaging, gives warning signs, and collaborates with the client.
scale.3: Declines mobilization and refers but is vague on urgency, neurological screening or warning signs.
scale.2: Mentions caution but performs gentle mobilization or waits for the scheduled appointment.
scale.1: Performs the requested mobilizations or dismisses the arm symptoms as unimportant.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would collaborate with the other professionals involved in Nadia's care. Identify who you would contact, what you would communicate, and how you would coordinate to support both her flare and her neck concern.

checklist.point: Contacts the rheumatologist promptly about the neck symptoms and flare, and shares objective findings
Communicates with her family physician about neck concern and imaging and her referral requests
Refers to or coordinates with occupational therapy for joint protection, splinting and work adaptations
Considers podiatry or orthotics for the forefeet and pharmacist input on medication questions
Obtains Nadia's consent for sharing information with each provider
Clarifies roles so the plan is not duplicated, such as who monitors disease activity and who manages splints and exercise
Uses clear written communication with specific questions and a time frame for response
Establishes how updates will be shared and who is the main contact, ideally Nadia
Considers community supports such as arthritis programs, given limited help at home

questions.model_answer:
Nadia has several people involved, and she has told me she has little help at home, so good collaboration will also lighten her load. I would start by asking her consent to share information with each provider, and explain who I intend to contact and why.

The first and most urgent contact is her rheumatologist, and her family physician, about her neck. I would call the rheumatologist's office today and follow with a short written note stating the neck ache, the electric sensations down both arms on neck flexion, my neurological findings, and my question: does she need urgent cervical imaging and assessment of stability? I would ask for a response within a day or two, and say that I am holding all neck techniques until then. I would also send a copy to her family physician and ask whether the physician can order the imaging if the rheumatologist cannot see her sooner. In the same note, I would tell the rheumatologist about the flare findings, including grip strength, joint swelling, morning stiffness and her HAQ-DI score, because they are useful for decisions about her medication, and I would leave the medication decisions to the rheumatologist and not comment on them.

Second, I would refer to occupational therapy, since Nadia's main goals are work and parenting. The occupational therapist can make resting splints, teach joint protection and fit work adaptations such as a keyboard setup. Splinting and exercise need to match, so I would send my plan and ask the occupational therapist to tell me which splints she has chosen.

Third, I would look at the feet. I would ask for a podiatry or orthotic referral for her forefeet, and ask the pharmacist to be available if she has questions about her medications.

To avoid duplication, I would state roles in my note: the rheumatologist manages disease activity and medications, the physician coordinates imaging, the occupational therapist handles splints and daily tasks, and I handle exercise and movement. I would make Nadia the centre of the communication: I would give her a one page summary of who is doing what, and ask her to share it. Given her limited coverage, I would point her to community arthritis programs that are free or low cost.

scale.4: Identifies the right providers with specific content and timing for each, prioritizes the urgent neck communication, obtains consent, clarifies roles and keeps the client at the centre.
scale.3: Names appropriate providers and purposes but is general on timing, roles or consent.
scale.2: Lists professionals to contact without explaining what to communicate or how to coordinate.
scale.1: Omits urgent contact about the neck, shares information without consent, or works in isolation.

safety_or_ethics_point: The buried issue is the new neck ache with electric sensations down both arms on neck flexion in a woman with nine years of rheumatoid arthritis, suggesting possible atlantoaxial instability or cord irritation. A competent candidate declines mobilization, screens neurologically without provoking symptoms, and arranges urgent medical review and imaging.
common_errors: Candidates agree to the requested neck mobilization or treat the arm symptoms as nerve irritation to be stretched. Others plan only the hand and wrist flare and never mention the neck, or wait for the rheumatologist visit in three weeks.
examiner_notes: A pass gives a flare-appropriate dosed plan, recognizes the neck symptoms as a stop signal and communicates urgently with the physician team. A fail performs or accepts neck manipulation or overlooks the symptom. Strong answers name roles clearly and keep Nadia at the centre of communication.

title: Day 1 hip hemiarthroplasty with delirium
setting: Orthopedic ward of a community acute care hospital
client_profile: Mrs. Margit Kovacs is an 84-year-old retired seamstress admitted two days ago after a fall at home with a displaced left femoral neck fracture. She had a cemented hemiarthroplasty via a posterior approach yesterday and is weight bearing as tolerated with posterior hip precautions. Past history: mild hypertension, osteoarthritis of both knees, and mild hearing loss. She lived alone in a bungalow and walked without an aid. Today she is drowsy, answers slowly, and the nurse's chart note says the Confusion Assessment Method was positive this morning with a quiet, withdrawn presentation. Vitals at rest in bed: BP 128/74, HR 84, SpO2 95% on room air, temperature 37.8 C. Hemoglobin this morning 88 g/L (96 g/L pre-operatively). Pain 4/10 at rest on regular acetaminophen and low-dose oral opioid as needed. Left hip dressing dry. Active ankle pumps and quadriceps contraction are present on both sides. Her glasses and hearing aids are on the bedside table, not in use.
clinical_scenario: It is 10:00 and you are the first physiotherapist to see her. Her daughter, Ilona, is at the bedside after driving two hours. She tells you her mother is just tired and lazy, that she managed to walk to the kitchen after her last surgery on her knee, and that she wants you to get her up and walking the length of the hallway today so she can go home on the weekend. Mrs. Kovacs speaks Hungarian first and English second, and she has been mostly silent since you arrived. A urinary catheter is still in place. The nurse is busy with another patient and the bed alarm is off.

questions.prompt: Describe your treatment plan for this client today and over the next two or three days. Explain how you will set your goals and progress her activity, and why you chose this approach given everything you know about her.

checklist.point: Sets short-term goals for today such as supervised bed mobility, sitting at the edge of bed and a safe transfer to a chair.
Links drowsiness, positive delirium screen and low hemoglobin to a cautious, graded progression rather than a hallway walk.
Includes posterior hip precautions in every bed mobility and transfer instruction, with assistance and a raised seat.
Plans frequent short sessions, not one long session, with rest breaks and monitoring of symptoms.
Plans early out-of-bed mobilization as part of delirium prevention and recovery, balanced against tolerance.
Includes non-pharmacological delirium strategies: glasses, hearing aids, orientation cues, daylight, familiar person, sleep protection.
Uses the same simple exercises: ankle pumps, quadriceps and gluteal sets, and assisted hip abduction within precautions.
Chooses a measurable outcome such as time to sit unsupported, transfer assistance level or distance walked with walker.
Names reassessment triggers: drop in blood pressure, symptoms, worsening confusion, pain not controlled, wound change.
Plans discharge-oriented thinking: home assessment, assistance at home or rehabilitation, without promising a weekend date.

questions.model_answer:
I will build today's plan around her delirium and her low blood count, because those two things decide how fast I can safely move her. My goal is regular, short, supported activity that gets her out of bed without taking her past what her body can handle today.

First, my goals. For today, I want her to roll and sit up at the edge of the bed with help, stand with a walker and a person on each side if she tolerates it, and transfer to a chair for meals. Over the next two or three days I would progress to standing at the walker several times, short walks in the room and then to the hallway, aiming at a transfer with one person and a walker.

Second, how I progress. I would not do one long session. She is drowsy, her hemoglobin has dropped to 88, and she is two days from a fracture and one day from surgery. I will check blood pressure lying and sitting, heart rate, oxygen saturation, how she looks, and whether she feels dizzy before I stand her, and again after. I stop and lay her back if she becomes pale, faint, short of breath or more confused. Several ten minute sessions across the day are safer and better than one long one, and I will agree on times with the nurse so that pain medication is working.

Third, her precautions. Because the approach was posterior, I will teach and cue no hip flexion past ninety degrees, no adduction past midline and no internal rotation. That means a raised chair seat, a pillow between her knees in bed, and assistance rolling. I will use simple, short words and demonstrate rather than explain at length. Between sessions she will do ankle pumps, quadriceps and gluteal sets in bed, and assisted hip abduction within her precautions.

Fourth, delirium. Moving out of bed in daylight is one of the best treatments for delirium, so activity is part of the plan, not a risk I accept. I will ask the nurse to put in her glasses and hearing aids, because she may be struggling to understand rather than failing to cooperate. I would use familiar cues, talk with her daughter about helpful routines, and ask about getting the catheter removed since it is a tether and an infection and delirium risk.

Fifth, I will measure progress with the level of assistance she needs for a transfer and the time she can sit up, and I will reassess each day. I will let the team know about the discharge goals only after she shows what she can do, so we do not set a weekend date that is not safe.

scale.4: Gives graded, staged goals and a clear progression, adjusts pace for delirium and low hemoglobin with monitoring, includes hip precautions and delirium strategies, and explains why with outcomes and reassessment.
scale.3: Sound plan with precautions and progression but thin on why delirium and hemoglobin change the pace or on outcome measures.
scale.2: Lists exercises and walking goals with little adjustment for her state, or omits precautions or monitoring.
scale.1: Plans a long walk or discharge target without regard to confusion or low hemoglobin, or ignores precautions.

questions.prompt: Mrs. Kovacs's daughter insists that you walk her mother along the hallway now. Explain how you will keep your client safe in this session and how you will respond to her daughter while still respecting your client's wishes.

checklist.point: Recognizes the client's own wishes and capacity matter, and tries to ask her directly in a way she can understand.
Does not mobilize beyond safe tolerance because of family pressure; explains the clinical reasons.
Checks vital signs including orthostatic symptoms and hemoglobin before standing her.
Recognizes that low hemoglobin with drowsiness raises fall and faint risk and adjusts the plan.
Arranges adequate assistance and equipment: gait belt, walker, chair following, bed alarm turned on.
Reinforces hip precautions during transfers.
Notes the elevated temperature of 37.8 C as common after surgery but monitors it and reports a rise.
Considers the catheter and lines before mobilizing.
Offers the daughter a role such as helping with orientation and being present at a short session.
Uses an interpreter or Hungarian words for key instructions rather than relying on the daughter.

questions.model_answer:
My first duty is to my client, and she is the person whose consent I need, not her daughter. So before anything else, I will turn to Mrs. Kovacs, make sure her glasses and hearing aids are in, and speak slowly and simply. I will ask her what she wants today and check whether she understands what I am proposing. If I need Hungarian, I would ask for a hospital interpreter or at least a phone service, because I should not depend on her daughter to translate when the daughter has her own goals. Delirium does not remove someone's right to be asked, and I will respect what she says and how she shows it.

Second, I will make this session safe. Before standing her I will check her blood pressure and pulse lying and then sitting, her oxygen level, and how she feels. Her hemoglobin has fallen to 88 and she is drowsy, so I expect she may feel faint on sitting up and I will take that seriously. I will not simply accept that this is laziness. I will turn on the bed alarm, put on a gait belt, use a walker, bring a chair close, and get a second staff member to help. I would also check the catheter bag, the dressing and any lines so nothing pulls. Throughout, I will cue her posterior hip precautions: a raised seat, no bending past ninety degrees, and no twisting to the operated side.

Her temperature of 37.8 is common one day after surgery, so I will not be alarmed by it alone, but I will tell the nurse and watch for a rise.

Third, I will explain to Ilona why I will not walk her mother down the hallway today. I would acknowledge that she drove a long way and is worried, and that wanting her mother home is a loving wish. Then I will explain in plain words that her mother's confusion is a medical condition after surgery and not a lack of effort, that the team is looking for the causes, and that rushing could cause a fall or a dislocation. Test results such as hemoglobin I will leave for the nurse or physician to share once her mother's consent or the substitute decision maker is clarified. I will say what we can do today: sit up, stand, and move to a chair, which is real progress and helps the confusion.

Finally, I will give her daughter a job. She can sit with her mother, help with familiar talk and routines, and come to the next session. I will offer to share my findings with the team so decisions about going home are made together, but I will not promise a date. If my client says no to getting up, I will respect that and try again later.

scale.4: Centres the client's voice and consent, makes the session physically safe with specific checks and equipment, explains clearly to the daughter and gives her a role.
scale.3: Safe plan and polite response to the daughter but does not address client consent or the interpreter issue clearly.
scale.2: Declines the daughter's request but with few specific safety measures or little attention to the client's wishes.
scale.1: Yields to family pressure, walks her mother despite findings, or dismisses the client's own voice.

questions.prompt: Later you meet Ilona in the corridor. She is tearful and says the hospital is not doing enough and that her mother will lose her independence. Discuss how you will communicate with her, including what you would say and how you would handle your professional limits.

checklist.point: Responds first to the emotion with empathy and active listening before giving information.
Uses plain language and checks understanding, avoiding jargon.
Explains what delirium is and that it is common and usually improves.
Describes the concrete rehabilitation plan and what she can expect without guaranteeing outcomes.
Respects confidentiality and consent: shares information with the daughter only as the client allows or per substitute decision maker rules.
Recognizes limits of scope; refers medical questions to the physician or nurse.
Invites her questions and addresses her specific worry about independence.
Offers a clear channel for ongoing communication such as a family meeting or a named contact.
Acknowledges cultural and language preferences and asks how the family wants to be involved.

questions.model_answer:
I will start by moving her somewhere quiet, sitting down so we are at the same level, and telling her I have a few minutes and would like to hear what is worrying her. I will not start with explanations. She is tired, frightened, and has driven a long way, so I would say something like, 'It is really hard to see your mother like this, and I can hear how much you care about her.' Then I will listen and let her finish, and reflect back what I hear: that she is afraid her mother will not get back to living in her own home.

Before I share anything about her mother, I would quietly check who Mrs. Kovacs has named as her substitute decision maker and what she would want shared. Once she feels heard, I will explain in general terms and simple words. I would say that her mother is in a state of confusion called delirium, that this is common in older people after a hip operation, that it is usually temporary, and that the team is looking for the causes of the confusion. I will tell her what I am doing: getting her mother up and moving a few times a day, helping with glasses and hearing aids, and using daylight and familiar voices. I would say what we expect over the next days but not promise an outcome, because I do not know how quickly she will recover. If she asks whether her mother will walk again, I would be honest: many people do well after this operation, and we will know more as the confusion clears and we see her progress.

Next, I will be careful about my role and about privacy. Mrs. Kovacs has the right to decide what is shared. If she can't give consent right now, I would check who the substitute decision maker is. Until that is clear I would share only general information about the rehabilitation plan and encourage Ilona to speak with the nurse or physician about medical details such as test results. I will not diagnose or guess about medication changes, because that belongs to the physician and I will tell her so.

I would then ask how she and her family want to be involved, and whether her mother prefers Hungarian, so we can arrange an interpreter and respect those wishes. I will offer to arrange a short family meeting with the nurse and the social worker to talk about home supports, and give her the name of the person to contact. I will end by thanking her and telling her what I will do tomorrow, so she knows what to expect.

scale.4: Leads with empathy and listening, explains delirium and the plan plainly and honestly, protects confidentiality, stays within scope and arranges follow-up.
scale.3: Empathetic and clear but weak on consent and confidentiality or on scope limits.
scale.2: Gives information with little empathy, or promises outcomes, or shares details without checking consent.
scale.1: Dismissive, defensive or breaches confidentiality or scope.

safety_or_ethics_point: Her hemoglobin is 88 g/L and she is drowsy with a positive delirium screen, so rapid mobilization is unsafe, and her daughter's pressure risks overriding her own wishes. A competent candidate notes the low hemoglobin, graduates activity with monitoring, asks the client directly, uses an interpreter rather than the daughter, and keeps information-sharing within consent.
common_errors: Candidates treat the case as a standard hip protocol and walk her down the hallway, or list precautions without adjusting for delirium and anemia. Many also answer the daughter's request with a purely technical refusal and never address the client's voice or language.
examiner_notes: A pass connects hemoglobin and delirium to a graded plan, puts the client's consent before the family's wishes, and communicates with empathy within scope. A fail ignores the red flags or relies on the daughter as interpreter and decision maker.

title: Lower leg cellulitis with chronic edema at home
setting: Client's home, community care program in a small rural town
client_profile: Mr. Dwayne Whitehorse is a 61-year-old retired school bus driver with type 2 diabetes, obesity (BMI 36) and long-standing bilateral leg edema, worse on the right. Five days ago his family physician diagnosed cellulitis of the right lower leg and prescribed oral antibiotics. The community nurse marked the edge of the redness with a pen three days ago. You were referred to start a program for edema management and mobility. Today: temperature 38.3 C, HR 108, BP 132/80, respiratory rate 20. The right shin and calf are hot, red and tender, and the redness now extends about 4 cm past the pen line. Both legs have pitting edema to the knee, right greater than left, with brawny skin changes and a small weeping area on the medial ankle. Pedal pulses are faint. Last HbA1c 8.4%. He walks short distances with a cane and has not been sleeping lying down because of leg discomfort.
clinical_scenario: He lives alone about 45 minutes from the nearest hospital and his truck is not running. The nurse visits twice a week and the family physician is in a clinic three days a week. Mr. Whitehorse says he is eager to start compression and exercise because the swelling keeps him from going to his daughter's home. He mentions he ran out of his antibiotic yesterday because the pharmacy is far and he did not want to bother anyone. A neighbour has been bringing groceries.

questions.prompt: Outline the plan you will put in place for this client's edema and mobility, and explain how and when you will introduce each part of the plan given what you found today.

checklist.point: Recognizes that active spreading infection with systemic signs means compression and manual lymphatic techniques are deferred.
Plans interim measures: leg elevation to a comfortable level (not above heart level until arterial supply is assessed), gentle ankle movements within comfort, skin care and avoiding friction.
Plans compression only after infection is controlled and arterial supply is judged adequate by assessment or medical clearance.
