Mentions checking arterial status (pulses, capillary refill, ankle brachial index or referral) because of diabetes and faint pulses.
Plans graded walking and exercise to activate the calf pump once infection settles.
Includes skin and wound care coordination with the nurse for the weeping area.
Includes education on infection prevention: skin hygiene, moisturizing, foot checks, early reporting.
Chooses outcome measures such as limb circumference, redness margin, pain and walking tolerance.
Sets clear triggers for reassessment and escalation.

questions.model_answer:
Today's findings change the plan, so I will split it into what I do now, what I do once the infection is controlled, and how I decide when to move on.

First, today. His redness has spread about four centimetres beyond the line the nurse drew, he has a fever of 38.3, and his heart rate is 108. Taken together this is a cellulitis that is not controlled, and he also ran out of his antibiotic yesterday. That means I will not apply compression, bandaging or manual lymphatic drainage today. Compression over an actively infected limb can push infection and cause pain, and I would not want to cause harm just because the swelling is what he is asking about. I will explain that to him honestly: I understand the swelling is stopping him from seeing his daughter, and we will get to it once the leg is safe. What I can do is show him gentle ankle pumps within comfort, leg elevation to a comfortable level when resting, but not above the level of my heart until I know his arterial supply is adequate, given his diabetes and faint pulses, and ways to avoid friction and trauma to the skin. I will also ask the nurse to look at the weeping area on the ankle.

Second, once the infection is settled. I will wait until the redness is shrinking, the fever is gone, and the physician or nurse agrees. Before compression I need to know his arterial supply. He has diabetes and faint pulses, so I would check capillary refill and skin temperature, and ask the physician for an ankle brachial index or vascular assessment. If the supply is poor, compression would need to be reduced or avoided. If it is adequate, I would begin with a light, comfortable level, applied by me or the nurse, and teach him to check for numbness, colour change and new pain.

Third, mobility. As the leg settles I will build a graded walking program, short walks several times daily, and calf pump exercises, since muscle contraction moves the fluid. I will track limb circumference at set points, the redness margin, pain, and the distance he can walk with the cane.

Fourth, prevention. I will teach daily skin checks, moisturizing, cleaning between toes, proper footwear and prompt reporting of redness or fever. This is also important because his diabetes is not well controlled.

I will reassess at each visit and escalate if the redness spreads, the fever persists or he feels unwell.

scale.4: Defers compression and drainage because of uncontrolled infection, gives interim measures, sets clear criteria including arterial assessment before compression, and ties outcomes and prevention to findings.
scale.3: Defers compression and gives a reasonable staged plan but lacks arterial check or clear criteria.
scale.2: Lists edema treatments with only partial adjustment for infection signs.
scale.1: Applies compression or drainage today or ignores signs of active spreading infection.

questions.prompt: Describe the safety actions you will take during this visit and before you leave. Include how you will involve Mr. Whitehorse in the decisions.

checklist.point: Identifies spreading redness, fever and tachycardia as signs needing prompt medical reassessment today.
Contacts the physician or arranges urgent assessment rather than waiting for the next scheduled visit.
Recognizes the missed antibiotic doses and raises how he can get medication.
Discusses transport options given the truck and distance, including ambulance or emergency if he deteriorates.
Explains his options and risks and respects his right to decide, with informed consent.
Gives clear return precautions: worsening redness, fever, chills, confusion, severe pain, dizziness.
Checks blood glucose management and symptoms of high blood sugar given infection and diabetes.
Ensures he is not alone without a plan: neighbour, phone, emergency numbers.
Documents findings and actions.

questions.model_answer:
The most important safety action is that I do not leave without making sure a physician knows what I found today. Spreading redness, a temperature of 38.3, a heart rate of 108 and a diabetic client who has missed his antibiotic add up to a cellulitis that is getting worse and may need intravenous antibiotics or hospital assessment. This cannot wait for the next scheduled nurse visit.

First, I will talk with Mr. Whitehorse. I will tell him plainly what I see: the redness has gone past the line, he has a fever, and the infection is not under control. I will ask when he last took his antibiotic, why he ran out, and whether he has chills, nausea, confusion or feels faint. I will also ask about his blood sugar readings, because infection can push glucose up, and ask about thirst, vomiting or drowsiness.

Second, I will call the family physician's office right away from his home, with my findings in a clear order: who he is, the reason for the call, vital signs, the spread beyond the marked line, the missed antibiotic, and my concern. I would ask for urgent assessment today and advice about whether he should go to the emergency department. If I cannot reach the physician or the advice is delayed, I will call the nurse supervisor, or arrange emergency transport if he looks unwell, since I am not able to assess him fully or prescribe.

Third, I will work through his options with him. His truck does not run and the hospital is forty-five minutes away. I will ask about his daughter, the neighbour, community transport, or the paramedics. I will explain the risk of waiting: infection can enter the blood and become life threatening, and a delay can mean a longer hospital stay. If he still prefers to stay home, I respect that as his decision once he understands the risks, and I make sure there is a safety net: a charged phone, emergency numbers, and a named person who checks in tonight.

Fourth, medication. I will tell the physician he missed doses so the prescription can be renewed and delivered, perhaps through the nurse or neighbour.

Finally, I will give return precautions in writing: spreading redness, higher fever or chills, confusion, severe pain, vomiting, dizziness, or a leg that turns dusky or numb. I will document my findings, my call and what was agreed.

scale.4: Acts the same day on the red flags with a structured medical call, addresses missed antibiotic and transport, informs and respects his choice with a safety net and clear return precautions.
scale.3: Recognizes the red flags and contacts a physician but misses medication, transport or safety-netting detail.
scale.2: Mentions monitoring or informing the nurse later without prompt action.
scale.1: Proceeds with treatment, ignores the red flags, or leaves without communicating with a physician.

questions.prompt: After the physician's office calls back, you need to work with the others involved in his care. Discuss who you will collaborate with, what information you will share and how you will divide responsibilities.

checklist.point: Names the family physician, community nurse and, if involved, home care coordinator and pharmacist.
Shares findings with a structured format such as SBAR, including measurements and changes since the last visit.
Clarifies who will manage wound care, who will monitor the infection and who will apply compression.
Agrees on criteria and timing for starting compression and a plan for vascular assessment.
Involves diabetes care, such as a nurse educator or physician, since glucose control affects healing.
Plans a shared communication method and schedule between visits.
Includes the client and neighbour or daughter, with his consent, in the plan.
Addresses access barriers: transport, medication delivery, rural distance.
Documents who was told what and when.

questions.model_answer:
I will approach this as a small team, with Mr. Whitehorse at the center, and my first step is to work out who needs to do what so nothing is missed because we each assume someone else has it.

First, who is involved. The family physician decides on antibiotics, blood tests and whether he needs hospital care, and I will also ask the physician about a vascular assessment, since his foot pulses are faint and he has diabetes. The community nurse manages wound care and dressings for the weeping area, checks the redness margin and vital signs between my visits, and knows when his next visit is. A pharmacist could help with delivering his medication, which solves the problem of the long trip. A diabetes nurse educator or the physician should look at his glucose management, because poor control slows healing. A home care coordinator may help with transportation and in-home support. With his permission, I would include his daughter or the neighbour for check-ins.

Second, what I share. I will use a structured message so that it is short and clear: the situation, which is spreading cellulitis with fever; the background, which is diabetes and a missed antibiotic; my assessment, which is that compression is on hold; and my recommendation, which is that we agree on criteria before I restart. I will include measurements I took, such as leg circumference, the redness margin and walking tolerance, so others can compare.

Third, who does what. I propose the nurse continues wound care and checks the redness at each visit, I will do the edema program once the physician and nurse agree the infection is controlled, the physician owns the antibiotic and vascular referral, and the pharmacist handles delivery. I would ask for criteria for starting compression, for example no fever, redness shrinking, and an adequate arterial result, and agree who decides.

Fourth, communication. We will agree on how we reach each other, a phone number or shared record, and a quick update after each visit. If one of us sees a red flag, we call the physician the same day.

Finally, I will tell Mr. Whitehorse what we agreed, make sure he consents to sharing his information with these people, and document who I spoke with and what was decided.

scale.4: Names the right team members with defined roles, shares findings in a structured way, sets criteria and ownership for compression and vascular assessment, and involves the client and addresses rural barriers.
scale.3: Identifies team and shares information but roles or criteria are vague.
scale.2: Lists professionals without clear roles or content of communication.
scale.1: Works in isolation, omits the physician or nurse, or shares information without consent.

safety_or_ethics_point: The redness has spread beyond the marked line with fever and tachycardia in a diabetic client who ran out of antibiotics, which is a worsening cellulitis needing same-day medical review. Candidates must hold compression, call the physician, address medication and transport, and respect his informed decision.
common_errors: Candidates are drawn to the edema and start compression or lymphatic drainage, or plan to monitor at the next visit. Many also never notice the missed antibiotic or the distance and transport barrier.
examiner_notes: A pass defers compression, escalates the same day with a clear message, and builds shared roles and criteria with the team. A fail treats the edema as the priority or leaves without medical contact.

title: Posterior heel pain in a recreational runner
setting: Private outpatient physiotherapy clinic in a mid-sized city
client_profile: Priya Raman is a 41-year-old accountant who runs about 35 km a week and is training for a half marathon in ten weeks. For six weeks she has had pain and morning stiffness in the right Achilles tendon, about 4 cm above the heel. Pain is 5/10 at the start of a run, eases, and returns that evening. She stepped up her weekly distance and added hill repeats two months ago. Medications: none regular. She completed a course of an antibiotic for a urinary tract infection about three weeks ago. On examination: a fusiform thickening 4 cm above the calcaneus, tender to palpation, painful arc sign present, positive single-leg heel raise reproduction at 12 repetitions versus 25 on the left. Ankle dorsiflexion with knee straight is 8 degrees on the right and 12 on the left. Calf squeeze test is negative and a palpable gap is absent. Foot posture is mildly pronated. VISA-A score is 62 out of 100.
clinical_scenario: Priya has extended health coverage with a yearly limit of eight physiotherapy visits. The clinic owner has asked all clinicians to sell a prepaid ten-session package that includes shockwave therapy, and the shockwave device was booked out for the next three weeks. Priya says she cannot afford to stop training and asks whether you can do whatever is fastest. She also mentions a cousin had a cortisone injection and was running within a week.

questions.prompt: Explain your clinical impression based on this client's history and examination. Describe which findings support it, which differentials you considered, and what further information you need.

checklist.point: States an impression of midportion Achilles tendinopathy.
Supports it with location 2 to 6 cm above insertion, thickening, painful arc, morning stiffness and load-related pain.
Links training load increase to onset.
Identifies recent fluoroquinolone antibiotic exposure as a risk factor for tendon injury and rupture and asks which antibiotic she took.
Considers and excludes Achilles tendon rupture or partial tear using Thompson or calf squeeze test and gap palpation.
Considers insertional tendinopathy, retrocalcaneal bursitis, plantaris involvement and paratenonitis as differentials.
Considers systemic causes such as inflammatory arthritis, familial hypercholesterolemia and diabetes when history suggests.
Uses VISA-A as a baseline outcome measure.
Notes calf strength endurance deficit and dorsiflexion limitation as contributors.
Recognizes mild foot pronation as a less important contributor than the load increase and calf strength endurance deficit.

questions.model_answer:
My impression is a midportion Achilles tendinopathy of the right side, and I will explain why, what else I considered and what I still need to ask.

First, what supports it. The pain sits about four centimetres above the heel, which is the midportion of the tendon. She has morning stiffness, pain at the start of a run that eases and returns later, a load history that fits, which is a recent jump in distance plus hill work, thickening of the tendon, and a painful arc sign where the swelling moves with the ankle. She also has a clear deficit on a single-leg heel raise, twelve repetitions against twenty-five on the good side, and reduced dorsiflexion. Her VISA-A score is 62 out of 100, which tells me this is a moderate problem and gives me a baseline.

Second, differentials. I considered insertional tendinopathy and retrocalcaneal bursitis, but pain at the heel bone and pain with dorsiflexion compression would be more typical, and hers is higher up. I considered plantaris involvement and paratenon irritation, which can look similar and are managed in a similar way. Most importantly, I looked for a tear or rupture. Her calf squeeze test is negative and there is no palpable gap, which makes a complete rupture very unlikely, though I would repeat the test.

Third, a key piece of history. She took an antibiotic three weeks ago for a urinary infection, and I need to know which one. Fluoroquinolone antibiotics are linked to tendon damage and rupture, even weeks after use, and that would raise my concern, change how aggressively I load, and mean I should tell her physician. I would also ask about steroid use, diabetes, high cholesterol, inflammatory conditions, a family history, and whether any pain comes in the other joints or the back.

Fourth, what contributes. Her calf endurance and range deficits and her fast increase in training load are likely drivers. Her mild pronation is probably not the main cause, so I would not make it my focus.

Fifth, what I need next: the antibiotic name, a repeat of the rupture tests, a look at the other leg, and baseline measures including VISA-A, heel raise count and pain on hopping. I would ask for imaging only if the picture does not fit or she does not respond.

scale.4: Gives a clear impression linked to specific findings, rules out rupture, identifies the antibiotic risk and asks the right questions, ranks differentials and contributors with a baseline measure.
scale.3: Correct impression and findings with reasonable differentials but misses the antibiotic or rupture screen.
scale.2: Names the diagnosis with little reasoning or an unfocused list of causes.
scale.1: Wrong impression, or misses the rupture possibility and medication risk.

questions.prompt: Priya wants to keep running and asks about the injection her cousin had. Explain how you will advise her about her activity and treatment options, and how you will keep her safe while respecting her goals.

checklist.point: Explains that she can usually keep some activity but load must be managed using pain as a guide.
Advises against corticosteroid injection into or around the tendon because of rupture risk.
Raises the antibiotic and tendon risk, advising her to stop high-load activity until the drug is identified and the physician consulted if it was a fluoroquinolone.
Gives a graded loading program with isometric then isotonic heavy slow resistance.
Sets acceptable pain levels and rules for next-day response.
Gives warning signs of rupture or worsening: sudden pop, calf pain, inability to push off, swelling.
Negotiates running changes: reduced hills, speed work and volume, with cross-training.
Uses shared decision making and links the plan to her half marathon goal.
Explains the expected timeline and gives realistic expectations for the race.

questions.model_answer:
I will work with her goal rather than against it, because telling a runner to stop completely usually means she stops listening. But I need to be clear about two safety issues first.

First, the injection. I understand why her cousin's story is appealing. A corticosteroid injected into or around the Achilles tendon can weaken it and has been linked to rupture, and it does not fix the underlying tendon problem. So I would not recommend it, and I would explain that in everyday words: the pain may settle for a while, but the tendon becomes more fragile at the very time she is asking it to carry heavy training. If she still wants to hear about injection options, she can discuss them with her physician, who can weigh the risks.

Second, the antibiotic. If the drug she took three weeks ago was a fluoroquinolone, her tendon may already be more vulnerable to damage, and then running through it is a bigger risk. I will ask for the name today. If it was one of those drugs, I would advise her to hold running and high-load training and speak with her physician before we go further, and I would explain why. If it was a different antibiotic, I would be more comfortable going ahead with careful loading.

Third, her activity plan. In tendinopathy, rest alone usually does not help and some loading usually does. I will start with isometric calf holds for pain relief, then progress to slow heavy calf raises in a straight and bent knee position, building over weeks, and we agree on a pain guide. For example, discomfort up to about four out of ten that settles within 24 hours and no worse stiffness the next morning. If the pain is worse than that, we reduce the load. For running, she can do shorter, flatter runs on alternate days for now, cut the hill repeats and speed work, and use cycling or swimming to hold fitness.

Fourth, warning signs. If she feels a sudden pop or snap, has sharp calf pain, cannot push off, or the swelling and pain rise sharply, she should stop and seek urgent assessment.

Fifth, expectations. Tendon recovery takes months, and the half marathon in ten weeks may need to be a slower, completion-based goal. We will review at each visit and decide together.

scale.4: Explains why not to inject, raises the antibiotic risk with action, gives a graded loading and running plan with pain rules and rupture warning signs, and respects her goal with realistic expectations.
scale.3: Safe advice and a reasonable plan but misses the antibiotic or rupture warning signs.
scale.2: Tells her to rest or continue running without a structured plan or risk explanation.
scale.1: Endorses injection or unrestricted running, or ignores medication and rupture risks.

questions.prompt: Your employer expects you to sell the ten-session package with shockwave, but her plan covers eight visits. Discuss how you will manage her care, your schedule, documentation and billing in an ethical way.

checklist.point: Puts the client's needs and informed choice ahead of clinic revenue targets.
Discloses fees, the insurance limit and the evidence for shockwave honestly, without pressure.
Does not bill for sessions not provided or code services inaccurately to fit coverage.
Plans visit spacing to use eight covered visits wisely with a home program between them.
Offers self-management and independent exercise to reduce reliance on visits.
Documents assessment, consent, treatment, advice and outcome measures clearly and on time.
Raises concerns with the owner about the conflict of interest and the package approach, referring to regulator standards if needed.
Manages scheduling and equipment availability honestly, with alternatives if the device is booked.
Considers delegation to a physiotherapist assistant only where appropriate and supervised.

questions.model_answer:
My obligation is to my client first, and to the standards of my regulator, so I will manage this in a way I would be comfortable explaining to either of them.

First, her care and the eight-visit limit. I will tell Priya plainly what her plan covers and what is not covered, so she can decide with the facts. Tendinopathy is mostly managed through a progressive loading program that she does herself, with visits to adjust and progress. So I would not spread the visits evenly. I might use two visits in the first two weeks to teach and set the program, then space the rest every two to three weeks to progress the load and review her outcome measures, keeping a couple in reserve in case of a flare. I would give her a written program with videos and a diary, and teach her how to adjust it, which also lowers her dependence on me.

Second, the shockwave package. I should not push it. I will tell her that shockwave is an option with mixed evidence as an add-on, usually after loading has been tried, and that it will cost extra and would not replace the loading program. If she would like it, I would explain the fees, the number of sessions and what might be expected, then let her decide without pressure. I also will not hold her to a ten-session prepayment she may not need. If the device is booked out for three weeks, I will say so and I will not delay her loading program, which does not depend on it.

Third, billing and documentation. I will bill only for the services that I actually provided, using accurate descriptions. I would not relabel a shockwave session or a home-program review as another service to fit into her coverage, because that would be misleading the insurer. My notes will record her history, the antibiotic question, findings, VISA-A score, consent, the advice given, her goals and the plan, completed on the same day.

Fourth, my employer. I would speak with the owner privately and respectfully, explain that I cannot promote a package where it is not in the client's interest, and that my regulator expects fees to be fair and transparent. I would suggest options that suit both, such as offering the package as a choice for those who want it.

Finally, if a physiotherapist assistant helps supervise exercise, they would work under my plan and direction, within their role, and I would remain responsible for reassessment.

scale.4: Puts the client first, plans visits within coverage with self-management, offers shockwave honestly, bills and documents accurately, and addresses the conflict with the employer professionally.
scale.3: Ethical approach and sound visit planning but weak on billing accuracy or employer conflict.
scale.2: Mentions ethics generally without concrete scheduling, billing or documentation decisions.
scale.1: Pressures the client into the package, misbills, or overlooks the conflict of interest.

safety_or_ethics_point: Her recent antibiotic course may have been a fluoroquinolone, which raises the risk of tendon damage and rupture, and she is considering a corticosteroid injection. A competent candidate asks which drug, screens for rupture, advises against injection and adjusts loading. The business pressure to sell a package is a separate conflict of interest.
common_errors: Candidates focus on foot posture and orthotics and never ask about medications, or go straight to loading without screening for rupture. In Q3 many repeat the package pressure as acceptable or avoid saying anything about billing accuracy.
examiner_notes: A pass identifies the antibiotic and rupture risks, advises against injection and gives a graded plan. In Q3 a pass puts the client's interest and honest billing ahead of revenue. A fail misses the medication cue or sells the package uncritically.

title: Chronic low back and buttock pain in a young adult
setting: Private outpatient physiotherapy clinic
client_profile: Kwame Mensah is a 29-year-old software developer with eight months of low back and deep buttock pain, sometimes alternating between the left and right sides. He wakes around 4 a.m. with pain and stiffness and needs to get up and move, and his morning stiffness lasts about 60 minutes. Pain improves with exercise and walking and worsens with rest and long sitting. Ibuprofen helps within a day. He has had two episodes of a red, painful, light-sensitive left eye over the past year, treated by an optometrist with drops. His father has psoriasis. Examination: BP 118/72, BMI 24. Lumbar flexion limited with a modified Schober of 3 cm (normal at least 5). Chest expansion 1.5 cm (normal at least 2.5). Lateral flexion reduced bilaterally. Sacroiliac provocation tests (compression, thigh thrust) reproduce buttock pain. Straight leg raise negative, neurological screen normal. Pain 4/10 today. He has been using a standing desk and has changed his chair twice without relief.
clinical_scenario: Kwame is employed by a company with a short-term disability plan and his manager has asked for a note stating his diagnosis and restrictions. He tells you he does not want his employer to know about any medical condition, as he fears being overlooked for promotion. He also asks you to confirm that it is just poor posture and says a friend told him a chiropractor would crack his back and fix it. He has booked a spinal manipulation at another clinic for tomorrow.

questions.prompt: Explain what you think is happening, based on the history and examination. Discuss the features that influence your thinking and what you would do next to clarify the problem.

checklist.point: Identifies an inflammatory back pain pattern rather than mechanical or postural pain.

Lists supporting features: age under 40, insidious onset over 3 months, night waking, morning stiffness over 30 minutes, improvement with exercise not rest, response to NSAIDs, alternating buttock pain.
Links the history of recurrent uveitis and family history of psoriasis as supporting features of a spondyloarthritis.
Notes reduced spinal mobility and positive sacroiliac provocation as consistent but not definitive.
Considers differentials: mechanical back pain, disc pathology, infection, malignancy, fracture.
Screens for red flags such as fever, weight loss, trauma, neurological signs.
Recognizes that postural or ergonomic factors are a distractor and not the primary explanation.
Plans referral for medical investigation such as imaging, HLA-B27 and inflammatory markers via the physician or rheumatologist.
Plans baseline outcome measures such as BASDAI, BASFI and spinal mobility measures.

questions.model_answer:
My thinking is that this is more likely an inflammatory back condition, such as axial spondyloarthritis, than a postural or ordinary mechanical problem. I cannot diagnose it on my own, but I can recognize the pattern and make sure he gets the right investigation.

First, the features that matter in the history. He is 29 and the pain began gradually over eight months. He wakes in the second half of the night and has to get up, he has about an hour of morning stiffness, and the pain improves with movement and gets worse with rest. Ibuprofen helps within a day. The pain alternates between the buttocks. Mechanical back pain usually behaves the other way: better with rest, worse with activity. Together these features fit inflammatory back pain.

Second, other clues outside the spine. He has had two episodes of a red, painful, light-sensitive eye, which sounds like anterior uveitis, a known association with this group of conditions. His father has psoriasis, which is another link. On examination, his spinal flexion is reduced, with a modified Schober of three centimetres, his chest expansion of 1.5 centimetres is reduced, and the sacroiliac tests reproduce his pain. None of these is proof alone, but they fit the same story.

Third, other possibilities. I considered a disc problem, but his straight leg raise is negative and there are no neurological changes. I considered infection, a tumour and fracture. He has no fever, weight loss or trauma that I know of, but I would check again, including asking about bowel or urinary change and numbness. His desk set-up is probably a distractor. Changing his chair twice did nothing, which tells me that sitting posture is not the cause.

Fourth, next steps. I will contact his family physician and recommend referral to a rheumatologist, with my findings in writing. They can arrange blood tests such as inflammatory markers and HLA-B27, and imaging of the sacroiliac joints, usually an MRI at this stage, since changes may not show on an X-ray early on. In the meantime I will collect baseline measures with the BASDAI for disease activity, the BASFI for function, and spinal measurements, so we can track change. I will explain all of this to him in plain language, and tell him that while the cause is uncertain, I take his symptoms seriously.

scale.4: Recognizes inflammatory back pain with specific supporting features, links the eye and family history, considers and screens differentials, dismisses posture as the explanation and plans referral and baseline measures.
scale.3: Recognizes an inflammatory pattern and refers but gives limited reasoning on extra-spinal clues or differentials.
scale.2: Lists findings but settles on mechanical or postural cause or gives vague next steps.
scale.1: Misses the inflammatory pattern and attributes it to posture, or fails to refer.

questions.prompt: Kwame plans to see a chiropractor tomorrow for a spinal manipulation. Describe how you will address this and what you will advise about activity and exercise, while respecting his choices.

checklist.point: Respects his right to choose his care and avoids dismissing the other profession.
Explains that high-velocity manipulation and end-range forces may be unsafe until the diagnosis is clarified, because inflamed spinal joints and possible low bone density raise fracture risk.
Advises him to tell any practitioner about his symptoms, suspected inflammatory condition and eye history.
Recommends delaying manipulation until medical assessment is completed.
Gives clear warning signs needing urgent care: red painful eye, sudden severe pain, new weakness, numbness, bowel or bladder change.
Recommends prompt eye assessment for the red painful light-sensitive eye if it recurs.
Encourages regular movement, mobility, aerobic and strengthening exercise suited to his condition.
Explains why prolonged rest is unhelpful for inflammatory back pain.
Uses shared decision making and checks understanding.

questions.model_answer:
I will start by acknowledging that it is his body and his decision, and that he is trying to get relief, which is reasonable after eight months of pain. I do not want him to feel judged for choosing another provider. But he needs to make that choice with full information, so I would explain my concerns plainly.

First, the risk. I think his back pain may be inflammatory, and the diagnosis is not yet confirmed. In conditions like that, the spinal joints can be inflamed and stiff, and over time the bones can become weaker. A high-velocity thrust or a forceful, end-range technique could injure an inflamed joint or, in rare cases, cause a fracture. That is why I would suggest waiting on manipulation until his doctor has assessed him and the results are back. I would not say that chiropractors are unsafe in general. I would say that in his particular situation I advise caution, and ask him to consider postponing tomorrow's appointment. If he still goes, I would ask him to tell the practitioner about his night pain, morning stiffness, recurrent eye inflammation and his family history, and to ask for gentle techniques only.

Second, warning signs. I will give him a written list: a red painful eye with light sensitivity should be seen by an eye specialist the same day, since uveitis can damage vision. He should seek urgent care for sudden severe back pain after a minor fall or manipulation, new leg weakness, numbness in the groin or legs, or changes in bladder or bowel control.

Third, what he can do. For this kind of back pain, rest makes things worse, and movement helps. I will prescribe a program that includes daily spinal mobility exercises, walking or cycling for cardiovascular fitness, and light strengthening for his trunk and hips, progressed with pain as a guide. I would encourage him to break up long periods of sitting every thirty minutes. I will teach him which exercise to avoid, such as end-range twisting under load or high-impact contact sports, until his doctor has seen him.

Finally, I will check that he understands, ask what he thinks he will do, and agree on a plan that he can follow.

scale.4: Respects his autonomy, explains risk of manipulation in a suspected inflammatory spine, gives specific warning signs including the eye, prescribes appropriate activity and checks understanding.
scale.3: Advises caution and activity with reasonable warning signs but lacks reasoning on bone risk or on informing the other practitioner.
scale.2: Tells him not to go or says it is fine without explaining, with limited safety advice.
scale.1: Endorses manipulation without caution or gives no warning signs.

questions.prompt: Kwame asks you to confirm posture as the cause and to write a note for his employer without revealing any diagnosis. Discuss your professional responsibilities in responding to these requests.

checklist.point: Will not state a cause or diagnosis that is unsupported, including 'poor posture'; documentation must be truthful.
Respects confidentiality and obtains informed consent before releasing any information to the employer.
Limits the note to what is necessary, such as functional limitations and duration, not diagnosis.
Reviews exactly what will be shared and lets the client approve it.
Stays within scope: does not make a medical diagnosis but states clinical findings and refers.
Documents the discussion, consent, findings and referral recommendation.
Communicates the referral to the physician with his consent.
Addresses his fear of discrimination and informs him of workplace accommodation and human rights protections in general terms.
Identifies the conflict if the employer or insurer asks for more information and directs requests through the client.

questions.model_answer:
These two requests pull in different directions, and my professional duty is to be honest in what I write and careful with what I share.

First, the cause. Kwame has asked me to confirm that it is posture. I can't do that, because the findings do not support it, and I should not say something I do not believe to be true, either to him or on paper. I would tell him kindly that his pattern suggests something other than posture, that I am not able to give a medical diagnosis, and that I have recommended further testing with his physician. Telling him what he hopes to hear would be false reassurance and could delay the care he needs.

Second, the employer's note. His health information is confidential, and I need his informed consent before I give anything to his manager or the disability plan. I will explain what a note could include and ask what he is comfortable with. A reasonable note may say that I am treating him for a musculoskeletal condition, which functional limits he has, such as the need to change position every thirty minutes, and how long they are expected to last. It does not need to include a diagnosis, the eye history or his family history. I will show him the note before sending it and send only what he approves. If the insurer asks for a diagnosis to process a claim, I would explain that to him first and let him decide, and ask the request to come in writing.

Third, my scope. I identify findings, make a clinical impression and refer, but a medical diagnosis belongs to his physician. I will write to his family physician, with his consent, to describe the inflammatory features I found, the eye episodes, my recommendation for rheumatology referral, and the baseline measures I took.

Fourth, his fear. I understand that he is worried about his career. I will explain that in general, employers have duties to accommodate health conditions and that he can seek advice from his workplace health office or a human rights resource. I will not make promises about specific legal outcomes.

Finally, I will document the findings, my advice, his consent and what was released.

scale.4: Declines to state an unsupported cause, obtains consent and limits the note to function, stays within scope, communicates with the physician, documents, and supports him on workplace concerns.
scale.3: Protects confidentiality and honesty but gives limited detail on note contents, scope or documentation.
scale.2: Writes a note or gives an answer without clear consent or truthfulness considerations.
scale.1: Writes that posture is the cause, discloses diagnosis without consent, or diagnoses outside scope.

safety_or_ethics_point: The history suggests an inflammatory spinal condition with recurrent uveitis, so high-velocity manipulation tomorrow carries fracture risk and a red painful eye needs urgent assessment. Professionally, the client asks the clinician to attribute his pain to posture and to write a note concealing the diagnosis, which tests honesty, consent and scope.
common_errors: Candidates diagnose a postural or mechanical problem and discuss ergonomics at length, missing the eye history and night pain. In Q3 many agree to write 'posture' to protect the client or simply send the full diagnosis to the employer.
examiner_notes: A pass recognizes the inflammatory pattern, protects the spine from manipulation, refers, and handles the note honestly with consent. A fail adopts the posture explanation or breaches confidentiality.

title: Incomplete thoracic spinal cord injury in rehabilitation
setting: Inpatient spinal cord rehabilitation unit
client_profile: Andre Gagnon is a 35-year-old electrician, six weeks after a fall from a ladder that caused a T10 burst fracture, stabilized surgically. He is now in inpatient rehabilitation. Sensation is reduced below the umbilicus. Light touch and pinprick sensory level is T10 on both sides. Anal sensation and voluntary anal contraction are present. Manual muscle testing on the right: hip flexors 3, knee extensors 3, ankle dorsiflexors 3, long toe extensors 3, plantar flexors 2. On the left: hip flexors 4, knee extensors 3, ankle dorsiflexors 3, long toe extensors 2, plantar flexors 2. Trunk control is fair in sitting. Upper limbs are normal. He transfers with moderate assistance and walks 10 m in parallel bars with bilateral knee-ankle-foot orthoses and one person. He uses a manual wheelchair. Bladder is managed with intermittent catheterization. Spasticity is mild. He is taking an anticoagulant for clot prevention that is due to finish in two days.
clinical_scenario: It is Monday morning after Andre's first weekend pass at home. He tells you the weekend went well, then quietly says he slipped transferring to the toilet on Saturday night and landed on his left side, but he did not tell the nurses because he did not want his pass privileges taken away and does not want his wife to worry. He asks you to keep it between the two of you. He mentions that his left calf has felt tight since Sunday. A student nurse is documenting nearby and the rehabilitation team plans a case conference on Thursday.

questions.prompt: Based on the examination findings, describe how you would classify his injury and explain how this classification guides your thinking about his rehabilitation and recovery.

checklist.point: States the neurological level of injury as T10 based on the sensory level and intact key muscles above.
Recognizes the injury as incomplete because of sacral sparing: anal sensation and voluntary anal contraction.
Applies the grading rule: at least half of the key muscles below the level have grade 3 or more.
Counts the key muscle grades correctly to reach an ASIA Impairment Scale D classification.
Notes that classification needs the full standardized International Standards examination and may change with recovery.
Explains the prognosis for walking is relatively favourable with AIS D, while remaining cautious in predictions.
Links findings to goals: lower limb strengthening, balance, gait training, orthoses, wheelchair skills as a backup.
Plans outcome measures such as walking index (WISCI II), 10 metre walk, Berg or Spinal Cord Independence Measure.
Considers secondary conditions: spasticity, bladder, bone health, skin, pain.

questions.model_answer:
I will classify his injury using the international standards, which look at the neurological level, whether the injury is complete or incomplete, and the impairment scale grade.

First, the level. His light touch and pinprick sensation is normal down to T10 and reduced below the umbilicus, and his arms are normal, so the sensory level is T10. There are no key muscles to test at T10, so the motor level is taken from the sensory level, and the neurological level of injury is T10.

Second, complete or incomplete. He has sensation around the anus and he can voluntarily contract the anal sphincter. That is sacral sparing, and it makes this an incomplete injury. A complete injury would have neither.

Third, the grade. The question is how many of the ten key muscles below the level have a grade of three or more. On the right side, hip flexors, knee extensors, ankle dorsiflexors and long toe extensors are three, so four of five. On the left, hip flexors are four, knee extensors three, ankle dorsiflexors three, long toe extensors two, and plantar flexors two, which gives three of five. Across both sides that is seven of ten muscles at grade three or more, which is at least half. Because the injury is motor incomplete and at least half the key muscles below the level are three or better, it is an ASIA Impairment Scale D. I would say this is my working classification, and I would confirm it by a full standardized examination, including the other myotomes, because recovery can change it.

Fourth, what it means for his rehabilitation. AIS D carries a relatively good outlook for walking, and many people with this grade walk functionally, although I will not promise an outcome. So my goals go beyond managing a wheelchair. I would aim at strengthening his hips, knees and ankles, working on trunk and standing balance, training weight shift and gait in parallel bars and then with a walker or crutches, adjusting or weaning the orthoses as he improves, and keeping wheelchair skills for long distances. Outcomes will include the ten-metre walk test, the walking index for spinal cord injury, a balance measure and the spinal cord independence measure, repeated every couple of weeks.

Finally, I will plan for spasticity management, skin checks, bone health and bladder issues alongside his therapy, working with the team.

scale.4: Correctly identifies T10 level, incomplete status from sacral sparing, and AIS D with the muscle count, qualifies the classification, and links to prognosis, goals and outcome measures.
scale.3: Reaches the correct classification with limited justification or without linking to rehabilitation goals.
scale.2: Partially correct classification or gives level without the grading rule.
scale.1: Classifies as complete or gives an incorrect level and grade.

questions.prompt: Andre has told you about the fall and the tight left calf. Describe the actions you will take in this session and how you will involve Andre in decisions.

checklist.point: Does not proceed with standing, walking or leg exercise until the possible clot and injury are assessed.
Recognizes calf tightness after immobility and an anticoagulant ending as a possible deep vein thrombosis and an urgent medical issue.
Assesses safely: calf and thigh circumference, warmth, swelling, tenderness, vital signs, without massaging or vigorous manipulation.
Screens for symptoms of pulmonary embolism: shortness of breath, chest pain, rapid heart rate, cough.
Considers fracture or spinal injury after the fall: asks about new back pain, checks surgical site, screens sensation and strength, checks hip and ankle.
Informs the nurse and physician immediately and arranges medical assessment and imaging.
Explains to Andre why this must be reported and invites his input on how it is communicated.
Keeps him comfortable and supported in a safe position with call bell, and watches him.
Considers other medical issues of his injury such as skin checks from the fall.

questions.model_answer:
The first thing I will do is stop and make sure he is safe, because a tight calf in someone with a spinal cord injury after a fall may mean a blood clot, and I need to treat that as urgent until it is shown otherwise.

First, no activity. I will not stand him, walk him or do leg exercises with that leg. Walking or vigorous movement with a clot could make the clot travel to the lungs. I will make sure he is comfortable and positioned safely in bed or his chair with the call bell within reach.

Second, a quick and gentle assessment, and no massage. I would check his pulse, blood pressure, breathing rate and oxygen saturation, and ask about chest pain, shortness of breath, cough or feeling faint, which could signal a clot in the lung. If he has any of those I will get help immediately. I would look at both calves and thighs for swelling, warmth, redness and tenderness, and measure the circumference at set points above and below the knee, comparing with the right leg. His reduced sensation means he may not feel pain properly, so tightness may be a significant sign. I would not squeeze or rub the calf. I would also check for the effects of his fall: bruising, deformity, swelling and pain around the hip, thigh and ankle, and his skin, because with reduced bone density and sensation a fracture can go unnoticed. He also landed on his stabilized spine, so I would ask about new back pain and whether he hit his head, look at the surgical site, and screen for any change in sensation or strength compared with last week, and tell the physician about the fall.

Third, escalate now. I will tell the nurse in charge and the physician right away, giving the facts in order: his injury, the slip on Saturday, the calf tightness since Sunday, the circumference difference, his vital signs, and that the anticoagulant ends in two days. I would suggest medical assessment, such as an ultrasound of the leg and imaging for a fracture, and I would not wait for Thursday's case conference.

Fourth, Andre's role. I will tell him honestly why I must report this: it is about his safety, and a missed clot or break could be serious. I understand that he is worried about losing his pass and about his wife. I will acknowledge those fears and explain that the team's priority is his health, and ask how he would like to tell his wife and what support he wants. I will offer to be with him when he speaks to the doctor.

Finally, I will stay with him or ask a colleague to stay until help arrives, and I will document everything.

scale.4: Stops mobilization, recognizes possible DVT and fracture, performs a safe focused assessment including pulmonary embolism screen, escalates immediately and brings Andre into the plan with empathy.
scale.3: Recognizes the concern and escalates but assessment is incomplete or Andre's involvement is limited.
scale.2: Reports later or continues modified therapy with partial awareness of the risk.
scale.1: Proceeds with standing or gait training, massages the calf, or does not report.

questions.prompt: Andre asks you to keep the fall between the two of you. Discuss your professional responsibilities and how you will handle this request, including documentation and communication with others.

checklist.point: Explains that confidentiality has limits and that you cannot agree to hide information that affects his safety.
Shares information with the care team on a need-to-know basis for his care, within privacy law.
Does not promise secrecy, and tells him before disclosing and explains why.
Reports the fall through the facility's incident reporting system.
Documents objectively: his account, findings, time, who was notified, and his response.
Respects his wishes about what is told to his wife, and does not disclose to family without his consent.
Addresses the pass privileges fear honestly and advocates fair, safety-focused handling of passes.
Recognizes the duty to communicate with team and student nurse appropriately, protecting his privacy in a shared space.
Reflects on trust and builds rapport so he feels able to report problems.

questions.model_answer:
I cannot agree to keep this between the two of us, and I will tell him that clearly and kindly. My duty is first to his safety and to the standards of my profession. A confidential relationship is not an absolute one, and when information affects a patient's safety and care, I am obliged to share it with the people who need it.

First, how I respond to the request. I will say something like, 'Thank you for telling me. I know that wasn't easy. I can't keep this secret, because a fall and a tight calf might need medical attention, and the team has to know. I will tell them only what they need to know to look after you.' I would not promise confidentiality I cannot keep, because that would break his trust later. I would tell him before I speak to the nurse so that he is not surprised, and ask whether he would prefer to tell them himself with me beside him.

Second, who I tell. I will tell the nurse in charge and the physician involved in his care, using the facts. I would not discuss it in a shared corridor or in front of the student nurse. I would find a private space. I will submit an incident report through the facility's system, because a fall is a reportable event and reports help prevent future falls, not to punish him.

Third, documentation. My note will be factual and timely: his account of the fall, the time and place, his symptoms, my findings including calf measurements, vital signs, who I notified and when, and his response. I will not speculate, and I will write what he said in his own words where it matters.

Fourth, his wife and his pass. His wife has no right to this information unless he agrees, so it is his choice what to tell her, though I can support him with how to say it. As for his pass, I will be honest that I cannot promise that nothing will change, but I will speak with the team about making any decision based on safety, such as bathroom equipment and training, rather than punishment.

Finally, I recognize why he hid it. I want him to know that telling us was the right decision, and I will make sure the team approaches him with respect so he keeps telling us when things go wrong.

scale.4: Declines secrecy while explaining limits, shares on a need-to-know basis, reports the incident, documents objectively, protects privacy from family and others, and supports trust.
scale.3: Declines secrecy and reports but weak on documentation, privacy detail or his concerns.
scale.2: Reports without explaining to the client, or partly agrees to confidentiality.
scale.1: Agrees to keep it secret, fails to report, or discloses inappropriately to family or in public.

safety_or_ethics_point: After an unreported fall with a tight calf in a person with spinal cord injury and an anticoagulant about to stop, possible DVT or fracture means no mobilization and same-day medical escalation. Ethically, the client asks for secrecy, which a competent candidate declines while explaining, reporting and protecting privacy.
common_errors: Candidates take the neurological classification as the whole case and carry on with gait training, or agree to monitor the calf themselves. In Q3 many promise confidentiality or lecture rather than explain and report.
examiner_notes: A pass classifies AIS D with the muscle count, stops activity and escalates for suspected clot and injury, and declines secrecy with honest, respectful communication. A fail continues therapy or keeps the secret.

title: Plantar forefoot ulcer in a man with long-standing diabetes
setting: Client's second-floor apartment, provincial home care program
client_profile: Mr. Harpreet Gill is 73, a retired bus mechanic, with type 2 diabetes for 18 years, hypertension and a previous right toe amputation of the fifth digit. HbA1c last month was 74 mmol/mol. He has a 2-week-old plantar ulcer under the right first metatarsal head, 1.5 cm by 1.2 cm, with yellow slough and a pink edge; it does not probe to bone. There is faint redness extending less than 1 cm from the edge. Temperature 37.6 degrees C. Monofilament sensation is absent at 6 of 10 sites on each foot. Right dorsalis pedis pulse is faint, posterior tibial not palpable; the right foot is cooler than the left and capillary refill in the toes is 4 seconds. Right ankle dorsiflexion is 5 degrees. He uses a single-point cane and walks in worn-out slippers.
clinical_scenario: Mr. Gill lives alone and walks barefoot to the bathroom at night because he fears tripping on his slippers. His daughter, who lives 40 minutes away, visits on weekends and has asked you to phone her with updates. A home care nurse changes the dressing twice a week and has asked you to take over the offloading plan. Mr. Gill says he does not want to be told to stay off his feet because he does his own groceries and cannot afford taxis. He has private coverage for only a small amount of footwear each year.

questions.prompt: Mr. Gill asks what can be done about his foot. Describe the plan of care you would put in place over the next four weeks, including your goals, interventions, outcome measures and the triggers that would make you change the plan.

checklist.point: Identifies the cool foot, weak pulses and slow capillary refill as a reason to seek medical vascular review before choosing an offloading device.
Recognizes mild redness and temperature as possible early infection and arranges prompt medical review of the wound.
Sets a short-term goal such as medical review within days and a four-week goal of a smaller, clean wound without spreading redness.
Selects offloading that fits perfusion and infection status, such as a removable forefoot offloading device, and explains why a rigid non-removable cast is not first choice here.
Problem-solves the night-time barefoot walking with a bedside option, lighting or footwear placed by the bed.
Addresses limited ankle dorsiflexion and forefoot pressure with gentle, non-weight-bearing mobility work only once cleared.
Plans education on daily foot inspection, never walking barefoot, avoiding heat and checking footwear.
Names measurable outcomes such as wound dimensions measured consistently, photographs with consent, adherence to the device and time spent on the feet.
States reassessment triggers: spreading redness, drainage, odour, fever, new pain, probing to bone, or wound not shrinking meaningfully in four weeks.
Coordinates with the home care nurse so that dressing and offloading plans match.

questions.model_answer:
My plan starts with what I do before I offload anything, because the findings change what is safe. His right foot is cooler than the left, capillary refill is four seconds, the posterior tibial pulse is not palpable, and there is some redness around the ulcer with a temperature of 37.6. That tells me I cannot assume the blood supply is adequate or that the wound is clean. So the first step is a same-day call to his family physician. I would explain that I am concerned about reduced arterial supply and early infection, and I would ask for urgent vascular assessment and a medical review of the wound. Everything else I do sits on top of that.

My goals are staged. Within the first week, the medical review is done and pressure is off the first metatarsal head. By four weeks, I want a smaller, cleaner wound with no spreading redness, and Mr. Gill walking safely at home without ever bearing weight on that spot unprotected.

For interventions, offloading is central, but the choice depends on perfusion and infection. A rigid cast that cannot be removed would hide the wound and is not suitable while blood supply and infection are unresolved. I would use a removable forefoot offloading shoe or boot, and I would be honest that it only works if he wears it every time he stands, including the night trips to the bathroom. We would solve that together: a night light along the path, the device kept beside the bed, or a bedside commode if he agrees. I would check that the device fits his cane use and that his gait is still safe.

His ankle dorsiflexion is only five degrees, which pushes load onto the forefoot at push-off. Once the doctor clears it, I would add gentle calf mobility in sitting, not forceful stretching. Meanwhile I would keep him active with seated exercise and a plan to cut unneeded steps, such as grocery delivery or a cart to carry items, because he says taxis are not affordable.

Education would cover daily foot checks with a mirror or his daughter, no barefoot walking, no heat packs, and checking the shoes for objects.

Outcome measures: wound length, width and depth measured the same way as the nurse does, photographs with his consent, how often he wears the device, and how many hours a day he is on his feet.

I would change the plan if there is spreading redness, drainage, odour, fever, new pain, bone on probing, or if the wound has not reduced by around half in four weeks, and then I would push for a diabetic foot or wound team referral.

scale.4: Starts with perfusion and infection concerns and a medical referral, then builds a staged offloading plan with goals, outcome measures and clear change triggers tied to this man's life.
scale.3: Offers a sound offloading and education plan with outcomes and triggers but is slow to link perfusion findings to the choice of device.
scale.2: Lists generic diabetic foot advice and offloading without goals, outcomes or any response to the vascular and infection findings.
scale.1: Chooses a non-removable device or aggressive stretching despite poor perfusion, or ignores the findings and the need for medical review.

questions.prompt: Mr. Gill says he will not stay off his feet and wants to keep doing his own shopping. Explain how you would respond, and what precautions you would take during this and your next visits.

checklist.point: Explores what shopping and independence mean to him before advising and asks what he is willing to do.
Explains in plain language the link between pressure on the ulcer, poor blood supply and risk of infection or amputation.
Uses shared decision-making to offer options that protect independence, such as grocery delivery, a cart, or fewer but protected trips.
Confirms he understands the risks and documents informed choice if he decides to continue with some risk.
Takes precautions with the foot at each visit: checks colour, temperature, swelling, drainage and any change from the last visit.
Does not apply heat, aggressive soft tissue work or compression to the right foot or leg while perfusion is unclear.
Checks fall risk with the offloading device, cane and stairs to the second-floor apartment.
Teaches him when to call same-day, such as fever, new redness, drainage or foot turning pale, dusky or cold.
Checks that he can reach help if he falls or becomes unwell while living alone.

questions.model_answer:
I would not lecture him. Staying independent matters to him, and if I start by telling him to stay off his feet, I will lose him. So I would begin by asking what shopping gives him, whether it is food choice, getting out of the apartment, or not depending on others. Then I would explain, in plain words, what I see: pressure on that spot keeps the wound open, the blood supply to the foot looks weaker on the right, and a wound in that situation can get infected quickly, which is how some people with diabetes end up losing part of the foot. I would check that he has understood by asking him to tell me back, in his own words, what worries him.

Then we would look for ways to protect his independence while lowering the load. Options might be a grocery delivery service, a wheeled cart so he does not carry bags while using the cane, shorter trips with the offloading device on, or going with his daughter once a week. I would offer these as choices and ask which he would try. If he decides he will still walk more than I recommend, he has the right to make that decision, as long as he understands the risk. I would say what I recommend, document that we discussed the risks and options, and what he chose, and keep offering support at each visit.

For precautions, at each visit I would look at the foot before I do anything else: colour, temperature compared with the other side, swelling, drainage, new redness. I would avoid heat, deep massage and compression on that leg while the blood supply is uncertain. I would watch his gait with the device, since forefoot offloading shoes change how he balances and he has a cane in one hand, and I would check the stairs to the second floor.

I would teach him warning signs that mean calling the same day: a fever, redness spreading, pus or smell, pain where he usually feels little, or the foot turning pale, bluish or cold. I would give those in writing in large print and agree who he calls. Finally, because he lives alone, I would ask how he would get help if he fell, and whether he has a phone he can reach from the floor or a personal alert device.

scale.4: Respects his goals, explains risk plainly, offers workable alternatives, documents informed choice and names specific foot and fall precautions with warning signs.
scale.3: Handles autonomy and education well but gives few concrete precautions or omits documentation of informed choice.
scale.2: Repeats instructions to stay off the foot with little exploration of his reasons or options, and few precautions.
scale.1: Dismisses his goals, pressures him, or applies heat or compression to an ischemic foot.

questions.prompt: Mr. Gill's daughter phones and asks for details of his condition and your plan because she is worried. Discuss your professional responsibilities in this situation and how you would act.

checklist.point: States that sharing his health information with his daughter needs his agreement, and that provincial privacy rules on family disclosure vary.
Asks Mr. Gill what he wants shared, with whom and how much, and records his decision.
Can listen to the daughter's concerns without disclosing his information until he has been asked.
Checks whether he has a substitute decision-maker, power of attorney or documented consent, and whether he has capacity to decide.
Refers to provincial health privacy legislation and the regulator's standards without citing invented sections.
Documents the phone call, the consent discussion and what was shared.
Reports the vascular and infection concern to the physician promptly and documents who was told and when.
Stays within physiotherapy scope: does not perform sharp debridement or direct wound treatment beyond your authorized role and training.
Offers a way for the daughter to be included, such as a joint visit or three-way call with his permission.

questions.model_answer:
My main responsibility here is to protect Mr. Gill's privacy while still being kind to a worried daughter. I do not have his permission to share his health information with her, and being family does not change that. Unless he has agreed, or named her as a substitute decision-maker, I would not share his diagnosis, findings or plan. Depending on the province and his wishes, limited information to family may be allowed, so I would ask him first and follow my regulator's and provincial privacy rules. On the phone, I can listen. I can thank her for calling, tell her I cannot share details without his permission, and say I will speak with him about it at our next visit or later today. I can also give general information, such as the importance of foot care in diabetes, without revealing anything about him.

Then I would speak with Mr. Gill. I would ask what he is comfortable with her knowing, whether that is everything, only the offloading plan, or only the warning signs. I would also check whether there is a power of attorney or substitute decision-maker, and whether I have any concern about his capacity to decide. Nothing I have seen suggests he cannot decide, so I would treat him as the decision-maker. If he agrees, I would write down what he consented to and with whom, and offer a joint visit or three-way call so she hears the plan with him present. I would follow my provincial health privacy legislation and my regulator's standards on consent and confidentiality.

I would document the daughter's call, what I said, my conversation with him and his decision, in the record, with the date and time.

The second responsibility is to act on my own findings. The foot is cool, pulses are weak and there is some redness and a slightly raised temperature. That is not something I leave until the next visit. I would contact his physician the same day, say what I found, and ask for review, then document who I spoke to and what was agreed. I would also let the home care nurse know, since we share responsibility for the wound.

Finally, I stay within my scope. My role is offloading, mobility and education. I would not debride tissue unless I am authorized and trained for that, and I would refer rather than attempt to manage infection myself.

scale.4: Protects privacy by seeking his consent, handles the daughter kindly, documents, and also acts on the clinical concern with a same-day physician report within scope.
scale.3: Handles consent and documentation correctly but gives limited attention to reporting the clinical findings or scope.
scale.2: Mentions confidentiality in general terms but is unclear about what may be said, to whom, or what to document.
scale.1: Discloses health information to the daughter without consent or ignores the need to report the clinical concern.

safety_or_ethics_point: The buried issue is a possibly ischemic and early infected foot hidden in a case that looks like a simple offloading problem. A competent candidate notices the cool foot, absent posterior tibial pulse, slow refill and redness, chooses a removable device rather than a rigid cast, and escalates to the physician the same day. The daughter's phone call adds a privacy test.
common_errors: Candidates jump straight to a total contact cast or a stretching program without commenting on perfusion and infection. Others answer the daughter's request by sharing the whole plan because she is family, or lecture about staying off the feet and ignore his reasons for walking.
examiner_notes: A pass connects the vascular and infection findings to the choice of device and a same-day physician contact, and treats the client as the decision-maker on both lifestyle and information sharing. A fail either offloads without recognizing perfusion risk or discloses information without consent.

title: Fever, low oxygen saturation and weak cough on post-operative day 3
setting: General surgical ward, acute care hospital
client_profile: Ms. Noor Haddad is 62 and had an open sigmoid colon resection three days ago for diverticular disease. She smokes about a pack a day (35 pack-years), BMI 33, and has no known lung disease. Day 1 SpO2 was 95 percent on room air. Today she is on 2 L/min by nasal prongs with SpO2 91 percent, RR 24, HR 108, BP 128/74, temperature 38.1 degrees C. She splints her abdomen when coughing and the cough is weak and mostly dry. Auscultation: reduced air entry at both bases, coarse crackles at the right base, dull to percussion on the right. Pain is 6 of 10 at rest with a PCA pump. She is on prophylactic low molecular weight heparin. Left calf is 2 cm larger than the right and mildly tender.
clinical_scenario: The ward is short-staffed. The nurse tells you the surgeon's order says 'chest physio and mobilize' and asks you to get her up and walking in the hallway now so the bed can be turned over for the afternoon. A physiotherapist assistant is on the unit and available. You have five other referrals today, including a patient post-hip fracture who is due to go home. Ms. Haddad says she feels 'a bit breathless' and wants to stay in bed.

questions.prompt: Explain your clinical impression of Ms. Haddad's presentation, the findings that support it, and what else you need to consider before you decide what to do.

checklist.point: Identifies the picture as consistent with post-operative pulmonary complications such as atelectasis, with possible pneumonia, linking crackles, dullness, fever and reduced air entry.
Links shallow breathing, weak cough, splinting, pain, obesity and smoking to the risk of retained secretions.
Notes the fall in SpO2 and rise in oxygen requirement since day 1 as a deterioration.
Recognizes tachycardia, tachypnea and fever as signs that the patient may be unwell beyond a simple chest problem.
Identifies the calf asymmetry and tenderness as a possible deep vein thrombosis and the risk of pulmonary embolism as an alternative or additional cause.
Considers other causes of hypoxia or fever such as pleural effusion, aspiration, wound or abdominal infection, or anastomotic complication.
Plans further information: full vitals trend, chest imaging and blood results, medications, and discussion with the nurse and surgeon.
States that physiotherapy treatment choice depends on ruling out the more dangerous cause first.
Considers pain control as a barrier and checks it before treatment.

questions.model_answer:
My impression is that Ms. Haddad has a post-operative pulmonary complication, most likely atelectasis with a possible developing chest infection, but I cannot stop there because she has a second finding that could mean something more dangerous.

First, what supports the chest picture. She is three days after open abdominal surgery, a smoker with a high BMI, and she is splinting and coughing weakly. On examination there is reduced air entry at both bases, crackles and dullness on the right, a respiratory rate of 24, a fever of 38.1, and her saturation has fallen from 95 percent on room air on day one to 91 percent on oxygen. That change matters to me because it shows she is getting worse, not just having a bad day. Her heart rate of 108 fits both infection and pain.

Second, the left calf is two centimetres larger than the right and tender. In someone after major abdominal surgery, being on prophylactic heparin lowers the risk but does not remove it. A deep vein thrombosis could have sent a clot to the lungs. Pulmonary embolism can give breathlessness, low saturations, tachycardia and a mild fever, and I cannot tell it apart from pneumonia by listening to her chest. So I would hold my impression as a working one, and I would treat the calf finding as a red flag.

Before I decide on treatment, I want more information. I would ask the nurse for her observation trend over the last 24 hours, check the chart for imaging and bloods already ordered, and review her medications and the timing of her last heparin dose. I would ask how her pain is controlled when she coughs, because poor pain control is probably a large part of why she is not clearing secretions. I would also think about other causes: a pleural effusion, aspiration, a wound or abdominal infection, or a leak at the join in the bowel, which can also cause fever and tachycardia.

My decision flows from that. I would tell the nurse and surgical team about the calf and the fall in oxygen before I start any treatment or ask her to walk, and I would wait for their assessment. Chest physiotherapy and mobilization are helpful for atelectasis, but they are not my first step if a clot is possible.

scale.4: Gives a reasoned primary impression, notes the deterioration, recognizes the calf asymmetry as a possible clot, lists other causes and states what to clarify before treating.
scale.3: Recognizes the pulmonary complication and notes the calf but gives limited differential reasoning or further information gathering.
scale.2: Names atelectasis or pneumonia from the chest findings and lists signs without noting the calf or the deterioration.
scale.1: Misses the calf finding or the oxygen deterioration and treats as a straightforward chest case.

questions.prompt: The nurse asks you to walk Ms. Haddad now, and Ms. Haddad says she would rather stay in bed. Explain how you would respond and what precautions you would take.

checklist.point: Does not begin walking or vigorous chest treatment until the possible deep vein thrombosis and the oxygen deterioration have been reported and assessed.
Tells the nurse and physician of the calf swelling, rising oxygen requirement and fever and asks for medical assessment before activity.
Explains clearly to Ms. Haddad what you found and why you are pausing, and listens to her breathlessness.
Does not massage or compress the left calf.
Monitors vital signs during any permitted activity: SpO2, heart rate, respiratory rate, symptoms, and sets stopping criteria.
Offers safe measures that remain appropriate, such as upright positioning, breathing exercises and supported cough with a pillow, once medically cleared.
Addresses pain control with the nurse before treatment.
Respects her preference and obtains consent for each intervention.
Checks lines, drains, wound and PCA before moving her.
Takes a full set of vitals, asks for an urgent medical call and follows the early warning or rapid response process if she worsens, staying with her.

questions.model_answer:
I would answer the nurse respectfully but clearly. I would say that I do not think walking her right now is safe until the team has looked at two findings. One is the fall in her oxygen levels with a fever and fast breathing, and the other is that her left calf is bigger and tender. I would take a full set of vitals myself, ask the nurse to call the surgical team urgently now, and follow the unit's early warning or rapid response process if she worsens. I would tell her that I am worried about a possible clot as well as a chest infection, and I would stay with Ms. Haddad until that is under way. I would be specific, using the numbers, because that helps the nurse act. I understand the bed pressure, but that cannot outweigh this. I would offer to come back as soon as the team has reviewed her, and write in the chart what I found and who I told.

With Ms. Haddad, I would take her shortness of breath seriously. She has told me she feels breathless and wants to stay in bed, and in this case her preference matches what I think is safest for now. I would tell her in plain words that I am going to pause walking while the doctors check her chest and her leg, that this is a precaution, and that I will be back. I would ask about chest pain, any sharp pain on breathing in, and any coughing up of blood, and pass that on straight away.

While we wait, I would take no action that could move a clot. I would not massage, rub or squeeze her calf, and I would not do vigorous leg exercises. Within what is safe, I would help her sit more upright in bed, because that improves lung expansion, and with the medical team's agreement, teach supported coughing with a folded pillow over the wound, and slow deep breaths. I would check with the nurse whether her pain medication is timed so that she is more comfortable.

Once she is cleared, I would restart with monitoring: oxygen saturation, heart rate, breathing rate and her symptoms before, during and after, with clear stopping points such as a fall in saturation below the agreed limit, new chest pain, dizziness or marked breathlessness. I would check the wound, drain, IV and PCA lines before moving her and get consent at each step.

scale.4: Holds activity and escalates the specific findings, protects the calf, explains calmly to the client, and describes monitoring and criteria for a later safe restart.
scale.3: Delays walking and informs the team but gives limited detail on precautions, monitoring or communication with the client.
scale.2: Reluctantly agrees to a modified walk or treatment with some monitoring but does not escalate the calf and oxygen findings.
scale.1: Walks or massages the leg, or begins vigorous treatment, without raising the calf and oxygen concerns.

questions.prompt: You have six patients to see today and a physiotherapist assistant is available. Discuss how you would organize your caseload, what you would delegate, and what you would document.

checklist.point: Prioritizes by acuity and risk, seeing the deteriorating patient and arranging review before routine or discharge work.
Says Ms. Haddad's treatment is not delegated to the assistant while her status is unclear.
Delegates only stable, predictable tasks matched to the assistant's training, with clear instructions and a plan to check.
Retains assessment, clinical decisions and plan changes as the physiotherapist's responsibility.
Plans the hip fracture discharge so it is safe, such as seeing that patient early or arranging equipment and teaching.
Communicates with the charge nurse about priorities and what cannot be done today.
Documents findings, who was informed, advice given and the rationale for holding treatment.
Uses infection prevention practices between patients, including hand hygiene and equipment cleaning.
Reflects on resources honestly, asking for help or documenting that care was limited by workload.

questions.model_answer:
I would organize the day by risk, not by the order of the referral list.
