Ms. Haddad is the patient who could deteriorate fastest, so I would deal with her first, which in practice means the phone call and communication with the nursing and surgical teams about the calf and the oxygen. I would then see the patient who is going home after the hip fracture early in the day, because discharge has a deadline and a delayed discharge teaching session, a missing walker or untested stairs creates risk of a fall at home. The remaining patients I would sort into those with a clear physiotherapy goal today and those where a visit could wait a day without harm, and I would tell the charge nurse what I cannot reach.

On delegation, I know the physiotherapist assistant is available, and I want to use them well. Delegation is not about who is free. It is about whether the patient is stable, whether the task is predictable, and whether the assistant has been trained for it. I would not hand over Ms. Haddad until she has been medically reviewed and I have reassessed her, because her status is changing and the decision whether it is safe to walk her is a clinical judgement that stays with me. I would give the assistant patients whose condition is stable, for example a patient on a repeat of a known exercise program or a gait practice session with a clear walking aid and distance, with written instructions on what to do, what to watch for and when to stop and call me. I would check back after the session and review their notes. I stay responsible for the assessment and the plan.

For documentation, for Ms. Haddad I would record my findings and the observations, the calf measurements, who I informed with the time, the advice I gave, the reason I held walking and what I will do when she is cleared. For the others, I would record what was done, by whom, and the outcome. If workload means some patients are not seen, I would document that and tell the charge nurse so that it is visible.

Between patients I would perform hand hygiene, clean shared equipment such as the pulse oximeter and walking aids, and use the correct precautions if any patient is on isolation.

scale.4: Prioritizes by risk with reasons, keeps the unstable patient out of delegation, delegates appropriately with supervision, plans the discharge and documents and communicates the workload limits.
scale.3: Prioritizes sensibly and delegates appropriately but gives limited documentation or communication detail.
scale.2: Lists tasks or delegates by availability with little explanation of risk, supervision or documentation.
scale.1: Delegates the unstable patient or ignores risk when ordering the caseload.

safety_or_ethics_point: The buried issue is the unilateral calf swelling and tenderness, which makes pulmonary embolism a possibility beside the more obvious post-operative chest infection. A safe candidate pauses mobilization, reports the findings by numbers to the team, avoids massaging the leg, and keeps the patient out of delegation until she has been medically assessed.
common_errors: Candidates treat the case as pure atelectasis and start vigorous chest physiotherapy and walking because the order says to. Others delegate the walk to the assistant to relieve workload, or mention the calf in passing and still go ahead with treatment.
examiner_notes: A pass gives a reasoned impression, treats the calf and the oxygen decline as reasons to escalate before treatment, and handles the workload by acuity with safe delegation. A fail walks or treats the patient without raising the calf finding.

title: Neck pain three weeks after a rear-end collision with insurer involvement
setting: Private outpatient clinic, auto insurer-funded
client_profile: Mr. Dmitri Volkov is 36, a warehouse supervisor, rear-ended at a traffic light three weeks ago. The emergency department cleared him with no fracture on x-ray after applying a validated cervical spine rule. He now has neck pain 6 of 10 and pain across both shoulders, with stiffness worst in the morning. Neck Disability Index score is 46 percent. Active rotation is 45 degrees right and 50 degrees left, extension is limited and painful, and cervical flexion is 35 degrees. Upper limb neurological screen is normal. He reports headaches most afternoons and occasional lightheadedness when he turns his head quickly to reverse his car. He has slept about four hours a night and says he has stopped playing hockey. He takes acetaminophen as needed.
clinical_scenario: The clinic is funded under a provincial auto insurance accident benefits system and the adjuster has already approved an initial block of visits. The clinic owner has told staff that passive modalities with a higher billing code are 'what the insurer expects.' Near the end of the session, Mr. Volkov quietly says that since the crash he feels on edge, replays it at night and, 'some days I wonder what the point is.' The adjuster has asked you to send complete clinical notes for the file and a prognosis for return to work.

questions.prompt: Describe the plan of care you would develop for Mr. Volkov over the next six weeks, including your goals, interventions, how you would progress them and how you would measure progress.

checklist.point: Sets patient-centred goals, such as sleep, driving comfort, return to work tasks and a graded return to hockey.
Uses education and reassurance about the expected course of whiplash associated disorder and encourages staying active.
Prescribes graded active movement and cervical, scapular and deep neck flexor exercise with dosage and progression.
Includes posture, ergonomic and work-task advice for the warehouse role.

Plans manual therapy only as an adjunct to active care, and only after the lightheadedness and neurological screen is completed and vascular or neurological causes are excluded or he is medically cleared.
Does not rely on passive modalities as the core of care.
Includes sleep strategies and graded return to driving and sport.
Names outcome measures such as the Neck Disability Index, pain scale, active range, and headache frequency, with timing of reassessment.
Identifies factors that may delay recovery and plans to address them, such as sleep loss, distress and fear of movement.
Sets reassessment triggers for referral, such as no change by a set time, worsening neurological signs or persistent distress.
Completes the neurological screen and addresses the lightheadedness before progressive neck loading, holding loading and manual therapy until medically cleared if it persists.

questions.model_answer:
My plan has a clear aim: help Mr. Volkov get moving, sleeping and working again, while watching for factors that can slow his recovery. His neck disability score of 46 percent, pain of six out of ten, limited rotation and afternoon headaches are in line with a moderate whiplash associated disorder without neurological signs, so I would build around education and active care.

Goals, agreed with him. In two weeks, better sleep, with at least five hours, and driving comfortable enough to check blind spots. In six weeks, a Neck Disability Index below 30 percent, pain no higher than three, neck rotation of at least 70 degrees to each side, back to full duties at work and a graded return to light hockey practice.

The first visit includes education. I would explain that most people with this kind of injury improve, that gentle movement is helpful and that rest in a collar is not. Reassurance has to be honest and specific, and I would answer his fears directly.

Before any loading, I would complete a neurological screen and ask about the lightheadedness when he turns his head quickly. If it comes with double vision, trouble speaking or swallowing, facial numbness or unsteadiness, he goes to emergency the same day. If it is isolated, I would arrange prompt medical review, keep to gentle active range within comfort, and hold progressive neck loading and manual therapy until vascular and neurological causes are excluded or he is medically cleared.

Exercise is the core. Early phase, daily and frequent short sets: active neck range in pain-tolerable ranges, ten slow repetitions in each direction two to three times a day, chin nods to start deep neck flexor work, and scapular setting. At around two weeks, if pain allows, I would progress to deep neck flexor holds increasing from 10 seconds, scapular strengthening with a band, thoracic mobility, and low-load postural endurance. From week four, once cleared, add resisted work and progress towards work-specific lifting practice and sport-specific drills. I would progress when pain settles to a mild level within an hour of exercising, not when a date arrives.

Manual therapy such as gentle mobilization can be added for a few visits to ease movement, but only alongside the exercises, and only once the lightheadedness has been cleared as described below. I would not use passive modalities as the main treatment, because they do not improve function and they build dependence.

For sleep, a pillow that keeps the neck neutral and a wind-down routine. For work, short micro-breaks and a plan for lifting and screen use. For driving, set up the mirrors and practise head turns in a parked car first.

I would measure the Neck Disability Index and pain every two weeks, rotation each visit, and his headache frequency. His poor sleep, mood and fear of movement predict slower recovery, so I would screen them and bring in other supports if they do not improve. If there is no improvement by about four to six weeks, or if neurological signs appear, I would refer back to the physician.

scale.4: Gives goals, education, dosed and progressed active exercise, adjunct-only manual therapy, work and sleep strategies, outcome measures and clear referral triggers.
scale.3: Provides a sound active plan with goals and measures but is vague on progression or on addressing recovery risk factors.
scale.2: Lists exercise and modalities without dosage, progression or outcome measures.
scale.1: Relies mainly on passive modalities, rest or a collar, or ignores function and recovery.

questions.prompt: At the end of the session Mr. Volkov says something that concerns you. Explain what you would do in response, and what other safety checks you would carry out.

checklist.point: Responds to the remark about 'what the point is' directly and calmly and asks him in plain words about thoughts of self-harm or suicide.
Listens without judgment and acknowledges his distress and sleep loss.
Assesses immediate risk by asking about plan, means and intent, and whether he has support.
Knows what to do if risk is high: stay with him, arrange urgent help through crisis services or emergency.
If risk is not immediate, creates a plan with him to see his physician or mental health support promptly and provides crisis line information.
Asks consent to inform his family physician and documents the conversation.
Screens for post-traumatic stress symptoms and considers how they affect recovery.

Treats lightheadedness with head turning after neck trauma as a possible vascular cause: sends him to emergency the same day if other neurological signs are present, otherwise arranges prompt medical review and holds neck loading and manual therapy.
Checks for neurological and other serious signs at each visit, such as new limb weakness, changes in speech, vision or swallowing.

questions.model_answer:
What he said at the end matters more to me than anything I did in the session. When someone three weeks after a crash says 'some days I wonder what the point is,' I take it seriously and I do not let the appointment time run out. I would stop what I am doing, sit with him and say something like: 'I want to come back to what you just said. I'm glad you told me. Sometimes when people are in pain and not sleeping, they have thoughts of ending their life. Is that something you have been thinking about?' Asking directly does not plant the idea. It lets him know I can listen.

Then I would listen to what he says, without hurrying, and acknowledge what he has been through: the pain, four hours of sleep, losing hockey, replaying the crash. I would ask whether he has thought about how he might harm himself, whether he has a plan or access to means, whether he intends to act, and who is around him. If he tells me he has a plan or intent, I would not leave him alone. I would stay with him, bring in a colleague or the clinic manager, and arrange urgent help according to our clinic's process, which means a crisis service or emergency department, and I would not send him home alone. If he has thoughts but no plan or intent, I would work out a safety plan with him: who he can talk to tonight, how to reach a crisis line, a same-day or next-day visit to his family physician, and removal of any means. I would offer to make that call with him, ask for his permission to tell his physician what he told me, and write down the conversation, my assessment, what I advised and what we agreed.

I would also ask about the other things that suggest post-traumatic stress: nightmares, replaying the event, avoiding driving, feeling on edge, and I would include these in the referral.

Other safety checks remain. The lightheadedness when he turns quickly deserves attention. It may come from the neck or from other causes, but I would ask if it comes with double vision, trouble speaking or swallowing, facial numbness, or unsteadiness, and if any of those signs are present I would stop treatment and send him to the emergency department or call 911 the same day. If the lightheadedness alone persists, I would arrange prompt medical review and hold neck loading and manual therapy until he is cleared. I would repeat a neurological screen at each visit and tell him which symptoms mean going to emergency right away.

scale.4: Asks directly about suicide risk, assesses plan and intent, acts proportionately including urgent help if needed, obtains consent to inform the physician, screens for stress symptoms and addresses the dizziness.
scale.3: Responds to the remark with a sound referral and documentation but explores risk or the dizziness less fully.
scale.2: Offers sympathy and a general suggestion to see a doctor without asking about suicide or setting a plan.
scale.1: Ignores or minimizes the remark, or ends the session without any risk assessment or follow-up.

questions.prompt: The adjuster has requested your complete clinical notes and a prognosis, and the clinic owner expects higher-billing treatments. Discuss your professional responsibilities in both situations and how you would proceed.

checklist.point: Obtains Mr. Volkov's informed consent before releasing information and tells him what will be sent.
Releases only information relevant to the claim and the purpose, and discusses whether sensitive disclosures such as his remark about the point of living should be shared.
Gives an honest, evidence-based prognosis within scope and says what is uncertain.
Bases treatment and billing on clinical need and the plan, not on the insurer's expectations or the clinic owner's preference.
Bills only for services actually provided and identifies passive modalities as not supported when they are not indicated.
Recognizes the conflict of interest and the physiotherapist's duty to the client over the employer or payer.
Documents accurately, objectively and at the time of care, including consent and what was released.
Raises the billing concern with the owner and, if unresolved, seeks guidance from the provincial regulator or professional association.
Refers to the regulator's standards and provincial health privacy legislation without inventing section numbers.

questions.model_answer:
There are two separate duties here, and in both my first responsibility is to Mr. Volkov, not to the insurer or the clinic.

Starting with the adjuster. The adjuster is a third party. I can only release his personal health information with his informed consent, and the consent should cover what is being sent, to whom and for what purpose. So before I send anything, I would sit down with him, explain what the adjuster has asked for, and show him what I plan to send. Many insurance arrangements include consent signed at intake, but I would still check that he understands it and that it covers what is being asked. I would send what is relevant to the claim: findings, treatment plan, progress, function and work capacity. I would not automatically send everything. His comment about feeling that there is no point is highly sensitive. I would talk with him about it, and unless he agrees or there is a legal reason, it stays out of the report to the adjuster, while remaining in my clinical record and being acted on through his physician. I would follow my provincial health privacy legislation and my regulator's standards.

For the prognosis, I would be honest and stay in my lane. Most people with this kind of injury improve over weeks to months, and he has some factors that may slow recovery, such as poor sleep and distress. I would give an estimate based on what I see, say what is uncertain, and describe it as a working view that I will update, rather than guaranteeing a date for return to work. I would also say what supports I recommend.

On the clinic's expectations, the plan of care is decided by his needs and the evidence, which supports active care and not passive modalities as the main treatment. I will not provide or bill for treatments I do not believe will help him, and I will bill only for what I actually did. That is a conflict of interest I have to manage openly: the clinic and the payer have financial interests, and my duty is to my client. I would raise it respectfully with the owner, pointing to my regulator's standards on billing and conflict of interest, and if the pressure continued I would contact my regulator or professional association for advice. Throughout, my notes must be accurate, timely and objective, with consent and releases recorded.

scale.4: Secures informed consent, limits disclosure to what is relevant and handles the sensitive remark, gives an honest prognosis, refuses unwarranted billing and escalates a conflict appropriately.
scale.3: Handles consent and honest billing but gives limited attention to the sensitive disclosure or to how to escalate.
scale.2: States that confidentiality and ethical billing matter without concrete actions or reasoning.
scale.1: Sends all notes without consent or agrees to bill unneeded treatments to satisfy the clinic or insurer.

safety_or_ethics_point: The buried issue is the quiet statement of hopelessness, which needs a direct suicide risk enquiry, proportionate action and consent-based follow-up. A second layer is the intermittent lightheadedness with head turning that deserves a vascular and neurological check. The insurer and clinic pressure tests consent, disclosure and billing integrity.
common_errors: Candidates build a good exercise plan and never respond to the remark, or respond only with sympathy and a card. Others agree to send the full file to the insurer and accept the owner's preference for passive modalities.
examiner_notes: A pass includes a direct, proportionate response to the risk statement, an active-care plan and clear separation between the client's interests and those of the payer or employer. A fail does not address the remark or discloses without consent.

title: Posterior thigh injury in a rugby player before a final
setting: Sport physiotherapy clinic
client_profile: Jamal Thompson is 24, a university rugby flanker, who felt a sudden tearing pain in the back of his right thigh while sprinting six days ago. There was visible bruising the next day. Pain is 4 of 10 walking and 7 of 10 on attempted sprinting. He is tender over the biceps femoris muscle belly about 12 cm below the ischial tuberosity. Active knee extension in supine with hip flexed to 90 degrees lacks 25 degrees on the right and 10 on the left. Prone knee flexion strength is 4 minus out of 5 on the right with pain. Slump test is negative, and there is no pain at the ischial tuberosity. He has no previous hamstring injury. He takes ibuprofen, 400 mg three times a day.
clinical_scenario: The team plays the provincial final in 10 days and the coach has texted him daily asking whether he will be ready. Jamal says his scholarship depends on this season and asks you to 'just tape it and get me back.' While discussing sleep, he adds that he was tackled in the same game and 'got his bell rung.' He has had headaches most days since, with some light sensitivity, and has not told the coach or the team doctor because he does not want to be benched.

questions.prompt: Describe the rehabilitation plan you would give Jamal for his thigh, including how you would set goals and criteria for progression, and what the timeline might look like.

checklist.point: Classifies the injury as a moderate muscle strain based on findings and sets a realistic range of return-to-play time rather than a promise.
Sets criteria-based progression rather than date-based, using pain, range, strength and function.
Includes early phase relative rest, pain-limited loading and gentle movement.
Progresses to isometric then eccentric hamstring loading, with sets, repetitions and progression.
Includes lumbopelvic control and trunk strengthening in the program.
Plans a graded running program leading to sprinting and sport-specific drills including contact only at the end.
Names outcome measures such as pain, active knee extension range, strength comparison with the other side and functional tests.
Addresses medication use, such as discussing with the physician or pharmacist the use of anti-inflammatories in early healing.
Plans return-to-play criteria and a hamstring injury prevention program after return.

questions.model_answer:
From the findings, this looks like a moderate hamstring strain of the biceps femoris, not a mild one. He has bruising, tenderness in the muscle belly, a 15 degree difference in the active knee extension test, weakness with pain on resisted flexion, and pain on sprinting. A moderate strain typically takes a few weeks to return to full sport, and I would tell him that honestly. A final in 10 days is very unlikely to be a safe target for full sprinting and contact, and I would frame the plan around readiness, not the date.

Goals, set with him: within a week, normal pain-free walking and full pain-free isometric contraction; by week three, pain-free jogging and running; by weeks four to six, sprint speed and sport-specific drills, then contact and a return to match play once criteria are met.

Phase one is the next several days. I would use relative rest, avoid stretching to the point of pain and keep him moving with walking in pain-free strides. I would start gentle isometrics at mid-range in prone or bridge position, such as holds of 20 to 30 seconds, five repetitions, and pain-free range exercise. I would also begin trunk and lumbopelvic work that does not load the thigh.

Phase two begins when he has pain-free isometrics. I would progress to bridges with a single leg, then eccentric loading such as slider hamstring curls or Nordic-type work in small ranges, three sets of six to eight, increasing range and load across sessions. I would add a progressive running program, going from jogging at modest speeds to progressive accelerations and then to sprinting at increasing percentages of maximum, with a rest day between loading sessions.

Phase three: change of direction, sport drills, and finally non-contact then contact training.

Progression depends on criteria: no pain at rest, walking and during the task, active knee extension within about 10 degrees of the left side, strength on the right at least 90 percent of the left, and the ability to complete sprint drills without pain or apprehension. I would measure these every visit.

I would ask him to talk to his physician or pharmacist about the ibuprofen, since evidence on anti-inflammatories early in muscle healing is mixed, and I would not tell him to start or stop it myself. After return, a hamstring strengthening program continues because reinjury risk is high.

scale.4: Classifies the injury, sets honest timelines, uses criteria-based phases with dosage, outcome measures and return-to-play criteria, and adds prevention.
scale.3: Provides sound phased rehabilitation with criteria but is limited in dosage detail or return-to-play criteria.
scale.2: Lists exercises generally with fixed dates and few outcome measures.
scale.1: Promises return by the final or uses stretching and heavy loading regardless of pain.

questions.prompt: Jamal mentions the tackle. Explain what you would do about this and how you would handle his request to be taped and returned to play.

checklist.point: Recognizes that headaches and light sensitivity since a head knock suggest a possible concussion and takes it as a priority above the thigh.
Asks about further symptoms: nausea, dizziness, sleep change, concentration problems, mood changes and worsening headache.
Advises him not to return to play or training and arranges prompt medical assessment by a physician or nurse practitioner.
Screens for red flags needing emergency care, such as repeated vomiting, worsening headache, confusion, seizure, weakness or drowsiness.
Explains that returning with a concussion risks worse injury and a longer recovery, in terms that connect to his goals.
Does not clear him for sport or tape him to play.
Advises that he tell the team doctor and coach and offers to help or, with consent, to do so.
Adjusts the thigh program to avoid high exertion until medically cleared.
Documents the disclosure, advice and referral.

questions.model_answer:
The concussion comes first. It is a bigger risk to him than the thigh, and I would put the hamstring aside for a few minutes to deal with it.

He told me he was tackled and 'got his bell rung,' and since then he has had headaches most days with light sensitivity. That is consistent with a concussion that has not been assessed. I would thank him for telling me, and then ask a set of questions: how the headache has changed, whether there is nausea, dizziness, trouble sleeping or sleeping more, trouble concentrating, irritability or feeling foggy. I would also check for red flags that mean going to the emergency department now: repeated vomiting, a headache that is getting worse, confusion, drowsiness that is hard to rouse, weakness or numbness, slurred speech, a seizure, or unequal pupils. If any of those are present, I would arrange emergency care straight away. If not, I would still tell him that he needs to see a physician or nurse practitioner for a proper concussion assessment in the next day or so, and I would help him book it.

I would also be clear with him that he should not play, train hard or do contact until he has been medically assessed and cleared through a graded return-to-sport process. I would explain this in terms that matter to him. Playing again with a concussion makes another injury more likely, can make symptoms worse and last longer, and can put his studies and long-term health at risk, which would hurt his season far more than missing the final.

On taping him to play, my answer is no, and I would say that kindly. I would not clear him to play, with either the thigh or the head. Tape would not make a moderate hamstring strain safe to sprint on, and I cannot send him out with an unassessed head injury. I would offer what I can do: a plan to get him back as quickly as it is safe, and my help in speaking with the team doctor and coach, if he agrees. It is better if he tells them himself, and I would support him in doing that. I would not tell them without his consent unless there were an immediate safety concern.

In the meantime I would keep his thigh program at low intensity: walking, gentle isometrics, no high-effort running or heavy exertion that could provoke head symptoms. I would document his disclosure, my screening, my advice and the referral.

scale.4: Treats the possible concussion as the priority, screens for red flags, refers for medical assessment, refuses to clear or tape him, links advice to his goals and adjusts exertion.
scale.3: Identifies concussion and refers him but gives limited red-flag screening or limited response to his request.
scale.2: Mentions seeing a doctor about the headaches but still plans to tape or progress him towards play.
scale.1: Ignores the head injury or agrees to tape and return him to play.

questions.prompt: Jamal is frustrated and says you are costing him his scholarship. Describe what you would say to him and how you would communicate, including how you would handle the coach's messages.

checklist.point: Acknowledges his frustration and fear about the scholarship before giving information.
Uses plain, specific language to explain findings and likely timeline without jargon.
Gives a clear, honest message that he is not cleared for the final, framed around his goals.
Uses open questions and reflective listening to understand what matters to him.
Offers options and next steps so that he has some control, such as the plan to return and ways to stay involved with the team.
Uses teach-back or checks understanding.
Explains that he decides what information is shared with the coach and that you will not share without his consent.
Suggests ways he can talk to the coach or offers a letter of recommended activity limits with his permission.
Stays calm and non-defensive and avoids false reassurance.

questions.model_answer:
I would start by listening, because his frustration makes sense. He has a scholarship, a team that is counting on him and a coach texting him daily. If I jump in with explanations, he will hear it as me taking something away from him. So I would say something like: 'It sounds like this final matters a lot, and that you feel stuck between your health and your season. Tell me what you're most worried about.' Then I would let him talk and reflect back what I hear: 'You're worried that if you miss this game, you lose your place and the scholarship.'

Then I would be clear and kind. 'Here is what I see. Your hamstring has a moderate tear. It's not just a bruise. If you sprint on it in ten days, there's a real chance it tears further and you lose the rest of the season, not just one game. And with the headaches since the tackle, I'm not comfortable with you playing until a doctor has checked your head. I know that's not what you wanted to hear.' I would use plain words, avoid medical jargon and not promise anything I cannot know, such as a particular return date.

Then I would give him control by offering choices. 'I can't clear you for the final, but here is what I can do. We can set up a plan to get you back as soon as it is safe, I can help you get a quick appointment about the headaches, and we can talk about staying involved with the team, for example in film review or training that does not load your leg or head.' I would ask what he thinks would help most, and check he has understood by asking him to tell me, in his own words, what the plan is and what he will do tomorrow.

About the coach: his health information belongs to him. I would explain that I will not share anything with the coach or the team without his permission. He may prefer to tell the coach himself, and I could help him prepare what to say. If he agrees, I can write a short note stating the activity limits without sharing diagnosis details. I would not reply to the coach's messages myself. If he feels pushed by the team, I would also tell him about the team doctor as another route.

I would stay calm if he stays upset, avoid arguing, and leave the door open: 'I'm on your side here, and I want you playing for years, not just this game.'

scale.4: Acknowledges feelings, delivers a clear honest message in plain language, offers choices and checks understanding, and protects his control over what is shared with the coach.
scale.3: Communicates clearly and empathically but gives less on choices, teach-back or the coach issue.
scale.2: Gives information correctly but in a clinical or defensive way with little acknowledgement of his concerns.
scale.1: Argues with him, gives false reassurance, or agrees to contact the coach without consent.

safety_or_ethics_point: The buried issue is a possible concussion that Jamal has hidden from the coach and team doctor, which outweighs the hamstring problem. A safe candidate screens for red flags, refers for medical assessment, refuses to clear or tape him, and respects his control over disclosure to the coach.
common_errors: Candidates write a thorough hamstring program and treat the concussion remark as a passing detail, or promise a return by the final. Others offer to phone the coach and share everything without asking Jamal.
examiner_notes: A pass prioritizes the head injury, gives an honest timeline for the thigh and communicates with empathy while protecting his consent. A fail tapes or clears him, or does not respond to the head injury.

title: Falls at home after stroke in an older man with new medication
setting: Client's home, community rehabilitation team
client_profile: Mr. Antoine Beaulieu is 77, retired farmer, five weeks after a left middle cerebral artery ischemic stroke, discharged home 11 days ago. He has right arm weakness (4 minus out of 5 shoulder, 3 out of 5 grip), mild right leg weakness (4 out of 5), and mild word-finding difficulty. Berg Balance Scale 38 of 56, Timed Up and Go 22 seconds with a four-wheeled walker. He walks short distances with supervision. His wife reports two falls in the past week, both at night on the way to the bathroom. At discharge his blood pressure medication was increased. Seated blood pressure today is 138/80 and standing at one minute is 112/66; he says he feels 'woozy' when he stands.
clinical_scenario: His wife, Colette, 75, is his only caregiver and has arthritis in her hands. She is exhausted and says she sleeps in short pieces because she listens for him at night. Their bedroom is upstairs and the only full bathroom is on the main floor. Mr. Beaulieu says he is fine and wants to be left alone with his wife. The community team includes an occupational therapist and a nurse case manager, and the family physician is a two-hour drive away in a regional centre, reachable by phone and fax.

questions.prompt: Explain what your assessment findings tell you about the reason for Mr. Beaulieu's falls, which factors you consider the most important and what further assessment you would do.

checklist.point: Identifies the drop in standing blood pressure with dizziness as a likely contributor to falls and links it to the recent medication increase.
Interprets the Berg score and Timed Up and Go time as showing impaired balance and increased fall risk.
Links right-sided weakness, reduced balance reactions and use of a walker to fall risk, especially in the dark.
Considers the night-time context: urgency to void, poor lighting, fatigue, medication timing, rushing and distance to the bathroom.
Distinguishes the contribution of stroke impairments from the medication-related low blood pressure, rather than blaming the stroke only.
Plans further assessment: lying to standing blood pressure at one and three minutes, heart rate, symptoms, gait observation, transfers and home hazards.
Screens for other contributors such as vision, visual field loss, sensation, cognition, mood and continence.
Considers fatigue and the effect on caregiver safety.
Identifies that medication decisions belong to the physician and plans to report the findings.

questions.model_answer:
My impression is that Mr. Beaulieu's falls come from several factors acting together, and the one I would take most seriously is a possible drop in blood pressure on standing, because it is both new and fixable.

Let me go through the findings. His blood pressure sitting is 138 over 80 and one minute after standing is 112 over 66. That is a fall of 26 in the systolic pressure, and he says he feels woozy when he stands. That is a pattern consistent with orthostatic hypotension, and it appeared after his blood pressure medication was increased at discharge. Both falls happened at night on the way to the bathroom, which is exactly when people stand up quickly from bed, often after lying for hours, and are hurrying. Low pressure on standing can cause dizziness and sudden loss of balance even in someone with otherwise reasonable function.

That said, the stroke also contributes. His Berg score of 38 out of 56 and his Timed Up and Go time of 22 seconds are both in the range associated with higher risk of falling. He has right leg and arm weakness, which affects his ability to respond to a loss of balance, and the walker, though helpful, is not always on hand at night. So I see the medication effect and the stroke impairments as working together, and I would not label the falls as just a stroke problem, since that would miss the part that his doctor can change.

For further assessment, I would measure lying and standing blood pressure and heart rate properly: after five minutes of lying, then at one and three minutes standing, noting his symptoms. I would observe his transfers from bed and toilet, how he turns, and how he uses the walker, and look at the route from bedroom to bathroom in the home, including lighting and floor surfaces. I would also screen his vision and visual fields, since stroke can affect these, any changes in sensation, thinking, mood and his need to urinate at night, because urgency leads to rushing.

I also see that Colette is exhausted. I would note that as a factor, because a tired caregiver assisting a transfer is another way someone gets hurt.

I cannot change his medication. What I can do is report my findings with the numbers to his physician promptly and ask for review, while I plan strategies that reduce the risk in the meantime.

scale.4: Links the orthostatic drop to the medication change and the night pattern, balances this with stroke impairments, uses the test scores correctly and plans specific further assessment and physician reporting.
scale.3: Identifies the blood pressure change and balance impairment but gives less on night context, differential factors or further assessment.
scale.2: Attributes falls to the stroke and balance scores alone with little comment on the standing blood pressure.
scale.1: Misses the blood pressure drop or suggests changing the medication yourself.

questions.prompt: Describe what you would put in place to reduce the risk of harm to Mr. Beaulieu and Colette in the next few days, and how you would involve them in the decisions.

checklist.point: Teaches slow staged position changes at night: sit at the edge of the bed, pause, then stand with support.
Reduces night-time hazards: lighting, clear path, walker within reach, bedside commode or urinal option.
Teaches the couple when to stop and sit or lie down, and what to do if he feels woozy.
Reviews safe assistance technique for Colette that respects her arthritis and limits lifting.
Arranges equipment or alternatives for the stairs and bathroom with the occupational therapist, such as sleeping on the main floor.
Plans for what to do after a fall: do not rush to lift, check for injury, call for help, and when to call emergency services.
Informs them when to contact the physician or emergency services, such as fainting, head strike, chest pain or new stroke symptoms.
Explores Mr. Beaulieu's priorities and Colette's capacity and respects their choices after explaining risks.
Uses language adapted to his word-finding difficulty and checks understanding.

questions.model_answer:
For the next few days I would focus on night time, because that is when both falls happened, and I would do it with both of them, not for them.

The first measure is how he gets up. I would teach and practise with him, in his own bed, a staged routine: sit up, count slowly to ten with feet on the floor, move his ankles up and down, stand with the walker already in place, and wait before walking. I would have him practise it while I watch and keep my hand ready. I would ask him to repeat it back to me or show me, since his word-finding difficulty means a demonstration is better than a long explanation, and I would leave a short picture sheet at the bedside.

The second measure is making the path safe and shorter. A night light between the bed and the bathroom, clear floor with no rugs, walker kept within arm's reach of the bed. The bathroom is downstairs and the bedroom upstairs, which is a risk in itself. With the occupational therapist, I would explore options such as setting up a bed on the main floor, a bedside commode or urinal for the night, a stair-use plan, and grab bars. I would present these as choices and ask what works for them. If he prefers to keep sleeping upstairs, I would explain the risk clearly, respect that it is their home and their decision, and do what I can to make it safer.

For Colette, I would watch how she helps him and teach her a technique that does not need lifting or pulling on his arm: guide at the waist belt, stand slightly behind and to his weaker side, and let him do the standing. Her hands have arthritis, so I would ask what she can safely do, and I would tell her she is not expected to catch him. If he starts to fall, she should guide him down rather than hold him up. After a fall, they should check for pain or injury, not try to lift him alone, and call for help. They should call emergency services for a blow to the head, chest pain, fainting, new weakness, trouble speaking or severe pain.

Throughout, I would ask what they want. He says he is fine, so I would listen to what independence means to him, and I would also ask Colette directly how she is coping.

scale.4: Gives specific night-time routines and environmental changes, safe caregiver technique and post-fall plan, and involves both partners in choices while adapting communication to aphasia.
scale.3: Provides sound safety measures but with limited caregiver guidance or limited involvement of the couple in decisions.
scale.2: Lists generic fall prevention advice without tailoring to the night-time pattern or caregiver capacity.
scale.1: Overrides their choices or advises Colette to lift or hold him up.

questions.prompt: Discuss how you would work with other members of the care team and the family to manage Mr. Beaulieu's situation, including who you would contact, what you would say and when.

checklist.point: Contacts the family physician promptly with specific findings, including lying and standing blood pressures, symptoms and the timing of the medication change, and asks for medication review.
Does not alter or advise stopping medication yourself.
Contacts the occupational therapist about home set-up, bathroom and stairs, equipment and caregiver strategies.
Informs the nurse case manager about caregiver strain and requests assessment for respite, home support or other community services.
Involves the pharmacist for medication review and timing, if available.
Considers the speech-language pathologist for aphasia and communication supports.
Obtains consent from Mr. Beaulieu to share information and includes Colette in team communication with his permission.
Uses clear structured communication and a fast channel since the physician is distant, and sets a time to follow up.
Clarifies roles and who will follow up on each item and documents communication.

questions.model_answer:
The most urgent contact is with his family physician, because the blood pressure finding needs a medical decision that I cannot make. The physician is two hours away, so I would not wait for a routine fax. I would phone the office the same day, ask to speak with the physician or the nurse who can bring it to them, and send the same information in writing. I would be brief and specific: 'Mr. Beaulieu is five weeks after a left MCA stroke and had his blood pressure medication increased at discharge. Since then he has had two night-time falls. Today his sitting pressure is 138 over 80 and one minute after standing it is 112 over 66, with dizziness. I am concerned about orthostatic hypotension contributing to falls. Could you review the medication and timing, and let me know any limits you want on activity in the meantime?' I would ask when to expect a reply and tell them I will call back by the next day if I have not heard. I would not change or advise him to stop any medication myself.

Next, the occupational therapist, today or tomorrow. I would ask them to see the home about the stairs, bathroom, equipment such as a commode and bed set-up, and to work on night-time routines. I would share my transfer teaching so we give the same message. With the nurse case manager, I would raise Colette's exhaustion and arthritis. Her sleep is broken and she is his only caregiver, and that is a safety risk for both of them. I would ask for an assessment for home support, respite and caregiver services. If a pharmacist is accessible, I would ask for a review of the medication timing and interactions. And if his word-finding difficulty is limiting how well he follows instructions, I would suggest a speech-language pathologist assess and advise us on communication strategies.

For the family, I would ask Mr. Beaulieu for permission to share information with the team and with Colette. I would include her in the conversation, because she is the person who sees him at night, and she can give us information on how things really are.

I would set roles: I follow up the physician response and balance work; the OT does the home changes; the case manager does caregiver support. I would document each contact with date, time, the information shared and the plan, and agree on a date for the team to check in again.

scale.4: Contacts the physician urgently with a structured, specific message, does not adjust medication, brings in the OT, case manager and others with clear roles, secures consent and follows up.
scale.3: Identifies the right team members and communicates well but with limited urgency, roles or follow-up planning.
scale.2: Names team members and says they would 'refer' without specifying content, timing or roles.
scale.1: Changes the medication, delays contact with the physician or excludes the client and caregiver.

safety_or_ethics_point: The buried issue is orthostatic hypotension after a recent medication increase, which looks like a stroke-related balance problem. A competent candidate measures it, reports it to the physician with numbers and does not alter medication. The exhausted sole caregiver is a second hidden risk that needs community services and safe assistance technique.
common_errors: Candidates build a balance and strengthening program and treat the falls as a stroke issue only. Others suggest he stop or delay the blood pressure tablets, or give Colette lifting instructions that her arthritis cannot meet.
examiner_notes: A pass connects the standing blood pressure drop and night timing to a targeted safety plan and a prompt, specific physician contact without altering medication, and includes the caregiver. A fail misses the blood pressure finding or advises on medication.

title: Neck and arm pain with hand symptoms in an office worker
setting: Private outpatient physiotherapy clinic, first visit
client_profile: Priya Raman is a 49 year old accountant who works about nine hours a day at a desk. For six weeks she has had left neck pain spreading into the posterior upper arm, forearm and the middle and index fingers, with tingling that is worse at night. She rates pain 6 out of 10. Her family doctor prescribed naproxen with partial relief. She has no trauma history. She takes naproxen 500 mg twice daily and a multivitamin. Vitals are normal. Cervical rotation is 50 degrees to the left and 70 degrees to the right, and the left arm symptoms increase with left rotation and extension. Spurling test on the left reproduces her arm pain. Distraction relieves it. Upper limb neurodynamic test for the median nerve is positive on the left. Triceps strength is 4 out of 5 on the left and triceps reflex is reduced. Sensation is reduced over the left middle finger. Grip is similar side to side. She mentions she has also been dropping her coffee cup lately. Neck Disability Index is 24 out of 50.
clinical_scenario: Priya's employer covers physiotherapy through a private plan that pays for ten visits a year and requires a progress report. The clinic owner has asked all therapists to offer a prepaid package of twelve visits. Priya says she cannot take much time off before a tax deadline in three weeks, and she asks whether the clinic can send her work notes without a full report. A physiotherapist assistant at the clinic is trained in mechanical traction and has open appointment times this week.

questions.prompt: Based on the history and examination findings, explain your clinical impression and justify how the findings support it. Then describe what further assessment you would complete today and why.

checklist.point: Identifies a left cervical radiculopathy, likely C7 root, using the cluster of Spurling, distraction relief, neurodynamic test, rotation limit and reflex change.
Links triceps weakness, reduced triceps reflex and middle finger sensory change to the C7 root level.
Explains that a positive cluster of tests raises the likelihood of radiculopathy more than any single test.
Recognizes dropping objects as a finding that does not fit a single root problem and raises possible spinal cord involvement.
Plans an upper motor neuron screen: hyperreflexia, Hoffmann sign, clonus, Babinski, gait and tandem walking, hand dexterity.
Plans a screen for other red flags: night pain, weight loss, fever, bladder or bowel change, history of cancer.
Considers differentials such as shoulder pathology, carpal tunnel syndrome and thoracic outlet syndrome and says how to differentiate them.
Plans baseline outcome measures and a patient specific functional goal, such as sitting tolerance at work.
States that imaging is not needed first for radiculopathy without red flags but that new cord signs change that.

questions.model_answer:
My impression is a left cervical radiculopathy, most likely at the C7 level. I will explain how I got there, and then tell you what I would add before I treat.

First, the pattern. Her arm pain follows a root distribution, with tingling in the middle and index fingers. Her pain is provoked by left rotation and extension, which narrow the foramen on that side. The Spurling test reproduces her arm pain, the distraction test relieves it, and the median nerve neurodynamic test is positive. No one of these is enough alone, but together they make a radiculopathy quite likely. Triceps weakness at 4 out of 5, a reduced triceps reflex and reduced sensation over the middle finger all point to C7 in particular. Her grip is symmetrical, so I am less worried about a C8 or a peripheral median nerve problem like carpal tunnel, although I would still check Phalen and Tinel tests at the wrist to rule it out. I would also screen the shoulder, because shoulder pain can refer into the arm, but rotation of the neck changing her symptoms makes the neck the main source.

Second, the detail that does not fit. She said she has been dropping her coffee cup. A single root problem rarely explains clumsy hands. This could be pain inhibition, but I must also consider that the spinal cord is being compressed, which is cervical myelopathy. So today I would add an upper motor neuron screen: deep tendon reflexes at the biceps, brachioradialis and knee, looking for brisk reflexes, then the Hoffmann sign, ankle clonus and the Babinski response. I would watch her walk, including tandem walking, and ask her to do fine tasks like buttoning or finger tapping. I would ask about balance, any change in walking, and bladder or bowel control.

Third, other red flags. I would ask about night pain unrelated to position, unexplained weight loss, fever, a history of cancer, and recent infection. Her vital signs are normal, which is reassuring.

Fourth, outcome measures. I have a Neck Disability Index of 24 out of 50, and I would add a pain rating and the Patient Specific Functional Scale, with a goal like working ninety minutes at the desk before symptoms rise, since that is what matters to her before her deadline.

If the cord screen is clear, I would not send her for imaging right away, because guidelines support a trial of conservative care for radiculopathy without red flags. If any upper motor neuron sign is present, my plan changes and she needs prompt medical assessment.

scale.4: Names a left C7 radiculopathy with reasoning from the test cluster, spots that dropping objects does not fit, and plans a specific cord screen and red flag questions, with outcome measures.
scale.3: Gives a sound radiculopathy impression with good test reasoning but treats the dropping objects as minor or gives only a brief cord screen.
scale.2: Lists tests and a diagnosis without explaining why they support it, and misses the dropping objects or the need to screen for cord involvement.
scale.1: Gives the wrong impression, ignores the neurological changes, or proposes treatment such as manipulation without further screening.

questions.prompt: Priya's upper motor neuron screen shows brisk knee reflexes and a positive Hoffmann sign on both sides. Describe how you would proceed and how you would speak with her about it.

checklist.point: Recognizes bilateral upper motor neuron signs as suggesting possible degenerative cervical myelopathy, needing urgent medical assessment.
Stops or withholds manual techniques such as thrust manipulation, end range mobilization, and mechanical traction.
Arranges prompt communication with her family physician or an urgent care pathway, based on local options, the same day.
Explains findings in plain language without alarming her and without promising or naming a diagnosis as certain.
Checks her understanding using teach back and invites questions and concerns.
Gives safety netting advice: worsening weakness, falls, loss of bladder or bowel control, or severe new pain needs emergency care.
Obtains consent to share information with her physician and explains what will be shared.
Respects her deadline pressure by offering to provide documentation but not allowing it to shape the safety decision.
Documents the findings, the advice given, her response and the communication with the physician.

questions.model_answer:
These findings change my plan. Bilateral brisk reflexes and a Hoffmann sign on both sides are upper motor neuron signs. With her clumsy hands, this makes me suspect that the spinal cord may be affected, a condition called degenerative cervical myelopathy. That is not something I should treat in the clinic as a simple pinched nerve, so my priority is getting her medical assessment promptly.

Here is what I would do in order. First, I stop any technique that could load the neck. That means no thrust manipulation, no end range mobilization and no mechanical traction, even though the assistant has time this week. I would also avoid sustained end range extension exercises. I would let her sit comfortably and finish the examination gently.

Second, I would talk with Priya before she leaves. I would sit down at her level and say something like, 'Some of your reflexes and hand signs tell me that the nerves in your neck might be under more pressure than I first thought. I cannot tell you the cause from my tests alone, and many people with these findings do well, but I want a doctor to look at this soon and probably arrange imaging.' I would avoid naming a frightening condition as certain. Then I would ask her to repeat back in her own words what we have found and what happens next, and I would ask what worries her most. I expect it may be the tax deadline, and I would tell her honestly that her health comes first and that I can provide a note for work.

Third, I would ask her permission to contact her family physician today, explain what I would share, and call or send a same day message with my findings. If the physician cannot see her within a short time, I would suggest an urgent care clinic or emergency department depending on local options, and I would not wait for her next appointment.

Fourth, safety netting. I would tell her to go to the emergency department right away if she notices new weakness in the arms or legs, trouble walking, falls, numbness in the groin or loss of control of bladder or bowel, or sudden severe neck pain.

Finally, I would document the examination, my reasoning, what I told her, her understanding, the consent for sharing information and who I contacted, and arrange a follow up call in a day or two to confirm that she has been seen.

scale.4: Identifies cord involvement, stops loading techniques, arranges same day medical contact with consent, uses clear language and teach back, and gives specific safety netting.
scale.3: Refers appropriately and avoids manipulation but gives less detail on communication, consent or safety netting.
scale.2: Mentions referral but continues some treatment, delays the referral to the next visit, or uses vague communication.
scale.1: Proceeds with manual therapy or traction, or minimizes the findings so that no medical assessment is arranged.

questions.prompt: Priya's physician sees her and starts the imaging process. She tells you she wants to keep seeing you. Discuss the practice management issues you must handle regarding visits, billing, documentation and your team.

checklist.point: Declines to sell or sign her up for the prepaid twelve visit package before the medical findings and plan are known.
Explains that fees and visit use must match clinical need and her insurance benefit, not clinic sales targets.
Tells her openly that her plan pays for ten visits and discusses how to use them, including costs beyond the cap.
Does not assign mechanical traction to the physiotherapist assistant, as the plan is on hold and the therapist must assess suitability.
Describes delegation principles: assessment and plan stay with the physiotherapist, with clear instructions and supervision for any task assigned.
Writes accurate, dated records of findings, decisions, communication and consent, kept as the college requires.
Provides the insurer report only with her consent and limits content to what the insurer needs.
Raises the conflict with the clinic owner if the package pressure continues, and follows the college standards on conflict of interest.
Schedules follow up to match the medical timeline, for instance a check after imaging results.

questions.model_answer:
There are several practice management issues here, and I will take them in turn.

First, the prepaid package. The clinic owner wants therapists to offer twelve visits up front. I would not offer Priya that package now. Her plan is not clear yet, because she may need surgical or other medical care, and a prepaid package would give her a financial reason to keep coming for treatment that may not be right. Under my college's standards, my duty is to the client, and fees and visits have to follow clinical need. I would tell her, 'Right now we do not know what the next step is, so I would rather book one visit at a time.' If the owner presses, I would explain the conflict of interest concern to the owner respectfully and, if needed, refer to the college's guidance on billing and conflicts.

Second, her insurance. Her plan covers ten visits a year. I would confirm with her and the insurer how many she has already used this year, so we both know how many remain. I would be open about this, including what each visit costs and what she would pay herself after the limit, so that she can choose how to use them. I would also keep a few visits available for after her medical assessment, when rehabilitation may be more clearly useful.

Third, the physiotherapist assistant. The assistant has time for mechanical traction, but I will not assign it. Delegation means I keep responsibility for assessment, diagnosis and the plan. A treatment can only be assigned when I judge that it is safe for this client, the task is within the assistant's training, and I give clear instructions and supervise. For Priya, traction is not safe to assign while cord involvement is unresolved. The assistant could help in other ways later, such as supervising a posture and strengthening program once I have cleared it.

Fourth, documentation. I would write clear, dated notes that cover her history, the upper motor neuron findings, my reasoning, the advice given, her consent to contact her physician, who I spoke with, and the safety advice. I keep the record for the length of time my college requires.

Fifth, reports. For her insurer, I would ask for her written consent and give only the information needed for payment and for work, not every detail of her health. If her employer asks for a note, I would write about function and restrictions, not the diagnosis, unless she agrees.

Finally, scheduling. I would book a short check after her imaging so that we adjust the plan to the results rather than to the clinic's calendar.

scale.4: Declines the package with a client centred reason, is open about benefit limits, refuses to delegate traction with reasons, and covers consent based reporting and documentation.
scale.3: Handles most issues correctly but gives thin reasoning on delegation or on reporting consent.
scale.2: Mentions billing and documentation in general terms, or agrees to the package or the delegated traction.
scale.1: Follows the clinic's sales target over client need or shares information with the employer without consent.

safety_or_ethics_point: The buried issue is the mention that Priya has been dropping her coffee cup, which hints at hand clumsiness and possible cervical myelopathy. A competent candidate notices it, adds an upper motor neuron screen, withholds traction and manipulation, arranges prompt medical review with her consent, and resists the package sales pressure.
common_errors: Candidates treat the case as a straightforward C7 radiculopathy and plan traction or manipulation without screening for cord signs. Others recognize the risk but give no plain language explanation, no safety netting, and no plan for consent, billing conflicts or delegation.
examiner_notes: A passing candidate links the pattern to C7, notices the dropped objects without prompting, and acts on the cord signs with a same day medical referral. A failing candidate continues with traction, or lists tests without reasoning. Practice management answers must refuse the package on ethical grounds, not just describe billing.

title: Freezing of gait and falls in Parkinson disease
setting: Hospital based outpatient neurological rehabilitation clinic
client_profile: Walter Okafor is a 68 year old retired bus mechanic with Parkinson disease diagnosed five years ago. He lives with his wife, Grace, in a two storey home with the bedroom upstairs. He takes carbidopa and levodopa four times daily and a dopamine agonist at night. Over three months he has had increased freezing of gait at doorways and when turning, with two near falls and one fall onto his knees without injury. He walks 25 metres with a rollator. Timed Up and Go is 19 seconds and 10 metre walk is 0.7 metres per second. He is at Hoehn and Yahr stage 3. Sitting blood pressure is 128 over 76 and standing at three minutes is 104 over 68, and he feels lightheaded. Freezing is worse when his medication is wearing off, usually mid morning. He rates mood as low and reports poor sleep. Montreal Cognitive Assessment is 24 out of 30.
clinical_scenario: Grace says Walter is stubborn and will not use his walker at home. She asks you to tell her everything about his test results so she can manage him. Walter says little during this part. He mentions that he drove to the clinic himself and nearly missed a stop sign last week when his legs would not move on the pedal. He asks whether you can help him stay active so that he can keep driving his grandchildren to hockey on Saturdays.

questions.prompt: Describe the physiotherapy plan you would develop with Walter, including goals, the main interventions, how you would address freezing, and how you would measure progress.

checklist.point: Sets patient centred goals with Walter, such as safe household mobility, fewer falls and continued community activity.
Schedules sessions and home practice during the on medication period, and notes the wearing off pattern for planning.
Includes cueing strategies for freezing: external visual, auditory (metronome) and attentional cues, with practice in doorways and turns.
Teaches turning strategies using wide arcs and avoiding pivoting, and rehearses dual task walking.
Prescribes progressive aerobic and strengthening exercise with intensity, frequency and progression stated.
Includes balance training and fall prevention education, and a plan for getting up from the floor.
Addresses the lightheadedness: orthostatic hypotension screening and referral to the physician and advice on slow position changes.
Reviews the home, including stairs and bedroom location, and walker use, with an occupational therapy referral if needed.
Selects outcome measures: Timed Up and Go, 10 metre walk, Mini BESTest or similar, fall diary, and sets reassessment timing.

questions.model_answer:
My plan is built around three goals that I would set with Walter himself, not only with Grace. I expect they would be to move safely in his house, to fall less, and to stay active enough to keep up his Saturday hockey trips. I would ask him to state in his own words which matters most.

I would start with timing. His freezing is worst when his medication wears off in the mid morning. I would schedule his visits and his home practice in his best on period, about an hour after a dose, and I would ask him to keep a simple diary of doses, freezing and falls for two weeks so that we can see the pattern.

For freezing itself, I would teach cueing. Cues are outside signals that help start movement. Visual cues could be strips of tape on the floor at doorways. Auditory cues could be a metronome app at a comfortable step rate, and attentional cues like thinking 'big step'. We would practise at the real trouble spots, doorways and turns, and we would add a second task such as carrying a cup. For turning, I would teach a wide arc rather than pivoting on the spot.

For exercise, evidence supports progressive training in Parkinson disease. I would start with aerobic work such as treadmill or bike at a moderate level, three times per week for thirty minutes, building slowly, along with lower limb strengthening twice a week, and balance work such as weight shifts, stepping in different directions, and standing up and sitting down. I would progress when he completes the work with good control. I would include a falls plan with him and Grace on how to get up from the floor.

I am concerned about his blood pressure dropping when he stands, from 128 to 104 systolic, with lightheadedness. This can cause falls independently of freezing. I would teach slow position changes and ankle pumps, and I would send a note to his neurologist or family doctor, because medication or hydration may need to be reviewed.

His home matters too. The bedroom is upstairs, and he is not using the walker indoors. I would ask about stairs, bathroom rails and lighting, and I would involve an occupational therapist for a home assessment.

For progress, I would repeat the Timed Up and Go and the 10 metre walk every four to six weeks, add the Mini BESTest, and count falls in his diary. I would reassess sooner if he falls or his medication changes.

scale.4: Gives goals set with Walter, on period timing, specific cueing and turning strategies, dosed exercise, orthostatic hypotension action, home review and outcome measures with a reassessment schedule.
scale.3: Provides a sound plan with cueing and exercise but misses the blood pressure issue, dosing, or reassessment timing.
scale.2: Lists generic exercises without cueing, timing or measures, and does not link choices to the case.
scale.1: Proposes unsafe or irrelevant interventions, or ignores freezing and fall risk.

questions.prompt: Grace asks you to give her all of Walter's results so she can manage him, and Walter stays silent. Explain how you would handle the conversation, including safety concerns and Walter's wishes.

checklist.point: Speaks directly with Walter and checks that he understands the discussion and wants Grace involved.
Obtains Walter's consent before sharing his personal health information with Grace, and agrees on what and how much.
Assesses capacity to consent in a respectful way, recognizing that a MoCA of 24 does not by itself mean incapacity.
Explores why Walter does not use the walker indoors, such as pride, space or freezing, using open questions.
Acknowledges Grace's stress and invites her view while keeping Walter at the centre of decisions.
Offers shared decision making on a fall plan: walker use, night time routes, bathroom set up, medical alert option.
Asks about the driving near miss and raises driving safety with Walter in a non judgemental way.
Provides information on caregiver supports and Parkinson organizations in his region.
Avoids labelling Walter as stubborn and describes behaviour in terms of barriers.

questions.model_answer:
The first thing I would do is turn toward Walter. Grace is asking for his information, but it belongs to him, and he has been quiet. So I would say, 'Walter, I would like to include Grace if you are comfortable. What would you like me to share with her?' If he agrees, I would also ask what level of detail he wants her to have, and I would write down his consent. If he says he wants some things kept private, I respect that. His MoCA of 24 out of 30 shows some mild difficulty, but that alone does not mean he cannot decide. I would assume he has capacity, explain things in short, clear steps, check his understanding, and only raise capacity more formally if I see real doubt about his ability to understand and weigh the information.

Next, I would try to understand the walker. Calling him stubborn does not help us. I would ask him, 'What makes the walker hard to use at home?' It might be narrow hallways, embarrassment, or because freezing happens at doorways where the walker catches. Then I would offer options: moving furniture, a different walker, or practice with cues. We would agree on a plan he chooses, like using it at night and on the stairs, and I would discuss night time routes to the bathroom, lighting, and a medical alert device. This is shared decision making, not a rule I set.

For Grace, I would thank her for her effort. I would tell her, with Walter's permission, what we are working on and how she can help, for instance by cueing rather than rushing him or pulling on him. I would also ask how she is coping and give her information about caregiver support and the regional Parkinson society.

The other safety issue is driving. Walter told me that his legs would not move on the pedal and he almost missed a stop sign. I would not ignore that. I would ask him gently, 'Tell me about that day. How do you feel about driving right now?' Freezing, slower reaction time, medication timing and sleepiness can all affect driving. I would explain my concern, encourage him to talk with his physician about a driving assessment, and ask him whether he can arrange alternatives for a while, like having Grace drive or using ride services. I would document the discussion and his decisions.

scale.4: Centres Walter, gets explicit consent before sharing, explores walker barriers, uses shared decision making, supports Grace, and raises the driving near miss with a clear plan.
scale.3: Handles consent and the walker well but gives limited attention to the driving issue or to Grace's needs.
scale.2: Shares information with Grace without clear consent, or lists safety advice without involving Walter.
scale.1: Shares results freely with Grace, dismisses Walter, or ignores the driving near miss.

questions.prompt: Walter declines to stop driving and asks you not to tell anyone about the near miss. Discuss your professional responsibilities, including confidentiality, reporting, scope and documentation.

checklist.point: States the duty of confidentiality and that disclosure without consent is allowed only where law permits or where serious risk requires it.
Says the physiotherapist assesses function but does not decide fitness to drive, which is a medical and licensing decision.
Recommends he speak with his physician and, with his consent, communicates the concern to the physician.
Checks the provincial rules on reporting unsafe drivers and what applies to physiotherapists versus physicians.
Explains the limits of confidentiality to Walter openly rather than acting behind his back.
Uses motivational and respectful communication to explore his reasons and offers alternatives to preserve his role with his grandchildren.
Documents what was said, advice given, his response and any discussion with others.
Seeks advice from the college, a manager or the privacy officer for a difficult decision.
Continues to treat him and keeps the relationship rather than discharging him because of the disagreement.

questions.model_answer:
This is a conflict between two duties: keeping Walter's information confidential, and protecting other people on the road. I would work through it step by step.

First, confidentiality. Walter's health information is protected under provincial health privacy law and my college's standards. I should not share it without his consent, unless the law allows or requires it, or there is a serious and immediate risk of harm. A single near miss that he told me about is not usually an immediate emergency, so I would begin by trying to get his agreement.

Second, scope. Deciding whether a person is fit to drive is not my role. That decision belongs to physicians and the provincial licensing authority, who can order a formal driving assessment. What I can contribute is my observations of function: freezing, slowed movement, and orthostatic changes. I would be honest with Walter that I cannot clear him or ban him from driving, but that I think the near miss matters.

Third, reporting rules. These differ by province. In some provinces, physicians are required to report certain medical conditions that affect driving, while other health professionals may have discretion or no duty at all. I would not guess. I would check my regulator's guidance, and if I am still unsure I would call the college or speak with my manager or the privacy officer before taking any step on my own.

Fourth, how I talk with him. I would not argue. I would say, 'I understand driving the grandchildren means a great deal to you. I am worried about what happened at the stop sign. Can we think together about how to keep you in that role safely?' I would explain that if I think the risk is serious I might need to speak with his doctor, so that nothing happens behind his back. I would ask for his consent to send his physician my observations. I would offer alternatives, such as a formal driving evaluation, driving only at his best medication times for now, or having Grace drive to hockey while he rides along and helps coach.

Fifth, documentation. I would record his statements, my advice, his decision, any consent or refusal, who I consulted, and my reasons.

And finally, I would keep treating him. Discharging him because he disagrees would remove a support and make things less safe.

scale.4: Balances confidentiality and public safety, states scope limits, checks provincial reporting rules, seeks consent and advice, offers alternatives, documents, and continues care.
scale.3: Identifies confidentiality and scope but is vague about provincial reporting rules or about seeking consultation.
scale.2: Either breaches confidentiality without a legal basis or ignores the safety concern, with little documentation.
scale.1: Reports without any process or consent, or decides Walter's fitness to drive on their own.

safety_or_ethics_point: The buried issue is the near miss while driving, in the context of freezing, orthostatic drops and mild cognitive change. A competent candidate raises it with Walter respectfully, explains the limits of confidentiality, respects scope, checks the provincial rules, and involves the physician with consent.
common_errors: Candidates give a generic exercise plan and forget cueing or the on medication timing. They also share information with Grace without asking Walter, or they either ignore the driving risk or decide he is unfit to drive themselves.
examiner_notes: A pass shows a tailored plan for freezing with on period timing, spots the blood pressure drop, puts Walter's consent first, and handles the driving dilemma within scope. A fail prescribes standard balance exercises only or breaches confidentiality.

title: Heel pain in an elementary school teacher
setting: Outpatient physiotherapy clinic
client_profile: Mei Ling Chow is a 46 year old elementary school teacher who stands and walks on hard floors for most of the day. For ten weeks she has had sharp pain under the medial heel on her right foot, worst with her first steps in the morning and after sitting. She rates pain 7 out of 10 at its worst and 3 out of 10 later in the day. She is 168 cm tall and weighs 84 kg. She stopped her walking program because of pain. Medications are a daily multivitamin and ibuprofen as needed. Five weeks ago she finished a seven day course of ciprofloxacin for a urinary tract infection. Examination shows tenderness at the medial calcaneal tubercle, pain on dorsiflexion of the toes with the ankle dorsiflexed, ankle dorsiflexion of 5 degrees on the right and 12 on the left, and a tight gastrocnemius. There is mild tenderness at the Achilles insertion. Foot Posture Index is mildly pronated. Neurological screen and the calf squeeze test are normal. Foot and Ankle Ability Measure sports sub-scale is not used. Foot Function Index pain subscale is 52 out of 100.
clinical_scenario: Mei Ling's family physician has told her that a corticosteroid injection is available if physiotherapy does not help within a few weeks. The school principal has told her she cannot sit during lessons, and teachers are expected to supervise outdoor recess on uneven ground. Her insurance covers custom orthotics only with a prescription from a physician or chiropodist. She is nervous about missing work and asks you to explain the plan in a way she can share with the principal.

questions.prompt: Describe the treatment plan you would develop for Mei Ling, including interventions, dosage and progression, outcome measures and how you would decide when to reassess or change the plan.

checklist.point: Sets goals with Mei Ling such as pain under 3 out of 10 for school days and a return to walking.
Educates on load management: reducing aggravating load without complete rest, footwear with support and cushioning, avoiding bare feet on hard floors.
Prescribes a calf stretching program with duration and frequency, and plantar fascia specific stretching.
Prescribes plantar fascia loading with sets, repetitions and tempo, starting with isometric or low load two leg work and holding added load until the Achilles tenderness settles.
Considers short term options: taping, a prefabricated insole or heel cup, and manual therapy for the calf, explaining modest evidence.
