Elicits his goals and uses shared decision-making about activity and school.

questions.model_answer:
My first step is to let the orthopedic team know about the sensory change and deltoid weakness today. I would phone, explain what I found and ask whether they want him seen sooner, or want nerve studies or imaging arranged. I would explain what I found and ask Mateo for his agreement to share it with the orthopedic team today, then phone. This does not change how kindly I treat him, but it does change what I can safely ask the shoulder to do.

For protection of the shoulder, I would avoid the position that puts the anterior capsule at risk, which is abduction combined with external rotation, like throwing or reaching behind the head. I would avoid forced stretching and passive pushing into end range. For the first weeks I would stay with gentle, pain-limited movement: pendulums only if tolerated, elbow, wrist and hand movement every day to prevent stiffness and swelling, scapular setting, and isometric rotator cuff work in neutral with the arm by his side. I would keep deltoid loading very light until I know the state of the nerve, because pushing a weak deltoid into big efforts leads to poor movement patterns and compensation. If the deltoid shows signs of recovery, I would progress to assisted elevation in the scapular plane, for example table slides, and later to light resisted work. For the sling, I would follow the physician's instruction, but in general a sling is for comfort and early protection, and I would encourage him to take it off to move his elbow and hand several times daily and when seated at his desk.

I need to be honest about rugby. He will not be ready in four weeks. A joint that recently dislocated, with a possible nerve injury and no strength or control yet, would be at high risk of dislocating again and of damaging the nerve or other structures. I would say that directly, and also explain what I can do: get him moving, keep his fitness up with lower body and cardio work that does not stress the shoulder, and let him help set the criteria for return, such as full motion, symmetrical strength, confidence, and a decision from the surgeon.

I would raise the idea of seeing an orthopedic shoulder surgeon early. In young contact athletes, surgical stabilization is often discussed after a first dislocation because recurrence is common. I would not decide for him. I would explain the choices, which are rehabilitation first or early surgery, with the risks and benefits of each, and encourage him to ask the surgeon about them.

As a safety net, I would teach him to tell me or the clinic promptly if numbness spreads, his hand becomes cold, pale or weak, he feels the shoulder slip, or pain worsens suddenly. I would ask what matters most to him, maybe school, work or sport, and make the plan around that.

scale.4: Communicates the nerve finding, specifies positions and loads to avoid, gives staged safe rehabilitation, gives a clear no on rugby with reasons, discusses surgical referral as a choice, and teaches warning signs.
scale.3: Safe plan with precautions and rugby advice, but incomplete on communication, nerve implications or shared decisions.
scale.2: Generic shoulder exercises without precautions or timeline.
scale.1: Clears rugby, applies aggressive stretching or strengthening, or ignores the neurological finding.

questions.prompt: Mateo asks you to explain what his friend called the surgery thing, and his father keeps answering for him. Describe how you would communicate with them.

checklist.point: Speaks directly to Mateo as the patient and invites his own understanding and preferences.
Asks Mateo privately or openly whether he wants an interpreter or his father to translate, and offers a professional interpreter.
Uses plain language and avoids jargon such as Bankart, labrum or capsule without simple explanation.
Explains recurrence risk and surgical stabilization in balanced terms, covering benefits and risks.
Uses teach-back and checks understanding rather than accepting yes.
Uses visuals or a model and gives written information in a language he prefers.
Acknowledges his anxiety and responds to emotion with empathy.
Includes his father respectfully while maintaining Mateo's privacy and consent.

questions.model_answer:
I would begin by setting up the conversation so that Mateo is at its center. I would greet both of them and then turn to Mateo, and say that I want to hear things from him, and that his father is welcome to help. I would ask him in a warm, non-pressuring way: Which language would you like to use for the health parts of today? Would you like a professional interpreter, or are you comfortable with me and your father helping? Many people are fluent in everyday English but find medical terms hard, and saying yes to a clinician does not always mean they understood. I would make clear that using an interpreter is normal, free and confidential, and it would let his father be a father instead of an interpreter. If Mateo prefers his father to help, I would respect that, and I would still check his understanding directly.

For the explanation, I would start by asking what he already knows from his friend and what worries him, because that tells me where to start. Then I would use plain words and a shoulder model or a simple drawing. I might say: The shoulder is like a golf ball sitting on a tee. When it came out the front, the soft rim of the socket, the tee, can tear, and the ball can get a small dent. After a first dislocation, especially in young men who play contact sports, the shoulder pops out again often, and each time there is more damage. Surgery is an operation to repair the rim and tighten the front so it is less likely to come out. Some people do very well with physiotherapy only, others have repeat dislocations and then choose surgery. Nobody can know ahead of time which way it will go, and I would not pressure him either way. I would describe benefits and risks of both options at a level he can follow: surgery lowers the chance of re-dislocation but involves anesthesia, recovery of several months and small risks of stiffness or infection, while rehabilitation alone avoids surgery but has a higher chance of the shoulder coming out again. I would tell him a surgeon is the right person to advise, and I can help with the referral.

I would use teach-back: Just so I know I explained it clearly, can you tell me in your own words what the choices are? If he repeats only yes, I would try again with a different explanation, not repeat the same one louder. I would give him a short written summary in Spanish if he wants it, and a diagram.

I would acknowledge his worry about the final games: it sounds like rugby matters a lot to you, and I want to help you get back to it safely. I would also include his father: I would ask him whether he has questions, and thank him for his support, while pointing out gently that Mateo decides about his own care. I would also tell them they can call the clinic with questions at any time.

scale.4: Centres Mateo, offers interpreter and explores language preference, explains surgery and recurrence in plain balanced terms with visuals, uses teach-back, handles anxiety and the father's role respectfully.
scale.3: Plain language and teach-back present but interpreter or role of the father not addressed.
scale.2: Explains with jargon, talks mostly to the father, or gives one-sided information.
scale.1: Pressures toward surgery or rehabilitation, ignores language barrier, or dismisses concerns.

safety_or_ethics_point: A new lateral upper arm sensory loss with a weak deltoid suggests an axillary nerve injury not noted at discharge. The candidate must find it, tell the physician, and avoid loading it. A communication layer is the risk of the father answering for the patient and Mateo's yes not meaning understanding.
common_errors: Concentrating on range of motion and instability tests and missing the nerve deficit, or allowing rugby return on a calendar. Using the father as interpreter without asking Mateo and accepting yes as understanding.
examiner_notes: Passes find and escalate the axillary nerve finding, give specific position precautions, say no to rugby with reasons, and communicate in plain language with an interpreter option. Failures treat this as a routine post-dislocation protocol.

title: Exercise rehabilitation for chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
setting: Hospital outpatient cardiac rehabilitation program
client_profile: Walter Okafor is a 74 year old retired bus driver with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, left ventricular ejection fraction 30 percent on echocardiogram 6 months ago, from ischemic cardiomyopathy. New York Heart Association class III. He takes ramipril, bisoprolol, spironolactone and furosemide. He lives with his wife. Today resting blood pressure is 104/64 mmHg, heart rate 78 beats per minute regular, SpO2 94 percent at rest. His weight is 2.1 kg above his dry weight recorded last week, gained over the past three days. He has trace pitting ankle edema, two pillows at night (previously one), and walks about 100 metres on level ground before stopping for breathlessness. Six minute walk distance at intake was 240 metres. He has mild dizziness on standing, with blood pressure falling from 104/64 sitting to 96/60 standing. He has an implantable cardioverter defibrillator placed two years ago.
clinical_scenario: Walter tells you he stopped taking his water pill on the weekend because he was tired of rushing to the toilet at his granddaughter's recital. His wife says he has had less energy and slept poorly. He wants to start the 12 week exercise program today and says the weight on the clinic scale must be wrong because his home scale showed less. He asks whether you can tell him whether he should stop the pills that make him dizzy.

questions.prompt: Describe the goals and the plan of care you would propose for Walter over the 12 week program, including how you would choose exercise intensity and measure progress.

checklist.point: Sets person-centred goals such as walking tolerance, ability to attend family events, symptom control, and self-management.
Includes baseline and repeat outcome measures such as six minute walk test, symptom scale, and NYHA class.
Chooses low to moderate intensity using RPE (about 11 to 13 on the Borg 6 to 20 scale) and talk test, not a heart rate target alone, as beta blockade limits heart rate.
Plans a longer warm-up and cool-down and gradual progression from short intervals with rest to continuous exercise.
Adds light resistance training and balance work as tolerated.
Specifies monitoring: weight, blood pressure, symptoms, SpO2, and rhythm if available, at each session.
Includes education on daily weights, symptom diary, fluid and sodium advice per team, and medication adherence.
States reassessment triggers for holding or modifying exercise, such as weight gain or worsening symptoms.
Confirms the ICD detection rate with the device clinic and keeps exercise heart rate at least 10 to 20 beats per minute below it.

questions.model_answer:
My goals would come from Walter, so I would begin by asking what he most wants to do. It sounds like attending family events without rushing, and walking farther. I would turn those into measurable goals over 12 weeks: for example to walk 400 metres on level ground without stopping, to climb one flight of stairs, to improve his six minute walk distance from 240 by a clinically meaningful amount such as 30 metres or more, to reduce symptoms, and to be able to manage his weights and medications himself. 

For outcome measures, I would use the six minute walk test, repeated at 6 and 12 weeks if he is stable, a symptom scale such as a Borg dyspnea rating, a heart failure quality of life questionnaire, and a functional test like the sit to stand. I would track NYHA class by history.

Intensity is the key decision. Because he takes bisoprolol, his heart rate response is blunted, so I would not prescribe by a percentage of maximum heart rate. I would prescribe by perceived exertion, aiming for about 11 to 13 on the Borg 6 to 20 scale, which is fairly light to somewhat hard, and use the talk test, where he can speak in short sentences. I would begin with short bouts of 3 to 5 minutes of walking or stationary cycling with equal or longer rests, accumulating 10 to 15 minutes in total, with a longer warm-up and cool-down of 5 to 10 minutes each to avoid sudden changes in blood pressure, especially given his drop on standing. Over several weeks I would increase duration first and then intensity, aiming for 20 to 30 minutes of continuous activity three times a week, along with daily walking at home. Once he is stable I would add light resistance exercise, for example sit to stand and light weights, with breathing throughout and no breath holding, and balance training, since he is dizzy and at risk of falls.

Because Walter has an ICD, I would confirm its detection rate with the device clinic and keep his exercise heart rate at least 10 to 20 beats per minute below it. At each visit I would check weight against his dry weight, blood pressure sitting and standing, heart rate, SpO2, symptoms such as breathlessness, orthopnea and swelling, and rhythm if monitoring is available. I would compare it to rules about when to hold exercise, such as a weight gain of more than about 2 kg over 3 days, worsening swelling or breathlessness, a drop in blood pressure with symptoms, or new chest pain or palpitations.

Education is part of the plan: daily morning weights on the same scale, a diary of symptoms and weights, the medications he takes and why, what the team has advised for sodium and fluids, and how to pace activity. I would use teach-back with Walter and his wife. I would reassess every few weeks and adjust, and I would talk with the heart failure team about any changes.

scale.4: Person-centred measurable goals, outcome measures, intensity by RPE with beta-blocker rationale, progression, monitoring, education and clear modification triggers.
scale.3: Sound exercise plan and measures but intensity rationale or monitoring and triggers are incomplete.
scale.2: Generic exercise prescription based on age-predicted heart rate or without monitoring.
scale.1: Prescribes high intensity or ignores heart failure specific safety.

questions.prompt: Walter wants to start the first session today. Explain your decision and how you would involve Walter and his wife in the plan for today.

checklist.point: Recognizes the weight gain of about 2 kg in 3 days, extra pillow and stopped diuretic as signs of possible decompensation.
Holds the exercise session today and explains why in plain words.
Contacts the heart failure clinic or responsible physician the same day for review, with consent.
Checks the clinic scale against the home scale and does not dismiss his concern, and does not assume the clinic scale is wrong.
Addresses orthostatic drop and dizziness, including fall prevention advice.

Gives warning signs requiring emergency care, such as chest pain, severe breathlessness, fainting, two or more ICD shocks or a shock with symptoms, and a same-day clinic call for a single shock when well.
Explores his reasons for skipping the diuretic and plans practical strategies with the team.
Offers a safe alternative today such as education, and rebooks promptly.

questions.model_answer:
I would not run an exercise session today, and I would explain it carefully so that Walter does not feel turned away. What I see together is a weight about 2 kilograms above his dry weight in three days, a second pillow at night, a bit more swelling, less energy, and he stopped his water pill over the weekend. In heart failure, those are the classic signs that fluid may be building up and the heart is not coping. A rise of around 2 kilograms in three days is the usual trigger for heart failure patients to call their team. Exercise now could worsen his breathlessness, and with an ejection fraction of 30 percent and an ICD, I would rather he be reviewed first. I would say that this is a pause to protect him, not a refusal to help.

He thinks our scale is wrong. I would take that seriously. I would recheck his weight on a second scale, with light clothing and no shoes, and I would ask him to tell me what his home reading was, when he weighs and what he wears. If the numbers differ, I would still contact the team, because the swelling, pillows and missed medication tell the same story. I would not dismiss him.

I would then call the heart failure clinic or his cardiologist the same day, with Walter's permission, give them the readings, the symptoms and the missed diuretic, and ask whether he should be seen today. If I cannot reach anyone, I would advise him to go to the emergency department or call his family doctor urgently, depending on his symptoms. I would pass on that he had dizziness on standing as well, since his pressure fell by only 8 over 4 on standing, below the usual 20 over 10 criterion for orthostatic hypotension, yet he is symptomatic, which may relate to his heart failure medications and is another reason for a physician to review. I would not tell him what to do about his medications, because that is the prescriber's decision. For the dizziness, I would suggest rising slowly, sitting at the edge first and holding a support.

I would give Walter and his wife clear warning signs. Call 911 for chest pain, severe breathlessness at rest, fainting, two or more ICD shocks, or a shock with symptoms such as feeling unwell or a fast irregular heartbeat. Call the clinic the same day for a single shock when he feels well, increased swelling, needing more pillows, or further weight gain. I would ask them to repeat these back.

I would also ask about the diuretic. It is common to skip it before an outing because of the urgency. Rather than judging, I would ask what makes it hard, and tell the team so they can adjust timing, which may solve it. His wife can help with a simple chart for weights and medications. Today I can use the visit for teaching, such as how to take daily weights, and for planning, and I would rebook for as soon as the team says it is safe, ideally within days.

scale.4: Recognizes decompensation signs, holds exercise, contacts team same day, gives clear emergency and call-the-clinic signs, respects his scale concern and explores the missed diuretic without judgement.
scale.3: Holds exercise and refers but warning signs, orthostatic issue or collaboration are incomplete.
scale.2: Modifies to light exercise or continues with monitoring only.
scale.1: Proceeds with the full session, tells him to restart or stop medications, or dismisses weight gain.

questions.prompt: Walter asks whether you can tell him to stop the medication that makes him dizzy, and his wife asks to see his chart. Discuss your professional responsibilities.

checklist.point: States that advising on starting, stopping or changing medication is outside physiotherapy scope and belongs to the prescriber.
Communicates the dizziness and orthostatic readings to the physician or pharmacist in writing or by phone.
Tells Walter not to stop medications on his own and why, and gives a plan to reach the team quickly.
Requires Walter's consent before sharing chart information with his wife, and asks what he wants her to know.
Explains how to access records through the proper process and respects his right of access.
Documents findings, advice, referral and conversations accurately and promptly.
Recognizes his wife's role as a support and involves her with his permission in education.
Keeps communication within the interprofessional team clear about who is responsible for follow-up.

questions.model_answer:
Two requests, two different professional issues. I will deal with the medication first. Deciding whether Walter should stop a medication is a prescribing decision, outside the scope of physiotherapy. I can observe and measure the effects, such as his dizziness on standing and the fall in blood pressure from 104 over 64 to 96 over 60, and I should report those, but I cannot tell him to stop or change anything. I would say that clearly and kindly: I know the dizziness is annoying and scary, and I take it seriously. I am not the right person to decide about the medications, but I will make sure the right person hears about it today. I would also tell him not to stop any heart medication on his own. Stopping drugs such as the beta blocker or ramipril suddenly can make heart failure worse, and the doctor may be able to adjust the dose or timing. I would link this to what he already did with the water pill, without blaming him, and say that this is exactly the kind of thing the team wants to hear about.

Then I would act. I would call or send a written message to his cardiologist or heart failure nurse, or his family doctor or pharmacist, whoever is responsible, with the readings, when the dizziness occurs, the missed diuretic, the weight gain and the swelling. I would write down who I spoke to and what they said, and I would tell Walter what to expect. If the response is delayed, I would follow up rather than assume it is dealt with. A pharmacist review of his medications could also help, and I could suggest that to him.

Now his wife's request. His health information belongs to him. His wife is clearly an important support, and she is welcome in sessions, but I need Walter's permission before showing her his chart or discussing details outside the room. So I would ask him privately or in front of her, depending on his preference: How much would you like your wife to know and see? Some people are happy to share everything. If he agrees, I would document his consent and what is covered. If he prefers that I share only certain things, I would respect that. A patient also has the right to see his own record, so I would explain how to request a copy from the hospital's health records department under the privacy rules, and I would not simply hand over my notes to someone else.

I would document everything accurately and promptly, including the objective findings, my education about warning signs, the advice that he should not stop his medications, the communication with the team, and his consent decisions. Finally, I would be clear with the team about who is following up, so that Walter is not left waiting.

scale.4: States medication scope boundary, advises against self-stopping, escalates findings to prescriber, handles wife's request through consent and record access rules, and documents.
scale.3: Recognizes scope and consent but does not communicate with the team or explain access to records.
scale.2: Gives general advice on medications or shares chart details with the wife without consent.
scale.1: Tells him to stop the medication, shares records freely, or fails to document.

safety_or_ethics_point: The buried issue is early decompensated heart failure: weight gain of about 2 kg in 3 days, an extra pillow, edema and a skipped diuretic. Exercise must be held and the team contacted the same day. The professional layer is medication advice being outside scope and consent before sharing information with the wife.
common_errors: Starting the exercise session at low intensity because he wants to, or using an age-predicted heart rate target despite a beta blocker. Telling him to stop the dizziness-causing medication, or showing the chart to his wife.
examiner_notes: A pass sets person-centred goals with RPE-based intensity, recognizes the decompensation signs, holds the session and escalates the same day, and respects scope and consent. Candidates who give a generic cardiac rehabilitation prescription fail.

title: Early mobilization after a left hemisphere stroke in inpatient rehabilitation
setting: Inpatient stroke rehabilitation unit in a regional hospital
client_profile: Harold Beaulieu is a 70 year old retired electrician, three weeks after an ischemic stroke affecting the left middle cerebral artery territory, with right hemiparesis. He has atrial fibrillation and hypertension, and takes an anticoagulant started after the stroke, plus an antihypertensive. He has mild expressive aphasia: he understands simple instructions and responds with single words. Right upper limb strength is 2 out of 5 proximally and 1 out of 5 distally. Right lower limb hip flexion is 3 out of 5, knee extension 3 out of 5, ankle dorsiflexion 1 out of 5. Tone is mildly increased at the right elbow flexors. Sitting balance is good, standing needs moderate assistance of one with a knee block. Berg Balance Scale 18 out of 56. A palpable gap is present at the right glenohumeral joint with the arm unsupported. Resting blood pressure is 128/78 mmHg, heart rate 72 irregular. He has had a urinary catheter removed 2 days ago. He wants to go home to his wife by the end of the month.
clinical_scenario: You are one of two physiotherapists on the unit, with 14 patients and one physiotherapy assistant shared with another team. The rehabilitation team plans to increase standing practice this week. This morning Harold's wife says his right leg looked bigger yesterday and he winced when the nurse touched his calf. The assistant has asked whether she can take Harold for standing and walking practice at 10 o'clock because your afternoon is full, and she says another assistant did that with him last week.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would approach your assessment today, including which findings you would prioritize and how you would interpret them for planning rehabilitation.

checklist.point: Examines the right calf for swelling, warmth, tenderness, redness, and compares circumference, because of the wife's report.
Recognizes immobility, stroke and age as risk factors for deep vein thrombosis and that anticoagulation does not exclude it.
Checks vital signs and asks about chest pain, breathlessness, or cough as screening for pulmonary embolism.
Interprets motor findings: distal weakness greater than proximal (ankle dorsiflexion and distal arm 1 out of 5), mild spasticity, foot drop, and expected recovery patterns.
Interprets Berg score of 18 as high fall risk and need for assisted transfers and walking.
Identifies the glenohumeral subluxation and its implications for handling and pain.
Chooses communication methods for aphasia such as short instructions, gestures and yes/no questions, and checks comprehension.
Plans additional measures such as 10 metre walk, sit to stand, cognitive and neglect screening, and orthostatic blood pressure.

questions.model_answer:
My first priority is the report from his wife about the right leg, because it might change everything else I do today. Harold has several strong risk factors for a deep vein thrombosis: a recent stroke, a paralysed leg, reduced mobility, and age. His anticoagulant lowers the risk, but it does not remove it, and the wife's observations of a bigger leg and wincing on touch are exactly what I need to take seriously. So before any standing practice I would look at the leg. I would compare both calves and thighs for swelling, warmth, redness, visible veins, and tenderness along the calf, and measure circumference 10 centimetres below the tibial tuberosity on both sides. I would not massage the calf or do any vigorous passive stretching. Physical examination alone cannot rule a DVT in or out, so a positive or even equivocal finding would be sent for a medical assessment rather than interpreted by me. I would also ask about chest pain, shortness of breath, cough or a fast heart rate, and check his heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate and oxygen saturation. His atrial fibrillation makes a pulse irregular, so I would pay attention to rate and symptoms.

If the leg looks normal, I would continue the rest of the assessment but with caution. For motor findings, he has right distal weakness greater than proximal: the arm is 2 out of 5 proximally and 1 out of 5 distally, and ankle dorsiflexion is 1 out of 5 against 3 out of 5 at the hip and knee, with increased tone in the elbow flexors. The fair hip and knee strength is helpful for standing and walking, but the foot drop needs an ankle foot orthosis or similar to manage the foot drop. A Berg score of 18 out of 56 puts him at high risk of falls, so I would plan for hands-on assistance with transfers and walking, and good footwear and a gait belt. The palpable gap at the shoulder suggests glenohumeral subluxation, which is common with a flaccid arm. I would avoid pulling on the arm during transfers, support the arm on a table or tray when sitting, and educate the nursing team and his wife.

Communication matters because of his aphasia. I would use short, clear sentences, gestures and demonstration, check that he has understood with yes or no questions or by asking him to show me, and allow time for his responses. I would screen for neglect and cognition as well, because they affect safety.

Additional measures include sit to stand tests, a 10 metre walk test when it is safe, orthostatic blood pressure, and the Berg for tracking. My plan would be that if the calf examination is positive or I am uncertain, no standing or walking happens until a physician has reviewed him, otherwise I proceed with a graded, assisted program.

scale.4: Prioritizes DVT and PE screening before mobilization, interprets motor, balance and shoulder findings, adapts for aphasia, and plans appropriate measures.
scale.3: Notes the calf concern but screening incomplete, or interprets findings without plan implications.
scale.2: Focuses on motor and balance without addressing the calf report.
scale.1: Ignores the calf or proposes massage or standing before assessment.

questions.prompt: On examination, the right calf is 3 cm larger than the left, warm and tender. Harold wants to keep practising standing because he is determined to go home. Explain what you would do and how you would involve him.

checklist.point: Stops standing, walking and vigorous leg exercise and keeps him at rest in a safe position pending medical review.
Notifies the physician or nurse in charge immediately, using clear information such as SBAR.
Does not massage or rub the calf.
Monitors for pulmonary embolism signs and tells nursing staff what to watch for.
Explains the situation to Harold and his wife using aphasia-friendly communication and obtains his understanding and assent.
Acknowledges his motivation and describes what can continue safely, such as upper body, trunk and seated activities as medically allowed.
Gives instructions for the team about positioning, arm support and fall prevention in the meantime.
Documents the findings, communication and the activity plan.

questions.model_answer:
Now that the right calf is 3 centimetres bigger than the left, warm and tender, with his risk factors, I would treat this as a possible deep vein thrombosis until a physician says otherwise. A clot can break loose and travel to the lungs, and exercise like standing and walking could make that more likely. So I would stop any standing, walking and vigorous leg exercise now. I would keep Harold resting in a comfortable position in bed or chair, with the leg supported, and I would not massage or rub the calf.

I would tell the physician and the nurse in charge right away, in person or by phone, not by leaving a note. I would use a clear structure. Situation: Mr. Beaulieu has a swollen, warm, tender right calf, 3 centimetres larger than the left. Background: three weeks post left MCA stroke, atrial fibrillation on an anticoagulant, reduced mobility, catheter removed two days ago. Assessment: I am concerned about a possible DVT, and I have stopped mobilization. Request: please review him today and consider a diagnostic ultrasound and decide on the activity plan. I would ask for clear instructions about activity until they decide.

I would also tell the nurse what to look for, so that the whole team is watching for a pulmonary embolism: sudden shortness of breath, chest pain, a fast heart rate, coughing blood, low oxygen saturation, or a sudden change in his condition. If any of those happen, the team should activate the emergency response right away.

For Harold, I would explain what I found and why we are pausing. Because he has aphasia, I would use short sentences, a calm voice, a drawing of a leg and a vein, and gestures. I would say something like: Your leg is swollen and sore. It may be a blood clot. We stop walking for now. The doctor will check. Then I would check that he understands by asking him to point to the leg that is the concern, and asking yes or no questions. I would include his wife, who noticed the swelling, and thank her, since it was her observation that mattered.

I know how determined he is to go home, so I would not leave him with only a no. I would tell him that his goal is still the goal, and that this pause is to keep him safe. I would offer what is safe, with the physician's agreement: seated trunk exercises, work on the left arm, positioning, and arm support for the right shoulder, plus ankle pumps on the left. I would not do ankle pumps on the right until a clot is excluded. Meanwhile I would ask the team to protect his shoulder and prevent falls, with a bed alarm if needed.

I would document my findings, who I contacted and when, what the physician ordered, my advice to staff, and my talk with Harold and his wife. I would ask when the result is expected, and plan to reassess as soon as he is cleared.

scale.4: Stops mobilization, escalates with a structured handoff, tells staff PE warning signs, uses aphasia-friendly explanation, offers safe alternatives and documents.
scale.3: Stops mobilization and informs physician but incomplete on PE monitoring, communication or alternatives.
scale.2: Reduces activity or continues light leg exercise while waiting.
scale.1: Proceeds with standing or massage, delays reporting, or leaves without explanation.

questions.prompt: The assistant asks to take Harold for standing and walking at 10 o'clock because your afternoon is full. Discuss how you would manage delegation, your caseload and your documentation.

checklist.point: Does not delegate standing and walking to the assistant until Harold's medical status is cleared and his condition is stable and predictable.
Explains that delegation depends on the patient's complexity, the assistant's training, and supervision, and that the physiotherapist remains accountable.
Gives the assistant a clear, specific plan for the day and tasks she can safely do, such as positioning, upper body or seated activity if cleared.
Ensures the assistant knows what to watch for and when to stop and call.
Reprioritizes the caseload by acuity, and asks the unit lead for help or redistribution when workload is unsafe.
Communicates the change in plan to nursing, the team and the wife, and updates the care plan visible at the bedside.
Documents the clinical reasoning, delegation decisions and communications accurately and on time.
Addresses the equipment and infection control needs such as gait belt, orthosis cleaning and shared equipment.

questions.model_answer:
I would not ask the assistant to take Harold for standing and walking this morning. Delegation is a decision I make as the physiotherapist, and it depends on three things: how stable and predictable the patient is, what the assistant has been trained to do, and what supervision is available. Harold is currently not stable and predictable. He may have a deep vein thrombosis, the physician has not reviewed him, and he has a high fall risk and a fragile right shoulder. Sending an assistant to walk him would put both of them at risk. The fact that another assistant did it with him last week does not change this, because his condition has changed. And although I am busy, I remain accountable for the plan even when I delegate, so I cannot hand over a decision I have not made.

I would explain this to her respectfully, because she is trying to help. I would thank her for asking, and say: Mr. Beaulieu has a new concern in his leg, so he is on hold for standing and walking until the physician reviews him. I would tell her what she can do. If the physician agrees, she could help with positioning, seated upper body exercises with the left arm, supported sitting practice, or ankle pumps on the left, using written instructions. I would tell her exactly what to watch for and when to stop and call me or the nurse, including sudden shortness of breath, chest pain, a change in alertness, or pain in the leg. I would make sure the plan is in his chart and at the bedside, so everyone gives the same message, and I would check in with her at an agreed time.

About my caseload: I have 14 patients and this change means I must re-prioritize. I would rank by acuity and risk. Harold needs the urgent handoff and a reassessment as soon as he is cleared. I would also see patients who are new, unstable or due for discharge decisions, and cluster stable patients' tasks for the assistant within her role. If I cannot safely cover my afternoon, I would tell the unit lead or my manager early, and ask for help from the other physiotherapist or to adjust the schedule, instead of cutting corners. I would not allow workload to pressure me into delegating tasks I should do myself.

Communication with the team: I would let nursing and the other staff know that Harold is not for standing practice, and ask them to keep the same restrictions. I would also update his wife, and explain that her observation helped.

Documentation: I would write the assessment findings, the circumference, my reasoning for stopping mobilization, who I notified and their response, the delegation decision and instructions to the assistant, and my reassessment plan. I would also note equipment needs when he restarts, such as a gait belt, a properly fitted ankle foot orthosis, and cleaning of shared equipment between patients according to infection prevention policy.

scale.4: Declines delegation with clear reasoning on accountability, gives assistant specific safe tasks and stop criteria, re-prioritizes caseload and escalates workload, updates team and documents fully.
scale.3: Declines delegation and documents but weak on caseload management or assistant instructions.
scale.2: Delegates with general instructions or ignores workload constraints.
scale.1: Delegates walking while the leg is unresolved or fails to document.

safety_or_ethics_point: The wife's report of a larger, tender right leg in a stroke patient with immobility is a possible DVT that must be examined and escalated before any standing practice. A second issue is delegating walking to an assistant while the patient's status is unresolved and workload pressure is high; the physiotherapist stays accountable.
common_errors: Starting the planned standing program without examining the calf, or massaging the leg. Delegating to the assistant because the schedule is full and a colleague did it before.
examiner_notes: Passing candidates act on the wife's observation, examine the calf, stop mobilization, escalate with clear communication and monitor for pulmonary embolism, then apply delegation principles correctly. Failing candidates treat the case as routine stroke rehabilitation.

title: Lateral ankle sprain in a rotating-shift nurse
setting: Walk-in physiotherapy clinic in a mid-sized Ontario city, late afternoon
client_profile: Amara Okafor is a 33-year-old registered nurse on a medical unit who works rotating 12-hour shifts. Five days ago she rolled her right ankle stepping off a curb. She has used a walking boot and crutches, mostly sitting at home. She takes a combined oral contraceptive and acetaminophen as needed. Pain is 5/10 on walking and 2/10 at rest. Ottawa ankle rules are negative: no bony tenderness at the malleoli, navicular or base of the fifth metatarsal, and she took four steps in the clinic. Lateral ankle swelling with bruising tracking to the heel. Figure-of-eight girth is 2.0 cm greater than the left. Dorsiflexion is 5 degrees on the right and 15 degrees on the left. Anterior drawer is positive with a soft end feel, talar tilt shows mild increased motion, squeeze and external rotation tests are negative. Right calf is tender along the posterior-medial belly and measures 2 cm larger than the left. Foot and Ankle Ability Measure daily living score is 54 percent. She wants to be back at work in three days.
clinical_scenario: Amara pays privately through her hospital extended health plan, which covers eight physiotherapy visits. She says nurses on her unit are short-staffed and she feels guilty being off. She asks whether you can write a note saying she is fit for regular duties, because she would rather not use more sick days. She mentions that her manager is a friend and has her cell number, and that she has been sitting with her leg up for most of the last four days because the boot is awkward in the car.

questions.prompt: Describe the physiotherapy plan of care you would develop with Amara for the next six weeks. Include your goals, the main interventions and how you would progress them, how you would measure change, and what would prompt you to modify the plan.

checklist.point: Sets a functional goal tied to her work: safely tolerating a full 12-hour shift of standing and walking, with a stated timeframe.
Starts with early protected weight bearing as tolerated, weaning from crutches and boot as pain and gait allow.
Addresses swelling with elevation, then compression and active ankle pumping once the calf is cleared, rather than prolonged rest.
Restores dorsiflexion range early with pain-limited mobilization and calf and ankle movement.
Progresses strengthening of peroneals and the whole lower limb from isometric to resisted to functional loading, only after the calf is medically cleared.
Includes balance and proprioceptive training with progression from stable to unstable surfaces and eyes closed.
Names outcome measures such as the Foot and Ankle Ability Measure, pain scale, dorsiflexion range, girth and gait quality, with reassessment points.
Proposes a graded return to shift work, such as shorter or lighter duties first, with supportive footwear or a lace-up brace or taping.
Gives self-management and home exercise dosage (sets, repetitions, frequency) and a plan for the eight covered visits.
States triggers to modify the plan: stalled range or strength, recurrent giving way, escalating swelling or pain, or new findings requiring other care.

questions.model_answer:
My plan has one aim: get Amara through a full 12-hour shift on her feet, confidently and without re-injury, in about six weeks, with a first check at two weeks. I will agree those goals with her, because her own priority is work.

First, the early phase, roughly the first two weeks. This is a grade 2 sprain, so the ligament is partly torn and needs load that is protective but not absent. The whole plan is conditional on one thing: her right calf must be medically assessed and a deep vein clot excluded first, which I explain in my next answer. Until then I offer only elevation and protected walking, and I wean her off the crutches and boot as gait allows, aiming for a normal heel-to-toe pattern in the clinic first. Once the calf is cleared, I add a compression sleeve and active ankle pumps, since movement drives fluid out better than rest does. After clearance I will start pain-limited dorsiflexion work and gentle joint mobilization, because her five degrees of dorsiflexion will otherwise distort her gait. Calf stretching, strengthening and progression all wait for that medical clearance.

Second, the strengthening phase, roughly weeks two to four, starting only once the calf is cleared. I will start with isometric peroneal and ankle strength, move to resisted eversion with a band, then heel raises and single-leg work. I will include hip and knee strength too, since nurses lose general conditioning quickly when off their feet.

Third, balance and control, which is the part that most reduces repeat sprains. We start with single-leg stance on a firm floor, add eyes closed, then foam, then reaching and hopping tasks. I will give her a home program of about ten to fifteen minutes, once or twice daily, written with sets and repetitions.

Fourth, return to work. I will suggest a graded plan: shorter shifts or lighter duties first if her employer can accommodate that, supportive footwear, and a lace-up brace or taping for the first weeks back. I will rehearse her actual tasks, such as walking fast, turning, and standing for long periods.

I will measure progress with the Foot and Ankle Ability Measure, starting at 54 percent, plus pain, dorsiflexion range, figure-of-eight girth and single-leg balance time, and I will repeat them at visits two, four and six. I have eight funded visits, so I will front-load them in the first two weeks, then space them out.

I will change the plan if range or strength stalls, if she reports the ankle giving way, if swelling or pain rises as load rises, or if any new finding changes my impression. In those cases I will reassess, adjust load, or refer to her physician for further assessment.

scale.4: Gives phased goals tied to a 12-hour shift, with early loading, range, strength, balance, dosage, outcome measures, graded return and clear triggers to modify, all justified for a grade 2 sprain.
scale.3: Covers most phases and a work goal with reasonable interventions but lacks dosage, progression criteria or modification triggers.
scale.2: Lists generic ankle exercises or rest and ice with little progression, measurement or link to her job.
scale.1: Recommends prolonged immobilization or full duty at once, or ignores function and measurement entirely.

questions.prompt: Discuss the safety considerations you would address with Amara before she leaves the clinic today, and explain how you would involve her in the decisions that follow.

checklist.point: Recognizes the calf tenderness and 2 cm girth difference as a possible deep vein thrombosis rather than part of the ankle sprain.
Links risk factors: recent reduced mobility, immobilization in a boot, and the combined oral contraceptive.
Stops or defers calf stretching, massage and vigorous exercise until the possibility is excluded.
Arranges same-day medical assessment, such as an emergency department or urgent care visit, rather than waiting for the next appointment.
Explains in plain language why she is being sent and what the physician is likely to do, such as a clinical risk score and ultrasound.
Gives warning signs of pulmonary embolism: sudden shortness of breath, chest pain, coughing blood, racing heart, and says to call 911.
Seeks Amara's consent to the plan and to any communication of her findings to the physician.
Discusses transport so she does not drive herself if unwell or without a plan, and offers a phone call to the facility.
Documents findings, the advice given, her response and who was informed.
Addresses her work guilt and respects her decision-making, offering choices about how to get assessed rather than imposing them.

questions.model_answer:
Before Amara leaves, my main safety concern is her right calf, not the ankle. She has tenderness over the posterior-medial belly of the calf and it measures 2 cm larger than the other side. She has also spent four days mostly sitting with the leg up, she wears a walking boot, and she takes a combined oral contraceptive. Together, those are risk factors for a blood clot in a deep vein. I cannot call it a clot, and I should not call it a stretched muscle either. The ankle sprain can explain swelling near the joint, but not tenderness in the calf belly, so I will treat this as needing medical assessment today.

I would stop what I was planning to do in the calf. No stretching, no massage and no strong calf exercise until a physician has had a look, because those could dislodge a clot if one is present.

Next I talk to her. I will say it plainly: your ankle sprain looks like it is healing, but I am concerned about your calf, and the safest thing is to have a doctor check it today. I will explain that the usual approach is a short clinical assessment and often an ultrasound of the leg veins, and that most people sent for this turn out to be fine. That helps her avoid panic and also avoid dismissing it.

I will give her options and let her choose among them: the closest emergency department, an urgent care that offers same-day ultrasound, or a call to her family doctor for a same-day slot. I will ask what works with her transportation, since she should not be left to decide that alone if she feels unwell. I will offer to phone ahead, with her permission, and to send a short written note describing my findings.

I also give her warning signs. If she develops sudden shortness of breath, sharp chest pain that worsens with breathing, coughing up blood, a racing heart or fainting, she should call 911 instead of driving. I will make sure she can repeat these back to me.

Finally, she is worried about missing work. I will acknowledge that, say that her health comes first, and tell her I will help with documentation so she does not feel she has failed her unit. I will record my findings, what I advised, her decision and who I contacted, and I will follow up by phone tomorrow with her consent.

scale.4: Identifies the calf findings and risk factors as a possible clot, stops calf loading, arranges same-day medical care, gives red-flag advice and shares decisions respectfully with her.
scale.3: Refers appropriately and gives advice but is vague about risk factors, urgency or warning signs.
scale.2: Mentions seeing a doctor eventually or monitoring the calf, with no urgency, no loading restriction or no explanation.
scale.1: Dismisses the calf as part of the sprain, continues calf stretching or massage, or lets her leave without advice.

questions.prompt: Later that day, the manager of Amara's hospital unit telephones the clinic and asks whether Amara can work her scheduled 12-hour shift on Thursday. Describe how you will respond and which professional responsibilities arise.

checklist.point: Does not release any health information to the manager without Amara's informed consent.
Explains that being a friend or colleague of the client does not change confidentiality obligations.
Offers to contact Amara and ask whether she wants any information shared, and what exactly.
If she consents, limits disclosure to functional information, such as restrictions, not diagnosis or investigation results.
Declines to write a fit-for-full-duty note while the calf concern is unresolved and the ankle is not yet at work-level function.
Suggests that fitness for duty be based on objective findings and a graded plan, possibly with occupational health.
Documents the call, what was said and the client's decision.
Respects the regulator's standards on honest, accurate reporting and avoiding pressure from employers or friends.
Acknowledges the staffing pressure empathically while keeping the decision with Amara and her physician.

questions.model_answer:
My first duty on that phone call is confidentiality. Amara has not told me I may speak to her manager. The fact that the manager is a friend of hers, or a colleague of other health professionals, does not matter. Under provincial health privacy legislation and my regulator's standards, information about a client's attendance, diagnosis or ability to work belongs to her unless she gives informed consent for me to share it. So I would say something like: I understand you are short-staffed and I appreciate your call, but I am not able to confirm whether she is a client here or share anything without her permission. I would then offer to pass on the request to her.

I would phone Amara and ask whether she wants me to share anything, and if so what and with whom. If she agrees, I would share only what is needed for the work decision, which is her functional restrictions and the expected time frame, not her diagnosis, her test results or the medical concern from today. I would document the consent, what she agreed to and what I said.

The second responsibility is honesty about fitness for work. Amara asked me for a note saying she is fit for regular duties. I cannot sign that. Her dorsiflexion is five degrees, her anterior drawer is positive, she still has swelling and pain of 5 out of 10 on walking, and the calf concern is unresolved. A twelve-hour shift on her feet is a heavy load for an ankle at this stage and, if there were a clot, the risk would be more serious. My regulator expects me to base statements on objective findings and to resist pressure from friends or employers. I would instead offer a note describing temporary restrictions only, if she consents, and suggest that her physician or occupational health decide on a return date once the calf is cleared.

Third, I should be sensitive to the system pressure. I would acknowledge the staffing strain to Amara without letting it direct her decision, and I would give her a graded return-to-work plan to take to her manager if she chooses.

Last, I document the call, the consent discussion and the note I did or did not issue, and I let the clinic's administrator know in case further calls arrive, so the same answer is given every time.

scale.4: Protects confidentiality, seeks consent and limits disclosure to function, refuses an unsupported fitness note, explains the reasoning and documents.
scale.3: Protects confidentiality and declines the note but is thin on consent scope, documentation or regulator standards.
scale.2: Is vague about confidentiality or gives partial information without consent, or declines without reasoning.
scale.1: Discloses diagnosis or attendance to the manager without consent or signs a full-duty note.

safety_or_ethics_point: The buried issue is a possible deep vein thrombosis: calf tenderness and girth difference with immobility, a boot and a combined oral contraceptive, hidden among ordinary sprain findings. A competent candidate recognizes it before any calf loading, arranges same-day medical assessment and gives red-flag advice. A second issue is the friend-manager call and the request for a fit-for-duty note, which tests confidentiality and honest reporting.
common_errors: Candidates describe an excellent ankle rehabilitation plan and never mention the calf, or they dismiss the calf as a bruise. In question 3 many answer the manager's question informally because the manager is a friend, or agree to write a full-duty note to be helpful.
examiner_notes: A pass requires the calf to be acted on the same day with clear reasoning and red-flag advice, plus consent before any contact with the employer. A candidate with a perfect rehabilitation plan who misses the calf should not pass this case.

title: Week 6 after ACL reconstruction in a teenage soccer player
setting: Private physiotherapy clinic in a suburb, after-school appointment
client_profile: Mateo Alvarez is a 17-year-old Grade 12 soccer player, six weeks after left anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction with a hamstring autograft. He has attended physiotherapy twice weekly and was independent with crutches by week 2. Today: pain 2/10, knee flexion 0 to 120 degrees, a 5-degree extension lag on straight leg raise, trace effusion, and a quadriceps limb symmetry index of 45 percent on handheld dynamometry. Gait shows reduced knee extension in stance. Patellar mobility is good. The hamstring harvest incision on the proximal medial shin is 6 cm long, with mild redness and warmth over about 3 cm at its lower end and a small amount of serous drainage on the dressing. Temperature is 37.9 degrees C; pulse 88. His International Knee Documentation Committee subjective score is 52 out of 100. He is anxious about playing in his school's spring tournament, which his father says is in 10 weeks. His mother wants him back to normal quickly so he can keep a university scholarship tryout.
clinical_scenario: Mateo's father, Luis, drove him and sits in the waiting room, then asks to come into the session. Luis coaches a local team and has been taking Mateo to gym drills at home with resistance bands and jumping 'to keep him sharp'. Mateo says he felt achy and tired yesterday and skipped dinner. His surgeon's next follow-up is not until week 12, and the clinic's bookings are on paper because the electronic system is down today.

questions.prompt: Describe the plan of care you would put in place for Mateo over the next six weeks, including your goals, how you will progress his rehabilitation, how you will measure change, and your criteria for advancing to the next stage.

checklist.point: Sets goals for full active knee extension, quadriceps strength and normal gait within the next phase, with measurable targets.
Prioritizes restoring terminal extension and eliminating the extension lag before adding higher loads.
Uses quadriceps strengthening progressing from isometric and neuromuscular electrical stimulation to closed-chain and open-chain exercise within the graft-protection limits of the surgeon's protocol.
Notes hamstring autograft implications: gradual hamstring loading, avoiding aggressive resisted knee flexion early.
Includes gait retraining, hip and trunk strength, and balance work.
States that running and jumping are not started on a calendar date but on criteria such as effusion, range, strength symmetry and movement quality.
Names outcome measures: quadriceps limb symmetry index, hop tests later, International Knee Documentation Committee score, and a psychological readiness measure.
Gives dosage for the home program (sets, repetitions, frequency) and rules for pain and swelling response.
Plans collaboration with the surgeon's protocol and restrictions and schedules reassessment points.
Addresses his fear of re-injury and goals for school and sport as part of the plan.

questions.model_answer:
At six weeks Mateo is in the strength and control phase, so I would set my plan around criteria, not dates. My goals with him, which I would confirm together, are full active extension with no lag within two weeks, a quadriceps symmetry moving toward 80 percent by week twelve, normal walking with a full heel strike, and a safe return to jogging only when he meets criteria, not simply because a tournament is coming.

First priority: extension. A five-degree lag with a trace effusion tells me the quadriceps is not yet driving the knee fully straight, and the loss of extension, if it persists, will alter his gait and load the patellofemoral joint. So I will start with heel props, quad sets with neuromuscular electrical stimulation, and straight leg raises until the lag is gone, together with effusion control.

Second, strength. Once the lag is gone I will add mini squats, leg press in a limited range, step-ups, and open-chain knee extension through the range allowed by his surgeon's protocol. His quadriceps are at 45 percent of the other side, so this is the main deficit. I will dose at three sets of eight to twelve repetitions, two or three times weekly in clinic and a lighter set daily at home, and increase the load when he completes the sets without pain above 3 out of 10, loss of form or more swelling the next morning.

Third, because the hamstring was the graft source, I will introduce hamstring loading gradually: bridges, then light curls, and I will avoid heavy resisted flexion early.

Fourth, movement and control: gait retraining in front of a mirror, hip abductor and trunk strengthening, and balance tasks progressing from firm to unstable surfaces.

I will measure change every two weeks with handheld dynamometry for the quadriceps symmetry index, active range and lag, effusion, the International Knee Documentation Committee score, and a readiness-to-return measure, because fear is a real barrier in teenagers. Later, once he meets strength and effusion criteria, I will add hop testing.

Criteria to advance: no effusion increase, full extension without lag, flexion near the other side, a symmetric walking pattern, and a quadriceps symmetry of at least about 80 percent, with no effusion and full extension, for light jogging, as agreed with his surgeon. Running and jumping come after, and return to sport later again.

Before I start the loading plan I need the surgeon to clear the wound, which I raise in the next answer. I will review his surgeon's protocol, send a short progress update, and revise the plan if he flares, plateaus, or has any concerns about the wound or his health.

scale.4: Criterion-based phased plan with extension first, quadriceps and hamstring-graft-aware strengthening, dosage, outcome measures, criteria to advance and links to the surgeon's protocol.
scale.3: Sound phases and measures but weak on criteria, dosage or the graft site.
scale.2: Generic knee rehabilitation list or a time-based plan with little measurement.
scale.1: Advances to running, cutting or jumping by calendar date to meet the tournament, or omits strength and range goals.

questions.prompt: Discuss the safety considerations you would address in today's session, and explain how you would make sure Mateo takes part in decisions about his care.

checklist.point: Notices the combination of a warm, red, draining harvest incision, low-grade fever and malaise as a possible surgical site infection.
Takes his temperature, inspects and palpates the wound and checks the dressing before exercising.
Defers the exercise session or stops loading the knee and hamstring until the wound is assessed by a physician.
Arranges same-day contact with the surgeon's office or urgent medical assessment and does not wait until week 12.
Gives warning signs: increasing redness, pus, fever, severe pain, calf swelling and shortness of breath.
Advises Mateo and his parents to stop the home band and jumping drills until cleared.
Explains findings to Mateo directly in plain language and asks what he understands and wants.
Obtains informed consent from Mateo, a mature 17-year-old, and invites but does not require his parents' involvement.
Documents findings, advice and who was contacted, and arranges follow-up despite the paper booking system.

questions.model_answer:
Before I start any exercise today, I want to look at his wound and his temperature, because several small things together worry me. Mateo said he felt achy and tired yesterday and skipped dinner. The harvest incision on his proximal shin is red and warm over a few centimetres and there was some drainage on the dressing. His temperature is 37.9. Any one of these could be ordinary, but together they are consistent with an early infection at the surgical site, and an infection near a new graft is serious. I will not progress his program or load the hamstring today.

So my plan is this. First, I take a full set of vitals, examine the wound without contaminating it, note its size and the drainage, and compare with my last record. Second, I stop any loading exercise that involves the hamstring and knee. I keep him comfortable, I might do gentle range and swelling control only if I am confident it will not worsen anything, but I would hold the session otherwise.

Third, I contact the surgeon's office the same day, not week 12. I describe what I found, ask for an urgent review, and if the office cannot see him that day, I advise urgent care or the emergency department. I would telephone ahead with his permission.

Fourth, I give clear warning signs: spreading redness, pus, fever above 38, worsening pain, a hot swollen joint, a swollen painful calf, or shortness of breath. Any of these means going straight to the emergency department.

Now, how Mateo takes part. He is 17. I would speak to him first, in plain words, and ask what he has noticed and what he thinks is going on. I would explain what I found and why I am worried, and let him say what he wants, including who should be in the room. Consent for assessment and sharing information rests on his capacity, which is expected at his age, so I would ask whether he is happy for his father to hear this, and I would encourage it, but the decision is his. I would also tell him that the band work and jumping drills his father has been doing need to stop until the wound is cleared, and explain why, so that this does not feel like blame.

Finally, because the electronic system is down, I document on paper, note the time of the call, and file it later in the record. I would also telephone him tomorrow to check on progress.

scale.4: Links wound, temperature and malaise to possible infection, holds loading, arranges same-day medical review, gives warning signs and engages Mateo as the decision-maker.
scale.3: Identifies the wound concern and refers but is vague on urgency, hold on loading or his role in decisions.
scale.2: Notes the wound and suggests monitoring, or talks mainly to the parent, or carries on the session.
scale.1: Ignores the signs, progresses the program as planned or defers all decisions to the father.

questions.prompt: Mateo's father then tells you he is frustrated and that Mateo should be jogging by now because he knows what pro players do. Describe how you will communicate with Mateo and his father, including the specific words and strategies you would use.

checklist.point: Acknowledges the father's concern and investment before responding.
Explains in plain language that return to running depends on criteria such as swelling, strength and movement quality, not on the calendar.
Uses concrete numbers from today, such as the 45 percent quadriceps strength and the extension lag, to show where Mateo is.
Directs the main conversation to Mateo and asks for his own goals and worries.
Uses teach-back or open questions to check understanding by both.
Offers a clear role for the father, such as supporting the home program, driving, and encouragement.
Addresses the wrong home drills gently and without blame.
Handles the scholarship pressure and tournament honestly without promising an outcome.
Offers a written summary and agrees on how updates will be shared, respecting Mateo's preferences.

questions.model_answer:
I would start by listening. I would say to Luis: I can hear how much you want Mateo back on the field, and I can see how much time you give him. That is a real strength. That small acknowledgement lowers the temperature before I explain anything.

Then I would speak to both of them, but I would look at Mateo when I speak about his knee. I would say: Mateo, I would like to show you and your dad where things are, and then ask what you think. I would use today's numbers. Your thigh muscle is working at about half the strength of the other leg, and your knee still lags about five degrees when you try to straighten it. Running with that gap puts more load through the new ligament and the joint, and that is when setbacks happen. I would put it as a map, not a no: we do not jog on a date, we jog when we reach these markers, and here they are in writing.

I would avoid jargon and keep sentences short. I would then ask each of them to say back what they understood: so, what would you tell your mom about when running starts? That is teach-back, and it shows me whether the message got through.

Next I would ask Mateo about his own goals. What matters most to you this spring: the tournament, the scholarship tryout, or being sure the knee is safe? A teenager is often more worried than he says. I would ask about fear of re-injury and tell him that this is common and can be worked on.

I would be honest about the schedule. I cannot promise a return for the tournament in ten weeks, and I will not guess a date, but I can promise a plan that gets him as far as safely possible and that we will review every two weeks together, and I will update the surgeon at key points. I would say the same about the scholarship tryout and suggest that, if he wants, we write a letter describing his progress.

About the home drills, I would say without blame: I know you did these to help. Right now, until his wound has been checked, the band work and jumping should wait, and I will give you a short home list that is safe, so you have something useful to do together.

Finally, I would offer a one-page written summary and ask Mateo how he would like updates shared, with his father in the room, by text, or after sessions.

scale.4: Acknowledges the father, centres Mateo, explains criteria with today's findings, checks understanding, gives the father a role and is honest about outcomes.
scale.3: Respectful and clear but lacks teach-back, concrete numbers or a defined role for the father.
scale.2: Defensive or technical language, or responds mainly to the father without checking Mateo.
scale.1: Promises a return date, dismisses the father or gives in to the pressure to start running.

safety_or_ethics_point: The buried issue is a possible surgical site infection: a warm, red, draining hamstring-harvest incision with low-grade fever and malaise, with no surgeon visit until week 12. A competent candidate examines the wound, holds loading, arranges same-day medical review and gives warning signs. A second thread is that a 17-year-old may be capable of consenting to his own care, so he is the person to inform and ask.
common_errors: Candidates produce a strong rehabilitation plan and never notice the wound, or note it and still plan to continue the exercises. In the communication question, candidates argue with the father about running or speak only to the parent and forget Mateo.
examiner_notes: The pass line is identifying the wound and fever as urgent, stopping loading and getting a medical review the same day, while keeping Mateo at the centre. Good rehabilitation reasoning cannot compensate for missing the infection.

title: Starting exercise with type 2 diabetes and hypoglycemia risk
setting: Hospital outpatient physiotherapy department, mid-morning appointment
client_profile: Gurpreet Dhillon is a 57-year-old long-haul truck driver referred by his family physician for a supervised exercise program for type 2 diabetes diagnosed 11 years ago. He takes metformin, gliclazide each morning and insulin glargine at bedtime. Last HbA1c was 69 mmol/mol (8.4 percent). Body mass index is 33 kg/m2. Resting blood pressure is 148/88 mmHg, heart rate 84 beats per minute, resting oxygen saturation 97 percent. Capillary glucose in the clinic is 5.1 mmol/L, three hours after breakfast. He reports two episodes of shakiness and sweating about 40 minutes into walks last week, which settled after he ate a banana. He denies chest pain, dyspnea or dizziness. Monofilament sensation is reduced under both forefeet and vibration sense is reduced at both great toes. There is a 1.5 cm callus with surrounding redness and a small intact blister under the left first metatarsal head, which he says does not hurt. His runners are worn flat. Six-minute walk distance is 360 m.
clinical_scenario: Gurpreet is on the road four nights a week and eats whenever he can. He is keen to start walking and wants a plan he can follow in truck stops and motel parking lots. He has not told his employer about the two low-sugar episodes and asks that you do not put anything about them in a letter. His wife phoned the clinic earlier asking you to confirm his program details, and the receptionist says she was told his diabetes details are 'fine to share with family'.

questions.prompt: Explain how you interpret Gurpreet's history and findings, which of them most influence how you will start an exercise program, and what further information or assessment you would gather today.

checklist.point: Recognizes the exercise-related shakiness and sweating as probable hypoglycemia in a person taking gliclazide and insulin.
Links hypoglycemia risk to medication timing, meal timing and exercise duration and intensity, and asks for his glucose log.
Interprets reduced monofilament and vibration sensation as peripheral neuropathy that raises foot injury risk.
Identifies the callus, erythema and blister as a pre-ulcer foot lesion needing protection and medical or foot-care follow-up.
Screens for cardiovascular red flags and notes that blood pressure 148/88 is elevated but not by itself a reason to withhold light to moderate exercise.
Considers autonomic neuropathy, retinopathy and kidney disease as factors that alter exercise precautions and asks about them.
Checks hypoglycemia awareness and what he carries to treat a low.
Uses the six-minute walk and perceived exertion to estimate fitness and set starting intensity.
Explores his work schedule, meals, preferences and barriers to adherence.

questions.model_answer:
I will reason from what could harm him first, then from what will help him.

The finding that most changes my plan is the pattern of shakiness and sweating after about 40 minutes of walking that settled with a banana. In a man taking gliclazide and bedtime insulin, that picture fits exercise-related hypoglycemia. Both drugs lower glucose, exercise increases glucose uptake in the muscles for hours afterwards, and his clinic reading today of 5.1 mmol/L is low-normal for starting exercise on these medications. So I need his glucose log, when he takes the gliclazide, what he ate today, how long and how hard the walks were, and whether he notices lows before they become severe. I also ask what he carries to treat a low, and I would plan for fast-acting carbohydrate within reach every session.

The second finding is the feet. Reduced monofilament and vibration sensation mean peripheral neuropathy. The callus with redness and a blister under the first metatarsal head is a pre-ulcer lesion he cannot feel, in worn shoes that offer no cushioning, and he is about to walk daily. Until it has been looked at by his physician or a foot-care clinic, I will not give a program that loads that foot repeatedly. I will check temperature, pulses and the skin between the toes, and consider non-weight-bearing options such as cycling or seated resistance work in the meantime.

Third, cardiovascular risk. He is 57, with long-standing diabetes, obesity and blood pressure of 148/88. He denies symptoms, which is reassuring, but diabetes can mask them. I would ask about exertional chest or arm discomfort, breathlessness, palpitations, and check whether his heart rate responds normally to the six-minute walk, since a blunted response could suggest autonomic neuropathy. The blood pressure alone is not a reason to withhold light to moderate activity, but I will tell his physician. I would also ask about eye disease and kidney problems because they affect how hard he should strain.

Fourth, his function and context. Six minutes of walking at 360 metres is below expected for his age and tells me to start low, around light to moderate effort on a perceived exertion scale, and build time gradually. I need to know what he can realistically do on the road: truck stops, parking lots, motel stairs and resistance bands.

So my impression is a man with type 2 diabetes at risk of exercise-related hypoglycemia and foot injury, with likely neuropathy and unclear cardiac status, who is ready and motivated to be active.

scale.4: Interprets the pattern as hypoglycemia, the foot findings as a pre-ulcer neuropathic lesion, weighs cardiovascular and other risks and states what to gather and how it changes the start.
scale.3: Identifies hypoglycemia and neuropathy but misses the foot lesion, the cardiovascular screen or the link to medication timing.
scale.2: Lists diabetes exercise facts with little linkage to his findings or no further assessment.
scale.1: Treats the findings as unremarkable or proceeds to an unrestricted program.

questions.prompt: Discuss the safety measures you will put in place today and over the coming weeks, and describe how you will plan them with Gurpreet so they fit his life.

checklist.point: Protects the left forefoot lesion: no repeated loading until assessed, and arranges a same-week medical or foot-care review.
Advises proper footwear, daily foot inspection and what to report, such as a new blister, redness or drainage.
Sets a hypoglycemia plan: check glucose before and after, carry fast-acting carbohydrate, and know symptoms and the treatment rule.
Explains the risk of delayed lows after exercise, including overnight, because he takes bedtime insulin.
Starts at a low to moderate intensity and short duration with gradual progression and a stop rule for symptoms.
States when to stop and seek help: chest discomfort, severe dyspnea, confusion, or a glucose that does not recover.
Shares information with his physician about the lows, the foot and the blood pressure with his consent.
Builds options that fit trucking life, such as walking breaks, resistance bands and stair work, with his input.
Uses shared decision-making and checks his understanding with teach-back.

questions.model_answer:
I want to set safety in three layers: today, the first few weeks, and his life on the road, and I want Gurpreet to choose the details.

Today. The first thing I protect is his left forefoot. A callus with redness and a blister that he cannot feel will turn into an ulcer if he walks on it daily in flat shoes. I will explain this by saying: you cannot feel this, so your eyes have to do the job your nerves are not doing. I would contact his family physician today, with his consent, to arrange a foot check within the week, and in the meantime I would choose exercise that spares that foot: cycling on a stationary bike with cushioned shoes, seated upper body work or leg work with bands. I would show him how to inspect his feet each evening with a mirror or his phone camera, and I would tell him to report any new redness, warmth, drainage, or blister.

Hypoglycemia. I would teach him that low glucose is the main exercise risk on gliclazide and insulin. Before sessions he checks his glucose; I would use the target his physician or diabetes educator gives, and ask them to confirm it. He carries fast-acting carbohydrate such as glucose tablets or juice at every session, and we practise the rule: treat, wait, recheck. I would also explain that lows can appear hours later or overnight, because exercise keeps sensitizing muscle to insulin and he takes insulin at bedtime. So after a session he checks again before sleep, and any pattern gets reported.

Intensity. We start with light to moderate effort, about ten minutes of walking or cycling and build slowly, with a stop rule: chest pain, severe shortness of breath, dizziness, confusion or glucose he cannot bring up means stop and call for help.

His life. I would ask him: what could you realistically do in a motel parking lot at 10 pm? Together we might pick a ten-minute walk after each driving block, a set of band exercises he keeps in the cab, and stairs at truck stops. He writes the plan in his own words, and I ask him to say it back to me, so that I know it is workable.

Finally, with his permission I send a short note to his physician about the lows, the foot, the blood pressure and what we agreed, and ask for guidance on medication adjustments, since that is not my decision to make.

scale.4: Protects the foot, builds a specific hypoglycemia plan including delayed lows, sets stop rules, coordinates with the physician and designs the plan with Gurpreet.
scale.3: Covers hypoglycemia and foot protection in general terms with some personalization.
scale.2: General diabetes exercise advice with little prioritization or without his input.
scale.1: Ignores the foot or the glucose risk, or imposes a fixed program.
