questions.prompt: Gurpreet asks you to leave any mention of his low-sugar episodes out of correspondence, and also asks how much he should cut back his insulin before walking. His wife's earlier call raises a further issue. Describe how you will respond and which professional responsibilities apply.

checklist.point: Declines to advise a specific insulin or gliclazide dose change and explains that this is outside physiotherapy scope and belongs to his prescriber or diabetes educator.
Offers to help him get a timely adjustment by contacting the prescriber with his consent.
Explains that the lows are clinically relevant and should go to his physician, and discusses what that means for his consent.
Does not share information with his employer without his consent, and does not fabricate or omit when reporting to the physician.
Discusses honestly the safety issue of hypoglycemia while driving a commercial vehicle and encourages him to talk to his physician about driving requirements.
Addresses the wife's call: no disclosure to family without his express consent and corrects the receptionist's assumption.
Reviews clinic practice on verifying consent before sharing and documents the incident.
Documents the discussion, advice and the client's decisions.

questions.model_answer:
There are three separate issues in what Gurpreet and his wife have asked, and I will deal with each.

First, the insulin question. He asks how much he should cut back before walking. That is a prescribing decision. Adjusting insulin or gliclazide is outside physiotherapy scope, and a wrong number could cause a severe low or a very high glucose. So I tell him kindly: I cannot give you a number, and I would not want to guess. What I can do is make it easy to get one. With his permission I will contact his physician or diabetes educator today, tell them about the two lows during walking, and ask for a written plan on his medication timing and pre-exercise carbohydrate for the exercise we are planning. I can help him write down the questions to ask.

Second, his request to keep the lows out of correspondence. I would respect that he decides what is shared with his employer, and I will not write to his employer without his consent. But the lows are clinically important, and the person who needs to know is his prescriber, because it changes his treatment. I would explain that omitting them from my report to his physician would be unsafe and not something I can do. I would also have an honest conversation about driving: a low blood sugar behind the wheel of a truck is dangerous to him and to others. I am not his driving authority, and I will not make a report on my own, but I would encourage him to discuss fitness to drive and any requirements with his physician, and I would document that I raised it. If I thought he was at imminent risk, my regulator's standards and provincial rules would guide me on whether disclosure without consent was justified, and I would seek advice from the college.

Third, his wife's call. Health information belongs to Gurpreet. Nobody told her he agreed. I would ask him whether he wants her to have information, and what kind, and I would record his answer. Until I know, no information is released. I would then speak to the receptionist and my manager so that we confirm consent before releasing any details, and I would note the incident in the record and follow the clinic's privacy procedure, including whether a breach report is needed.

Finally, I would record the conversation, my advice, his decisions and every contact I made.

scale.4: Stays within scope, refers the insulin question, insists on physician communication, addresses driving risk and consent properly, handles the wife's call and documents.
scale.3: Handles scope and consent adequately but misses the driving issue, the clinic privacy process or documentation.
scale.2: Partially addresses scope or confidentiality, vague about the physician or the wife.
scale.1: Gives an insulin dose, agrees to hide the lows from the physician, or shares details with the wife.

safety_or_ethics_point: Two buried issues: a pre-ulcer neuropathic foot lesion he cannot feel, and exercise-related hypoglycemia in a commercial driver on a sulfonylurea and insulin, plus an unauthorized family disclosure assumption at reception. A competent candidate protects the foot, builds a hypoglycemia plan, keeps medication decisions with the prescriber and secures consent before any disclosure.
common_errors: Candidates design a generic aerobic program with no foot lesion management, or tell him how to adjust insulin. They also tend to overlook the receptionist-wife disclosure and the driving hazard when they answer the professional question.
examiner_notes: Passing responses connect the lows to medications, protect the foot, stay in scope and handle consent cleanly. A response that adjusts medication doses, or ignores the foot, is a fail on this case.

title: Hip pain in a retired farmer with long travel to care
setting: Rural community health centre with a physiotherapist on site one day a week
client_profile: Walter Kowalchuk is a 63-year-old retired grain farmer who still works his land with his son. He lives 160 km from this centre and has driven in with his wife, Irene. He reports eight months of right groin and thigh pain, worse over the last three months. Pain is 6/10 walking and 5/10 at night, and it wakes him most nights even when he is lying still. Morning stiffness lasts 20 minutes. A radiograph a year ago showed moderate joint space narrowing of the right hip. He had a radical prostatectomy for prostate cancer five years ago and says his last blood test was 'a couple of years back'. Weight has dropped from 92 to 86 kg in three months and he is more tired. Right hip flexion is 90 degrees and internal rotation 5 degrees with pain at end range; FADIR is painful. Gentle heel strike percussion reproduces deep thigh pain. Strength is hip flexion 4/5, abduction 4/5. Hip Disability and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score pain subscale is 48 out of 100.
clinical_scenario: Walter is stoic and says he does not want to make a fuss. He wears bilateral hearing aids and often answers 'yes' before the question is finished. The centre's physiotherapist visits weekly, there is no broadband at his farm, and the nearest orthopedic clinic is a five-hour drive. Irene schedules his appointments and says he will 'probably not come back unless it is really bad'. Seeding season starts in three weeks and he wants strength and exercises to get through it.

questions.prompt: Describe the plan of care you would develop with Walter for the coming weeks, including goals, interventions, and how you would deliver and follow up care given where he lives. Include how you would measure change and when you would alter the plan.

checklist.point: Sets goals that Walter values, such as sleeping through the night and doing farm tasks, with measurable targets and a timeframe.
Makes loading, strengthening and walking progression conditional on medical clearance of the night pain and weight loss, keeping interim care protective.

Limits interim care to pain-limited non-resisted range, protected weight bearing with a cane in the opposite hand, and falls avoidance, deferring strengthening and walking targets until medical review.
Gives activity modification advice for farm work, such as limiting lifting, climbing in and out of equipment and prolonged driving.
Offers a short written or illustrated home program with dosage that needs no equipment and no broadband.
Plans follow-up by telephone or in-person clustered visits, and arranges contact points before the next weekly clinic day.
Names outcome measures such as hip pain score, the Hip Disability and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score, walking tolerance and night pain frequency.
States triggers to change the plan: pain not easing, night pain persisting, new findings, falls, or imaging and investigations that alter the diagnosis.
Considers weight, nutrition and general fitness within the context of unexplained weight loss, without recommending weight loss as a goal.

questions.model_answer:
My plan has to work for a man who lives 160 km away, who will not make a fuss, and who has a clear deadline: seeding in three weeks. It also has to respect that his night pain and weight loss are not what I would expect from simple osteoarthritis, so my plan is a safe, simple bridge while that question is answered.

Goals. I would ask Walter what he wants and write it down. Likely: sleep through the night, walk to the barn and back without stopping, climb into the tractor, and get through seeding with a plan. I would set targets like pain at night no more than 2 out of 10, with walking and strength goals set only after the bone is cleared, and review them in one and in three weeks.

Interventions. Because I want medical clarification before any real loading progress, I would start low-risk and unaggravating. First, positions and pacing: breaks every hour in the tractor cab, a footstool or cushion, getting out and moving, and avoiding long lifting and twisting. Second, protected weight bearing: a cane in the left hand, the side opposite the sore hip, which I would fit today, and care to avoid falls. Third, a short program of about ten minutes of pain-limited, non-resisted hip range that he can do lying or seated, with a simple rule that pain should settle within an hour and should not be worse the next morning. I would hold off on strengthening, bridging, sit-to-stand loading, walking-duration targets, impact and resisted hip movements until imaging and medical review show the bone is safe.

Delivery. Because he will not come back often, I would give him a printed, picture-based program with large type, and put dosage in plain words: one set of ten slow movements, once a day. I would book a telephone check in one week, because he has a telephone even if he has no broadband, ask Irene to be part of the call with his permission, and offer a slot on the next clinic day, grouped with other visits to cut the driving.

Weight and nutrition. His loss of 6 kg in three months is unexplained, so I would not treat it as a goal to encourage and I would not advise him to lose weight. I would ask his physician to review it, and suggest a dietitian if the physician agrees.

Measurement. I would record numeric pain at night and walking, the Hip Disability and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score, and his own report of how far he can walk, and repeat at each contact.

Modification. I would change the plan if night pain continues or worsens, if he falls, if the leg feels weak, or if the physician's investigations give a different explanation for his hip. If the answer is osteoarthritis alone, once cleared I would progress to strengthening, a walking program and a work-conditioning plan. If not, the plan follows the diagnosis.

scale.4: Builds a plan around his goals with conservative interim care, conditional progression, dosage, remote follow-up, outcome measures and clear triggers to change the plan in light of the red flags.
scale.3: Sound plan with some personalization but progression is not tied to the unexplained findings or follow-up is not realistic.
scale.2: Standard hip osteoarthritis exercises with no regard to his location, goals or measurement.
scale.1: Prescribes heavy loading and impact or a plan he cannot access, with no follow-up.

questions.prompt: Discuss the safety considerations in Walter's case, including what you would do today and what you would tell him, and explain how you will involve Walter in deciding what happens next.

checklist.point: Recognizes night pain unrelieved by rest, unintentional weight loss, fatigue and a cancer history as red flags that make a serious cause, such as a bone metastasis, possible.
Does not attribute everything to the radiographic osteoarthritis and recognizes that the old x-ray does not explain the new pattern.
Recommends urgent medical assessment and investigations, such as bloodwork including prostate-specific antigen and updated imaging, and contacts his physician promptly.
Considers pathological fracture risk and gives advice on protected loading, such as avoiding falls, heavy lifting and impact.
Gives clear warning signs: sudden severe pain, inability to bear weight, a new deformity, leg shortening, neurological symptoms or bladder changes.
Explains this honestly without causing alarm, in plain language and at a pace Walter can follow.
Asks what Walter understands and what matters to him, including seeding, and explores his fear and barriers to attending.
Obtains consent for referral, and for involving Irene, and respects his decision, including a decision to wait.
Documents the findings, advice and plan to ensure follow-up is not left to chance.

questions.model_answer:
The safety question here is whether Walter's hip pain is osteoarthritis only, and my answer is that I cannot be sure. Some of what he describes fits osteoarthritis: the groin pain, the morning stiffness of twenty minutes, the limited internal rotation and the old x-ray. But several things do not: pain that wakes him most nights even when he lies still, a loss of 6 kg in three months without trying, new tiredness, and pain on gentle heel strike that suggests the bone itself may be irritated. He also had prostate cancer five years ago, and prostate cancer commonly spreads to bone, including the upper femur and pelvis. A year-old x-ray cannot tell me what is happening now. So I treat this as possible serious pathology until a physician has ruled it out.

What I do today. I contact his family physician by phone today, explain what I found and why I am worried, and ask for urgent assessment, including blood tests such as a prostate-specific antigen and an updated hip and pelvis image. If the physician cannot see him within days, I would ask for a plan for urgent imaging. I would give him a letter to carry.

I protect the bone in the meantime. I would advise him to avoid heavy lifting, jumping, climbing on and off equipment where he could fall, and to use a cane. I give warning signs: sudden severe pain, inability to put weight on the leg, a leg that looks shorter or turned, new numbness or weakness in the legs, or trouble passing urine. These mean going straight to the nearest emergency department.

Now how I involve him. He is stoic and might nod without understanding, so I would speak slowly, face him, make sure his hearing aids are in, and use short sentences. I would say: Walter, I think your hip arthritis is real, but some things you told me are not typical for arthritis alone, and I want a doctor to check, because it is better to find out now. Then I would ask what he thinks and what worries him. I expect he will say seeding. I would not dismiss that. I would explain that if there is a problem in the bone, working through seeding could lead to a break that would cost him far more time, and ask what help his son could give.

I ask his permission to speak to Irene and to send information to his physician. If he chooses to wait, I respect that, document it, repeat the warning signs and book a call in a few days. I record all of it in the chart.

scale.4: Identifies the cluster of red flags and cancer history, arranges prompt medical investigation, protects the bone, gives warning signs and engages Walter with tailored communication and respect for his choice.
scale.3: Recognizes red flags and refers but is vague about urgency, fracture precautions or his participation.
scale.2: Mentions seeing a physician at some point but treats the case as osteoarthritis and carries on.
scale.1: Attributes all findings to the osteoarthritis, with no referral, or pressures him without explanation.

questions.prompt: Describe the specific communication strategies and words you would use with Walter and Irene to explain your concerns and the next steps, given his hearing, his stoicism and the distance he lives from care.

checklist.point: Sets up the conversation for hearing: face-to-face, good lighting, hearing aids on, reduced background noise, slow clear speech.
Uses plain language and short sentences, avoiding words such as metastasis or pathology unless explained.
Uses teach-back and asks Walter to say in his own words what happens next.
Gives key points in writing in large print, including who will call him, and when.
Asks permission before involving Irene and checks what he wants her to know.
Responds to stoicism by normalizing concerns and inviting questions without pushing him.
Acknowledges his farm responsibilities and links the plan to what he values.
Addresses travel barriers with telephone follow-up, a named contact person and clustering of only non-urgent visits, without delaying the urgent physician assessment.
Shows cultural humility by asking about his preferences, transport and finances rather than assuming rural life, means or capacity.

questions.model_answer:
Three things shape how I speak to Walter: he is hard of hearing and tends to say yes quickly, he does not like to make a fuss, and he lives 160 km from the centre. I plan for each.

First, hearing. I would ask him to put his hearing aids in, sit facing me in good light, and move to a quieter room. I would speak slowly, in short sentences, and look at him, not at the chart or at Irene. I would not rely on him saying yes. I would ask him instead to tell me what he heard.

Second, words. I would say: Walter, your hip has some arthritis, and that is real. But you also told me about night pain and about losing weight without trying, and with your history of prostate cancer, I want your doctor to look at the bone in your leg. I will not use the words metastasis or pathology unless he asks, and if he asks I will answer honestly and simply. I would use plain pictures of the hip and femur to show where I am concerned. I would stop after each point and ask: does that make sense? What questions do you have?

Third, his stoicism. I would say that many people put up with pain and hope it passes, and that it is not a fuss to ask for a test, it is how we find the right treatment. I would name his seeding season out loud, because I expect it is his main worry: I know seeding matters. If there is a problem in the bone, finding it now protects your ability to work this spring. I would ask what his son could do to help.

For Irene, I would ask Walter first whether he is happy for me to include her, then speak to both. She books his appointments, so I would ask her to help with the plan, such as who will drive him and how they will reach me.

For distance, I would write a one-page summary in large print: what I found, what the doctor will do, what to do if the pain suddenly worsens, and my clinic phone number. I would say, I will call you on Thursday at 10, is that a good time? The physician assessment cannot wait for a combined trip, so I would arrange it as soon as possible, locally or by phone referral, and only cluster non-urgent follow-up with it. I would ask what he prefers and what transport he has, rather than assuming how far he can travel or what he can afford.

To close, I would ask: to be sure I explained well, can you tell me what will happen next, and what would make you call 911? If anything is missing, I explain again in different words.

scale.4: Adapts to hearing and stoicism, uses plain language and teach-back, includes Irene with consent, gives written information and solves distance with specific follow-up.
scale.3: Clear and respectful but misses hearing adaptation, teach-back or a concrete remote follow-up plan.
scale.2: Generic communication advice without specific words or adaptation to Walter.
scale.1: Uses jargon, relies on a yes from Walter, or dismisses his concerns about seeding.

safety_or_ethics_point: The buried issue is a red-flag cluster: night pain at rest, unintentional weight loss, fatigue and a prior prostate cancer in a man whose hip radiograph shows osteoarthritis. A competent candidate does not anchor on the x-ray, arranges prompt medical investigation, protects against fracture and explains this in a way Walter can understand.
common_errors: Candidates anchor on the visible osteoarthritis and write a strengthening program without raising the red flags. Others raise the concern but leave the plan vague on timing, or use jargon with a patient who has hearing loss and says yes automatically.
examiner_notes: A pass identifies the red-flag cluster and acts on it with urgency while still giving Walter a workable interim plan. Failing to recognize the cancer history and night pain is a fail on this case.

title: Fatigue in relapsing remitting multiple sclerosis
setting: Hospital-based outpatient neurology rehabilitation clinic
client_profile: Esi Mensah is a 38-year-old elementary school teacher with relapsing remitting multiple sclerosis diagnosed six years ago. She was referred for fatigue that limits her afternoons and her after-school duties. She is on baclofen at night for leg stiffness. Her disease-modifying therapy was stopped three months ago when her drug coverage lapsed between contracts. Her last neurology letter, 14 months ago, recorded mild disability. Modified Fatigue Impact Scale is 52 out of 84, worse in the afternoon and in hot weather. She sleeps about six hours, wakes unrefreshed, and her partner says she snores. Six-minute walk is 380 m with a rise in effort rating late in the test. Timed 25-foot walk is 7.8 seconds. Timed Up and Go is 10 seconds. Right ankle dorsiflexion is 4/5 and left is 5/5. Right knee reflex is brisker than left. She mentions her right toes have been catching on stairs for four days and that her right eye has felt blurry and sore on looking sideways for five days. She thinks this is the fatigue.
clinical_scenario: Esi is anxious about money and about her principal noticing. She asks if you will complete the long-term disability form her private insurer sent, which asks for a diagnosis, prognosis and her functional abilities, and says she has not told her employer she stopped treatment. She would like to start a gym program on her own and hot yoga on weekends, and asks whether she should avoid exercise because it makes her more tired. She has not seen her neurologist since the coverage gap.

questions.prompt: Explain your clinical impression of what is contributing to Esi's presentation, which findings from today most influence your thinking, and what further assessment you would carry out or arrange.

checklist.point: Identifies several contributors to fatigue: primary multiple sclerosis fatigue, heat sensitivity, possible sleep disorder (snoring, unrefreshing sleep), deconditioning, mood, medication effects.
Notes the new right foot catching, mild right dorsiflexion weakness, brisker right reflex and eye pain with movement as findings that may represent new neurological deficits rather than fatigue.
Recognizes that new symptoms lasting more than 24 hours may indicate a relapse and asks about onset, duration, heat or infection triggers and progression.
Considers the lapse in disease-modifying therapy as increasing the risk of new disease activity.
Explains why heat-related transient worsening (Uhthoff phenomenon) does not fit symptoms lasting days.
Plans screening for sleep apnea, depression, anemia or thyroid problems by arranging medical follow-up rather than diagnosing them.
Uses and interprets standardized measures: fatigue scale, six-minute walk, timed walk, Timed Up and Go, with a view to a baseline.
Describes further neurological examination: tone, sensation, coordination, gait and visual screening.
Identifies the unmet need for a neurology follow-up.

questions.model_answer:
Esi came because of fatigue, and fatigue is very common in multiple sclerosis, so I will take it seriously. But my impression is that fatigue is probably not the only thing happening, and the findings that most influence my thinking are not the fatigue score.

First, the fatigue. Her Modified Fatigue Impact Scale is 52 out of 84, worse in the afternoon and when it is hot, which fits primary multiple sclerosis fatigue and heat sensitivity. But other things add to it. She snores, wakes unrefreshed and sleeps six hours, which makes me think of a sleep disorder such as sleep apnea. She is also anxious and under financial strain, so mood could contribute. Deconditioning from avoiding activity, the night baclofen, and medical problems like low iron or thyroid disease can also play a part. I cannot diagnose these, but I can ask about them and ask her physician to test.

Second, the findings that matter more. For four days her right toes have been catching on stairs, her right ankle dorsiflexion is 4 out of 5 and the right knee reflex is brisker than the left. For five days her right eye has been blurry and sore when she looks sideways. These are new neurological symptoms on one side, lasting days. Heat-related worsening of old symptoms usually fades within an hour of cooling and does not last four or five days. New or worsening deficits lasting over 24 hours, without fever or infection, raise the possibility of a relapse, and pain with eye movement and blurred vision could be optic neuritis. Her disease-modifying therapy lapsed three months ago, which raises the chance of new activity. I will not call it a relapse, but I will treat it as a possible one.

Further assessment today. I would ask when each symptom started, whether they come and go with heat, any recent infection, fever, or a new urinary or bowel problem, and any other new numbness or imbalance. I would examine tone, sensation, coordination, gait, and do a basic visual screen including acuity with her glasses and eye movements, without going beyond my scope. I would record the six-minute walk, 25-foot walk and Timed Up and Go as baselines.

And I would arrange what I cannot do myself: contact her neurologist or family physician the same day about possible new activity, and ask about sleep and blood testing, since both matter for her fatigue.

scale.4: Gives a multifactorial view of fatigue and identifies the new unilateral deficits and visual symptoms as a possible relapse, explaining why heat sensitivity does not fit, with specific further assessment and referral.
scale.3: Identifies multiple fatigue contributors and flags some new findings but is unclear on relapse or urgency.
scale.2: Attributes all findings to MS fatigue and heat with standard measures only.
scale.1: Misses the new deficits or advises that symptoms are expected and will pass.

questions.prompt: Discuss the safety considerations in this case, including Esi's wish to start a gym program and hot yoga, and explain how you will involve her in decisions.

checklist.point: Advises same-day contact with her neurologist or physician for the possible relapse, and not waiting for a routine appointment.
Explains that vision symptoms or worsening weakness should lead to urgent care and gives clear warning signs.
Holds new intense exercise until medical assessment but advises against complete inactivity and supports safe movement.
Advises against hot yoga because heat can worsen symptoms and fatigue, and offers cooling strategies and cooler options.
Addresses fall risk with the right foot catching and offers gait aid or footwear advice and stair safety.
Explains that exercise is beneficial in multiple sclerosis when dosed carefully and fatigue pacing is used.
Addresses driving safety if vision is affected and discusses with her physician.
Uses shared decision-making, explores her fears about cost and work, and checks understanding.
Obtains consent before contacting the physician and documents the plan.

questions.model_answer:
My first safety concern is that Esi may be having a relapse and may be treating it as tiredness. She told me about new right foot catching and eye pain and blurring, and I found mild weakness and a brisker reflex on the right. Because relapses can be treated, and early assessment can protect vision and function, I want her seen by a physician quickly. So I would say to Esi: I am glad you told me about your foot and eye. I do not think this is just fatigue, and I would like your neurologist or a doctor to look at it today or tomorrow. I would offer to call with her permission from the clinic while she is here, and give her a short written summary to take along. I would give her warning signs: if her vision gets worse, if she loses vision in either eye, if the weakness spreads or she cannot walk safely, if she develops new numbness, a loss of bladder or bowel control, or severe dizziness, she should go to the emergency department.

Second, her wish to start a gym program and hot yoga. I would explain that exercise is good for multiple sclerosis and is not the cause of her fatigue, and that I want to help her become active. But I would hold new intense exercise for a few days until a doctor has looked at her, because if she is relapsing, a strenuous program could worsen things and fatigue could make her fall. Meanwhile, light activity such as short walks in a cool place is fine. Hot yoga I would advise against, and I would say why: heat raises body temperature, and in multiple sclerosis a small rise can temporarily worsen vision, weakness and fatigue. I would suggest alternatives such as cooler pools, fans, cooling vests or neck wraps, and exercise in the morning when she is freshest.

Third, falls. Her right toes are catching, and she uses stairs at school every day. I would check her footwear, teach her to use the handrail, discuss an ankle-foot orthosis if the foot drop persists, and ask her to tell me about any near-falls.

If her vision is blurry, driving may be unsafe. I would ask her to discuss this with her physician and not drive if it is hard to see.

How she takes part. I would ask her what worries her most. I suspect money and work. I would ask what she understands, offer choices on how to reach her doctor, such as phoning now or going to a walk-in clinic, and check that she can repeat the plan. I would document it all, with her consent for every contact.

scale.4: Arranges prompt medical review of possible relapse, gives warning signs, holds intense exercise, advises against heat exposure, addresses falls and driving and shares decisions with Esi.
scale.3: Makes a medical referral and advises on heat and exercise but lacks urgency, fall or driving safety or shared decision-making.
scale.2: Gives general MS exercise and heat advice with only a routine neurology referral.
scale.1: Approves hot yoga or a vigorous program, or does not address the new deficits.

questions.prompt: Esi asks you to complete her insurer's long-term disability form and says she has not told her employer she stopped treatment. Describe how you will respond and which professional responsibilities apply.

checklist.point: Obtains explicit written consent before releasing any information to the insurer, and limits it to what the form requires.
Completes only the parts within physiotherapy scope, such as observed function and measures, and defers diagnosis and prognosis to the physician.
Reports accurately and objectively, without exaggerating or omitting findings, including the date of assessment.
Does not disclose to the employer that she stopped treatment and does not pressure her either way.
Discusses without judgment the lapse in therapy and encourages her to resolve it with her neurologist, including coverage options and social work.
Offers to refer to social work or patient navigation for drug coverage and benefits.
Discloses fees for form completion according to clinic policy and the regulator's standards.
Documents the request, consent, what was completed and what was deferred.

questions.model_answer:
The disability form raises scope, honesty and consent, and the treatment lapse raises advocacy.

Consent first. The form asks for diagnosis, prognosis and functional abilities, and it goes to her insurer. I will not send anything until Esi has read what I plan to include and signed consent that names the insurer, the purpose and the information to be shared. If the form asks for more than it needs, I would share only what is relevant and explain why. This follows provincial health privacy legislation and my regulator's standards.

Scope. I can describe what I assessed: her walking measures, balance, strength, fatigue scores and what she can do in a session, and I can describe those observations with dates. I cannot provide a diagnosis or a prognosis, since those belong to her neurologist or physician. I would say: I can fill in the functional parts based on what I observed, and I will ask your neurologist to complete the diagnosis and outlook. Because her symptoms may be changing, I would mark my findings as of today's date and say that they may change after medical review. I will write only what I measured. I will not exaggerate to help her claim, and I will not leave out findings that she may not want mentioned. Accuracy protects her and me, and fraud or misleading statements would breach professional standards.

Employer. She has not told her employer she stopped treatment. That is her information. I would not contact the employer, and I would not push her to disclose. I would explain what the insurer form will and will not tell the employer, and I would suggest she think about how to talk to her workplace about accommodations such as scheduling and cooling.

The treatment lapse is the more important issue. I would not judge her. I would say that I understand money is tight and that stopping her disease-modifying therapy raises the chance of new disease activity, especially with the new symptoms we found today. I would encourage her to talk with her neurologist about restarting and offer to refer her to social work or a patient navigator who can look at public drug programs and manufacturer assistance. With her permission I would include the lapse in my communication to her physician.

Finally, I would disclose any fee for completing forms before I do the work, according to clinic policy, and document the request, her consent, what I completed and what I deferred.

scale.4: Secures consent, stays within scope, reports objectively, respects her control of employer information, addresses the treatment lapse supportively and documents.
scale.3: Handles consent and scope but is thin on accuracy, the treatment lapse or documentation.
scale.2: Completes the form with little concern for scope or consent, or refuses without helping.
scale.1: Provides diagnosis and prognosis, shares information with the employer or inflates findings.

safety_or_ethics_point: The buried issue is a possible multiple sclerosis relapse: new right foot catching, dorsiflexion weakness, brisker reflex and eye pain with movement for days, in a woman who has been off disease-modifying therapy for three months and who attributes it all to fatigue. A competent candidate flags it, arranges same-day medical review, advises against heat exposure and respects consent and scope on the insurer form.
common_errors: Candidates design a fatigue-management program (pacing, exercise, cooling) and never question the new neurological signs. In question 3 they complete the diagnosis and prognosis parts of the insurer form themselves or share details without written consent.
examiner_notes: A pass notices that the new unilateral deficits and visual symptoms are not just fatigue and acts the same day, while keeping scope and consent sound. A fatigue-only answer is a fail on this case.

title: Widespread pain and fatigue in a retail worker in a pain program
setting: Hospital-based interdisciplinary chronic pain program, outpatient physiotherapy clinic room
client_profile: Priya Nair is a 51 year old woman who works part time as a cashier and stockroom clerk. Three years ago her family physician diagnosed fibromyalgia after widespread pain, unrefreshing sleep and fatigue with normal bloodwork. She takes duloxetine 60 mg daily and acetaminophen as needed. Her Revised Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire score is 62 out of 100 (higher is worse). Pain averages 6 out of 10 on a numeric scale. She sleeps about 5 hours and wakes tired. She can walk 10 minutes before pain flares for the next two days, so she either does too much on a good day or nothing for days. Examination shows diffuse tenderness, full joint range, normal strength, a normal neurological screen and a 6-minute walk of 340 m. She has not exercised regularly in two years.
clinical_scenario: The program offers eight weekly group sessions with a psychologist, an occupational therapist and you, publicly funded. Priya's private plan also covers ten individual physiotherapy visits per year. Her manager wants her back to five full shifts a week, which she thinks is impossible. She cares for her mother in the evenings, which cuts her sleep further. At the end of the visit, while picking up her coat, she says quietly that she is so tired of all this that some nights she thinks it would be easier not to wake up, then laughs it off and asks about next week's time.

questions.prompt: Describe the physiotherapy care plan you would develop with this client over the first eight weeks. Include goals, the main interventions, how you would set the exercise dosage and progress it, and how you would measure change.

checklist.point: Sets collaborative, functional goals tied to her work and caregiving roles, such as walking duration and shift tolerance
Provides pain neuroscience and condition education to explain that hurt does not always mean harm
Prescribes low-intensity aerobic exercise starting well below the current flare threshold, for example 5 to 10 minutes
Teaches pacing with planned rest and a fixed baseline rather than boom and bust activity
Progresses gradually, about 10 percent or 1 to 2 minutes per week, with a flare plan that avoids full rest
Adds light resistance and flexibility work after tolerance to aerobic exercise is established
Includes sleep hygiene and links with the psychologist and occupational therapist on shared goals
Uses outcome measures such as the Revised Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire, 6-minute walk and pain scale and sets reassessment points
Plans a graded return to work discussion rather than an immediate full schedule

questions.model_answer: Thank you. My plan is built around what Priya wants to be able to do, so first I would agree on goals with her. She told me she wants to get through a shift, keep helping her mother, and stop crashing after good days. I would set a goal such as walking 15 minutes at an easy pace within eight weeks, building toward 30 minutes over the following months, and tolerating a four hour shift without a multi-day flare. Second, education. I would explain in plain words that fibromyalgia involves a sensitive pain system, that her tests are normal because her joints and muscles are not being damaged, and that carefully dosed movement calms the system over time. That reduces fear, and fear of movement is a major reason people stop. Third, aerobic exercise, which has the best evidence in this condition. Because she flares after 10 minutes, I would start at about half of that, five minutes of easy walking or stationary cycling, at an effort she can talk through, roughly 3 out of 10 on a perceived exertion scale. I would have her do it most days, and add one or two minutes per week only if she has no worse than a mild increase in pain the next day. If she flares, she drops back one step rather than stopping. Fourth, pacing. We would find her baseline, the amount she can do on a bad day, and have her do that amount every day, so good days no longer trigger crashes. Fifth, from about week three or four I would add light resistance exercises for large muscle groups, such as sit to stand and band rows, two sets of eight to ten at low load, and gentle stretching. Sixth, sleep and stress. I would give basic sleep routines, coordinate with the psychologist on cognitive behavioural strategies, and with the occupational therapist on how she organizes her evenings with her mother and her workstation. Seventh, measurement. I would repeat the Revised Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire and the 6-minute walk at week four and week eight, and track her daily walking minutes and pain in a simple diary. A change of about 14 percent on the questionnaire or a clear gain in walking distance would tell us the plan is working. If there is no change by week four, I would review dosage, adherence, mood and sleep, rather than just pushing harder. Finally, I would use her private visits to supervise progression between group sessions and help her prepare a graded return to work letter for her physician and employer.

scale.4: Gives a collaborative plan with functional goals, education, a low starting dose below the flare threshold, specific progression and flare rules, pacing, and named outcome measures with reassessment, linked to her case.
scale.3: Sound plan with education, exercise and pacing, but dosage, flare management or measurement is vague.
scale.2: Lists interventions such as exercise and modalities without a dose, progression or reasoning tied to the flare pattern.
scale.1: Prescribes vigorous exercise or passive treatment only, ignores the boom and bust pattern, or imposes goals without her input.

questions.prompt: As the client is leaving, she makes a comment that concerns you. Describe how you would respond right then and what steps you would take afterward, while keeping her at the centre of decisions.

checklist.point: Recognizes the comment as possible suicidal ideation and does not let her leave without a response
Pauses the exit, sits down with her, and asks directly and calmly whether she is thinking of ending her life
Asks about plan, means, intent, timing, past attempts and protective factors in a non-judgmental way
Acknowledges her exhaustion and thanks her for telling you before offering any solutions
Knows the clinic procedure and involves the program psychologist or physician the same day when risk is present
Provides crisis resources such as 9-8-8 and the local emergency department and does not leave an at-risk client alone
Seeks her consent to share information and explains the limits of confidentiality if safety is at risk
Documents her words, your questions, her answers, actions and follow-up objectively
Arranges a specific follow-up contact rather than waiting for next week's session

questions.model_answer: I would not let that comment pass. Even though she laughed it off, saying some nights it would be easier not to wake up can mean passive or active thoughts of suicide, and asking about it does not plant the idea. So I would put down my notes, ask her to sit with me for a few minutes, and say something like: I heard what you said at the door and I am glad you told me. You sound exhausted. Are you having thoughts of ending your life? I would ask it directly, in plain words, and then listen. Next I would find out how serious it is. Does she have a plan, access to means such as stored medication, a sense of when, any past attempts, and what keeps her going, such as her mother, her family, her work? I would also ask about her sleep, her mood, and whether she has told her physician. If she says the thoughts are fleeting, with no plan or intent and strong reasons to live, I would still involve the team. I would tell her what I am going to do and why, and ask permission to bring in the program psychologist today, who is already part of her care, and to let her family physician know. I would explain that confidentiality has limits, and that if I believed she was in immediate danger I would have to get help even without her agreement. If she tells me she has a plan or intent, I would not leave her alone, I would call the program psychologist or physician or the emergency department and follow our clinic crisis procedure, and I would help her get there safely. In either case I would give her the 9-8-8 Suicide Crisis Helpline number, which is available by call or text at any hour, and write it down for her, and encourage her to include a trusted person. I would collaborate with her on a safety plan rather than imposing one: what she will do on a bad night, who she will call, and how her medication is stored. Afterward I would document her exact words, my questions, her answers, who I contacted and what we agreed, and I would arrange a call or visit within a day or two rather than waiting a week. Her exercise plan would be paused or reduced until she is supported, because her wellbeing comes first.

scale.4: Responds immediately and directly, assesses risk with specific questions, involves the right team members with consent, provides crisis resources, plans follow-up and documents, all in a warm client-centred way.
scale.3: Recognizes the risk and refers appropriately but misses direct questioning of plan or means, or follow-up detail.
scale.2: Notes concern and suggests she see her physician later without assessing risk or acting the same day.
scale.1: Ignores the comment, treats it as a joke, or reassures without assessing safety.

questions.prompt: Discuss how you would organize her physiotherapy services across the group program and her insurance-funded visits, including scheduling, documentation, and what you would delegate or not delegate.

checklist.point: Coordinates group sessions and individual visits so they complement rather than duplicate each other
Uses the ten individual visits strategically, such as early dosing, week four review and transition to self-management
Bills only for services actually delivered and does not extend visits or add unnecessary treatments to use up coverage
Documents assessments, goals, dosage, progression, consent, outcome measures and safety discussions in the shared record
Delegates supervised exercise practice to a physiotherapist assistant with clear written instructions and keeps assessment and plan changes
Keeps risk-related decisions and the progression of the plan with the physiotherapist
Books longer sessions or flexible times around her shifts and caregiving, with reminders and a cancellation plan
Uses an interpreted or written home program and tracks adherence with a simple diary

questions.model_answer: There are two streams of care, the publicly funded group program and her ten private visits, and my job is to make them work as one plan. First, scheduling. Her group sessions are weekly and fixed, so I would schedule her individual visits around her shifts and her evenings with her mother. I would offer early morning or late afternoon times, send a reminder, and discuss a clear cancellation approach, because missed visits are common when someone has unpredictable pain and caregiving duties. Second, I would plan the use of the ten visits rather than spending them evenly. I would use the first for individual assessment and to set her exercise dose, since group classes cannot be dosed to one person, then visits in weeks two, four and six to progress her program and review her flare plan. I would reserve the last few for the transition to independent exercise and a return to work letter. Third, billing. Her insurer covers ten visits, but I would only bill for care I actually deliver and that she needs. I would not add passive treatments or extend the program because coverage remains, and if she needs fewer visits I would say so. If a service is delivered by an assistant, it should be billed accurately as such. Fourth, delegation. A physiotherapist assistant could supervise her walking and strengthening practice in the gym once I have set the dose and written clear instructions with stop and flare rules. The assessment, interpretation of her response, decisions about progression, and the safety follow-up from today all remain with me, because those require clinical judgement. I would check in with the assistant after the first sessions and review her notes. Fifth, documentation. I would record the assessment, goals agreed with her, dosage, outcome measures, education, consent, and the safety discussion and actions, in the shared program record following the privacy rules, and share only what the team needs, with her consent. Finally, I would give her a written home program and a simple diary so progress between visits is visible to her and to the team, and I would review caseload so I have time for brief phone follow-ups when she flares.

scale.4: Describes coordinated scheduling around her life, deliberate use of limited visits, honest billing, safe delegation with retained clinical decisions, and thorough documentation and privacy.
scale.3: Covers scheduling, documentation and delegation but with limited detail on billing ethics or how the visits are used.
scale.2: Lists administrative tasks without reasoning or without separating what can and cannot be delegated.
scale.1: Delegates assessment or safety decisions, bills for unneeded services, or ignores coordination.

safety_or_ethics_point: The buried issue is her remark that some nights it would be easier not to wake up, said as she leaves. A competent candidate catches it, asks directly about suicide, assesses plan and means, uses crisis resources, involves the team with consent, and documents. Treating it as a joke or deferring it to next week is unsafe.
common_errors: Candidates spend all their time on exercise detail and never mention her comment, or note it and only advise seeing her doctor without direct questions. Others prescribe an aerobic dose that matches her good day, which triggers flares.
examiner_notes: A pass shows a low starting dose with pacing and measurement, plus a clear, direct, same-day response to the suicide comment. Missing the comment is a fail on Question 2 even with a strong care plan.

title: Airway clearance and exercise planning in a young adult with a chronic lung condition
setting: Outpatient specialty clinic, shared waiting area and physiotherapy room
client_profile: Jasmine Tremblay is a 19 year old university student living in residence. She has had cystic fibrosis since infancy and chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa in her sputum. Two weeks ago she finished 14 days of intravenous antibiotics for an exacerbation. Today FEV1 is 62 percent predicted (it was 71 percent a year ago), resting SpO2 is 94 percent on room air and respiratory rate is 18. She reports a daily productive cough with thick green sputum, mostly in the morning. She admits she does airway clearance once a day instead of twice, because of lectures and roommates. Her body mass index is 19.5. She takes pancreatic enzymes with meals and an inhaled hypertonic saline before treatment. Chest sounds show scattered crackles in the upper zones. On the 3-minute step test her SpO2 falls from 94 to 90 percent with mild breathlessness.
clinical_scenario: Jasmine uses an oscillating positive expiratory pressure device and has an active cycle of breathing technique she was taught as a child. She wants to join the university hockey intramurals and the gym. She mentions she rinsed her device only occasionally. She says the last few mornings there were pink streaks in her sputum, but she did not want to "make a big deal". In the waiting area today she sat close to another young woman with cystic fibrosis and they chatted before her appointment. Her mother lives four hours away and she manages her own appointments.

questions.prompt: Outline the airway clearance and exercise plan you would develop with Jasmine. Include techniques, schedule, how you would set and progress exercise, and how you would support her adherence and monitor her response.

checklist.point: Reinforces twice daily airway clearance and extra sessions during exacerbations, timed around her lecture schedule
Reviews her technique with the oscillating device and active cycle of breathing, checking pressure, huff and cough effectiveness
Sequences inhaled therapy before airway clearance, as already prescribed, and coordinates timing with the team
Prescribes regular aerobic exercise, with strength training, using a graded program based on her tolerance and a measured baseline, started once the team has cleared the sputum bleeding
Sets oxygen saturation monitoring during exercise and a stop threshold agreed with the respiratory team
Addresses hydration, enzyme timing and fuelling around exercise, linked to the dietitian
Uses motivational strategies and shared goals, such as playing intramurals, to support adherence
Sets outcome measures and review points such as sputum volume, FEV1 trend, exercise test and adherence log
Teaches cleaning and drying of equipment per manufacturer and clinic guidance

questions.model_answer: I would plan this with Jasmine, because she is an adult who manages her own care and has her own priorities. Her main goal is to play intramurals and go to the gym, so I would use that as the thread. First, airway clearance. She is doing it once a day and her lung function has fallen from 71 to 62 percent over a year, with a recent exacerbation, so I would aim for twice daily, morning and evening, each lasting about 20 to 30 minutes once her team has advised on the bleeding, and until then I would use only gentle techniques, relaxed breathing control and gentle huffing, as in my safety answer, with extra sessions if she has more sputum or feels unwell. Together we would look at her calendar and choose fixed times that fit lectures, such as a session on waking before class and one before bed, and discuss a private space in residence. I would watch her do a session with her oscillating device and active cycle of breathing, checking her breathing control, thoracic expansion, and a forced expiration technique that produces sputum rather than just noise, and correct anything that needs correcting. She would take her hypertonic saline first, as prescribed, then clear her airway. Second, exercise. Exercise supports airway clearance and fitness. I would test her baseline, such as a 6-minute walk or the step test, with SpO2 monitoring. Her saturation fell from 94 to 90 percent, so I would agree with her respiratory physician on a threshold, and teach her to use a pulse oximeter and stop and rest if she drops below it, or has more than the usual breathlessness. Because she told me about pink streaks in her sputum, which I address in my safety answer, I would keep clearance gentle and hold high-intensity exercise until her cystic fibrosis team has assessed it. Once they have cleared her, I would start with 20 minutes of aerobic exercise three times a week at a moderate effort, around 3 to 4 out of 10 on a dyspnea scale at first, add two sessions of strength work, and progress duration by about 5 minutes every week or two. She can join intramurals as her tolerance improves, with a plan for hydration, salt and enzymes around sessions. Third, adherence. I would use motivational interviewing, explore what makes the second session hard, and agree a small written plan with specific times. A simple log or phone reminder would help. Fourth, equipment. I would teach her to wash the device after each use, air dry it, and follow the manufacturer's disinfection steps, because her chronic Pseudomonas makes contamination matter. Finally, I would monitor her response with her sputum volume, FEV1 at clinic visits, exercise tolerance, and her own log, and review in four weeks.

scale.4: Gives a specific, client-centred plan covering twice daily airway clearance with technique check, graded exercise with SpO2 limits, adherence strategies, equipment care and monitoring tied to her findings.
scale.3: Covers airway clearance and exercise reasonably but dose, saturation limits or adherence strategy is thin.
scale.2: Lists techniques and exercise in general terms without schedule, progression or monitoring.
scale.1: Recommends unmonitored vigorous exercise, drops airway clearance, or ignores her desaturation and goals.

questions.prompt: What safety concerns do you have with this client at this visit and what would you do about each of them, including how you would speak with her about them?

checklist.point: Recognizes pink streaks in sputum as possible hemoptysis and asks about amount, frequency, pain, fever and trend
Withholds or modifies vigorous airway clearance and intensive exercise until the respirologist assesses the bleeding
Contacts the cystic fibrosis team the same day and explains the urgency, with a plan for large bleeds and emergency services
Recognizes cross-infection risk from close contact with another person with cystic fibrosis and applies masking and separation
Explains that people with cystic fibrosis should keep distance, avoid shared spaces and equipment, and corrects this without blame
Reviews desaturation on exertion and sets monitoring and stopping rules
Addresses hand hygiene, equipment cleaning and clinic cleaning between patients
Uses plain language, thanks her for mentioning the blood and respects her autonomy while explaining the reasons

questions.model_answer: I have three safety concerns, and the first one is the most urgent. First, the pink streaks in her sputum. She mentioned it almost in passing, but blood in the sputum can be a sign of airway bleeding in cystic fibrosis, and vigorous airway clearance, forceful coughing, or intense exercise could worsen it. I would thank her for telling me, then ask specific questions: how much, a streak or a teaspoon or more, how many days, whether it is increasing, any chest pain, fever, or more breathlessness. For small streaks with no distress I would hold the more forceful elements of clearance and any high-intensity exercise for now, and call her cystic fibrosis team, the respirologist or nurse coordinator, the same day to report it and ask whether she needs to be seen sooner. I would explain this to her plainly: this is not a punishment, I am trying to keep her safe, and the decision about how to continue treatment will be made together with her team. If the bleeding were larger or increasing, I would hold airway clearance completely and arrange urgent assessment the same day. If it were heavy, meaning large amounts of fresh red blood, or she were dizzy, very breathless or unstable, I would call 911 and not wait for a clinic call. Second, cross-infection. She sat close to another person with cystic fibrosis and they chatted. People with cystic fibrosis can pass resistant organisms such as Pseudomonas to each other, so current practice is to keep them apart, usually at least two metres, with masks, and without shared rooms. I would gently explain this to her, not blame her, and tell her I will arrange separate times or waiting areas, and make sure my room is cleaned between patients. I would also review hand hygiene and discuss with her how this applies in residence and at the gym. Third, her desaturation from 94 to 90 percent on a step test. That is mild, but I would set clear rules: use a pulse oximeter during exercise, stop and rest if below the threshold the team agrees, and report persistent changes. Last, I would remind her to clean and dry her devices after each use. Throughout, I would check she understands and agrees with the plan, and document the discussion and who I contacted.

scale.4: Identifies hemoptysis as the priority, modifies treatment, contacts the team the same day and sets emergency criteria, also addresses cross-infection and exertional desaturation, with respectful plain communication.
scale.3: Identifies hemoptysis and cross-infection and acts reasonably but with gaps in urgency, specifics or communication.
scale.2: Notes one concern, or mentions several without a clear action or explanation to the client.
scale.1: Misses the bleeding or continues vigorous clearance and exercise without assessment.

questions.prompt: Explain how you would collaborate with the team and others to support Jasmine over the next few months. Include who you would involve, what you would share, and how you would keep the communication clear.

checklist.point: Identifies the cystic fibrosis multidisciplinary team members and their roles, including respirologist, nurse, dietitian, respiratory therapist, social worker and pharmacist
Obtains Jasmine's consent about what is shared with whom, including the university
Communicates the bleeding report and findings clearly to the respirologist with a structured summary
Coordinates exercise limits and oxygen saturation thresholds with the medical team
Involves the dietitian about low body mass index, enzymes and exercise fuelling
Suggests contacting university accessibility or health services for scheduling and space for treatments, with her permission
Considers social work for psychosocial support, adherence barriers and transition from pediatric care
Plans how and when team members will follow up and share updates, including with Jasmine herself

questions.model_answer: Jasmine's care depends on a team, and my role is to be one clear part of it. First, I would ask her consent: who she is happy for me to talk to and what can be shared. She is an adult managing her own care, and she may not want her university to know details of her health, so I would explain what I would like to share and why, and respect her decisions. Second, the cystic fibrosis clinic team. The respirologist needs to know about the pink-streaked sputum today, so I would phone and give a short structured report: who she is, what I found, what I did, and what I am asking. That would be that she is 19 with cystic fibrosis and chronic Pseudomonas, finished intravenous antibiotics two weeks ago, FEV1 is 62 percent and down from 71 percent, saturation drops from 94 to 90 percent on a step test, she reports several days of pink streaks, and I have held vigorous clearance and exercise until I hear back. I would ask for advice on her exercise limits and saturation threshold. The clinic nurse coordinator is a good first contact for follow-up. Third, the dietitian. Her body mass index is 19.5, and exercise increases energy needs, so I would ask for advice on calories, salt, hydration, and enzyme timing around exercise. Fourth, the social worker or psychologist on the team, because she lives away from her mother in residence, is skipping treatments, and may be struggling with the burden of daily care. Fifth, with her permission, the university accessibility or health services could help with a private space for treatments, flexible lecture schedules, and a plan for exacerbations. Sixth, her pharmacist and the respiratory therapist on devices and inhaled therapy timing. For clear communication, I would send written notes after each visit, agree who contacts Jasmine about what so she is not given conflicting messages, and set a review date in four weeks. I would also tell Jasmine what I report back, so she is part of the conversation, and ask her which method of contact she prefers, such as text or email.

scale.4: Names the right team members with their roles, obtains consent first, gives a structured urgent report on the bleeding, coordinates exercise limits, nutrition and psychosocial support, and sets clear follow-up with Jasmine included.
scale.3: Names the team and shares appropriate information but with limited consent discussion, structure or follow-up.
scale.2: Lists professionals without explaining what is shared, why or how.
scale.1: Shares information without consent, omits the medical team, or does not communicate the bleeding concern.

safety_or_ethics_point: Two issues are buried. Pink streaks in the sputum are possible hemoptysis and need same-day team contact and modified treatment. Her chat with another person with cystic fibrosis is a cross-infection risk. A competent candidate asks questions, holds vigorous clearance, calls the team, and corrects the contact kindly.
common_errors: Candidates focus on airway clearance technique and exercise and never pick up the pink streaks, or they note it but continue the planned program. Others lecture her about the waiting room contact in a way that shames her.
examiner_notes: A pass identifies the blood and the infection risk, modifies treatment and communicates with the team and consent. The candidate who writes an excellent exercise plan but ignores the sputum fails the safety question.

title: Profound weakness after prolonged critical illness on an acute care ward
setting: Medical-surgical acute care ward, bedside, day 3 after transfer from the intensive care unit
client_profile: Gordon Leclerc is a 66 year old retired bus driver admitted 4 weeks ago with septic shock from pneumonia. He spent 16 days in the intensive care unit, 9 of them on a ventilator with sedation and a short course of corticosteroids. He was previously independent and walked daily. He has type 2 diabetes and hypertension. Today he is alert, oriented and cooperative. He cannot lift his arms against gravity for long, cannot sit unsupported for more than a minute and needs two staff to transfer. Strength on the Medical Research Council sum score (12 muscles, maximum 60) is 38. Grip is 8 kg on the right and 10 kg on the left. Reflexes are reduced, sensation to light touch is intact, and facial and eye movements are normal. Resting heart rate is 98, BP 128/74, SpO2 96 percent on room air. Platelets were 62 x 10^9/L yesterday and prophylactic anticoagulation is on hold.
clinical_scenario: The ward is short staffed and you are carrying 14 patients today with one physiotherapist assistant. Gordon is on contact precautions because he grew methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus in a nasal swab. His wife is anxious and asks if he will walk again. Nursing mentions that he complained of some "cramping" in his right calf this morning, and the calf looks a little fuller than the left, but he has had pain in both legs for days. A mechanical lift and a tilt table are available but shared across two floors.

questions.prompt: Explain your clinical impression of Gordon's weakness and describe the further assessment you would do to support or refine it, including how you would interpret the findings you have so far.

checklist.point: Interprets a sum score of 38 out of 60 as significant weakness, below the threshold of 48 used to identify acquired weakness
States an impression of ICU-acquired weakness and distinguishes likely polyneuropathy, myopathy or both
Identifies risk factors in his history such as sepsis, ventilation, sedation, steroids, hyperglycemia and immobility
Considers differentials such as stroke, spinal cord, Guillain-Barre syndrome, electrolyte problems, medication effect and deconditioning
Notes symmetric, proximal and distal weakness with preserved cranial nerves and sensation as consistent with the impression
Plans standardized measures such as repeat sum score, grip dynamometry, sit-to-stand and functional mobility scales, and tracks change
Examines the right calf: circumference, tenderness, warmth, swelling, and considers deep vein thrombosis risk with anticoagulation on hold
Checks respiratory muscle function, orthostatic response, delirium, nutrition and skin
Recommends discussion with the team about electrophysiology or other testing if the picture is unclear

questions.model_answer: Based on what I have, my working impression is intensive care unit acquired weakness, most likely critical illness polyneuropathy, myopathy, or a combination of the two, on top of deconditioning. I will explain why. First, his history carries the classic risk factors: sepsis, 9 days of mechanical ventilation, sedation, a course of corticosteroids, diabetes, and 16 days in intensive care with limited movement. Second, the pattern fits. His weakness is symmetrical and affects both arms and legs, his cranial nerves and eye movements are normal, his sensation is intact, his reflexes are reduced rather than absent or brisk, and he is alert, so this is not a central problem. His Medical Research Council sum score is 38 out of 60. A score below 48 is the usual threshold for clinically significant acquired weakness, so he is well into that range, and a score at this level predicts a longer recovery and higher risk of complications. His grip, 8 and 10 kilograms, supports this because values under about 11 kilograms in men also indicate weakness. I would keep other possibilities in mind: a stroke or spinal cord problem, though symmetrical weakness with normal cranial nerves argues against them, Guillain-Barre syndrome, which would usually show absent reflexes and progress, electrolyte disturbances such as low potassium or phosphate, medication effects, and simple deconditioning, which does not usually produce this degree of weakness. Next steps in assessment. I would repeat the sum score and grip at consistent times, assess sitting balance, sit to stand with assistance, and use a functional scale suited to the ward, such as the Physical Function in ICU Test or the Functional Status Score for the ICU, so I can track change. I would check his breathing pattern and cough for respiratory muscle weakness, his blood pressure and heart rate when moving from lying to sitting, his cognition for delirium, his nutrition and skin. I would ask the physician whether electrophysiological testing or review of his electrolytes and creatine kinase would help. I would also examine his right calf now. It looks fuller than the left and he reports cramping. Pain in both legs can be from weakness, but with his anticoagulation on hold because of low platelets, I need to measure the calf, check warmth and tenderness, and talk to the nurse and physician today, before any mobilizing, about whether he needs imaging.

scale.4: Gives a clear impression of ICU-acquired weakness with reasons from history and findings, interprets the sum score and grip, names differentials, plans specific measures and recognizes the calf finding as needing assessment.
scale.3: Reaches the correct impression with some support but limited differentials, measures or attention to the calf.
scale.2: Names the condition or lists tests without interpreting the findings.
scale.1: Misattributes the weakness, ignores the findings or overlooks the calf.

questions.prompt: Describe the precautions you would take and the decisions you would make about whether and how to mobilize Gordon today, and how you would involve him and his wife in these decisions.

checklist.point: Holds mobilization of the legs until the calf has been assessed and a possible deep vein thrombosis has been discussed with the physician
Communicates the concern to the nurse and physician the same day and requests imaging and an anticoagulation decision
Continues safe bed-level activity that does not stress the right leg, such as upper limb and left leg active exercise, with clinician agreement
Uses contact precautions with correct personal protective equipment and equipment cleaning
Monitors heart rate, blood pressure, SpO2 and fatigue and sets stop criteria
Plans safe handling with a mechanical lift or sufficient staff once cleared, to avoid falls and injury to the shoulders
Explains risks and options to Gordon and his wife in plain language and respects his preferences
Addresses his wife's question honestly about recovery without false promises

questions.model_answer: My main decision today is that I will not mobilize his legs until his right calf has been assessed, and I will not wait to raise it. His right calf is fuller than the left, he reports cramping, he has been immobile for weeks, he has sepsis and diabetes, and his preventive anticoagulation is on hold because of low platelets. That makes a deep vein thrombosis a real possibility, and walking, standing or vigorous leg exercise could dislodge a clot and cause a pulmonary embolism. So first I would examine the calf quickly and gently, measuring circumference at a marked point, checking warmth, tenderness and swelling. Whatever I find, I would tell his nurse and the physician today and ask for a decision about imaging and about whether anticoagulation can be restarted. Until I hear back, I would avoid active or passive exercise of the right leg and no standing, tilt table or transfers to chair. I can still do useful things safely: active and assisted exercises for his arms, deep breathing, positioning, and gentle active movement of the left leg, as the team agrees. Once there is no clot or it is treated, I would start sitting at the edge of the bed and progress. Second, his vital signs. I would check heart rate, blood pressure and SpO2 before, during and after activity, and stop if heart rate rises above an agreed limit, blood pressure drops, SpO2 falls below 90 percent, or he feels dizzy or very fatigued. His resting heart rate of 98 is a little high and I would watch it. Third, infection control. He is on contact precautions, so I would put on gown and gloves before entering and clean equipment such as the lift sling and any dynamometer afterward. Fourth, safe handling. When he is cleared, I would use the mechanical lift or enough staff, because with his weak shoulder girdle, pulling on his arms could injure him, and a fall would be serious. Finally, I would speak with Gordon and his wife in simple words. I would tell them I noticed something in the leg that needs checking first, that this delay is about keeping him safe, and ask what matters to him. About walking again, I would say that most people improve, but it can take weeks to months, and I would not promise a timeline.

scale.4: Withholds leg mobilization pending assessment of a possible clot, escalates same day, offers safe alternatives, sets monitoring and stop criteria, applies infection and handling precautions, and communicates honestly with Gordon and his wife.
scale.3: Recognizes the calf risk and takes appropriate precautions but is vague on escalation, monitoring or communication.
scale.2: Mentions precautions in general without addressing the calf or setting criteria.
scale.1: Mobilizes him on the legs without addressing the calf, or promises full recovery.

questions.prompt: Discuss how you would manage your workload and the resources available today, including prioritization of patients, delegation to the physiotherapist assistant, equipment, infection control and documentation.

checklist.point: Prioritizes patients by acuity and risk, with those at risk of deterioration or needing urgent decisions seen first
Sees Gordon's calf concern early and communicates it before routine caseload
Delegates only stable, predictable tasks to the assistant with clear instructions, limits and a way to report concerns
Keeps assessment, clinical decision making and any patient with unclear status with the physiotherapist
Books shared equipment such as the lift and tilt table and cleans it between patients
Applies contact precautions, hand hygiene and equipment cleaning, including for the assistant
Documents findings, escalations, who was informed, treatment given and plan, in a timely manner
Communicates with nursing about the schedule and informs the manager if safe coverage is not possible

questions.model_answer: With 14 patients and one assistant, I cannot give everyone equal time, so I would prioritize by risk and urgency. First, I would take two minutes at the start of the shift to review my list with the charge nurse, ask who is unstable, who has new orders, and who is going home. Patients who are deteriorating, who have new respiratory problems, or who need a discharge decision come first. Gordon would be near the top, not because he needs long treatment, but because of his calf and the decision about imaging and anticoagulation. I would assess and report his calf early so that the team can act while I see others, instead of discovering it at the end of the day. Second, delegation. The assistant can safely supervise stable patients with clear programs, for example a patient who is already walking with a cane and has an established exercise routine, or provide upper-limb range of motion for Gordon if I have specified exactly what is permitted. For each task I would give written, specific instructions, name the limits, such as heart rate, saturation, and pain, tell the assistant to stop and call me if anything changes, and tell them I will be reachable. I would not delegate the assessment of Gordon's calf, his first mobilizations after clearance, or any patient whose status is uncertain, because those need clinical judgement. Third, equipment. The lift and tilt table are shared across two floors, so I would book them in advance with the other ward, plan Gordon's use for when he is cleared, and clean them between patients. Fourth, infection control. For Gordon I would use gown and gloves under contact precautions, and I would tell the assistant the same rules and check that they clean shared equipment. Hand hygiene before and after every patient. Fifth, documentation. I would write my assessment, the calf measurements, who I informed and when, what the physician decided, what treatment I gave or held, and the plan, as soon as possible after each visit, not at the end of the day. Finally, if I cannot safely see everyone, I would tell the manager and the nurses which patients will not be seen today and why, so that nobody is unaware.

scale.4: Prioritizes by risk, acts early on the calf, delegates appropriate tasks with explicit limits and retains judgement tasks, plans shared equipment and infection control, documents promptly and escalates workload limits.
scale.3: Describes sound prioritization and delegation but is less detailed on equipment, infection control or documentation.
scale.2: Lists management tasks generally without linking to this workload or showing reasoning.
scale.1: Delegates unsafe tasks, ignores priority, or leaves Gordon's concern unaddressed.

safety_or_ethics_point: The buried issue is the fuller, cramping right calf in a bedbound patient whose anticoagulation is on hold for low platelets. It may be a deep vein thrombosis. A competent candidate examines the calf, holds leg mobilization, escalates the same day and prioritizes Gordon early.
common_errors: Candidates give a good account of weakness and an exercise program but start standing or leg exercises without looking at the calf. Others delegate Gordon's first mobilization to the assistant.
examiner_notes: A pass links the calf to the held anticoagulation and acts before mobilizing. Naming ICU-acquired weakness with the sum score of 38 is expected. Missing the calf is a fail on safety even with a strong assessment answer.

title: Hot, swollen knee with fever in a restaurant owner at a community clinic
setting: Private community physiotherapy clinic, direct access, late Thursday afternoon
client_profile: Rashid Hussein is a 55 year old man who owns a restaurant. He booked for a "knee problem". Two days ago his right knee became swollen, hot and painful, and he now cannot bear weight without severe pain. He has had mild osteoarthritis in both knees for years. Ten days ago he received a corticosteroid injection in the right knee from another clinic. He has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin and takes ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day for the knee. Temperature today is 38.4 C, heart rate 102, blood pressure 126/78. The knee is visibly swollen with a large effusion, warm and red, held at about 30 degrees of flexion, and he resists any passive motion beyond a few degrees because of severe pain. A small scab is visible over the medial joint line. He says an X-ray from last year showed "wear and tear".
clinical_scenario: Rashid says the restaurant has a big banquet tomorrow evening and he is the only one who can run the kitchen.
