He tells you he just wants some "treatment to loosen it up" so he can get through tomorrow, and he will see his doctor on Monday. He lives alone and his wife is travelling. He asks you to please not call anyone because he does not want his staff to hear he is unwell. He is alert and speaks clearly, and shows he understands what you tell him.

questions.prompt: Explain your clinical reasoning about the cause of this knee presentation. Include what findings are most important, what other conditions you considered, and what you would conclude from the assessment.

checklist.point: Identifies acute monoarthritis with fever, warmth, large effusion and severe pain on any motion as consistent with joint infection until proven otherwise
Lists risk factors: diabetes, recent intra-articular injection, possible skin break, age and existing joint disease
Notes that ibuprofen can mask fever and symptoms and that the temperature may understate the problem
Considers differentials such as gout, pseudogout, inflammatory arthritis, hemarthrosis, cellulitis and osteoarthritis flare
Explains why the old X-ray finding of wear and tear does not explain this presentation
Explains that infection cannot be excluded by physical examination and needs joint fluid analysis, blood tests and urgent medical assessment
Notes systemic signs such as heart rate 102 and fever suggesting possible sepsis
Avoids further provocative testing and limits examination to what is needed

questions.model_answer: My conclusion is that Rashid has a hot, swollen joint with fever that must be treated as a joint infection until a physician proves otherwise, and that this is a medical emergency, not something I can treat or wait on. I will explain how I got there. First, the pattern. He has an acute single joint problem over two days with a large effusion, warmth and redness, and he holds the knee semi-flexed and resists passive motion because even small movement is very painful. That severe pain with any movement is what raises my concern most. Second, he has a temperature of 38.4 and a heart rate of 102, which suggest the body is reacting to something systemic. And he is taking ibuprofen three times a day, which lowers fever, so his real temperature may be higher and his picture may be worse than it looks. Third, his risk factors. He is 55 with diabetes, which lowers resistance to infection, he had a corticosteroid injection into this knee ten days ago, which is a recognized route for bacteria to enter the joint, and there is a small scab near the joint line, a possible skin entry point. Fourth, what else it could be. Gout or pseudogout can look the same, with a hot red joint and sometimes fever. An inflammatory arthritis, bleeding into the joint, cellulitis over the knee, or a flare of his osteoarthritis are possible, and a reaction to the injection can occur. But these cannot be separated from infection by looking at the knee or by the old X-ray, which only shows that he has osteoarthritis, not what is happening now. In fact, someone can have gout and infection together. Only joint fluid analysis, with cell count, Gram stain, culture and crystals, along with blood tests such as white cell count and inflammatory markers and blood cultures, can tell. A delay of even a day or two can destroy cartilage and lead to bone infection or sepsis. So my conclusion is that he needs urgent same-day medical assessment at an emergency department, where the joint can be aspirated. I would not push on the joint further, I would not do any special tests that move it, and I would not try to treat it with manual therapy, heat or exercise.

scale.4: Concludes joint infection must be assumed, reasons from fever, severe pain on movement, effusion, diabetes, recent injection and masked fever, considers differentials but explains why they cannot be excluded, and states the need for same-day fluid analysis.
scale.3: Identifies infection as the leading concern and urgency but reasoning on risk factors or differentials is thin.
scale.2: Lists possible diagnoses without prioritizing infection or explaining the urgency.
scale.1: Concludes osteoarthritis flare or strain, or proposes treatment.

questions.prompt: Rashid says he wants to be treated now and will see his doctor on Monday. Describe what you would say and do in response, including how you would handle the situation and support his decision making.

checklist.point: Declines to provide treatment such as manual therapy, heat, exercise or taping and explains that it could cause harm
Explains in plain language the risk of joint destruction, spread of infection and sepsis if care is delayed
Recommends same-day emergency assessment and does not suggest waiting until Monday
Assesses decision-making capacity and confirms understanding using teach-back
Explores his reasons, such as the banquet and staff, and works on solutions such as asking a manager or a friend to take over
Offers to arrange transport or ambulance, and advises not to drive himself given pain and possible sepsis
If he still refuses, respects the informed refusal, explains return warning signs, gives written information and plans follow-up
Asks about someone who can be with him because he lives alone and his wife is away

questions.model_answer: I would begin by acknowledging his situation, the banquet, the pressure, being the only one who can run the kitchen, because he is more likely to listen if he feels heard. Then I would be direct and clear. I would say: Rashid, I am worried about your knee. Your knee is hot and swollen, you have a fever, and you have diabetes and had an injection in this joint ten days ago. These together can mean the joint is infected. That is serious. An infected joint can be damaged permanently within days, and the infection can spread to your blood. I cannot treat this in my clinic, and treatments like massage, heat or exercises could make it worse. I recommend that you go to the emergency department today, so a doctor can drain a sample of fluid and decide on antibiotics. Waiting until Monday is not safe. I would ask him to tell me in his own words what he understands, which is the teach-back, and ask what worries him most about going. If the worry is the banquet, we could problem-solve together: could a sous chef, a friend, a family member, or a caterer cover? Could the restaurant postpone? I would also ask who can take him and whether a friend or family member can stay with him tonight, since he lives alone and his wife is away, and I would check his emergency contact. He should not drive himself in severe pain with a fever. If he is unsteady or looks unwell, I would call an ambulance. He is alert and understands what I say, so I think he has capacity to decide, and it is his right to decide even if I disagree. If he still refuses after clear explanation, I would not argue or pressure him further, and I would still not provide treatment. I would document that he was informed of the risks, including permanent joint damage, sepsis, and death, and that he chose to decline. I would give him a written summary, tell him exactly what signs mean he must go immediately, such as shaking chills, a rising fever or heart rate, confusion, faintness or spreading redness, which means he must call 911 at once, and I would keep urging the emergency department tonight, not a walk-in clinic and not Monday, and ask him to let me phone him this evening to check. I would also ask permission to speak to his physician or the emergency doctor, since that is the safest thing for him.

scale.4: Respectfully explains the risk in plain words, recommends same-day emergency care, declines treatment, assesses capacity with teach-back, problem-solves his barriers, and if he refuses documents informed refusal with return precautions.
scale.3: Recommends urgent care and explains the risk but is less thorough on capacity, barriers or informed refusal.
scale.2: Suggests seeing the doctor soon or monitoring without urgency, or lectures without exploring his concerns.
scale.1: Provides treatment, agrees to wait until Monday, or overrides his choice without information.

questions.prompt: Rashid asks you not to contact anyone. Discuss your professional responsibilities in this situation regarding consent, confidentiality, communication with other clinicians, documentation and your follow-up plan.

checklist.point: Seeks consent before sharing information and explains why contacting the emergency department or physician protects him
Recognizes that confidentiality has limits when there is serious risk and acts proportionately if he lacks capacity or is in imminent danger
Shares only the information needed with the receiving clinicians, such as findings, risk factors and timing
Reassures him that his staff will not be told and respects his privacy wishes where possible
Records his presentation, findings, advice, his decision, capacity, and the discussion in a timely and objective way
Acts within scope: does not diagnose definitively, aspirate or prescribe, and refers to the appropriate service
Arranges follow-up contact and confirms what happened, within what he agrees to
Reflects on whether the earlier injection or other events require reporting through the clinic or provider channels

questions.model_answer: My professional responsibilities here begin with respect for Rashid's autonomy and privacy and end with his safety, and I would work to meet both. First, consent. His information is his, so I would ask permission before I contact anyone. I would explain what I would like to do and why: phone the emergency department or his physician so that they know he is coming with a possibly infected joint and can see him quickly. I would explain that this helps him get care sooner, and ask if that is acceptable. I would be honest about what I will share, and I would tell him I will share only what is needed, such as his symptoms, temperature and heart rate, my findings, his diabetes and the recent injection, and nothing about his business or other personal details. I would assure him that I will not contact his staff or anyone he does not name, and that my clinic keeps his information private under provincial health privacy legislation. Second, the limits of confidentiality. If he declines but has capacity, I respect that wherever possible and keep urging urgent care, because adults have the right to refuse. I would only consider the minimum necessary disclosure if provincial privacy law and my regulator's standards allow it for a significant risk of serious harm, and I would tell him first. But if his condition worsened, if he became confused, faint, or could not decide, I would call emergency services, because disclosure to protect a person from serious harm is permitted when he cannot consent, and I would share the minimum needed. Third, scope. I am not able to diagnose an infection definitively, aspirate the knee or prescribe antibiotics, so my responsibility is to recognize the red flag, avoid harm, and refer to the right service promptly. Fourth, documentation. I would record the time, his history, vital signs, examination, my reasoning, my advice, his understanding and decision, capacity, who I contacted with consent, any written information I gave, and the follow-up plan, in clear objective language, and sign it. Fifth, follow-up. I would ask him to tell me where he is going, call him that evening with his permission, and if I cannot reach him I would follow my clinic's procedure. Finally, because he had an injection at another clinic, I would suggest he tell the treating doctor about it, and with his consent the treating physician and the clinic that gave the injection should be informed, so a possible post-injection infection can be reviewed and reported through their incident process. I would also reflect on whether anything in my own clinic process could help clients like him get seen faster.

scale.4: Seeks consent and explains the benefit, states limits of confidentiality accurately, shares minimum information, stays within scope, documents capacity and decisions, and arranges follow-up.
scale.3: Covers consent, confidentiality and documentation correctly but with limited detail on disclosure limits or follow-up.
scale.2: Names responsibilities in general terms without applying them to his request.
scale.1: Breaches his privacy without justification, agrees to do nothing, or oversteps scope.

safety_or_ethics_point: The buried issues are ibuprofen masking fever and the recent steroid injection with a possible skin entry point, together with his plan to wait three days. A competent candidate recognizes probable septic arthritis, declines treatment, urges same-day emergency care, respects capacity and consent, and documents.
common_errors: Candidates treat it as an osteoarthritis flare and offer gentle mobilization, or recommend a doctor visit on Monday. Others override his confidentiality request and phone his staff without thought.
examiner_notes: A pass names infection as the working concern, refuses to treat, recommends the emergency department today, and handles consent and refusal properly. Offering any physical treatment or accepting a delay until Monday is a fail.

title: Recovery from a rapidly progressive nerve condition at transfer to rehabilitation
setting: Inpatient rehabilitation unit, first assessment on admission from acute care
client_profile: Ana Rodrigues is a 42 year old high school teacher and mother of two. Five weeks ago she developed tingling in her feet, then leg and arm weakness over ten days after a stomach illness. She was diagnosed with Guillain-Barre syndrome, treated with intravenous immunoglobulin, and was ventilated in intensive care for six days. She is now transferred to rehabilitation. Examination shows generalized weakness, worse distally: Medical Research Council sum score 46 out of 60, bilateral foot drop with ankle dorsiflexion grade 2, hand grip 12 kg bilaterally, absent ankle reflexes, reduced knee reflexes, and reduced light touch and vibration in the feet. Berg Balance Scale is 24 out of 56. She stands for 30 seconds with a walker and two assists. Forced vital capacity is 2.1 L (about 65 percent predicted). She reports burning pain in the feet at night, rated 5 out of 10, and marked tiredness after any activity.
clinical_scenario: The acute care discharge summary mentions that her heart rate was "variable" and that she was "sometimes dizzy". At rest today her heart rate is 112 and blood pressure is 134/82 lying. When you sit her up for the balance test, her blood pressure drops to 92/58 and she becomes pale and says she feels faint. She wants to work hard and says she should be pushing through the tiredness. Her husband mentions that her school board wants an update on when she might return and that her sister is a nurse who is asking for information.

questions.prompt: Explain how you would interpret Ana's current findings and what additional assessment you would carry out, including what the main problems are, which findings are expected and which concern you.

checklist.point: Identifies the pattern as consistent with recovery from an acute demyelinating polyneuropathy with distal predominance, absent ankle reflexes and sensory loss
Recognizes the heart rate of 112 and the blood pressure fall from 134/82 to 92/58 on sitting as autonomic dysfunction with orthostatic hypotension
Notes symptoms of presyncope and pallor and treats them as a safety finding rather than deconditioning
Plans repeat orthostatic vital signs at stages of lying, sitting and standing, with timing, and identifies other autonomic signs such as sweating, bowel and bladder changes
Interprets the forced vital capacity of 2.1 L as reduced and plans monitoring of respiratory function
Plans standardized measures such as sum score, grip, Berg Balance Scale, 10-metre walk when possible, and a fatigue scale
Assesses neuropathic pain, joint range, skin, and foot drop impacts on gait and sets orthotic needs
Considers other causes of tachycardia and hypotension such as dehydration, infection, pulmonary embolism, medication and pain

questions.model_answer: Let me separate what I expect from what worries me. What I expect: Ana's findings fit someone recovering from Guillain-Barre syndrome. Her weakness is symmetrical and more distal, her ankle reflexes are absent, her knee reflexes are reduced, her sensation is reduced in the feet, and she has foot drop. A sum score of 46 out of 60, grip of 12 kilograms, and a Berg of 24 out of 56 tell me she has moderate weakness and a high fall risk. She stands only with a walker and two helpers. Her burning foot pain at night is common, as is severe fatigue after small amounts of activity. Her forced vital capacity of 2.1 litres, about 65 percent of predicted, shows some residual respiratory muscle weakness after ventilation, so I would measure it regularly. What worries me most is not her strength. It is that her resting heart rate is 112 and that when I sat her up, her blood pressure fell from 134/82 to 92/58, and she turned pale and felt faint. That is a drop of 42 systolic, well over the 20 systolic or 10 diastolic that defines orthostatic hypotension. In this condition it points to autonomic dysfunction, which can cause both fast heart rates and unstable blood pressure, and the discharge summary has hints that this was seen before. It is a safety problem, because it can lead to fainting, falls and, in severe cases, dangerous arrhythmias. I would not call it deconditioning. I also have to rule out other contributors that could produce the same picture: dehydration, infection, a blood clot in the lung, pain, medication such as pain medication or blood pressure drugs, and bleeding. I would report to the physician today. For my assessment, I would repeat blood pressure and heart rate lying and then in staged head-up positions or on the tilt table at one and three minutes, progressing to standing only after the physician has advised and readings are stable, and ask about sweating, bowel and bladder function, and vision changes. I would also complete the rest of my examination in a staged way: repeat the sum score and grip, monitor fatigue with a scale, check her ankle and knee range, skin on her heels, and test sensation. I would use the Berg Balance Scale and, when she can, a 10-metre walk and sit to stand. And I would assess her foot drop and decide with the orthotist whether ankle-foot orthoses are needed. I would document the baseline so that we can show change.

scale.4: Separates expected neuropathy findings from the autonomic instability, quantifies orthostatic hypotension, recognizes it as a safety problem, plans staged assessment and measures, and considers other causes.
scale.3: Interprets the neuropathy well and recognizes blood pressure change but is thin on plan or differentials.
scale.2: Describes weakness and balance only, with limited mention of the blood pressure and heart rate change.
scale.1: Attributes dizziness to deconditioning or ignores the vital sign findings.

questions.prompt: Describe the safety precautions and decisions you would make for Ana's therapy this week, and how you would discuss her wish to push through the tiredness.

checklist.point: Reports the autonomic findings to the physician the same day and obtains guidance before progressing upright activity
Monitors blood pressure and heart rate lying, sitting and standing before and during therapy, with stop criteria
Uses gradual position changes, a tilt table or supported sitting, compression garments if the team agrees, and fluids as directed
Prescribes low-intensity, short, frequent sessions with rest, avoiding exhaustive or high-resistance exercise that can cause overwork weakness
Explains why pushing through fatigue can set back recovery and teaches energy conservation
Prevents falls: assistance, walker, gait belt, bed alarm and safe footwear or orthoses
Protects insensate feet and skin and positions joints to prevent contractures
Involves Ana in setting goals and uses motivational language to respect her drive

questions.model_answer: My priorities this week are to keep her safe from her blood pressure changes and from overdoing it, and to do that together with Ana. First, the blood pressure. I would call the rehabilitation physician today, describe the numbers, 134/82 lying and 92/58 sitting with pallor and faintness, along with her resting heart rate of 112, and ask for guidance on monitoring, fluids, whether to use compression stockings or an abdominal binder, and any medication review. Until I hear back I would lay her flat, check her vital signs again, and not stand her up. After that, I would use gradual changes in position, for example raising the head of the bed in stages or using a tilt table, and check blood pressure and heart rate lying, then one and three minutes after each change. I would stop and lay her flat if the systolic falls by more than about 20 mmHg with symptoms, if she is pale, sweaty or dizzy, if her heart rate rises abnormally, or if she reports chest pain. I would keep a nurse informed so that nobody sits her up quickly on the ward. Second, the exercise dose. In this condition, too much exercise too soon can cause overwork weakness and a longer recovery. So I would plan short sessions of 10 to 15 minutes, several times a day, at light effort, no more than moderate on a perceived exertion scale, with rests, and avoid training to exhaustion or heavy resistance. I would stop when she is tired, not when she is exhausted, and monitor for a drop in strength or more pain the next day. I would talk to Ana directly about her wish to push through. I would say that I can see how determined she is, that this will help her recovery, but that her nerves are healing and tired nerves and muscles recover best with pacing, and that the tiredness she feels is a signal. We would set goals together, for example sitting in a chair for her meals, and I would show her how to track her fatigue. Third, falls and skin. I would use two assistants, a gait belt, and a walker when she stands, and a good-fitting ankle support for the foot drop. I would check her feet and heels for pressure because her sensation is reduced, and position her joints to prevent stiffness.

scale.4: Reports and responds to autonomic instability before upright progression, sets monitoring and stop criteria, prescribes low-intensity paced exercise, prevents falls and skin injury, and discusses her determination respectfully.
scale.3: Covers monitoring and pacing with reasonable safety measures but less detail on stop criteria, reporting or communication.
scale.2: Mentions general safety, falls and energy conservation without addressing blood pressure instability.
scale.1: Progresses standing and exercise despite hypotension or encourages pushing through fatigue.

questions.prompt: Explain how you would collaborate with the rehabilitation team, Ana's family and her workplace, including who would be involved, what information would be shared, and how you would organize communication.

checklist.point: Identifies rehabilitation team members and roles: physician, nursing, occupational therapist, speech-language pathologist, psychologist, dietitian, orthotist and social worker
Gives a structured report of the autonomic findings to physician and nursing and agrees shared monitoring rules
Obtains Ana's consent about what is shared with her husband, sister and employer
Holds a family meeting or teaching session with Ana's agreement, explaining expected recovery and pacing in plain language
Communicates with the school board only through what Ana authorizes, such as a general update from her physician rather than detailed health information
Agrees with occupational therapy on fatigue, self-care, and return to work planning, and with the psychologist on coping
Sets regular team goals review and a shared goals board or note
Plans for discharge and community follow-up, including home assessment and outpatient therapy

questions.model_answer: Ana's recovery involves many people, so I would be clear about who does what and what each person needs from me. First, consent. She is an adult, awake and able to decide, so I would ask her what she would like me to share and with whom. Her husband is here and her sister is a nurse who is asking questions, but I would not give health details to her sister or her employer without Ana's agreement. I would ask Ana if she wants a family meeting, who she wants there, and what she wants discussed. Second, the rehabilitation team. The physician is the first person I need today, to report the blood pressure drop and the heart rate. I would give a short structured message: Ana, 42, Guillain-Barre syndrome five weeks ago, transferred today, heart rate 112 at rest, blood pressure 134/82 lying and 92/58 sitting with pallor and faintness, I have returned her to lying and I am holding upright activity, and I would like advice on monitoring and treatment. I would agree with nursing on shared rules: how often to check vital signs, how to change her position, and who to call. The occupational therapist and I would plan together so that fatigue, energy conservation, self-care and positioning are consistent and we are not both asking her to do the same tiring task on the same day. The psychologist can support her adjustment, since she is a mother and teacher facing a long recovery. The speech-language pathologist may be needed if she has swallowing or voice difficulty after ventilation. The dietitian can help with intake and weight. The orthotist can assess her foot drop for ankle-foot orthoses. A social worker can help with family needs and funding. Third, her family. With her agreement, I would run a session to explain the likely course: recovery can take months, may be incomplete, fatigue and pain are common, and pacing is important. I would use plain language, invite questions, and avoid promising a date. Fourth, work. The school board needs to know when she might return, but not the details. With her consent, her physician can provide a general update, and the occupational therapist can plan a graded return later. Finally, I would suggest a weekly team meeting with shared goals written in one place that Ana can see, and begin early discharge planning, including a home assessment and outpatient follow-up.

scale.4: Names team roles, gives a structured urgent report, obtains consent before sharing with family or employer, plans family education and a limited workplace update, coordinates with occupational therapy and others and includes discharge planning.
scale.3: Covers team and family communication with consent but with limited detail on structure, workplace or discharge.
scale.2: Lists professionals without describing communication, roles or consent.
scale.1: Shares details with the sister or employer without consent or omits the physician report.

safety_or_ethics_point: The buried issue is autonomic dysfunction: resting heart rate 112 and a blood pressure fall from 134/82 to 92/58 with pallor and faintness on sitting. A competent candidate recognizes it, returns her to lying, reports to the physician, monitors with stop criteria, and does not mistake it for deconditioning.
common_errors: Candidates concentrate on strength, balance and gait training and never address the blood pressure, or they plan vigorous strengthening to match her drive. Others share information with the sister and school board freely.
examiner_notes: A pass recognizes the autonomic instability, acts and reports it, and prescribes paced, low-intensity exercise. Planning upright and strengthening work without addressing the hypotension is a fail on safety.

title: Adolescent with a spinal curve found at school screening
setting: Pediatric outpatient physiotherapy clinic in a regional children's centre
client_profile: Amara, 13, is brought by her father after a school nurse noticed uneven shoulders. She plays competitive volleyball, reports occasional ache between the shoulder blades after long practices, rates it 2 out of 10, and has no night pain. Menarche was 5 months ago and she grew 6 cm this year. Height is 158 cm. Forward bend shows a right thoracic rib prominence, with a scoliometer reading of 9 degrees at T8. Shoulder height is uneven, with the right higher. Pelvis is level and leg lengths are equal. Neurological screen shows normal strength and reflexes, but the abdominal skin reflexes are present on the right and absent on the left. A standing radiograph from her family physician reports a right thoracic curve with a Cobb angle of 28 degrees and a Risser grade of 1. Her mother has mild scoliosis that never needed treatment.
clinical_scenario: The clinic has one physiotherapist, one physiotherapist assistant and a waiting list of eight weeks for new pediatric patients. Amara's father works shifts and can attend only on Thursdays. Amara is anxious about wearing anything that shows under her uniform and asks whether she can quit volleyball. The family has private insurance that covers ten visits a year. The family physician's referral says only 'scoliosis, please treat'.

questions.prompt: Using the findings provided, explain what you conclude about Amara's spinal presentation, what you would still need to rule out, and how you would decide on your next steps.

checklist.point: Identifies a right thoracic curve of 28 degrees with Risser 1 as consistent with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis with significant growth remaining.
Recognizes idiopathic scoliosis is a diagnosis of exclusion and that atypical features need further workup.
Flags the asymmetric abdominal skin reflexes as an atypical neurological finding that does not fit idiopathic scoliosis.
Links recent menarche and rapid growth to a higher risk of curve progression.
Explains that a 28 degree curve in a skeletally immature adolescent sits in the range where bracing is usually considered.
Proposes further questions about headache, back pain at night, sensory changes, bladder or bowel changes and gait.
Plans a full neurological exam including cranial nerves, tone, clonus, plantar responses and gait.
States that a neurological abnormality leads to prompt communication with the physician for referral rather than starting treatment.
Mentions the scoliometer is a screening tool and does not replace the radiograph for measuring the curve.
Treats the volleyball ache and backpack use as minor contributors rather than causes of the curve.

questions.model_answer:
First, my impression. The right thoracic rib hump, the shoulder asymmetry and a Cobb angle of 28 degrees fit adolescent idiopathic scoliosis. Her Risser grade of 1 means she has a lot of growth left, and she has just had her first period and grown 6 centimetres this year. Those are the factors that make a curve more likely to progress, so I treat this as a curve that needs active management, not simple watching. The scoliometer reading of 9 degrees is only a screen; the radiograph Cobb angle of 28 degrees is what measures the curve.

Second, and this is what I would not let slide, idiopathic scoliosis is what we call it only after other causes are excluded. One finding does not fit. The abdominal skin reflexes are present on the right and absent on the left. A one sided loss of these reflexes can point to a problem in the spinal cord or brainstem, such as a syrinx or a Chiari type malformation, and such conditions can come with a curve. It is not a diagnosis, but it is enough to stop me from simply starting an exercise program.

Third, I would extend my screening. I would ask about headaches, especially with coughing, neck pain, numbness, hand clumsiness, changes in how she walks, and any bladder or bowel changes. I would examine cranial nerves, tone, deep tendon reflexes, clonus, plantar responses, sensation, and look for a foot deformity such as a high arch. I would watch her walk and do a tandem walk.

Fourth, the decision. If I find any other neurological sign, or if the reflex finding holds up, I contact the family physician the same day, explain exactly what I found, and ask for further assessment, which may include MRI and a pediatric spine referral. I would not delay that referral to run a trial of exercise. If the exam is otherwise completely normal, I would still tell the physician about the reflex asymmetry, because the decision about imaging belongs with them, and I would ask for a pediatric spine opinion because a curve of 28 degrees at Risser 1 is in the range where bracing is usually considered.

Finally, I would be honest with Amara and her father, in plain words, that the shape of her back is a spinal curve, that this is common, that it is not caused by volleyball or her backpack, and that I want one more check before we plan treatment. That keeps them informed and avoids frightening them.

scale.4: Names probable adolescent idiopathic scoliosis with progression risk factors, identifies the asymmetric abdominal reflex as atypical, outlines a targeted neurological screen, and commits to physician communication before treatment.
scale.3: Recognizes the curve and progression risk and mentions the reflex, but is vague about the action or the reasoning behind it.
scale.2: Describes scoliosis and treatment options but treats the reflex finding as minor or does not plan further screening.
scale.1: Proceeds to treatment without addressing the neurological finding, or blames sport or posture for the curve.

questions.prompt: Amara says she is afraid of a brace and wants to stop volleyball. Discuss how you would respond, including the safety considerations and how you would involve Amara in the decisions.

checklist.point: Acknowledges Amara's fear and body image concerns before giving information.
Speaks to Amara directly as the person affected, while including her father.
Explains that bracing aims to stop progression, not to correct the curve, and is worn for set hours.
Clarifies that the brace decision belongs to the spine specialist team and the family, not to the physiotherapist alone.
States that volleyball does not cause or worsen scoliosis and that sport is generally encouraged.
Explains why any activity limit is temporary and minimal, advises stopping and reporting new symptoms, and gives clear return criteria.
Asks what matters most to Amara and what she is most worried about being seen.
Offers options to ease brace concerns such as clothing advice, peer support or talking with other teens who wear a brace.
Screens for low mood or anxiety linked to appearance and plans to share concerns with the physician if present.
Checks understanding using teach back, assesses Amara's capacity to consent, and involves her father with her agreement.

questions.model_answer:
I would start with Amara, not with the curve. I would turn to her, since she is the one who will live with this, and say that it makes sense to be worried about a brace, and ask her to tell me what she imagines. Often a teen has a picture of an old metal device, and today's braces are different. I would ask what matters most to her. If it is volleyball and her friends, that tells me what a good plan has to protect.

On the volleyball question, I would be direct. Volleyball did not cause her curve, and nothing she does in practice will make it worse. Staying active is good for her, so she can keep doing light, pain-free activity, and her usual volleyball if my full examination finds nothing new, while the physician reviews one finding I want checked. The only limit is to stop and tell me if anything new appears, such as numbness, weakness, new back pain or a change in how she moves. I would tell her what the check is for, in simple terms, so it does not sound like a punishment, and I would say that any restriction would be temporary and minimal, with a clear point at which she is cleared.

On bracing, I would explain what I know and the limits of my role. A brace is meant to hold the curve where it is while she finishes growing, not to straighten it. Whether she needs one is decided with the spine specialist team, using her X-ray and how much growing she has left. I am not the one deciding this alone, and I would not promise that she will or will not need one. What I can do is make sure she understands the options so that she can take part in the conversation.

I would offer practical help. Many teens wear a brace under loose clothing, and worn hours can often be set around school and sport. I could connect her with a peer support group or another teen who has worn one, if she wants that.

I would watch for how she is coping. Body image worries in adolescents with scoliosis are real, and if I notice withdrawal, low mood or persistent anxiety, I would tell her father and the family physician so they can help.

Finally, I would ask her and her father to explain back to me what we agreed, so I know my words made sense. I would assess Amara's capacity to consent, which in Canada depends on understanding rather than a set age. If she is capable, her consent is what counts, and I would still involve her father with her agreement. I would write down what each of them decided.

scale.4: Centres Amara's voice, explains brace aims accurately, corrects the sport myth while keeping any activity limit minimal, temporary and explained, and checks understanding and consent.
scale.3: Handles the emotional side and sport advice well but is vague about the specialist decision or consent.
scale.2: Gives information on bracing and sport but speaks mainly to the father or ignores the reason for the pending medical review.
scale.1: Dismisses her fear, says she must quit sport indefinitely, or promises a brace outcome.

questions.prompt: Your clinic has a long waiting list, limited insurance coverage and a physiotherapist assistant. Describe how you would organize Amara's care and documentation, including what you would and would not delegate.

checklist.point: Prioritizes Amara's visit and follow up based on clinical risk rather than the order of the waiting list.
Documents the abdominal reflex asymmetry, the examination findings and the communication with the physician with dates and times.
Does not delegate assessment, interpretation of neurological findings or changes to the plan to the assistant.
Identifies tasks suitable for delegation once the plan is set, such as supervised exercise practice with a written program.
Describes supervising and checking in with the assistant, and clear criteria for the assistant to stop and call the physiotherapist.
Plans scheduling around the father's Thursday availability and makes the best use of ten insured visits.
Requests clarification of the vague referral and sends a clear written summary to the physician.
Records a baseline outcome measure such as a scoliosis quality of life questionnaire and asks the physician to set the plan for repeat curve monitoring.
Avoids ordering or arranging repeated radiographs herself and defers imaging decisions to the physician.
Explains fees and coverage honestly and avoids proposing unneeded visits to use up insurance.

questions.model_answer:
I would organize this in three parts: what happens first, what is documented, and who does what.

First, scheduling. Amara has a finding that needs action, so she does not wait her turn on the list. I would complete the full neurological exam at this visit and contact the family physician promptly, then book her next visit soon, on a Thursday so her father can come. I would not tuck this into a routine slot. The referral just says to treat scoliosis, so I would write back to the physician with a clear summary: the curve, the Cobb angle and Risser grade, the absent left abdominal reflex, what I tested, and my request for further assessment and a pediatric spine opinion. I would ask them to confirm they received it.

Second, documentation. I would record the history, the scoliometer reading, the full neurological findings including the reflex asymmetry, the advice I gave Amara and her father about activity, their questions, their agreement, and the time I contacted the physician and what was said. If the physician does not reply in the time I expect, I would follow up and note it. Good notes protect Amara, because another clinician reading them will see at once that something was flagged.

Third, delegation. I would not delegate the assessment, the interpretation of any neurological finding, or any decision to change the plan. Those need my judgment and are mine to answer for. Once the physician has weighed in and the plan is set, my assistant can supervise Amara practicing a written exercise program that I design and teach first. I would show the assistant exactly what to watch for and give clear stop rules: new pain, numbness, weakness, dizziness, or anything the assistant is unsure about means stop and get me. I would watch the first session, then check in regularly and review notes.

I would record a baseline outcome measure such as the SRS-22 questionnaire and ask the physician to set the plan for repeat radiographs to monitor the curve. On funding, the ten insured visits are limited, so I would be upfront with the family about how I plan to use them, spacing visits with a home program rather than filling the calendar. I would not book extra visits just because coverage exists. Repeat X-rays are the physician's decision, so I would not arrange them myself.

scale.4: Prioritizes by clinical risk, documents the flagged finding and the physician contact, delegates only after a plan with explicit boundaries and supervision, and handles funding honestly.
scale.3: Covers scheduling, documentation and delegation sensibly but with thin boundaries or no stop rules.
scale.2: Lists generic administrative tasks without linking them to Amara's risk or the assistant's limits.
scale.1: Delegates the assessment or neurological findings to the assistant, or books visits to use coverage.

safety_or_ethics_point: The absent left abdominal skin reflex is an atypical neurological sign that can accompany a syrinx or Chiari malformation. A candidate who treats this as classic idiopathic scoliosis and starts exercise has missed the buried issue. The competent path is a full neurological exam, same day communication with the physician and a request for imaging and specialist review before treatment.
common_errors: Starting a scoliosis specific exercise program straight away without addressing the reflex finding, and promising the family that exercise will correct the curve. A second error is delegating the follow up screening to the assistant or saying volleyball must stop without a clear reason.
examiner_notes: A pass identifies the reflex asymmetry as a reason to escalate before treating, speaks to Amara directly, and sets firm limits on delegation. A fail treats this as straightforward idiopathic scoliosis or gives a brace or cure promise.

title: Positional spinning after a neck adjustment
setting: Outpatient physiotherapy clinic in a community health centre
client_profile: Marguerite, 59, is a bookkeeper who drives to client sites. For 4 days she has had brief spinning when she rolls over in bed to the left or looks up to a high shelf. Each episode lasts about 20 to 30 seconds with nausea but no hearing loss, ringing or ear fullness. She has hypertension treated with ramipril, and her clinic blood pressure today is 152/94 mmHg, heart rate 78. Five days ago she saw a wellness clinic practitioner for neck stiffness who performed a rapid neck rotation adjustment. She mentions a dull headache at the back of her head since then, which she rates 4 out of 10. Neurological screen today shows normal cranial nerves, strength, sensation and finger to nose testing. Gait is steady. She has not yet had any positioning tests. Her family physician has not seen her for this problem.
clinical_scenario: Marguerite is anxious because she nearly fell last week reaching for a cupboard, and she worries about losing work if she cannot drive. She asks you to 'do the manoeuvre my friend had, it fixed her in five minutes'. Her workplace plan pays only after a physician's note. The clinic is quiet today, the only other staff member is a receptionist, and the nearest emergency department is 15 minutes away.

questions.prompt: Based on the history and screening findings, explain your working impression, what must be considered before you perform positional testing, and how you would proceed.

checklist.point: States that the brief positional spinning with no hearing symptoms fits benign paroxysmal positional vertigo as a probable cause.
Recognizes the recent rapid cervical rotation with new occipital headache and neck pain as a possible sign of cervical artery injury.
Explains that vertebral artery dissection can present with vertigo and headache and can cause stroke.
Decides not to proceed with provocative neck extension and rotation testing until the vascular concern is addressed.
Plans to ask about neck pain, visual changes, double vision, difficulty speaking or swallowing, facial numbness and drop attacks.
Notes that blood pressure is elevated and checks both arms or repeats the measurement.
Recommends same-day emergency assessment with vascular imaging and communicates with the emergency department and physician.
Distinguishes peripheral from central causes using nystagmus pattern, persistence and associated neurological signs.
Mentions that BPPV can be confirmed later with positional testing and supine roll tests once safe.

questions.model_answer:
My working impression has two layers, and the second one drives what I do.

The first layer is what her symptoms look like. Short spells of spinning, 20 to 30 seconds, brought on by rolling over or looking up, with nausea and no hearing loss or ear fullness, fit benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, most likely the posterior canal. That is the most common cause of this story in her age group, and it is very treatable.

The second layer is what the history also contains. Five days ago she had a rapid neck rotation adjustment, and since then she has a dull occipital headache. The spinning began the day after, and the headache has been there since. Neck manipulation is a recognized risk factor for injury to the vertebral artery, and a dissection can present with vertigo, neck pain and a back of the head headache, sometimes before any other sign. She also has hypertension that is not well controlled today. Her neurological screen is normal, which is reassuring, but a normal screen does not rule out a dissection, and the main danger is a stroke in the days that follow.

So before I do anything that puts her neck in extension and rotation, as a Dix-Hallpike does, I want to question and screen further. I would ask about neck pain, visual disturbance, double vision, trouble speaking or swallowing, facial numbness, limb weakness, and any episode of near fainting. I would check blood pressure again, and in both arms. I would look for nystagmus at rest, since persistent or vertical nystagmus would point to a central cause.

I would not do the positional test today. Even a test that is usually safe is not worth the risk until a vascular cause has been considered. Given a new headache and neck pain after a manipulation, I suspect a cervical artery dissection, so I would recommend same-day emergency assessment with vascular imaging, and I would phone ahead to the emergency department with my findings and let her physician know. If she has any neurological symptom, she goes by ambulance, and in every case not by her own driving.

Once a dissection has been properly excluded by the medical team, I would come back and confirm BPPV with positional testing and treat it.

scale.4: Names BPPV as probable, identifies the manipulation plus headache as a possible vertebral artery injury, withholds provocative testing, and acts on urgent medical communication.
scale.3: Recognizes both BPPV and the vascular concern but is hesitant about withholding the test or about urgency.
scale.2: Focuses on BPPV and mentions the neck adjustment without letting it change the plan.
scale.1: Performs positioning tests or the manoeuvre without addressing the vascular risk.

questions.prompt: Marguerite asks you to perform the manoeuvre her friend had and says she needs to keep driving. Explain how you would respond, including her safety and her involvement in the decision.

checklist.point: Acknowledges her wish for quick relief and her work worries without dismissing them.
Explains in plain language why you are not doing the manoeuvre today and what you are concerned about.
Avoids frightening language while being clear about the possible seriousness of her symptoms.
Advises her not to drive until medically cleared and explains why.
Gives red flag symptoms and exactly what to do if they occur, including calling emergency services.
Arranges safe transport home or to the emergency department and does not leave her unsupported.
Gives fall prevention advice for the interim such as rising slowly and avoiding heights.
Recommends emergency assessment today and involves her in how she gets there and who accompanies her.
Checks her understanding with teach back and obtains her consent to share information with her physician.

questions.model_answer:
I would begin by telling her I understand. Spinning is frightening, her job depends on driving, and her friend got better quickly. Wanting the same thing is reasonable and I would say so.

Then I would explain, in plain words, why I am not doing it today. I would say something like: your symptoms are very likely from a small problem in the inner ear that I can treat, and I expect to be able to help you. But you also had a quick twist of the neck five days ago and you now have a headache at the back of your head. Sometimes that kind of neck movement can injure a blood vessel in the neck. It is uncommon, but it matters because it can lead to a stroke. The manoeuvre puts the neck in a position I do not want to use until a doctor has checked that. I would not hide the reason, and I would not say she has a serious problem, because I do not know that.

On driving, I would be clear. Until a physician has assessed her, she should not drive. Sudden spinning at the wheel is a danger to her and to others. I would offer to help with practical steps, such as arranging a ride, and I would explain that I can provide a note stating she needs medical assessment, which may also help her workplace plan.

I would give her the warning signs: sudden severe headache, worsening neck pain, double vision, slurred speech, trouble swallowing, numbness of the face or limbs, weakness, loss of balance, or fainting. If any of these happens she calls 911 and does not drive herself.

I would let her take part in the decision. I recommend emergency assessment today. I would explain my reasoning and ask her how she would like to get there and who can go with her. For the days until she is seen, I would suggest rising slowly, sitting to dress, and avoiding ladders or reaching overhead.

I would ask her to repeat back the plan and warning signs, and ask her permission to phone her physician and share my findings.

scale.4: Responds with empathy, explains the reason for withholding the manoeuvre truthfully, stops driving, gives clear red flags and emergency instructions, and confirms consent and understanding.
scale.3: Explains and advises on driving and red flags but with limited shared decision making or no teach back.
scale.2: Declines the manoeuvre with little explanation or gives incomplete safety advice.
scale.1: Agrees to do the manoeuvre, permits driving, or alarms her without a clear plan.

questions.prompt: Marguerite's workplace plan wants a note saying she can return to driving next week, and she asks you not to tell her physician about the neck adjustment. Describe how you would handle your professional responsibilities in this situation.

checklist.point: States that you cannot certify fitness to drive or make a return to driving decision that is outside your scope in this situation.
Explains that withholding the neck adjustment history from the physician could harm her and that you will share it with her knowledge.
Describes seeking her informed consent for disclosure and what to do if she refuses, within provincial privacy law.
Recognizes duty of care to act on an urgent safety concern even if the client is reluctant, using the least disclosure needed.
Documents the history, the findings, the advice given, the driving advice and her response.
Offers a factual note describing what you found and recommended, without stating she is fit to drive.
Notes that the provincial driver licensing authority and medical reporting rules are a matter for the physician.
Avoids criticizing the practitioner who did the adjustment and, if appropriate, advises on how she can raise concerns through the proper regulator.
Keeps follow up and treatment planning dependent on medical clearance.

questions.model_answer:
There are two requests here, and I would treat them separately.

The first is the note saying she can drive next week. I cannot write that. Deciding whether someone is fit to drive is a medical judgment that depends on a diagnosis I do not yet have, and in my province it sits with her physician and the licensing authority, not with me. If I wrote it and she had an episode on the road, I would have put her and others at risk and stepped outside my scope. What I can do is write a factual letter for her workplace plan stating that she was seen on this date, that she has symptoms requiring medical assessment, and that she has been advised not to drive until a physician has assessed her. That is true and it supports her claim without overstating anything.

The second is her request that I not tell her physician about the neck adjustment. This is her information, and I would respect her right to control it, but I would not simply agree. I would explain why it matters: her physician needs that detail to decide what tests she needs, and without it she could be missed or delayed. I would ask for her consent to share, and ask what her worry is. Sometimes people fear being blamed or embarrassed. I would reassure her that nobody is blaming her. If she agrees, I phone and also send a written summary, sharing what is needed for the assessment and nothing more.

If she still refuses, I would not act behind her back as a first step. I would explain again, keep my advice clear, and document her decision and my explanation. However, if I judged there was a serious and imminent risk to her life, such as new neurological signs, I would follow my regulator's standards and provincial privacy legislation, which allow limited disclosure to prevent serious harm, disclosing only what is necessary, and I would tell her what I was doing. I would consult my regulator or my employer's privacy officer if I was unsure.

I would document everything: the history, the findings, my reasoning for not testing, the driving advice, her consent decisions, and who I contacted and when. I would not criticize the other practitioner. If she has concerns about that care, I would tell her how a complaint can be made to the relevant regulator, and leave the choice to her.

scale.4: Declines to certify driving, offers an accurate factual note, secures consent for disclosure with a reasoned approach to refusal, documents fully and avoids blaming.
scale.3: Handles the note and disclosure appropriately but is vague on privacy law, refusal or documentation.
scale.2: Raises scope or confidentiality but gives an incomplete or inconsistent resolution.
scale.1: Writes the return to drive note, or agrees to conceal a safety relevant history.

safety_or_ethics_point: A rapid neck rotation adjustment followed by new occipital headache and vertigo raises the possibility of cervical artery dissection. The candidate must find this, withhold provocative neck positioning, advise against driving and involve medical care urgently. The distractor is the classic BPPV story that invites an immediate Epley manoeuvre.
common_errors: Performing a Dix-Hallpike and Epley manoeuvre because the story sounds like BPPV, and agreeing to the return to drive note. A second error is accepting the client's request to keep the neck adjustment from the physician.
examiner_notes: A pass holds two diagnoses in mind, withholds the test, advises against driving and handles disclosure and the note within scope. A fail treats the case as routine BPPV.

title: Young adult with epilepsy starting a fitness program
setting: Outpatient neurology rehabilitation clinic in a university hospital
client_profile: Tomas, 24, is a graduate student with focal epilepsy with impaired awareness seizures diagnosed 3 years ago. He had his last seizure 7 months ago, a 90 second episode of staring and lip smacking while sitting in a lecture. He takes lamotrigine, increased by his neurologist 3 weeks ago from 150 mg to 200 mg daily. He wants to start running, a spin class and lap swimming to manage stress and weight. Resting blood pressure is 118/72 mmHg and heart rate 70. Gait, balance, strength and coordination are normal. Six minute walk distance is 640 m. He reports poor sleep, about 5 hours a night during exams, and two missed doses this month. He mentions fatigue and some itchy skin on his chest and back that he attributes to a new laundry soap. He drinks 3 to 4 beers on weekends.
clinical_scenario: Tomas lives alone in a student residence and prefers to swim at 6 a.m. when the pool is quiet. The campus recreation centre has a physiotherapy-led exercise program and a lifeguard on duty only at peak hours. He says his neurologist 'just told me to exercise' and he has not told his friends or the gym about his epilepsy because he fears being treated differently. He asks you to write a plan he can follow on his own.

questions.prompt: Explain what you would conclude from Tomas's history and examination about his readiness to exercise, and which findings you would explore further before finalizing a plan.

checklist.point: States that regular exercise is generally recommended for people with epilepsy and that Tomas has no neuromotor limitations on testing.
Identifies the possible rash after a recent lamotrigine dose increase as needing medical review before exercise begins.
Explains that rash with lamotrigine can signal a serious hypersensitivity reaction, so the itchy skin is not assumed to be laundry soap.
Plans to inspect the skin and ask about fever, mouth sores, swollen glands, sore throat or blistering.
Recognizes missed doses, short sleep and alcohol as seizure triggers affecting risk.
Asks about seizure triggers, auras, warning time, injuries and seizure types, and whether exercise has ever triggered one.
Notes that 7 months seizure free is not long enough to treat him as low risk for water activities without precautions.
Uses vital signs and a submaximal walk test to set a baseline exercise intensity.
Identifies the need to communicate with the neurologist about the rash and about clearance for the specific activities.

questions.model_answer:
My conclusion has two parts: he is physically ready, and he is not yet ready to start because of something in the history.

Physically, Tomas has a normal examination. His strength, balance, coordination and gait are fine, blood pressure and heart rate are normal, and he walked 640 metres in six minutes, which is a good base for a young adult. Exercise is generally recommended in epilepsy. It supports mood, sleep and fitness, and it does not usually raise seizure frequency. So I support the goal.

The finding I would pursue first is the itchy skin on his chest and back. He thinks it is laundry soap, but the timing matters. His lamotrigine was raised three weeks ago, and rash is a known effect of this drug, usually in the first weeks after starting or increasing it. Most rashes are mild, but a small number are the start of a serious hypersensitivity reaction such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and that can get worse fast. I cannot tell the difference by looking, and it is not my role to decide. So I would look at the skin today with his permission, and ask about fever, sore throat, mouth or eye sores, blistering, swollen glands, and feeling unwell. If he has any of those, he needs same day emergency care. Even if he does not, I would contact his neurologist or physician today and say what I saw. I would hold the start of exercise until the rash is reviewed.

Second, I want to understand his seizure risk. Seven months without a seizure is encouraging but not long, and I would ask about auras, how much warning he gets, whether he has ever injured himself, and whether exercise or overheating has ever set one off. Sleeping five hours, missing two doses this month and drinking on weekends are all recognized triggers, so these raise his risk more than the exercise itself.

Third, I would use his resting vitals and walk test to choose a starting intensity, using the talk test and perceived effort.

Finally, I would ask his neurologist to confirm clearance for the specific activities, especially swimming.

scale.4: Finds him physically ready, treats the rash after the lamotrigine increase as a medical priority, explores triggers and seizure risk, and plans neurologist contact.
scale.3: Identifies rash and triggers but is slow to prioritize the rash or lacks reasoning on its seriousness.
scale.2: Assesses fitness and seizure triggers but accepts the soap explanation or does not escalate.
scale.1: Clears him to begin training without addressing the rash.

questions.prompt: Tomas wants to swim alone at 6 a.m. and does not want anyone at the gym to know about his epilepsy. Discuss how you would advise him on safe activity and respect his preferences.

checklist.point: Advises against swimming alone and explains that a seizure in water can lead to drowning.
Recommends a supervised setting with a lifeguard present, or a swim buddy who knows what to do.
Respects his right to decide who is told about his epilepsy and explores options for limited disclosure.
Explores the reasons for his fear of stigma without judgment.
Offers safer alternatives while swimming is not cleared, such as walking, stationary cycling or running on a track with company.
Gives precautions for cycling and running such as avoiding unsupervised heights, traffic and extreme heat and dehydration.
Addresses sleep, medication adherence and alcohol as part of safe participation.
Describes a basic seizure first aid plan and suggests he carry medical identification.
Confirms understanding and agreement and records his choices.

questions.model_answer:
I would begin by saying that I want him to be active, and that my goal is a plan he will actually follow. That keeps the conversation about what he can do.

On swimming alone at 6 a.m., I would be firm and honest. Of all the activities he mentioned, water is the one where a seizure can be fatal, because a person who loses awareness can go under and not be noticed, and with only a lifeguard at peak hours nobody would be watching at that time. Seven months without a seizure does not remove the risk. So I would advise him not to swim alone, and not to swim at that hour unless a lifeguard is on duty. I would explain the choices that would let him swim: swimming at staffed times, or with a buddy who knows what to do and stays close, and a conversation with his neurologist about clearance. Until that is sorted, I would suggest he begin with land activities.

For the land activities, I would give specific precautions. For the spin class, a stationary bike is reasonable, as long as he is not riding to the point of dehydration or overheating. For running, I would suggest a track or a familiar route with a running partner, away from traffic, ravines and water, and I would suggest avoiding heat and keeping up fluids. I would add that sleep, taking his medication every day and limiting alcohol matter as much as the exercise plan.

On disclosure, I would respect that it is his information and his choice. I would ask what worries him. Many people fear being treated differently. I would not tell the gym. I would explain that telling one trusted person, like a swim partner or class instructor, can make a big difference in an emergency, and he decides who and how much to say. I could help him word a short statement such as, 'I have epilepsy that is controlled. If I have a seizure, I need time and space, and I should not be restrained.'

I would also review basic seizure first aid, suggest a medical alert bracelet, and ask him to repeat back the plan. I would note his decisions in the chart.

scale.4: Clearly advises against swimming alone with reasons, offers safer options, respects confidentiality while explaining the value of limited disclosure, and addresses triggers.
scale.3: Gives sound safety advice but is thin on respecting disclosure choices or alternatives.
scale.2: Lists generic precautions without firm advice on the swimming risk.
scale.1: Allows solo swimming or discloses his condition without his consent.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would collaborate with the other people involved in Tomas's care, including what you would communicate, to whom, and how you would manage his privacy.

checklist.point: Obtains Tomas's consent before contacting anyone and specifies what will be shared.
Contacts his neurologist or prescribing physician promptly about the rash and the missed doses.
Gives the neurologist objective information such as the timing of the dose increase, skin findings and symptoms.
Asks the neurologist for specific clearance and limits for swimming, cycling and running.
Involves the family physician or student health service as appropriate and clarifies who is the lead for follow up.
Considers a pharmacist for medication adherence strategies such as reminders or blister packs.
Describes how to work with the campus recreation staff without revealing diagnosis unless Tomas agrees.
Offers a referral to a social worker or counsellor for stress, sleep and stigma concerns.
Agrees on a feedback loop with a time frame and documents the communication.

questions.model_answer:
I would begin with Tomas. Before I speak to anyone, I would ask his permission and tell him what I want to share and with whom. He is worried about being treated differently, so how I handle his privacy will decide whether he trusts the plan.

The first call is to his neurologist, today, because of the rash. I would say clearly what I saw and when: that his lamotrigine went from 150 to 200 milligrams three weeks ago, that he now has an itchy rash on the chest and back, whether or not he has fever or mouth sores, that he has missed two doses and is sleeping five hours. I would give facts and not guess at the cause. I would ask whether he needs to be seen the same day, and I would ask what instructions I should give him in the meantime. I would also ask for specific guidance on exercise: whether he is cleared for swimming and under what conditions, and any limits on intensity or heat.

Then I would ask who leads his care. If the neurologist is the lead for his epilepsy, I update them, and I let his family physician or student health clinic know if he is also followed there, so that nobody assumes someone else is watching the rash. I would agree on when I will hear back and what I will do if I do not.

I would suggest to Tomas that a pharmacist can help with missed doses, with reminders, a pill organizer or blister packs, and can advise on drug interactions and alcohol. A counsellor or social worker at student health could support his stress, sleep and worry about stigma, and I would offer that as an option, not a requirement.

With campus recreation, I would only share what he agrees to. If he is comfortable, I could ask staff to arrange for a lifeguard at a time he can swim, without naming his diagnosis, or he might choose to tell one instructor. His choice stands.

I would document what I shared, with whom, his consent, and the replies, and I would review progress with him at the next visit.

scale.4: Seeks consent, contacts the neurologist promptly with factual information and specific questions, clarifies the lead, uses allied professionals sensibly, and protects privacy at the gym.
scale.3: Includes the right people and consent but is vague on content, timing or the lead.
scale.2: Names team members without a clear purpose or ignores his privacy preferences.
scale.1: Shares his diagnosis with the gym without consent or does not involve the prescriber about the rash.

safety_or_ethics_point: The itchy rash three weeks after a lamotrigine dose increase is the buried issue: it may be an early serious hypersensitivity reaction and must be reviewed medically before exercise starts. The second issue is the unsupervised early morning swim. A competent candidate finds both and respects the client's control over disclosure.
common_errors: Accepting the laundry soap explanation and writing a training program, and forbidding all exercise on the basis of epilepsy alone. A second error is telling the gym about his diagnosis without consent.
examiner_notes: A pass escalates the rash, forbids solo swimming with reasons, and keeps Tomas in charge of disclosure. A fail clears him for exercise without raising the rash or breaches his privacy.

title: Calf swelling nine days after hip replacement
setting: Outpatient physiotherapy clinic attached to a community hospital
client_profile: Priya, 58, a school custodian, had a right total hip replacement 9 days ago and was discharged on day 2 with a prescription for a direct oral anticoagulant for 14 days. She attends her second outpatient visit. She reports her right lower leg has been heavier and sore for 3 days. She admits she stopped the anticoagulant 4 days ago because of bruising and stomach upset, and did not tell the surgeon. Right calf circumference is 3.5 cm greater than the left, measured 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity. There is pitting edema of the right ankle and calf, localized tenderness along the deep calf, and warmth. The surgical wound is dry and closed. Resting heart rate is 102, blood pressure 128/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 and oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. Hip flexion is 80 degrees and she walks with a walker.
clinical_scenario: Priya is the main caregiver for her young grandson three afternoons a week and her daughter is at work today. She says, 'I only came for my exercises, I do not want to go to the hospital.' While undressing she mentions that she has felt a bit short of breath on the stairs since yesterday and put it down to being out of shape. The surgeon's office is closed until Monday and it is Friday at 3:30 p.m.

questions.prompt: Outline your plan of care for today's visit and the next 48 hours, and explain the reasoning behind your priorities.

checklist.point: Recognizes calf swelling, pitting edema, tenderness and recent surgery as making deep vein thrombosis likely, using a clinical prediction rule.
Holds all exercise, manual therapy, massage and compression of the leg today.
Recognizes shortness of breath, a heart rate of 102 and saturation of 94 percent as possible signs of pulmonary embolism.
Explains that same day diagnostic imaging and medical assessment are required and she should not wait until Monday.
Notes that stopping the anticoagulant without telling the surgeon increases the risk of clot formation.
Plans repeat vital signs and monitoring of symptoms while arranging transfer.
Sets goals for the next 48 hours focused on safety and assessment rather than hip rehabilitation.
Plans to resume the hip rehabilitation program only after medical clearance, with reassessment triggers.
Describes the information to give the receiving team: timeline, surgery, medication change, findings and vitals.
Arranges ambulance transport rather than a private vehicle and keeps her at rest and monitored until paramedics arrive.

questions.model_answer:
My plan has one main priority for today, which is to get Priya assessed for a blood clot, and everything else waits.

Here is my reasoning. Nine days after hip surgery, she has a right calf that is 3.5 centimetres bigger than the left, pitting edema, tenderness over the deep calf, warmth, and she has had these for three days. Using a prediction rule such as the Wells criteria, surgery in the last 12 weeks, calf swelling over 3 centimetres, pitting edema and localized tenderness already add up to a score that makes a deep vein thrombosis likely. On top of that, she stopped her anticoagulant four days ago. I cannot confirm or exclude a clot in the clinic. That needs imaging, usually an ultrasound, and that is a medical decision.

The breathlessness changes things further. Shortness of breath on stairs since yesterday, a heart rate of 102 and an oxygen saturation of 94 percent could mean a clot has reached the lungs. I would not wait for the surgeon's office to open on Monday.

So today, I stop the session. No exercise, no manual therapy, no massage and no compression wrap or stocking over that leg, because these could move a clot. I keep her sitting or lying comfortably, recheck her vital signs, and ask about chest pain, cough, blood in the sputum, light-headedness or fainting. With a likely clot and possible pulmonary embolism, I call 911 now for ambulance transfer, and she does not drive or go by private vehicle. I keep her at rest and monitored until the paramedics arrive, and if she is worse I tell the dispatcher right away. She has the right to decide, so I explain the risk plainly and ask what worries her about going, but I make a clear recommendation.

In the next 48 hours, my goals are safety, a diagnosis and restarting the anticoagulant, if the medical team decides that. I would hand over the history clearly: date of surgery, the drug and the date she stopped it, the findings, the vital signs and the breathing symptoms.

Only after medical clearance would I restart the hip program. I would then check with the treating team on what activity is permitted, and reassess if the leg swells again or breathlessness returns.

scale.4: Identifies a likely DVT with possible PE, stops treatment, arranges ambulance transfer for emergency assessment, plans monitoring and a clear handover, and defers rehabilitation until cleared.
scale.3: Recognizes the DVT and urgency but is slower to link the breathlessness or the medication lapse, or has a thin handover.
scale.2: Suspects a clot but proposes to continue modified treatment or to wait for the surgeon on Monday.
scale.1: Continues rehabilitation, massages the leg or treats it as routine post operative swelling.

questions.prompt: Priya says she does not want to go to the hospital because she must care for her grandson. Describe how you would respond, including the precautions you would take while she is in your care.

checklist.point: Acknowledges her caregiving obligations and offers practical help to arrange cover.
Explains in plain language the possibility of a clot in the leg and the lung and the danger of delay.
Checks her understanding of the risks and her capacity to make the decision.
Respects her right to make her own decision while making a clear recommendation for same day care.
Keeps her at rest, monitors vital signs and breathing and does not leave her alone.
Recognizes the symptoms that mean call 911 now, such as chest pain, worsening breathlessness, fainting or coughing blood.
Recommends she not drive herself and arranges safe transport.
Helps contact her daughter or another person to care for the child.
Documents an informed refusal if she still declines, with advice given and a safety net.

questions.model_answer:
I would start by recognizing that her worry is genuine. She looks after her grandson, and nobody else is available this afternoon. I would say that and ask her to tell me about the arrangements, because if I can solve the child care problem, the hospital stops being the barrier.

Then I would explain what I think, calmly and in everyday words. I would say that her leg and her breathing have me concerned that she may have a blood clot in her leg, and that a piece of a clot can travel to the lungs, which can be life threatening. I would say I cannot tell for sure in the clinic, and the only way to find out is a scan and blood work at the hospital today. I would explain that waiting until Monday risks the clot moving, and that treatment, if she needs it, works well when started early.

I would make a clear recommendation: go to the emergency department now. I would check that she understands, by asking her to say in her own words what could happen. I want to know she can weigh this decision, and I would be satisfied that she understands the risk, the options and the consequences. If she can, the choice is hers.

While she is with me, I would keep her resting, not walking around, and stay with her. I would recheck pulse, saturation and breathing every few minutes and ask about chest pain or light-headedness. If any red flag appears, I call 911 immediately. I would not allow her to drive herself.

Then I would help with the practical side. I would offer to phone her daughter or a neighbour, or the school, to arrange care for her grandson, and ask whether a family member could take her.

If she still refuses, I would not argue or threaten. I would tell her she can change her mind at any time, give her the warning signs in writing, ask her to have someone stay with her, and offer a call back this evening. I would document her refusal, the information I gave, her understanding and her decision, and inform her physician.

scale.4: Combines empathy and practical problem solving with a clear recommendation, checks understanding and capacity, monitors her, and handles refusal respectfully with safety netting.
scale.3: Explains the risk and recommends care but has gaps in capacity, monitoring or practical help.
scale.2: Gives a general warning but accepts her refusal quickly or neglects monitoring.
scale.1: Agrees to treat her or lets her leave without warning signs or transport.

questions.prompt: Describe your professional responsibilities after Priya leaves your clinic, including communication, documentation and any follow up related to her medication and your own practice.

checklist.point: Communicates findings directly to the receiving emergency team and to the surgeon or responsible physician.
Documents the history, objective findings, vital signs, advice given, the time she left and the mode of transport.
Reports that the anticoagulant was stopped by the client and does not advise her to restart it herself.
Stays within scope by not changing, restarting or advising on dose of the medication.
Follows up with the client or the hospital to confirm she was assessed.
Respects confidentiality by sharing information only with those involved in her care.
Considers whether a post operative adverse event should be reported through the clinic's incident or patient safety process.
Reflects on whether earlier screening at the first visit could have been better and what practice changes might follow.
Updates the rehabilitation plan only after receiving medical instructions.

questions.model_answer:
My responsibilities continue after she leaves, and I would organize them in order of urgency.

First, communication. Before she goes, or as soon as she is on her way, I would phone the emergency department and speak to the nurse or physician who will receive her. I would not rely on her to explain it.
