I would give a short, clear handover: she is 9 days after a right total hip replacement, has a swollen, tender right calf 3.5 centimetres larger than the left with pitting edema, she has had shortness of breath on stairs since yesterday, heart rate 102 and saturation 94 percent, and she stopped her anticoagulant four days ago without telling the surgeon. I would also contact the surgeon's service, using the on call number since it is after hours on a Friday, so the person responsible for her operation knows. Sharing this information is justified because it is needed for her care, and I would tell her I was doing it.

Second, the medication. She stopped the drug herself. I do not advise her to restart it, change the dose or choose another drug. That belongs to the physician or pharmacist. My role is to report that she stopped it and why, because she said it caused bruising and stomach upset, and let the team decide.

Third, documentation. I would write the history, my findings with measurements and times, the vital signs, the reasoning for holding treatment, the advice I gave, her response and decision, who accompanied her and how she travelled, and every call I made with names and times. I would record that I held treatment and why.

Fourth, follow up. I would phone the hospital or Priya in the evening or next morning to confirm that she was seen, and I would hold any further bookings until I receive instructions on activity.

Fifth, my own practice. I would follow the clinic's process for a significant safety event, and reflect on whether the leg and her symptoms could have been screened for at her first visit, for example by routinely checking calf swelling, medication adherence and breathlessness at every post operative visit. I would share my learning with colleagues.

scale.4: Handles urgent direct communication with receiving and responsible clinicians, stays within scope on medication, documents thoroughly, follows up, and reflects on practice.
scale.3: Covers communication and documentation but is vague about scope on medication or follow up.
scale.2: Describes routine documentation without direct handover or without addressing the medication.
scale.1: Advises restarting or changing the medication, or relies on the client to pass on the information.

safety_or_ethics_point: The likely deep vein thrombosis with signs suggesting pulmonary embolism, plus an anticoagulant stopped without the surgeon's knowledge, requires stopping treatment and arranging same day emergency care. The breathlessness is mentioned in passing and is the buried issue. The competent candidate also respects her right to decide while making a clear recommendation.
common_errors: Continuing gentle hip exercises or applying compression to the leg, and waiting for the surgeon on Monday. A second error is advising the client to restart her anticoagulant, which is outside physiotherapy scope.
examiner_notes: A pass picks up the breathlessness, stops all treatment and arranges same day assessment with direct handover. A fail treats the swelling as routine post operative edema or modifies the exercise program.

title: Severe hand pain and swelling after wrist fracture
setting: Outpatient hand and upper limb physiotherapy clinic
client_profile: Dolores, 56, a hair stylist, fractured her left distal radius in a fall 10 weeks ago and had 6 weeks in a cast followed by 4 weeks of limited use. She reports burning pain of 8 out of 10 in the hand that began within days of the fracture and is far worse than the injury seemed to warrant. Light touch from her sleeve and cold air hurt. The left hand looks swollen, shiny and blotchy red, and feels warmer than the right. Skin temperature is 2.5 degrees C higher on the left. She notices sweating on the left hand only. Active finger flexion reaches 50 percent of the right, wrist extension is 20 degrees, and there is a fine tremor with weakness of grip. Hair and nail growth on the left hand are increased. A follow up radiograph from her family physician reports a healed fracture in good alignment with patchy bone loss. She takes acetaminophen and ibuprofen.
clinical_scenario: Dolores is self-employed, has had no income for 10 weeks and has no private insurance. She has been avoiding using the hand and keeps it in a sling to protect it. She tells you quietly that she has not been sleeping, that she cries often, and that 'my family would be better off if I were not here'. Her husband is waiting in the car park and she asks you not to tell him. The workers' compensation board does not apply as the fall happened at home.

questions.prompt: Explain what you conclude from Dolores's presentation, the findings that support your conclusion, and what you would do next with respect to assessment.

checklist.point: Identifies the presentation as consistent with complex regional pain syndrome type 1 using the clinical diagnostic criteria.
Links continuing pain out of proportion to the injury and allodynia to the sensory category.
Identifies temperature asymmetry and skin colour change as vasomotor signs.
Identifies edema and sweating asymmetry as sudomotor signs.
Identifies reduced range, weakness, tremor and hair and nail changes as motor and trophic signs.
States that the diagnosis is clinical, that other causes must be excluded, and that the diagnosis is confirmed by the physician.
Differentiates from expected post fracture stiffness, infection, a missed injury, nerve injury or a vascular problem.
Recognizes the statement about her family being better off without her as a possible suicide risk requiring direct inquiry.
Plans baseline measures such as pain scores, edema volume or circumference, range of motion, grip and a function questionnaire.

questions.model_answer:
My conclusion is that Dolores has the pattern of complex regional pain syndrome after her wrist fracture, most likely type 1 since there is no known nerve injury. I base this on the recognized clinical criteria, which look for pain that continues and is out of proportion to the original injury, along with symptoms in several categories and signs in at least two.

Her sensory category is clear: burning pain at 8 out of 10, and allodynia, where light touch from a sleeve and cold air hurt. The vasomotor category fits too: the left hand is blotchy red and warmer by 2.5 degrees. For the sudomotor category, she has swelling and sweating on the left hand only. The motor and trophic category includes reduced finger and wrist range, weak grip, a fine tremor, and increased hair and nail growth. That is signs in all four categories, which is a strong picture. The patchy bone loss on the X-ray fits as well.

I would be careful about how I frame this. The diagnosis is clinical and made by excluding other causes, and the confirming diagnosis belongs to her physician. Ordinary stiffness after cast removal would not explain the colour change, the temperature difference or the allodynia. I would still consider infection, a missed fracture or tendon problem, nerve entrapment, a vascular problem such as arterial or venous obstruction, and a lymphedema picture, and I would ask about fever, wound problems and any numbness in a nerve distribution.

My next steps in assessment are baseline measures that I can repeat: pain scores at rest and with movement, allodynia mapping, skin temperature and colour, hand circumference or volume, range of motion, grip strength, and a functional questionnaire such as the QuickDASH. I would observe how she holds and uses the hand.

Separately, something she said matters more than any measure. She said her family would be better off if she were not here. I would not let that pass. I would ask her directly and kindly whether she is thinking of ending her life, because asking does not plant the idea and it is the only way to know. I would let that guide the rest of the visit.

scale.4: Applies the diagnostic criteria across all four categories, frames the diagnosis as clinical and physician confirmed, considers alternatives, plans repeatable measures, and picks up the suicide risk statement.
scale.3: Identifies complex regional pain syndrome and supporting findings but is thin on alternatives or misses the risk statement in the assessment.
scale.2: Lists findings and names the syndrome without linking categories or with overconfident diagnosis.
scale.1: Treats as ordinary post cast stiffness or does not address the risk statement.

questions.prompt: Dolores has just told you her family would be better off without her and asks you not to tell her husband. Describe how you would respond right now, including safety and her involvement in decisions.

checklist.point: Responds with calm, empathy and attention, and gives her time to talk.
Asks directly about thoughts of suicide, including whether she has a plan, means and intent.
Explains the limits of confidentiality in a safety situation in a respectful way.
Does not leave her alone if she is at risk and does not promise secrecy.
Involves her in deciding who will be contacted and how, while prioritizing her safety.
Describes a next step according to risk such as contacting a crisis line, her physician, or emergency services for imminent risk.
Asks about supports, protective factors and access to medications or other means.
Acknowledges her pain, sleep loss and money worries as real stressors without minimizing them.
Documents the discussion and the actions taken.

questions.model_answer:
I would stop the physical assessment and turn my attention to her. I would say something like, 'Thank you for telling me that. It sounds like things have been very heavy.' I would sit, lower my voice and give her time.

Then I would ask directly: 'Are you having thoughts of ending your life?' I would not soften it so much that it is unclear. If she says yes, I would ask whether she has thought about how, whether she has the means, such as medications at home, whether she has a time in mind, and whether she has ever tried before. I would also ask what has kept her going, such as her family or her work, because her protective factors matter. I would listen without arguing or lecturing and without saying that things will be fine.

On her request not to tell her husband, I would be honest. I would tell her that I care about her privacy and that most of what she tells me stays with me, but that if I think her life is at risk I cannot keep that secret. I would not promise silence. I would say it kindly: 'I want to keep you safe, and I do not want to do that behind your back.' Then I would invite her to help decide. She might prefer to tell her husband herself with me beside her, or I might offer to do it with her consent.

What I do depends on what she says. If she has a plan, the means and intent, or I cannot be confident she is safe, I stay with her, and I arrange emergency help, either calling 911 or taking her to the nearest emergency department with someone accompanying her. If the risk is lower, I would still arrange same day contact with her family physician or a mental health crisis service, give her the crisis line number, and agree on a safety plan with her, including limiting access to medications at home. I would involve her husband with her permission, or without it if the risk is imminent.

I would acknowledge that her pain, her lack of sleep and her loss of income are real and heavy, and that treatment exists for all three. I would document her words, my questions, her answers, my actions and who I contacted.

scale.4: Asks directly about suicide, explores plan and means, explains limits of confidentiality without promising secrecy, scales response to risk, and keeps her involved.
scale.3: Takes the statement seriously and gets help but is indirect in questioning or unclear about confidentiality.
scale.2: Expresses concern and suggests counselling without assessing risk or setting up a same day plan.
scale.1: Agrees to keep it secret, ignores the statement, or continues the physical assessment.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would work with other professionals and people in Dolores's life to coordinate her care, explaining who, why, and how you would communicate.

checklist.point: Contacts the family physician promptly to confirm the diagnosis, address mental health risk and review pain management.
Obtains Dolores's consent for each communication and explains what will be shared.
Proposes referral to a pain clinic or physician experienced with complex regional pain syndrome.
Includes an occupational therapist for desensitization, hand function and work adaptation.
Includes a psychologist or counsellor for mood, sleep and pain coping.
Describes how physiotherapy will fit with graded activity, mirror therapy or graded motor imagery and desensitization, as the team agrees.
Suggests a social worker or financial support resources for her income loss.
Engages her husband as a support with her agreement and gives him clear information.
Sets shared goals, roles and a communication schedule among providers.

questions.model_answer:
Coordinating this well matters because complex regional pain syndrome responds best to a team that works to a common plan, and because Dolores has more than a hand problem. She is in pain, not sleeping, low in mood and short of money.

I would start with her family physician, today. I want them to confirm the diagnosis and rule out other causes, and I want them to know about her statement about her family and the safety steps we have taken, so mental health follow up is not lost. I would ask them to review her pain medication, since acetaminophen and ibuprofen are probably not enough, and to decide on a referral. I would ask for consent from Dolores first and tell her exactly what I will share.

I would suggest a referral to a pain clinic or a physician with experience in this condition, since medical options, such as medications or nerve blocks, are decided there and not by me. I would send a clear summary with measurements.

An occupational therapist would be a key partner for desensitization, safe use of the hand in daily tasks, splinting advice, and adapting her work as a stylist. A psychologist or counsellor can help with mood, sleep and pain coping, which has been shown to matter in this condition. I would present it as part of treatment for pain and not as a sign that her pain is imagined.

Within physiotherapy, I would agree with the team on a graded plan: desensitization, mirror therapy or graded motor imagery, gentle active movement within tolerable limits, and edema control, progressing as pain allows, and I would say that I will adjust based on her responses. I would ask her to stop using the sling all day, with the team's agreement.

A social worker could help with income supports and benefits, since stress from money is feeding her pain.

With her permission, I would speak to her husband so he understands the condition and how to support her. Finally, I would write down who does what, share goals, and agree on how often we update one another, for example a brief message after each key visit.

scale.4: Seeks consent, prioritizes the physician for diagnosis and risk, names appropriate team roles with reasons, and sets shared goals and communication.
scale.3: Names suitable team members and reasons but with limited detail on roles, consent or communication.
scale.2: Lists professionals with little explanation of purpose or no consent process.
scale.1: Proceeds alone, shares information without consent, or omits mental health follow up.

safety_or_ethics_point: The statement that her family would be better off if she were not here is a possible suicide risk, tucked into a visit about a hand. A competent candidate asks directly, explains the limits of confidentiality, does not promise secrecy and arranges help matched to risk. The classic complex regional pain syndrome picture is the distractor.
common_errors: Concentrating on the diagnostic criteria and exercise progression while moving past her remark, and promising not to tell her husband. A second error is recommending aggressive stretching or forced range of motion.
examiner_notes: A pass asks directly about suicide and sets up appropriate help, and frames the diagnosis as clinical with team care. A fail treats the remark as background or promises secrecy.

title: Walking limited by leg heaviness in a retired man
setting: Community outpatient physiotherapy clinic
client_profile: Mr. Harpreet Gill is a 72 year old retired bus mechanic who lives with his wife. For two years he has had bilateral buttock and thigh heaviness and aching when he walks or stands, settling within about five minutes of sitting or leaning forward on a shopping cart. He can walk 150 m before stopping, down from 600 m last year. He has no back pain at rest. Medical history: hypertension, mild hearing loss, no diabetes. Medications: ramipril and amlodipine. MRI reported by his family physician: multilevel degenerative changes with severe central canal narrowing at L3 to L4 and L4 to L5. Objective: lumbar extension reproduces thigh symptoms within 20 seconds, flexion eases them, straight leg raise negative, ankle dorsiflexion strength 5/5 bilaterally, knee reflexes symmetrical but reduced, pedal pulses palpable, Timed Up and Go 13 seconds, two-minute walk test 88 m.
clinical_scenario: Mr. Gill wants to keep walking the dog with his wife and has asked about surgery because his neighbour had a good result. His wife attends every visit and often answers for him because he struggles to hear in the clinic room. At the end of today's visit, while putting on his coat, he mentions that he has needed to wait longer to start passing urine for about two weeks, which he blames on his age, and that his legs feel more 'rubbery' on the stairs. His family physician has a three month wait for a follow-up.

questions.prompt: Describe the physiotherapy plan you would develop with Mr. Gill for the first six weeks, including the main interventions, how you would progress them, and the outcome measures you would use to judge change.

checklist.point: States goals linked to the client: longer walking tolerance, dog walking, stairs, and independence with self-management.
Selects flexion-biased positions and strategies such as forward-leaning walking, cycling or stationary bike, and pacing between rests.
Prescribes a graded walking or body-weight-supported treadmill program using time or distance targets that extend gradually.
Includes hip mobility and lower limb and trunk strengthening, with dosage such as sets, repetitions and frequency.
Includes balance and falls-prevention work given the reduced reflexes and the stairs complaint.
Names repeatable outcome measures such as walking distance or time to symptoms, two-minute or six-minute walk, Timed Up and Go, and a patient-reported scale.
Defines reassessment triggers and a plan to refer or reconsider if function does not improve or neurological signs worsen.
Recognizes that the new urinary hesitancy and rubbery legs change the plan and must be acted on before progressive loading.
Includes education on self-management, activity pacing and realistic expectations about natural course.

questions.model_answer:
I would build the plan around what Mr. Gill wants, which is to walk the dog with his wife and manage stairs safely. Before I describe the exercise, I want to say that the new urinary hesitancy and the rubbery legs he mentioned are not part of a routine stenosis plan, so I would address that first and treat everything I describe as the plan once those are looked at by a physician. I will explain that reasoning in the next question.

First, goals. In six weeks I would aim for a two-minute walk test that has improved by a meaningful margin from 88 m, walking 400 m with pacing, and managing a flight of stairs with a rail without legs giving way. We would agree these together.

Second, interventions. His symptoms ease in flexion, so I would teach him to use that. He can lean on a cart, use a pole or walker temporarily, and rest in a forward-leaning posture rather than just sitting. I would use a stationary bicycle or recumbent bike, because it keeps the spine flexed and lets him build aerobic capacity without provoking symptoms. For walking I would use intervals: for example, walk until symptoms reach a mild level, rest in flexion until they settle, then repeat, three to four times a week. Over weeks I would lengthen the walking intervals rather than the rest, and consider body-weight-supported treadmill walking if the clinic has it.

Third, strengthening and mobility. I would work on hip flexor and hamstring flexibility, glute and core strength in neutral or slightly flexed positions, and sit to stand practice, two or three sets of eight to twelve, two to three days a week, increasing load when he can finish the set with good control. I would add balance work, such as tandem stance and single leg stance near a counter, because of his reduced reflexes and stair complaint.

Fourth, education. I would explain that stenosis changes slowly, that exercise helps function even when imaging stays the same, and how to pace activity. I would give a written plan with large print, as he has hearing difficulty.

Fifth, measurement. At each visit I would record distance or time to first symptoms, the two-minute walk, Timed Up and Go, and a patient-reported scale. I would reassess at three weeks. If there is no improvement by six weeks, or if neurological signs progress, I would refer back to his physician about a surgical opinion rather than continue the same plan.

scale.4: Gives a prioritized, individualized plan with flexion-based strategies, walking intervals, strengthening and balance dosage, named outcome measures, and clear reassessment triggers, while linking the new urinary and leg symptoms to the plan.
scale.3: Sound plan with appropriate interventions and measures but weak on dosage, progression, or the link to the new symptoms.
scale.2: Lists generic exercises or modalities without tying them to stenosis, progression or measurement.
scale.1: Prescribes extension-based or high-load work, ignores the new symptoms, or suggests a plan that would be unsafe.

questions.prompt: Mr. Gill has just told you about changes in his urine and his legs. Explain what you would do next in this visit, how you would involve him in the decision, and what precautions you would apply to his activity.

checklist.point: Recognizes the combination of new urinary hesitancy and worsening leg heaviness as a possible serious neurological compromise needing urgent medical assessment.
Performs or arranges a focused neurological screen: perianal or saddle sensation, lower limb myotomes and dermatomes, reflexes, gait, and asks about bowel function and sexual function.
Asks specific questions about retention, incontinence, onset, progression, and falls.
Explains the concern in plain words and asks permission to contact his physician or arrange same-day assessment.
Decides who to contact and how, such as phoning the family physician, clinic physician or sending him to emergency, based on findings, rather than waiting for the three month appointment.
Holds off on progressive loading or high-intensity exercise until medical clearance, offering safe activity such as walking with rests.
Involves his wife with his consent and checks his understanding with teach-back.
Gives red flag advice about going to emergency if retention, incontinence, saddle numbness or sudden weakness occurs.
Documents findings, advice given, and the communication with the physician.

questions.model_answer:
I would stop the end of the visit from becoming a casual goodbye, because what he said matters. New difficulty starting urine over two weeks, together with legs that feel rubbery, could mean more serious compression of the nerves in his canal. I should not assume it is age or the prostate, and I should not wait for a three month appointment.

Here is what I would do. I would sit him back down, face him so he can see my lips, speak slowly, and tell him that I would like to ask a few more questions and do a short check, and ask if that is acceptable. I would ask about the stream: hesitancy, dribbling, feeling that the bladder is not empty, any leaking, and any change in bowel control, numbness in the groin or inner thighs, or sexual function. I would ask if his legs have given way or if he has fallen.

Then I would do a focused neurological screen: sensation around the saddle area if he agrees and a chaperone is offered, lower limb strength by myotome including ankle dorsiflexion, great toe extension, and knee extension, sensation by dermatome, reflexes, and his gait including heel and toe walking. I would compare with the baseline I already recorded today, where strength was normal.

If the screen is abnormal, or if he describes retention, incontinence or saddle numbness, I would explain that he needs to be seen today and I would help him go to the emergency department, phoning ahead with my findings. If the screen is normal and symptoms are mild, I would still contact his physician the same day by phone, explain the new urinary change and leg change together, ask for an expedited assessment, and agree a timeframe with Mr. Gill. I would tell him in plain words why, and ask his permission to share the information. I would use teach-back: 'Tell me what you will do if the passing of urine gets harder.'

With his consent, I would include Mrs. Gill so that she can reinforce the plan, but I would speak to him directly.

For activity, I would not progress him to harder exercise or loaded treadmill work until a physician has reviewed him. He can keep gentle walking with rests, as that is low risk, and I would ask him to stop and call if he notices any new weakness, tripping, or numbness. I would give him written advice in large print about going straight to the emergency department if he cannot pass urine, loses control of bladder or bowel, or notices numbness in the groin.

Finally, I would document my questions, findings, who I contacted, the advice given, and his decisions.

scale.4: Identifies the pairing of urinary and leg change as a red flag, screens neurologically, acts the same day with the physician or emergency, respects his consent, and sets clear activity limits and return precautions.
scale.3: Recognizes the concern and refers but misses part of the screen, the consent process, or specific activity precautions.
scale.2: Notes the issue but advises waiting for the scheduled appointment or only gives general advice.
scale.1: Dismisses the symptoms as age related or continues progressive exercise without assessment.

questions.prompt: Mr. Gill has hearing loss, his wife often answers for him, and he is asking whether surgery is the answer. Describe how you would communicate with him in your next conversation so that he understands his options and can make his own decision.

checklist.point: Sets up the environment to support hearing: quiet room, face to face, good lighting, reduced background noise.
Speaks clearly and at a measured pace, avoids shouting, and checks whether he uses hearing aids or an amplifier.
Addresses Mr. Gill directly and invites his wife to add information only with his agreement.
Uses plain language and avoids jargon such as stenosis without explaining it.
Provides written or pictorial information in large print.
Presents options neutrally: exercise program, medical review, injections and surgery as decisions for the physician or surgeon, with general benefits and risks.
Stays within scope by not promising a surgical result or advising for or against surgery.
Uses teach-back and open questions to confirm understanding.
Explores his values, goals and fears and responds to emotion.

questions.model_answer:
My aim is that Mr. Gill leaves this conversation understanding his options in his own words and feeling that the decision is his.

I would start with the setting. I would use a quiet room, close the door, sit at his level about one metre away so he can see my face, and have good light on me. I would ask him what helps him hear best, whether he has hearing aids that he is not wearing, and whether there is a pocket amplifier I could use. I would speak at a steady, slightly slower pace and a normal volume, not shout, and I would pause between ideas.

Next, his role. I would greet him first, and look at him when I ask questions. I would say, 'Mr. Gill, I'd like to hear from you first, and then your wife can add anything you would like her to.' I would ask him privately, at the start of the visit, whether he is happy for his wife to speak for him or to stay in the room, because I want to respect his choice rather than assume. If she answers for him, I would gently redirect: 'Thank you, I would like to hear how that is for Mr. Gill.'

Then the content. I would explain the problem in everyday words: 'The channel the nerves run through in your lower back has become narrow, which is why your legs get heavy when you stand and ease when you bend forward.' I would draw a simple picture and give him a one page summary in large print. On surgery, I would explain that I am a physiotherapist, so the decision about surgery belongs to him and a surgeon. I can describe in general that some people choose surgery when walking stays very limited despite exercise and that others improve with exercise, and that a physician can explain risks and likely results for him. I would not promise an outcome or tell him what to choose. I would also tell him I want his physician to see him about the urinary change before we plan further, and that this may affect which options are suitable.

I would ask open questions: 'What matters most to you about walking again?' and 'What worries you about surgery?' If he seems anxious or says he fears becoming dependent, I would acknowledge that.

Finally, I would use teach-back: 'So that I explained it clearly, can you tell me what the next steps will be?' I would write the next steps on the page and invite him to bring questions to the appointment with his physician or surgeon.

scale.4: Adapts the environment and style to hearing loss, speaks directly to the client with his wife included by consent, gives neutral information within scope, and confirms understanding with teach-back.
scale.3: Uses good communication strategies but misses one of consent for his wife's role, scope limits, or understanding checks.
scale.2: General statements about being clear with little tailoring to hearing loss or autonomy.
scale.1: Speaks mainly to the wife, advises for or against surgery, or uses jargon throughout.

safety_or_ethics_point: The buried issue is the new urinary hesitancy for two weeks and rubbery legs, mentioned casually at the end. Together with severe multilevel stenosis they may signal progressive neural compression, so the candidate should recognize it, screen, contact the physician or send him to emergency the same day, and pause progressive loading. The imaging report is the distractor.
common_errors: Candidates write a complete exercise plan and treat the urinary comment as a footnote, or they say they will 'monitor' it. Others answer the communication question with generic advice and forget hearing loss, his autonomy and scope.
examiner_notes: A pass requires a safe, reasoned stenosis plan and clear recognition of the red flag with same-day action. Strong candidates connect the urinary change to the exercise plan and communicate within scope and with his consent.

title: Lateral elbow pain in a carpenter with a workplace claim
setting: Private clinic accepting workplace compensation board claims
client_profile: Mr. Dmitri Kowalczuk is a 44 year old finish carpenter with six weeks of right lateral elbow pain, gradual onset after a large trim job. Pain is 6 out of 10 with gripping a hammer or power driver and 2 out of 10 at rest. He is right-hand dominant. No numbness, no neck pain. Past history: none; no medications except occasional ibuprofen. Findings: tenderness over the lateral epicondyle and proximal common extensor tendon; pain with resisted wrist extension and resisted middle finger extension; full elbow range; grip strength right 28 kg, left 46 kg; pain-free grip not possible; Spurling's negative; neurological screen normal. Patient-Rated Tennis Elbow Evaluation score 58 out of 100. He had one corticosteroid injection from a walk-in physician three weeks ago with brief relief.
clinical_scenario: The claim was accepted by the provincial workers' compensation board, and the board's case manager has asked for a progress report within seven days. The employer's supervisor phoned the clinic yesterday asking for the diagnosis, the treatment plan and whether Mr. Kowalczuk can go back to full duty on Monday. Mr. Kowalczuk currently works modified duties but told you today that he is working on ladders and dropped a nail gun last week when his hand 'let go'. A physiotherapist assistant is available to help in the clinic.

questions.prompt: Describe the treatment plan you would set for Mr. Kowalczuk over the next eight weeks, including the interventions, how you would dose and progress them, and how you would know if the plan is working.

checklist.point: Sets function and work-based goals, such as pain-free tool grip and return to full duties.
Advises load management and temporary modification of aggravating tasks rather than complete rest.
Prescribes progressive tendon loading, beginning with isometric holds and moving to isotonic and eccentric or heavy slow resistance work, with dosage.
Includes grip, forearm and shoulder or scapular strengthening and addresses kinetic chain contributors.
Mentions work technique and tool adjustments such as handle size, neutral wrist posture or counterforce bracing as options.
Uses pain as a guide with an acceptable threshold during and after loading and a 24 hour response rule.
Names outcome measures: PRTEE, pain-free grip, grip dynamometry, and work tasks.
Explains the natural course and sets a timeframe for reassessment and escalation if not improving.

questions.model_answer:
I would organize the plan around getting his tendon able to take the loads of his trade again, not just settling pain. His goals are likely to be gripping tools without pain and working a full day, and I would confirm that with him.

First, load management. Complete rest would weaken the tendon, so I would not take him off everything. I would identify the tasks that provoke most symptoms, such as repetitive hammering and power driving with a tight grip, and reduce the volume of these while keeping other work. I would discuss tool changes with him: a larger diameter handle, a lighter driver, keeping the wrist in neutral, and trying a forearm counterforce strap for work tasks as an option for short term relief, not a cure.

Second, progressive loading, which is the core of treatment. In weeks one to two I would begin isometric wrist extension holds, for example five holds of 30 to 45 seconds, once or twice a day, at an effort that gives pain no more than 3 or 4 out of 10 and that is settled by the next morning. Once holds are comfortable and grip is improving, I would move in weeks three to six to slow isotonic loading: wrist extension with a dumbbell or resistance band, about three sets of 10 to 15 with three seconds up and three seconds down, three to four days a week, adding load when he completes all sets with pain at or below the agreed threshold. In the last phase I would add heavy, slow resistance work, grip work with a dynamometer or putty, and functional tasks like holding a hammer at different grips and weights, then work-specific simulations.

Third, other regions. I would include shoulder and scapular strengthening, because poor proximal control raises load on the forearm, and I would look at his neck and wrist as contributors.

Fourth, I would explain the course. This condition usually improves over months, not weeks, and the injection gave brief relief but is not a long term solution, so I would not rely on repeat injections.

Fifth, measurement. I would repeat the PRTEE, pain-free grip and grip strength every two weeks, and use a task test such as hammering a set number of times at a given weight. I would expect a clear change by six weeks. If there is no improvement at six to eight weeks, or if he develops neurological signs, I would discuss imaging or referral to a physician for other options.

scale.4: Gives a staged loading program with dosage, load management, work modification, outcome measures, and a clear review point, tied to the client's trade.
scale.3: Appropriate interventions but incomplete dosage, progression or measurement.
scale.2: Mostly modalities, rest or stretching with little progressive loading.
scale.1: Recommends complete rest, repeated injections as the plan, or an unsafe approach.

questions.prompt: Discuss what you would do about the safety concerns that arise from Mr. Kowalczuk's current work, and how you would make decisions with him about what he does at work this week.

checklist.point: Identifies that dropping a tool while working on a ladder is a risk to him and others.
Asks specific questions about the dropping: frequency, weakness versus pain inhibition, other neurological symptoms, and tasks at height.
Re-examines for neurological or other causes of the 'letting go', such as cervical or radial nerve involvement.
Advises to avoid ladder and overhead power tool work or use alternatives until grip is reliable, explaining why.
Respects his autonomy and finances by discussing options such as modified duties and the likelihood of income effects.
Explains the workplace modification in a way he can take to his employer, with his consent.
Discusses medication safety, including the injection history and analgesic use.
Documents the safety discussion and decisions.

questions.model_answer:
The safety concern is that his hand let go of a nail gun while he was working on a ladder. That is a risk of a fall and of the tool striking someone, and it needs to be handled before the plan. I would raise it directly and calmly with him.

I would begin by asking him to tell me about it in his own words. How often has his grip let go? Is it sudden weakness, or is the pain making him drop things? What was he doing, how high was he, and who was nearby? Any numbness, tingling, neck pain or weakness elsewhere? I have already done a neurological screen today, which was normal, but I would repeat a quick check of the radial nerve and C6 to C8 myotomes, and test grip and wrist extension for a true loss of strength, so that I am not assuming this is only tendon pain. If the drop was a pain-related reflex, the risk is still real, because it could happen again at height.

Then I would give him my professional advice. I would say that until his grip is reliable and he can hold his tools without his hand giving out, I recommend that he avoids ladder work and overhead use of heavy power tools, or works with another person to hold or use a tool lanyard and a lighter tool. I would explain why in practical terms: a fall from a ladder could be far more harmful to him than a few days of reduced hours.

Then I would involve him in the decision. He knows his worksite and his financial pressures. I would ask what tasks he could do at ground level, whether the employer has other work, and what he is worried about. I would explain that the board and employer have processes for modified duties, and that I can provide a functional abilities note listing what he can and cannot do, with no diagnosis, if he agrees. The final decision about whether to follow the advice is his, but I would make sure he understands the risk and document that.

I would also check on analgesics: how much ibuprofen he takes, because of stomach and kidney effects, and I would remind him that I cannot advise on further injections but his physician can discuss them.

At the end, I would summarize the agreement in his words, ask him to repeat the safety plan, and book a short follow-up within one week to review his grip and work.

scale.4: Identifies the ladder and tool risk, screens for the cause, gives clear advice to modify work, supports his decision-making, and documents.
scale.3: Recognizes the risk and advises modification but with limited exploration or limited shared decision-making.
scale.2: Mentions safety in general terms or only passes on a work note.
scale.1: Ignores the dropped tool or tells him to continue full duties.

questions.prompt: The board and the employer are both asking for information, and you have an assistant available. Discuss how you would manage reporting, documentation, privacy, delegation and billing for this claim.

checklist.point: Provides the board with the required progress report by the deadline using accurate, objective information.
Obtains and documents consent before sharing health information and limits what is shared with the employer to functional abilities and restrictions, not diagnosis or treatment detail.
Redirects the employer's request for diagnosis to the proper channel and explains why.
Documents each visit contemporaneously: findings, plan, response, advice, communications.
Delegates appropriately to the assistant, such as supervised exercise instruction and measurement of grip, while retaining assessment, plan and progression.
Ensures the assistant is trained, supervised and the client agrees to the assistant's involvement.
Bills only for services provided at the board's agreed rates and codes, without charging the worker for covered services or inflating items.
Retains records and stores them securely according to regulator and provincial privacy requirements.

questions.model_answer:
There are three audiences here: the board, the employer and Mr. Kowalczuk himself, and each has a different right to information. I would manage them separately.

First, the board. They are funding the claim and have asked for a progress report in seven days. I would put that date in my schedule today. The report would be objective and brief: findings at the initial assessment, measures such as grip strength and PRTEE, the plan, response so far, restrictions, and expected timeline. I would stick to what I measured and avoid speculation, and I would sign it with my name and registration number. I would send it by the board's secure method.

Second, the employer. The supervisor has no automatic right to the diagnosis or the plan. I would not give details by phone. Questions about the diagnosis or claim status should go through Mr. Kowalczuk himself or the board's case manager. I would tell the supervisor, politely, that I need the worker's consent to release information and that I can provide, with his consent, a functional abilities form, with his written consent, that lists what he can do, such as no ladder work and limited gripping with power tools, and the expected review date. For the question about full duty on Monday, I would say that return to full duty depends on reassessment and I would not commit on a date. I would tell Mr. Kowalczuk what was asked and what I shared, and note that in the record.

Third, documentation. I would write notes at the time of each visit, including the history, findings, safety discussion, advice, his decisions and every communication with the board and employer. Notes should be clear enough that another therapist could continue care.

Fourth, delegation. The assistant can supervise his exercises, teach technique, record grip measures, and apply tools like a strap under my direction. I would remain responsible for the assessment, diagnosis, plan and progression, and I would tell Mr. Kowalczuk who the assistant is and obtain his agreement. I would not delegate the reassessment, the decision about safety or the report.

Fifth, billing. I would bill the board only for sessions and items that took place, using the codes in the board's fee schedule, and I would not bill the worker for covered services or add charges for items the board does not approve. If he needs a larger sleeve or strap that the board does not cover, I would discuss that cost with him before purchase.

Finally, I would keep the record secure and kept for the length of time my regulator requires.

scale.4: Separates board, employer and client information needs, protects privacy and consent, delegates within scope with supervision, documents and bills ethically.
scale.3: Covers most elements but is vague on consent, delegation limits or billing ethics.
scale.2: Mentions reporting and documentation in general terms without handling the employer request or delegation.
scale.1: Shares diagnosis with the employer without consent, delegates assessment, or bills inappropriately.

safety_or_ethics_point: The buried issue is that Mr. Kowalczuk dropped a nail gun while on a ladder because his hand let go. The candidate should recognize the fall and tool hazard, screen for a neurological cause, advise work modification, and respect his decision. The employer's request for diagnosis is a related privacy issue.
common_errors: Candidates give a long exercise plan and treat the dropped tool as background, or they send the diagnosis to the employer to be helpful. Others delegate assessment to the assistant or forget billing ethics.
examiner_notes: A pass needs evidence-based loading with dosage, a clear safety response to the ladder risk, and firm privacy boundaries with the employer. Strong answers keep roles for the assistant specific.

title: Thigh contusion in a university hockey player
setting: University varsity athletics clinic
client_profile: Mr. Amara Okoye is a 19 year old defenceman on the varsity hockey team. Two days ago he took a hard knee to his right anterior mid-thigh during a game. He played on for ten minutes, then iced it. Today he reports a deep, tight ache of 6 out of 10, a limp, and trouble with stairs. Right thigh circumference at 15 cm above the patella is 3.5 cm greater than the left. There is a firm, tender area over the mid quadriceps about 8 cm across with no visible skin discolouration yet. Active right knee flexion is 55 degrees in prone, left 140 degrees. Straight leg raise is possible with pain. Sensation in the leg and foot is normal, dorsalis pedis pulse is palpable, and foot colour and temperature are normal. He is otherwise healthy, takes no medications, and has no previous thigh injury.
clinical_scenario: The head coach is asking for him to dress for Saturday's game in five days, as two defencemen are already out. Before coming in, the athlete's teammate applied a heat pack and a deep massage last night 'to loosen it', and Mr. Okoye has been taking ibuprofen from a friend for two days. He tells you that the leg felt tighter this morning than last night, and that he is scared of losing his spot on the team. His parents live in another province and he lives in residence.

questions.prompt: Describe the phases of your management plan for Mr. Okoye over the coming weeks, including what you would do now, how you would progress, and the criteria you would use for return to play.

checklist.point: Grades the injury as moderate based on knee flexion range and swelling and explains why this guides the plan.
Initial phase: relative rest, protection, light non-constricting compression only after a same-day recheck shows no increasing tightness, cold in short applications, avoiding heat and massage.
Advises to avoid deep massage, heat, and aggressive stretching early because of the risk of heterotopic ossification.
Uses pain-free progression: active range of motion within tolerance, isometrics, then strengthening, then sport-specific work.
Gives criteria for progressing between phases, such as pain-free flexion range, symmetrical strength, and swelling reduced.
Gives return to play criteria: full pain-free range, near symmetrical strength, sport-specific drills and contact tolerance with padding.
Names a reassessment schedule and measures, such as thigh circumference, knee flexion range, hop and strength tests.
States that return before day five is unrealistic for this grade, with an expected timeline range.

questions.model_answer:
From what I found today this is a moderate quadriceps contusion. I base that on knee flexion limited to 55 degrees, the 3.5 cm increase in thigh circumference, and a limp. This grade usually needs about three to six weeks in an athlete, not five days. The main thing I want to protect against is a bad complication called myositis ossificans, where bone forms inside the muscle. So the plan is staged, and what we avoid early matters as much as what we do.

Phase one, the first 48 to 72 hours, is the acute phase and we are in it. The aim is to limit bleeding and swelling. He should rest from sport, walk with crutches if he cannot walk without a limp, and, once the same-day recheck I describe next shows no increase in tightness, I would apply a light compression wrap that is snug but never tight, with the knee resting in as much flexion as is comfortable. I would take the wrap off and send him to emergency if the thigh gets tighter or more painful, or if he notices numbness or colour change. I would use ice for ten to fifteen minutes with a barrier at a time, several times a day. I would stop the heat and the massage, and ask him to check with the team physician or a pharmacist about the ibuprofen, and avoid aggressive or forced passive stretching early, and explain why: heat and deep massage can increase bleeding and are linked to bone forming in the muscle, and forced stretching raises that risk too, and anti-inflammatory drugs early on are a question for his physician or the team doctor.

Phase two begins once swelling is settling and he can move without strong pain, usually after several days. I would begin gentle active knee flexion and extension within comfort, pain-free quadriceps isometrics, stationary bicycle with a high seat, and gradual weight-bearing. Progress when flexion is at least 90 degrees, he walks without a limp, and pain at rest is low.

Phase three is strengthening: closed chain exercise such as leg press and squats, eccentric work, hip and core strength, and then straight line running when he has near full pain-free range and strength about 80 to 90 percent of the other leg. Phase four is sport-specific: skating, cutting, shooting, and drills, then non-contact and contact practice with a thigh pad.

Return to play criteria are full pain-free flexion, no tenderness or palpable firmness, strength and hop tests close to symmetrical, and tolerance of full practice. I would reassess every few days, measuring thigh circumference, flexion range and function, and if the firm area is not softening by week three, or range stalls, I would arrange medical review and possible imaging. I would tell the coach, with his permission, that he will not be ready by Saturday, and give the three to six week range.

scale.4: Gives phased plan with specific precautions against heterotopic ossification, objective progression and return to play criteria, and a realistic timeline.
scale.3: Appropriate phases and avoids harmful treatments but with limited criteria or dosage.
scale.2: Generic RICE or exercise list without phases, criteria or the myositis ossificans link.
scale.1: Recommends heat, massage, aggressive stretching or early return to sport.

questions.prompt: Discuss the safety precautions you would take with Mr. Okoye today, and how you would make decisions with him, given what he has told you about the last two days.

checklist.point: Recognizes that increasing tightness and tension in the thigh at 48 hours requires screening for compartment syndrome.
Checks for the signs: severe pain out of proportion, tense swelling, pain on passive stretch, paresthesia, weakness, pulses and capillary refill.
Gives clear instructions to go to emergency immediately if these signs appear or worsen, and defers compression until a same-day recheck shows no increase.
Advises to stop heat and massage and explains the reason.
Raises the use of ibuprofen and advises him to speak to the team physician or pharmacist.
Screens for other injuries such as head injury or knee injury from the hit.
Respects his autonomy and addresses his fear of losing his spot with open questions and shared decision-making.
Arranges a same-day recheck and a check on him tonight, involves the team physician, and documents the discussion.

questions.model_answer:
The thing that stands out is that his thigh felt tighter this morning than last night. After two days I would expect a bruise to be stabilizing, not tightening. That is a warning sign that bleeding may be continuing inside the muscle, and a rare but serious complication is compartment syndrome, where pressure inside the thigh compartment cuts off blood supply to nerves and muscle. I will not treat that as a minor detail.

So first I would check. I would ask him about the pain: is it worsening, is it out of proportion to what I see, does it wake him at night, and does he have numbness, tingling, or weakness in the leg or foot? On examination I would feel for a tense, hard or tight compartment compared with the other side, I would repeat the thigh circumference and compare it with my earlier number, I would check how much pain is provoked by passively bending the knee, test sensation in the thigh and foot, look at the colour and temperature of the foot, and check the dorsalis pedis pulse and capillary refill. Today those were normal, which is reassuring, but findings can change over hours.

If I find a very tense thigh, rapidly increasing swelling, disproportionate pain, or any numbness or weakness, I would send him to the emergency department right now rather than wait, and call ahead. If findings remain reassuring, I would not apply compression yet, because compression over a tightening thigh could make pressure worse. I would keep the leg rested and supported at about heart level, not raised high, and avoid compression and heat, recheck tightness and circumference in a few hours the same day, and apply only light compression if nothing has increased. I would give him the warning signs in plain language: rising tightness, pain out of proportion, numbness, weakness or a cold, pale foot. If any occur he goes to emergency immediately. I would ask the team physician to see him today, and arrange for a friend or the team athletic therapist to check on him tonight, since he lives in residence away from family.

Second, I would explain that heat and deep massage should stop, because heat can increase bleeding and massage can damage the injured muscle and raise the chance of bone forming in it. On the ibuprofen, I would ask how much he has taken and tell him that it is best to speak to the team doctor or a pharmacist about whether to continue, since that is a medication decision. I would also ask whether he hit his head or injured his knee in the collision.

Third, his choice. I would ask him how he feels about being out. I would say, 'It sounds like you are worried about your place on the team. Tell me more.' I would give him options and let him decide how to communicate with his coach, supporting him with a note.

scale.4: Identifies the worsening tightness as a possible compartment syndrome, screens with specific findings, gives clear escalation criteria, stops harmful treatments and supports his choices.
scale.3: Notes the concern and advises monitoring but with limited screening or escalation detail.
scale.2: Gives general RICE safety advice without considering compartment syndrome.
scale.1: Does not recognize the warning sign or advises continued heat or massage.

questions.prompt: The coach wants him back on Saturday and Mr. Okoye is anxious about his place on the team. Describe how you would communicate with each of them, and what you would say.

checklist.point: Speaks with Mr. Okoye first, privately, listening to his concerns before explaining the plan.
Obtains his consent to share information with the coach and agrees what will be shared.
Explains the injury and the reason for the timeline in plain language, with a clear message that Saturday is not safe.
Uses an empathetic response to his fear and focuses on what he can still contribute and control.
Gives the coach functional information such as expected timeline and phases, not unnecessary detail, and holds the position if pressured.
Offers alternatives, such as training upper body, bike, team meetings, and a defined reassessment date.
Uses teach-back or asks him to restate the plan.
Documents the communication and follows up.

questions.model_answer:
I would talk to Mr. Okoye before anyone else. I would find a private room and start with listening: 'You mentioned that you are worried about your spot. What is on your mind?' He is nineteen, away from home, and he may fear that being hurt makes him replaceable. I would acknowledge that: 'That sounds stressful, and it makes sense that you want to be out there.'

Then I would explain the injury with plain words and a drawing if helpful. 'You have a deep bruise in the big muscle at the front of your thigh. The muscle has bled inside, and that is why it is tight and why bending your knee is limited. If we push too early, the bleeding can continue, you can get a scar or even bone growing in the muscle, and a short injury can become a season ending one.' I would be clear: 'I cannot clear you for Saturday, and I would not want you to play.' I would say it kindly and without hedging, because mixed messages invite pressure.

Next, I would give him things he can control. He can keep training upper body, use the bike once I clear it, attend video sessions and team meetings, and follow a phased plan that has clear steps toward being back. I would tell him the usual range of weeks for this grade and that I would reassess in a few days so he can see progress.

I would then ask permission to speak with the coach, and agree what I will share: that he is out for Saturday, a general timeline in phases, what he can do in practice, and the date of the next review. I would not share more than that without his consent.

For the coach, I would speak calmly and directly, and say, 'He has a moderate thigh injury, and playing on Saturday would put him at real risk of a longer absence. I can give you a plan and a date when we will reassess.' If the coach pushes, I would repeat the same message and refer to the team physician for the final medical decision, rather than negotiate on the safety issue. I would offer to put the information in writing.

Finally, I would check Mr. Okoye's understanding with, 'So that I explained it well, tell me how you will describe this to your coach.' I would document both conversations and follow up.

scale.4: Listens to the athlete first, gets consent, gives a clear and consistent no-play message, supports him emotionally, and communicates limited, appropriate information to the coach.
scale.3: Communicates the message clearly but with limited emotional response or consent process.
scale.2: Focuses on informing the coach with little attention to the athlete's fear or consent.
scale.1: Yields to the coach's pressure, shares excessive information, or uses blaming language.

safety_or_ethics_point: The buried issue is the thigh feeling tighter this morning two days after the injury, along with heat and massage use. The candidate should screen for compartment syndrome with specific signs, set escalation criteria, and stop heat and massage because of myositis ossificans risk. The coach's pressure is related but secondary.
common_errors: Candidates give a standard sprain-style RICE plan and neglect the worsening tightness, or agree to a return date to please the coach. Others forget the myositis ossificans precautions.
examiner_notes: A pass requires a phased plan with the precautions, recognition of the compartment syndrome risk, and firm, empathetic communication that protects the athlete's consent.

title: Arm swelling and fatigue after breast cancer treatment
setting: Hospital-based oncology rehabilitation clinic
client_profile: Ms. Lucia Ferreira is a 52 year old elementary school teacher who finished treatment for left breast cancer 14 months ago: mastectomy with axillary node dissection of 12 nodes, adjuvant chemotherapy, and radiation to the chest wall and axilla. She is on an aromatase inhibitor. For four months her left arm has felt heavy and swollen. She also reports fatigue rated 7 out of 10 that limits her work to three days a week. Measurements: left arm circumference at 10 cm above the elbow is 3 cm greater than the right, forearm 2 cm greater, pitting is minimal, skin is intact, and shoulder flexion is 140 degrees on the left versus 165 on the right. There is no redness or warmth. Pulse 72, blood pressure 118 over 74 mmHg right arm, SpO2 98 percent. She walks 20 minutes a few times a week.
clinical_scenario: Ms. Ferreira sleeps poorly and is anxious before each follow-up. During the interview she mentions a new dull ache in her mid back over the past six weeks that wakes her at night and does not improve when she changes position, and that she has lost about 4 kg without trying. She thinks it is from sleeping badly and carrying her school bag. Her next oncology appointment is in four months. She asks you not to mention the back pain to anyone because she does not want to hear that the cancer is back. She also asks about wearing a compression sleeve to a flight next month.

questions.prompt: Based on what Ms. Ferreira has told you and your findings, explain your clinical impression, the further assessment you would perform, and how you would sort out the contributors to her symptoms.

checklist.point: Identifies probable secondary upper limb lymphedema, early stage, based on swelling, risk factors (node dissection, radiation) and circumference difference.
Notes that circumference difference and minimal pitting suggest an early or mild stage and plans further staging.
Uses additional measures: bilateral arm circumferences at standard points or volumetry, skin and tissue assessment, and function.
Identifies the night-time, non-mechanical mid back pain with unexplained weight loss as a red flag for possible metastatic disease or other serious pathology.
Recognizes that the lymphedema is not the explanation for the back pain and the weight loss.
Proposes a screen of the thoracic spine and neurological status and other systemic symptoms.
Considers fatigue contributors: treatment effects, sleep, anxiety, deconditioning, medications, anemia, and thyroid, and the need for medical input.
Considers other causes of swelling such as infection, venous thrombosis, and recurrence, and the findings that would distinguish them.

questions.model_answer:
My clinical impression has two parts, and I want to keep them separate. The first part is that she most likely has mild secondary lymphedema in the left arm. She had a 12 node axillary dissection and radiation to the axilla, which are two of the biggest risk factors, the swelling has been present for four months, the arm is 3 cm bigger above the elbow and 2 cm bigger in the forearm, and there is only minimal pitting, no redness and no warmth. That fits an early stage, where swelling comes and goes and the tissue is still soft. The shoulder flexion loss may reflect scar and radiation changes in the chest wall and fascia.

To stage the lymphedema I would measure both arms at the same landmarks every 4 cm or use volume measurement if available, record the skin, the presence of fibrosis, and the effect on her hand function and daily activity. I would also check for signs that would point away from lymphedema: redness, heat and pain would suggest cellulitis; a sudden swelling with a tender cord would suggest a clot; and a hard or fixed supraclavicular or axillary mass or arm swelling that increases quickly could mean recurrence or compression.

The second part is more important. A new mid back ache that wakes her at night, does not change with position, and comes with 4 kg unintentional weight loss in someone who has had breast cancer is a red flag combination for possible bone metastasis or other serious disease. That is not explained by lymphedema or by carrying a school bag. I would ask more: when it started, how severe, whether it is constant, any other pain, cough or breathlessness, appetite, fever, abdominal symptoms, headaches, or weakness or numbness. I would examine her thoracic spine for tenderness, percuss gently, screen her neurology for strength, sensation, reflexes and gait, and ask about bladder and bowel function. I would not try to diagnose it, but I would conclude that this needs medical assessment soon.

Fatigue has many contributors: effects of chemotherapy and radiation, aromatase inhibitor, poor sleep, anxiety, low activity and sometimes anemia or thyroid problems. I would use a fatigue scale, and ask about sleep, mood, and activity, and ask her physician to check for medical causes. But I would not attribute the fatigue to treatment effects until the red flag is dealt with.

So my working impression is mild lymphedema plus a possibly serious unexplained symptom cluster that needs prompt medical review.

scale.4: Separates the probable lymphedema from the red flag cluster, names specific assessments, and explains why the back pain and weight loss need prompt medical review.
scale.3: Identifies lymphedema and red flags but with limited differential reasoning or assessment detail.
scale.2: Focuses on lymphedema and fatigue with minimal attention to the back pain.
scale.1: Attributes the back pain to posture or the school bag, or misses the red flags.

questions.prompt: Explain the precautions and advice you would give Ms. Ferreira about her arm, her activity and her upcoming flight, and how you would involve her in decisions.

checklist.point: Gives skin care and infection precautions and instructs on signs of cellulitis that require urgent medical care.
Discusses compression: fitting by a qualified person, sleeve and glove options, and wearing for flights as a reasonable measure to discuss with the clinician.
Advises on safe exercise: gradual progression, monitoring arm response, and avoiding overloading, rather than avoiding exercise entirely.
Advises on holding off on loading the thoracic spine or strenuous strengthening until the back pain is assessed.
Provides red flags to seek urgent care: back pain with weakness or numbness, bladder or bowel change, sudden swelling, fever, or breathlessness.
Addresses travel: hydration, movement, and a plan for the flight, and carrying advice for swelling.
Elicits her fears and preferences and uses shared decision-making.
Explains the limits of what physiotherapy can do and checks understanding.

questions.model_answer:
My safety advice would cover her arm, her activity and her back, and I would start by asking what matters to her about the flight and about staying active, so that my advice fits her life.

For the arm, the main risk is infection. An arm with lymphedema has slower fluid drainage and a higher chance of cellulitis, which can progress quickly. I would teach her to keep the skin clean and moisturized, treat small cuts and insect bites right away, use gloves for gardening, avoid very hot baths and saunas on that arm, and to call her physician or go to emergency the same day if she sees redness, warmth, pain, fever or sudden increase in swelling. I would not tell her never to have blood pressure taken on that arm as an absolute rule, but I would mention that she can ask staff to use the other arm.

For compression, a well-fitted sleeve and glove can control swelling, and many people wear one on flights because of pressure changes. I would explain that she should be measured and fitted by a certified fitter so that it is the right size and class, and I would discuss with her whether to wear one on the flight, with her lymphedema therapist or physician. I would also suggest hydration, moving about the cabin, simple arm movements, and not carrying a heavy bag on the left arm.

For exercise, I would encourage regular aerobic activity and gradual strengthening, because both are safe with lymphedema when progressed slowly. I would say to watch for increases in heaviness or swelling for 24 hours after, and adjust. But today I would hold off on any thoracic loading, resisted work or manual techniques to her back until her physician has assessed the new back pain, because I do not yet know the cause. Walking is fine.

I would explain the red flags: back pain that gets worse, numbness or weakness in the legs, trouble with bladder or bowel, new breathlessness, or fever. If any occur, she should go to emergency.

Throughout, I would ask her for her thoughts, give her choices about compression and activity, and have her tell me back the plan in her own words. I would tell her honestly what I can and cannot do: I can help with swelling, movement and activity, but I cannot determine why her back hurts, and that is why I want her doctors to check it.

scale.4: Gives specific infection, compression, exercise and travel advice, defers loading of the spine pending assessment, lists red flags, and involves her in decisions.
scale.3: Gives sound lymphedema advice but weak on the back pain precaution or shared decisions.
scale.2: General lymphedema precautions with little tailoring.
scale.1: Gives unsafe advice such as heavy loading or ignoring the back pain.

questions.prompt: Ms. Ferreira has asked you not to tell anyone about her back pain. Discuss your professional responsibilities in this situation and what you would do.

checklist.point: Acknowledges her right to autonomy and confidentiality and explores her reasons and fears.
Explains the clinical concern honestly and the reason that prompt medical assessment matters.
Attempts to obtain her informed consent to communicate with her physician or oncologist, offering options such as her calling or a joint call.
Does not diagnose or tell her it is a recurrence and stays within scope.

Recognizes that if she refuses, she has the capacity to decide, and the physiotherapist must respect it, document the discussion and the advice, and keep the door open, unless a legal exception applies.
Does not disclose without consent unless required by law or there is serious risk to her or others that meets the legal threshold.
Documents the history, red flags, advice, her decision and follow-up plan.
Plans follow-up, including a time-limited recheck and offers to help with the appointment.

questions.model_answer:
This is a conflict between respecting her wishes and my duty to act on a possible serious problem. I would handle it by working with her, not around her.

First I would listen. I would say, 'I hear that you do not want this to be shared. Can you tell me what worries you most?' She is probably frightened of hearing the word recurrence, and she may feel she cannot go through more treatment. I would acknowledge that, and I would not hurry. I would remind her that what she tells me is confidential and that I will not share her information without her permission, except in the rare situations the law requires.

Then I would be honest and clear about my concern, in plain words and without alarming her or giving a diagnosis. 'A back pain that wakes you at night and does not ease with position, together with the weight loss, is not something I can explain from physiotherapy. Most of the time causes are manageable, but because of your history, it is important that your doctor looks at it soon, not in four months.' I would tell her that I cannot treat or assess the cause of this, and that continuing physiotherapy on the back without knowing could be unsafe.

Next I would ask for her consent. I would offer choices: she could call her family physician or oncology nurse line from my office with me present, I could call with her permission, or I could write a note she brings. I would offer to help her book it and to go over what to say. I would ask what would make this easier.

If she still refuses, I would respect that, since she is an adult with capacity and the decision is hers. I would not contact her oncologist behind her back, because the situation does not meet the threshold for disclosure without consent. I would make sure that she understands the possible consequences of waiting, give her the red flags that mean emergency, and tell her that she can change her mind at any time. I would document the history, my findings, my advice, her understanding, her refusal and the reasons she gave. I would hold off on any treatment to the spine and book a short follow-up within a week to revisit.

I would also check with my regulator's guidance or a senior colleague if I was unsure about disclosure requirements.

scale.4: Balances autonomy and duty, seeks consent with options, explains the concern honestly within scope, respects capacity if she refuses, documents, and plans follow-up.
scale.3: Seeks consent and documents but explores her fears or legal limits less fully.
scale.2: Either simply accepts her request or says she will contact the oncologist without consent.
scale.1: Breaches confidentiality without justification or ignores the issue.

safety_or_ethics_point: The buried issue is the new night-time mid back pain with 4 kg unintentional weight loss in a breast cancer survivor, with a request for secrecy. The candidate should treat it as a red flag for possible metastasis, separate it from the lymphedema, seek consent for medical referral, and respect capacity if she refuses while documenting. The arm circumference is the distractor.
common_errors: Candidates focus on lymphedema staging and compression and treat the back pain as a minor comment, or they promise secrecy or breach confidentiality. Some tell her it is probably a recurrence.
examiner_notes: A pass requires recognizing the red flag cluster, separating it from lymphedema, and handling the confidentiality conflict with consent seeking, honesty and documentation. Strong answers do not diagnose.

title: Calf pain on walking in a man with type 2 diabetes
setting: Community outpatient physiotherapy clinic
client_profile: Mr. Walter Nakamura is a 67 year old retired electrician with type 2 diabetes for 12 years, hypertension and a 40 pack-year smoking history; he currently smokes about eight cigarettes a day. Medications: metformin, an ACE inhibitor and a statin. For one year he has had right calf cramping after about 120 m of walking, which settles within three minutes of standing still. Findings: right dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are weak, left diminished; the right foot is cool with shiny, hairless skin; ankle-brachial index right 0.62, left 0.78; monofilament sensation reduced at both forefeet; capillary refill 3 seconds on the right. Six-minute walk distance 290 m with stops. Lumbar spine is unremarkable, and low back pain has been present on and off for years, with an MRI report showing mild degenerative changes. He wants to walk more with his grandchildren.
clinical_scenario: He does not have a family physician and uses walk-in clinics when he needs to, last about eight months ago. As he removes his sock, you notice a small dry, dark area on the tip of his right second toe that he says has been there for about three weeks, and that his right foot aches at night in bed, which he relieves by hanging the foot over the edge of the bed. He says it is nothing and asks only for exercise to improve his walking. His private insurance covers 10 physiotherapy visits.

questions.prompt: Describe the exercise-based plan you would develop for Mr. Nakamura, including the type, dosage and progression of the exercise, the other strategies you would include, and how you would measure change.

checklist.point: Sets goals linked to the client such as walking with grandchildren and increasing pain-free walking distance.
Prescribes a structured walking program to moderate claudication pain with rest between bouts, for example 30 to 60 minutes total, at least three times a week, for 12 weeks or more.
Describes progression by increasing time or distance or intensity as pain-free or moderate-pain walking improves.
Includes lower limb strengthening and optionally cycling or arm ergometry if walking is limited.
Includes risk factor education: smoking cessation support, foot care, glucose and blood pressure management with his health care team.
Names outcome measures: treadmill or six-minute walk, pain-free and maximum walking distance, a claudication scale, ABI by appropriate provider, and a function questionnaire.
Plans reassessment and criteria for modifying or stopping, including signs of limb threat.
Acknowledges limits of 10 visits and plans home program and community exercise support.

questions.model_answer:
I would plan around the goal of walking with his grandchildren, and I would be upfront that this plan is for exercise therapy for claudication, and that I would set it up only after the foot concerns are dealt with, which I describe in the next question. Assuming that is done, this is the plan.

The central intervention is supervised or structured walking. The best-supported approach for claudication is walking to a moderate level of calf discomfort, resting until it settles, and repeating. I would start with intervals: walk until the pain reaches about 3 out of 4 on a claudication scale, rest standing or sitting for a few minutes, and repeat, building up to 30 minutes of total walking time at the start and progressing toward 45 to 60 minutes, three or more times a week, for at least 12 weeks. Because he can manage about 120 m, I would begin with a time target, perhaps 20 to 30 minutes of walking plus rests, then progress by adding about five minutes every one to two weeks as the walking time to pain improves, and then raise speed or add a slight incline. With only 10 insured visits, I would use them to teach, supervise the first sessions, monitor and adjust, and I would build a home program with a log, and look for a community program or a track for the rest.

Second, I would add leg strengthening twice a week: calf raises, sit to stand, step ups, two sets of 10 to 12, progressing as tolerated. If walking is limited by pain, he can do stationary cycling or arm cranking as a complement.

Third, the risk factors. I would explain that walking helps the legs but that smoking, glucose and blood pressure drive the disease. I would offer support for quitting, with the recommendation that he talk to a physician or pharmacist about cessation aids, and encourage him to establish a family physician. I would teach daily foot checks, proper shoes, and never walking barefoot, given his reduced sensation and diabetes.

Fourth, measurement. At the start, at four weeks, at 12 weeks, I would record the six-minute walk, time to first pain and to maximal pain, a claudication rating, and a function questionnaire. The ABI would be repeated by the appropriate provider if needed. I expect the walking time to improve over the first weeks.

Fifth, I would set triggers to stop and refer: any new wound, color change, rest pain, or a drop in walking tolerance. If there is no improvement at 12 weeks, I would discuss with his physician about further vascular assessment.

scale.4: Gives an exercise plan with intervals to moderate pain, dosage and progression, risk factor and foot education, named outcome measures and referral triggers, and notes the visit limit.
scale.3: Sound exercise plan but with limited dosage, progression or measurement.
scale.2: Generic exercise advice without claudication-specific dosing or risk factor management.
