scale.1: Prescribes unsafe or unrelated treatment such as lumbar traction or high-intensity exercise through limb threat signs.

questions.prompt: Explain how you would respond to what you noticed on his toe and what he told you about night pain, including your precautions with exercise and how you would involve him in the decision.

checklist.point: Recognizes the combination of a non-healing dark toe lesion and rest pain with low ABI as suggesting chronic limb-threatening ischemia needing urgent vascular assessment.
Examines the foot further: lesion size, colour, temperature, signs of infection, pulses, capillary refill and sensation.
Explains to Mr. Nakamura in plain language why this is not just a claudication problem and may risk the toe or foot.
Holds exercise program and walking to tolerance until medically cleared, and avoids anything that could injure or load the foot.
Gives wound and foot protection advice and the signs of infection or worsening that need emergency care.

Arranges same-day urgent assessment (emergency department or urgent vascular or wound clinic), by phone with him present or by sending him directly, because rest pain with tissue loss threatens the limb.
Addresses his minimization and fear, uses shared decision-making, and checks understanding.
Documents findings and advice.

questions.model_answer:
What I noticed changes the visit. A dark, dry area on the tip of the toe that has not healed in three weeks, in a man with diabetes, reduced sensation, weak pulses and an ankle brachial index of 0.62, together with an ache in the foot at night that he relieves by hanging the foot down, is a pattern that suggests the blood supply is no longer enough to keep the tissue healthy at rest. That is different from claudication, and it can progress to infection, gangrene and loss of the toe or foot. I would not begin an exercise program until a physician has assessed it.

I would begin by examining the foot more fully, with his permission. I would look at the lesion: size, depth, colour, edges, any drainage, odour, or redness spreading up the foot. I would compare skin temperature, colour on elevation and dependency, capillary refill, and pulses, and I would check sensation again. The night pain and the posture he uses to relieve it help me understand how severe it is.

Then I would talk to him. 'Mr. Nakamura, I am glad you showed me this. The mark on your toe and the night ache tell me your foot is not getting enough blood, and that needs to be looked at by a doctor soon, not just treated with walking. I know you wanted exercise, and I will help with that, but I want to make sure your foot is safe first.' I would ask what worries him. People often minimize this because they fear amputation, and I would acknowledge that fear honestly, and explain that early treatment gives the best chance of keeping the foot.

Because he has no family physician, I would not just tell him to book something. I would phone a walk-in clinic or a vascular referral line with him present if possible, or send him to the emergency department or an urgent vascular or wound clinic the same day. Rest pain with a dark toe lesion threatens the limb even if the foot looks stable, and it is more urgent still with infection, spreading redness, a wet or painful wound, or a cold, pale foot. I would give him a letter with my findings.

For exercise, I would pause the walking program. He can still do gentle, non-weight-bearing movement if comfortable. I would ask him to protect the foot, wear closed shoes with clean socks, not walk barefoot, avoid heat packs, not cut the lesion or use corn remedies, and go to emergency if he sees pus, redness, or increasing pain. I would ask him to repeat the plan, and document everything.

scale.4: Identifies chronic limb-threatening ischemia features, examines further, arranges urgent assessment despite no physician, pauses exercise, gives protection advice, and engages his fear and choices.
scale.3: Recognizes the problem and refers but with limited examination, safety advice or engagement of his minimization.
scale.2: Notes the toe but continues exercise or advises routine follow-up.
scale.1: Ignores the lesion and night pain or applies heat or debridement.

questions.prompt: Mr. Nakamura has no family physician and says he will not go anywhere. Discuss your professional responsibilities and what you would do to see that he gets the assessment he needs.

checklist.point: Acknowledges his right to make decisions and explores barriers such as cost, transport, past experiences and fear.
Takes reasonable active steps to connect him to care, such as calling a clinic, providing a written referral letter, or arranging transport, and does not just advise.
Stays within scope by describing findings and concerns without diagnosing or prescribing.
Obtains his consent before sharing information with other providers and explains what will be shared.
If he declines, confirms capacity and informed refusal, explains the risks, documents the discussion, and keeps follow-up open.
Considers cultural safety and respectful communication and avoids blame or judgment about smoking.
Documents findings, advice, actions taken, his decisions and the plan.
Follows up within a defined period to check whether he was seen.

questions.model_answer:
My responsibility here is greater than giving advice. I have found something that could threaten his foot, and he has no physician to hand it to. As a physiotherapist I cannot diagnose or treat it, so I have a duty to take reasonable steps to see that someone who can does, while respecting his choices.

First I would understand why he says he will not go anywhere. I would ask, 'Help me understand what makes it hard to see a doctor.' It might be cost, a bad experience, difficulty with transport, long waits, or fear of what he will hear about his foot. Understanding the barrier lets me address it. I would avoid blame about his smoking, because judgment will make him close up, and I would use respectful language and ask what he understands about his own health.

Then I would take active steps. I would offer to phone a walk-in clinic or an after-hours vascular or wound clinic from our office while he is here, explain the situation briefly, and arrange a time. If there is a regional nurse navigator or a primary care attachment program, I could help him register. I would write a short referral letter with my findings: the toe lesion, duration, ankle brachial index, pulses, rest pain, and diabetes, and ask for assessment for peripheral arterial disease. Before I share any of this I would ask for his permission, tell him what I will include, and who will see it. If he wants, I could help with transport, such as asking a family member, a taxi voucher, or a community service.

I would stay in my scope. I would say what I observed and what it could mean, but I would not tell him he has gangrene or that he will lose the toe, and I would not prescribe or treat the wound beyond protective advice.

If he still refuses, he is an adult with capacity and it is his decision. I would make sure he truly understands the risks of waiting, in plain words, and tell him that the door stays open. I would give him written red flags and a number to call, document what I observed, what I advised, what I offered, his reasons and decision, and I would pause exercise. I would call him within two or three days to ask whether he went, and to offer help again. Using more of his insured visits for that follow up is reasonable.

I would also consider talking with my clinical lead or regulator guidance if I was unsure about what more I should do.

scale.4: Takes active steps to connect him to care with consent, stays within scope, explores barriers, respects capacity if he declines, documents, and follows up.
scale.3: Refers and documents but is passive about connecting him or limited on consent and scope.
scale.2: Simply advises him to see a doctor and notes it in the chart.
scale.1: Discharges him, treats the wound beyond scope, or shares information without consent.

safety_or_ethics_point: The buried issue is a three week non-healing dark toe lesion with night rest pain in a man with diabetes, neuropathy and an ABI of 0.62, which suggests chronic limb-threatening ischemia. The candidate should pause exercise, examine, arrange urgent assessment despite no physician, and respect his consent. The low back MRI is the distractor.
common_errors: Candidates write a full claudication walking program and mention the toe in passing, or tell him to see a doctor without taking steps to connect him. Some treat the wound beyond scope.
examiner_notes: A pass needs a correct claudication exercise plan, recognition of limb threat with urgent action, and a professional response to the lack of a physician that goes beyond advice. Strong answers keep his consent and capacity central.

title: Dupuytren fasciectomy, hand therapy, retired welder
setting: Outpatient hand therapy clinic in a community hospital
client_profile: Mr. Joao Medeiros is a 66 year old right hand dominant retired welder who now does weekend woodworking. Ten days ago he had a partial fasciectomy of the right ring and small fingers for Dupuytren contracture. Portuguese is his first language and he reads English slowly. He takes metformin. Pre-operative PIP flexion contracture was 50 degrees in the small finger and 35 degrees in the ring finger. Today the small finger PIP extension lag is 30 degrees and the ring finger lag is 20 degrees. MCP joints extend fully. PIP flexion is 80 degrees in both. Grip strength is 18 kg right and 38 kg left. The palmar wound is mostly closed with a 1 cm open area, and the dressing has a small amount of serous drainage. The skin over the digits is slightly shiny. He rates pain 6 out of 10 at rest, and light touch from a cotton ball to the ring finger makes him pull away. Temperature is 36.8 degrees C.
clinical_scenario: The surgeon's referral asks for a night extension splint, scar management and range of motion exercises. Mr. Medeiros says he does not need a pamphlet because he worked with his hands for 40 years and he plans to help his son move a heavy workbench next week. His daughter usually drives him but cannot attend today. He has been skipping his evening splint because it is uncomfortable and he has been taking extra acetaminophen to sleep. He wants to know whether he can stop therapy once his fingers look straight. He gives permission to speak to the surgeon's office.

questions.prompt: Describe the treatment plan you would set up for Mr. Medeiros over the next six weeks, including your goals, the interventions you would choose, how you would progress them and how you would measure progress.

checklist.point: States goals tied to the case: maintain finger extension, restore PIP flexion, control swelling and scar, return to woodworking.
Plans a custom thermoplastic extension splint for night wear with a schedule and a plan to check fit and skin.
Addresses edema and scar with elevation, light compression, gentle massage once the wound is closed.
Prescribes active, pain limited range of motion exercises several times daily, avoiding forceful passive stretching of the fresh wound.
Sets progression by wound healing and symptoms, with strengthening delayed until the wound is closed and pain settles.
Names outcome measures such as total active motion, extension lag, grip strength and a patient reported hand function scale.
Plans reassessment at set visits and states triggers to modify the plan, such as rising pain, swelling or worsening lag.
Links work and hobby demands to a graded return, including lifting limits until cleared by the surgeon.

questions.model_answer: My goals for the next six weeks are to protect the surgical result, keep the fingers straight, get the bent range back, settle swelling and scar, and get Mr. Medeiros safely back to woodworking. First, the splint. I would make a custom thermoplastic night splint that holds the ring and small fingers in extension, and I would check the fit and the skin at every visit because he already finds it uncomfortable. I would ask what exactly bothers him, and adjust edges or padding, because a splint he does not wear gives him no benefit. The plan would usually continue for several months, and I would explain that this is the usual course and not a punishment. Second, swelling and scar. I would teach elevation, light compression with a sleeve if the surgeon agrees, and gentle scar massage with silicone once the open area is closed. Third, exercise. I would prescribe active range of motion several times a day in short sets, working PIP and DIP flexion, then full extension against the splint plate. I would avoid forceful passive stretching right now, because the wound is still partly open and his pain is high for ten days after surgery. Fourth, progression. I would progress by tissue healing and symptoms, not by a calendar. Once the wound is closed and pain is settling, I would add tendon gliding, then light putty, then grip work, and finally lifting and tool use in steps. Heavy lifting stays off the table until the surgeon clears it, and I would say that plainly about the workbench. Fifth, outcome measures. I would record extension lag at the PIP joints, total active motion, grip strength compared with his left side, and a patient reported measure of hand function so we can see change that matters to him. I would also set a goal in his own words, such as using his chisels comfortably. Sixth, reassessment. I would see him two or three times a week at first, then weekly. If pain stays high, if swelling or lag increases, or if the wound changes, I would slow down, stop loading and contact the surgeon. If lag stays stable and motion improves, I would progress and space visits out. Finally, I would answer his question about stopping therapy honestly. Straight fingers at six weeks do not mean finished, because contracture can return, so we would agree on a splint and review schedule and a plan for what to do if the fingers start to curl again.

scale.4: Gives case-specific goals, splint, edema and scar care, graded exercise, progression tied to wound healing, named outcome measures and clear triggers to modify, all linked to his woodworking and family role.
scale.3: A sound plan covering most elements with reasoning, but lacking named outcome measures, triggers to modify, or a clear link between progression and the state of the wound.
scale.2: Lists generic hand therapy items such as a splint and exercises without dose, progression logic or links to the case, or overlooks the open wound and the high pain level.
scale.1: Plans forceful stretching or early heavy strengthening, or leaves out splinting and reassessment, so the plan could damage the surgical result or ignore the findings.

questions.prompt: While you work, Mr. Medeiros asks how his hand compares with other patients and whether the pain and sensitivity you noticed are normal. Discuss how you would respond and what safety steps you would take before he leaves.

checklist.point: Recognizes that pain at rest that is high for this stage plus light touch pain, shiny skin and swelling are not typical.
Considers early complex regional pain syndrome and also infection from the open wound drainage as possible explanations.
Takes a focused history of pain pattern, temperature and colour change, sweating, nights, fever, drainage and medication use.
Examines wound, colour, temperature, swelling and sensation, and compares with the opposite hand.
Avoids aggressive stretching or modalities that provoke pain while symptoms are unexplained.
Contacts the surgeon the same day to report findings and seeks medical assessment, with his permission.
Asks about acetaminophen dose and discusses safe daily limits without prescribing or changing medication.
Gives clear return precautions about fever, spreading redness, pus and sudden worsening pain.
Respects autonomy by explaining findings, checking understanding and agreeing next steps with him.

questions.model_answer: I would answer him honestly and not just reassure him. I would say that stiff fingers and some soreness are expected after this operation, but pain this strong at rest and a hand that hurts from a light touch is more than I would expect at ten days, so I want to look more closely and get the surgeon involved. First, I would take a focused history. When did the pain change, is it burning or throbbing, does it keep him awake, has the colour or temperature of the fingers changed, is there more sweating, any fever or chills, and what has the drainage looked like. I would ask how many acetaminophen he is taking and how often, because he said he is taking extra, and I would remind him of the daily maximum on the label and ask him to check with his pharmacist or doctor. I would not change his medication myself. Second, I would examine. I would look at the wound for redness, warmth, swelling, smell and the type of drainage, compare skin colour, temperature and swelling with the left hand, and test light touch and sensation. I am thinking about two possibilities. One is an early wound infection, because there is drainage from the open area. The other is an early pain syndrome such as complex regional pain syndrome, because the pain is out of proportion, the skin is shiny and light touch hurts. I cannot diagnose either, and both need a physician. Third, I would change what I do today. I would stop any forceful stretching, deep massage or heat, and keep to gentle active movement within comfort, plus elevation. If I push into pain, I could make an inflamed or sensitized hand worse. Fourth, communication. With his permission, which he has given, I would call the surgeon's office before he leaves and ask for a same day or next day assessment, giving my findings in short, clear terms. I would write down what I told him. Fifth, return precautions. I would tell him in plain words to go to emergency or call the surgeon immediately if he gets a fever, redness spreading up the hand, pus, a bad smell, or pain that suddenly gets much worse. I would ask him to say it back to me. Finally, I would check that he feels heard. He is proud of his hands, so I would invite his questions and tell him that checking early is the best way to protect the result he had surgery for.

scale.4: Identifies the abnormal pain and skin pattern, names infection and early pain syndrome as concerns, stops provocative treatment, contacts the surgeon and gives precautions while respecting his autonomy.
scale.3: Recognizes the problem and refers, but leaves out one of the infection or pain syndrome reasoning, medication safety advice, or clear return precautions for him to follow.
scale.2: Treats the findings as normal post-operative stiffness or only reassures him, with a thin history, no same day contact with the surgeon or no change to the treatment.
scale.1: Continues stretching or treats through the pain, or fails to inform the surgeon, leaving a possible infection or pain syndrome unaddressed and the client at risk.

questions.prompt: Mr. Medeiros becomes irritated and says he has used his hands for 40 years and does not need to be told what to do. Explain how you would communicate with him to reach agreement on splint wear, home exercises and activity limits.

checklist.point: Acknowledges his expertise and frustration without defensiveness before giving any advice.
Uses open questions to explore why the splint is uncomfortable and what matters most to him.
Uses plain language, short sentences and avoids jargon, checking reading comfort in English.
Offers an interpreter or Portuguese materials and the option to include his daughter by phone or video.
Uses teach back to confirm he understands exercises, splint schedule and lifting limits.
Frames advice around his goals, such as woodworking and helping his son, using shared decision making.
Gives demonstrations and written or pictorial home program with large print instead of a dense pamphlet.
Explains the reason for each limit, including why the workbench lift must wait, and negotiates alternatives.
Sets a follow up plan and invites him to call with concerns.

questions.model_answer: I would start by slowing down and listening. He is irritated because he feels talked down to, and he is right that he knows his hands. So I would say something like, you know your hands better than anyone, and I want to use that. I would not defend my pamphlet. Then I would ask open questions. What has made the splint hard to wear? What does a good week look like for you? What are you hoping to be doing with your hands in two months? His answers tell me what to build the plan around, probably woodworking and helping his son. Second, language and literacy. He reads English slowly, so I would ask in a respectful way which language he prefers for instructions, and offer a professional interpreter or Portuguese materials. I would also offer to phone his daughter or have her join by video so the plan is shared at home. I would use short sentences and plain words, such as straighten, bend and rest, not terms like extension lag. Third, I would show instead of tell. I would do the exercises with him, hand over hand if he agrees, and give a large print sheet with photos of his own hand in the positions, with three or four exercises, not a long pamphlet. Fourth, teach back. I would say, I want to be sure I explained this well, can you show me how you will do your exercises and tell me when you will wear the splint? If something is missing, I would take responsibility for the explanation and try again. Fifth, the splint. Because it is uncomfortable, I would look at the fit with him and adjust it, then agree on a realistic schedule, for example every night and only a short trial for the days. We would agree on what to do if he cannot tolerate it. Sixth, the workbench. I would not simply say no. I would explain that the palm wound and the fascia are still healing, that a heavy pull can open the wound or bring back swelling and pain, and that the surgeon will tell us when lifting is safe. Then I would offer ways he can still help, such as directing the move, carrying light items with the other hand, or doing it in a few weeks. Finally, I would ask him what is still unclear and agree on when we meet next, so he knows the decisions remain his.

scale.4: Acknowledges his expertise, explores barriers, adapts language and format to his needs, uses teach back, explains the reasons for limits and negotiates alternatives tied to his own goals.
scale.3: Communicates respectfully and checks understanding, but misses his language or literacy needs, or does not negotiate the lifting limit and splint plan with him. The reasoning is mostly sound, but the answer lacks depth in one important area.
scale.2: Mostly instructs or repeats advice with little exploration of his concerns, uses jargon, or does not check that he has understood the plan before he leaves.
scale.1: Dismisses or argues with him, talks down to him, or lets him leave with unclear instructions and no agreement on the splint, exercises or lifting limits.

safety_or_ethics_point: Pain at rest of 6 out of 10, allodynia, shiny skin, swelling and wound drainage at ten days may signal early infection or complex regional pain syndrome. A competent candidate notices the cluster, stops provocative treatment, contacts the surgeon the same day and gives return precautions. The extra acetaminophen use also needs a safe-dose conversation.
common_errors: Candidates treat the case as routine post-fasciectomy stiffness and push stretching or strengthening. They also list a generic plan without tying progression to wound healing, and respond to his irritation with more instructions instead of exploring his goals.
examiner_notes: A pass notices the abnormal pain and skin signs without being told, changes treatment and escalates the same day. Strong responses also adapt communication to a proud, first-language Portuguese speaker. Failing responses stretch through pain or miss the escalation.

title: Transtibial amputation, prosthetic training, diabetes
setting: Inpatient and day program at a regional rehabilitation centre
client_profile: Mr. Dale Kowalchuk is a 60 year old long haul trucker with type 2 diabetes for 20 years. Eleven weeks ago he had a left transtibial amputation for a non-healing heel ulcer with osteomyelitis. He lives with his wife in a two storey house with six entry steps. He takes metformin, insulin glargine and atorvastatin. Last HbA1c was 8.4 percent. The residual limb is cylindrical with the incision healed. Edema is mild, and the distal end has a 1 cm area of pink, warm skin that blanches. Residual limb knee extension strength is 4 out of 5 and hip extension is 4 minus. Knee flexion contracture is 8 degrees. He has a temporary prosthesis with a patellar tendon bearing socket and a pin lock liner, worn about 5 hours daily. With parallel bars he walks 20 m with close supervision. His right foot has reduced monofilament sensation and a 2 cm callus under the first metatarsal head. Berg Balance Scale is 38 out of 56.
clinical_scenario: The team plans discharge in two weeks because of bed pressure. Mr. Kowalchuk wants to return to driving a truck within three months and says his right foot is fine, only a bit sore in the evening. He asked you not to mention the sore spot to the nurses because they might delay his discharge. His wife works days and he will be alone at home. He does not like using the walker and wants to walk with a cane. A physiotherapist assistant has been walking him in the hall twice daily.

questions.prompt: Explain how you would interpret these assessment findings for Mr. Kowalchuk and decide what further assessments you would complete today to guide prosthetic training and discharge planning.

checklist.point: Interprets the knee flexion contracture as a barrier to prosthetic alignment and gait, and plans management.
Notes mild edema and limb shape as appropriate for the temporary prosthesis and monitors volume change and socket fit.
Identifies the pink, warm distal area as a possible early pressure injury needing monitoring and socket review.
Recognizes the right foot callus and reduced sensation as high risk for ulceration of the remaining limb.
Interprets the Berg score as a fall risk and plans additional balance and mobility testing.
Plans a functional mobility measure such as the Amputee Mobility Predictor or a timed walk test, and pre-prosthetic strength testing.
Reviews glycemic control, cardiovascular status and exercise tolerance with the team.
Considers home environment, steps, support and driving requirements in the assessment.
Plans to inspect both limbs fully, including skin, temperature and pulses.

questions.model_answer: I would interpret the findings in order of what could harm him, then what limits his walking. First, skin. The pink, warm, blanching area at the end of the residual limb tells me the tissue is under load. Blanching is reassuring because it is not a deep tissue injury yet, but warmth and redness after 5 hours of wear could be early pressure from the socket. I would remove the prosthesis, look at the whole limb, mark the area, take a photo if the centre policy allows, and check socket fit and liner with the prosthetist. The right foot worries me just as much. He has diabetes, reduced sensation and a callus under the first metatarsal head, and now he puts more weight through that foot. Those are the conditions in which an ulcer forms, and he told me it is sore in the evenings. Today I would do a full foot inspection, check skin temperature, pulses and sensation, and look at his footwear. Second, the contracture. Eight degrees of knee flexion limits terminal extension, which changes alignment and increases load on the end of the limb. I would measure it again, look at hamstring and soft tissue tightness and at how he sits, and plan stretching and positioning. Third, strength and balance. Hip extension at 4 minus and knee extension at 4 out of 5 are fair, but his Berg of 38 puts him at risk of falls, especially on stairs. I would add a validated mobility measure such as the Amputee Mobility Predictor to help predict his prosthetic mobility level, a timed walk and a single leg stance on the right. I would also test his transfers and how he manages the six entry steps. Fourth, general health. His HbA1c of 8.4 percent suggests healing and infection risk, so I would check blood glucose records and ask about hypoglycemia during exercise, and talk to the team about his cardiovascular fitness. Fifth, function and goals. I would ask about the truck, the bed height, the pedals and the hours he sits. Driving a commercial vehicle will have medical and licensing steps that depend on his province, so I would flag that early to him and his physician. Together, I would say his current status is a safe walker with a temporary prosthesis, a limb that needs close monitoring, and a high risk remaining foot, and that these findings should shape the discharge plan, not just the walking program.

scale.4: Interprets skin, remaining foot, contracture, strength and balance with clear reasoning, chooses specific further measures and links the findings to prosthetic training and the discharge plan.
scale.3: Interprets most findings and selects relevant tests, but gives the remaining foot or the distal skin area too little weight, or offers limited reasoning for the tests.
scale.2: Lists tests and findings without interpretation, misses the foot or distal skin concern, or treats the findings only as a strength and gait training problem.
scale.1: Dismisses the skin and foot findings, or proceeds with full prosthetic loading without further assessment, creating a risk of harm to the limb and the other foot.

questions.prompt: Discuss how you would manage safety during today's prosthetic training session and how you would respond to what Mr. Kowalchuk has asked you to do about his symptoms.

checklist.point: Does not agree to keep the foot and skin findings secret and explains why in a respectful, non-judgemental way.
Explores his fear that discharge will be delayed and explains that early care prevents a bigger setback.
Modifies training: shortens wear time, offloads the distal limb and reduces weight bearing on the sore areas until reviewed.
Arranges review of the remaining foot and residual limb by the nurse or physician and a footwear check.
Protects against falls with guarding, a gait belt, appropriate walking aid and environmental setup.
Monitors blood glucose, hypoglycemia symptoms and vital signs before and during exercise.
Teaches daily skin checks of both limbs with a mirror and what to do when a spot looks wrong.
Respects autonomy by sharing decisions about the walking aid and goals, while explaining safety limits.

questions.model_answer: I would begin with what he asked, because it shapes everything. I would tell him kindly that I cannot keep this from his team. I would say that I understand he is worried about being sent home late, and that I want him walking at home too. But a sore spot on the foot he now depends on can turn into an ulcer quickly, and an ulcer on the right foot is the thing that would really delay his plans and could threaten the other leg. Telling the nurse and physician is how we protect his discharge date, not how we lose it. I would ask if he would like to be in the room when I tell them, so he stays part of the decision. Second, the session itself. Before we start I would check his blood glucose, because he is on insulin and exercise can drop it, and I would have juice and a snack at hand. I would take a baseline blood pressure and heart rate. I would inspect the residual limb and his right foot first. Because the distal limb is pink and warm, I would shorten wear time to what the skin allows, check the socket and liner with the prosthetist, and remove the prosthesis if the area reddens more or does not blanch within a few minutes after doffing. For the right foot, I would reduce time on it, check his shoe for room and a good insole, and avoid barefoot standing in the parallel bars. Third, falls. He walked 20 m with close supervision in the bars and his Berg is 38. I would keep the gait belt on, stand on the side of the prosthesis, use the parallel bars or a walker rather than a cane for now, and set the room so a chair is behind him for rest. I would explain why the walker comes first and set criteria to progress to a cane, for example when his balance, step length and walking speed meet targets, because the cane is his goal and that gives him something to work toward. Fourth, teaching. I would show him how to inspect both limbs each day with a mirror, how to wash and dry, how to manage sock ply, and I would tell him to stop wearing the prosthesis and call us if a spot stays red, opens, drains or hurts. I would ask him to repeat the plan back. Finally, I would document my findings and communicate them the same day.

scale.4: Declines secrecy with empathy, modifies the session, arranges review, covers glucose, falls and skin teaching, and keeps him involved in decisions about his walking aid and goals.
scale.3: Reports the findings and modifies the session appropriately, but omits glucose monitoring, fall precautions, or the explanation of why the information cannot be kept private.
scale.2: Reports or modifies the plan in part, but gives generic safety statements, does not address his request directly, or fails to offload the foot and the residual limb.
scale.1: Agrees to hide the findings or continues full training on a threatened foot and limb, creating a clear risk of harm and breaking professional duties.

questions.prompt: The team leader asks you to support the planned discharge date and to have the assistant continue the hallway walking program unchanged. Discuss your professional responsibilities in this situation.

checklist.point: States that the clinical findings, not bed pressure, determine safe discharge and advocates for the client.
Communicates concerns to the team leader and physician clearly, objectively and in a timely way.
Reassesses the delegation to the physiotherapist assistant and provides updated written instructions.
Explains that accountability for the plan remains with the physiotherapist and that tasks require competence and supervision.
Documents findings, communication, the client's wishes and the changes made.
Considers shared information with the client's consent and respects privacy within the team.
Uses an escalation route, such as the manager or professional practice lead, if the concern is not addressed.
Offers solutions such as a short delay, enhanced home care, outpatient follow up and prosthetist visits.

questions.model_answer: My first responsibility is to the client, and my professional standards require me to act on what I have found even when the system is under pressure. I would tell the team leader that I understand bed pressure is real and that I want to help find a safe route, but I cannot support the date until the distal limb area and the right foot are reviewed. I would not present it as a complaint. I would give clear facts: a warm, pink, blanching area at the end of the residual limb after 5 hours of wear, a callus and reduced sensation on his right foot with evening soreness, a Berg of 38, and no one at home during the day. I would ask for a physician or nurse review of both limbs today and a prosthetist visit to check the socket. Second, the assistant. I can delegate gait practice, but I remain accountable for the plan, so delegation has to match the client's current condition. Since my assessment changed today, I would update the assistant in person and in writing: shorter sessions, check both limbs before and after every walk, use the walker, gait belt always, and report any redness, pain, drainage or change in glucose to me at once. I would confirm the assistant understands, and I would increase my supervision. If I judged the assistant could not manage the new risk safely, I would do the walking myself for now. Third, I would be honest and open with the client. I would tell him what I am sharing and why, and ask what he wants the team to know about his goals, including the truck. Information is shared within the care team for his care, but I would keep it to what the team needs. Fourth, documentation. I would record my findings, who I contacted and when, the plan changes, his concerns and what he was told. Fifth, if the leader still pressed discharge without review, I would escalate to the clinical manager or the professional practice lead, and I would recognize my regulator's standards say I must advocate for safe care. Finally, I would offer solutions: a few extra days, home care nursing for foot checks, outpatient prosthetic follow up with transport, and a clear plan for what to do if a spot opens. That shows I am solving the same problem as the team, safely.

scale.4: Puts client safety ahead of discharge pressure, communicates objectively, updates delegation and supervision, documents, escalates appropriately and offers workable alternatives to the team. The answer is organized, prioritizes safety and explains the reasoning clearly.
scale.3: Advocates for the client and addresses delegation, but lacks clear escalation steps, documentation of the discussion, or constructive solutions to offer the team leader. The reasoning is mostly sound, but the answer lacks depth in one important area.
scale.2: Mentions advocacy or delegation only in general terms, or complies with the date while noting a concern but taking no action to change the plan.
scale.1: Agrees to the discharge date and the unchanged delegation despite known risks, or breaches confidentiality or scope of practice in handling the request. The answer misses the intent of the question or includes an unsafe element.

safety_or_ethics_point: The client asks the therapist to hide a sore remaining foot and a warm distal limb area to protect his discharge date. The therapist must decline secrecy, explain why, offload the areas, arrange medical review and update the assistant's delegated tasks. Safe care and honest advocacy outrank discharge pressure.
common_errors: Candidates focus only on strength and gait training and overlook the remaining foot and the distal skin area. Others agree to the client's request for secrecy or accept the team leader's plan without reassessing the assistant's delegation.
examiner_notes: A pass finds the two skin risks without being told, declines secrecy with empathy and links delegation to the changed risk. A fail trains toward the cane and the driving goal while missing the foot, or defers entirely to discharge pressure.

title: Crohn disease with fatigue and low bone density, young adult
setting: Outpatient physiotherapy clinic in a community health centre
client_profile: Ms. Amara Okafor is a 26 year old graduate student and part time barista. She was diagnosed with Crohn disease four years ago and was started on prednisone 30 mg daily seven weeks ago for a flare, now tapering by 5 mg every week. She also takes an infliximab infusion every eight weeks and a daily vitamin D supplement. Her gastroenterologist referred her for exercise guidance because of fatigue and a bone density scan showing a lumbar spine Z-score of minus 2.3. Hemoglobin from last week was 98 g/L and ferritin was low. Standing heart rate rises from 78 to 112 beats per minute with light dizziness. BMI is 18.9 kg per square metre. She reports sleeping nine hours but waking tired. Grip strength is 22 kg bilaterally, and five repetition sit to stand takes 12 seconds. She walks 20 minutes twice weekly. She has intermittent abdominal cramping and loose stools about four times daily.
clinical_scenario: Ms. Okafor wants to start lifting weights and running to build bone. Last week she lifted a 25 kg box of milk crates at work and felt a sharp pain in her mid back. She says it is better with rest but it still catches when she twists. A friend who follows a wellness influencer has told her prednisone is poisoning her bones and that she should quit it. She asks whether she can keep her diagnosis from her manager but still get lighter duties.

questions.prompt: Describe the exercise program you would design for Ms. Okafor, including your goals, the types of exercise, how you would dose and progress them, and how you would monitor her response.

checklist.point: Sets goals for bone health, fatigue, strength and function that match her priorities and condition.
Plans progressive resistance training and gradual weight bearing impact, with spinal loading patterns added only after medical clearance.
Starts at a lower load and volume, with a defined frequency and progression by symptoms and tolerance.
Limits the program to walking and spine-sparing work, with no spinal loading or impact until the back pain is medically reviewed and imaged.
Adds low to moderate aerobic work and flexibility with pacing based on fatigue and hemoglobin.
Plans for bathroom access, hydration, fuelling and flare days when exercise is reduced.
Names monitoring tools such as rate of perceived exertion, sit to stand time, grip strength, fatigue scale and pain.
Sets triggers to pause exercise and asks her physician to review the orthostatic heart rate rise, dizziness and anemia.
Educates on protein and calcium adequacy through the dietitian and gastroenterology team.

questions.model_answer: My goals are to build strength and bone loading safely, reduce fatigue, and keep her active through flares. I would set them with her, for example lifting at work without back pain and feeling less wiped out by afternoon. First, I would start lower than she expects. She is on prednisone, her bone density is low for her age, her hemoglobin is 98 and her standing heart rate rises to 112. So I would begin with two or three sessions a week of about 30 to 40 minutes. Second, resistance training, in stages. Until her back pain is medically reviewed and imaged, I would limit this to sit to stand, supported leg work and gentle pain free movement that does not load the spine. Once she is cleared, I would add hip hinge, row and press patterns with machines or light free weights, at a load she can lift for 10 to 12 repetitions with good form, two sets, and progress about 5 percent every week or two if there is no pain increase the next day. These patterns are bone loading and useful for work. I would not ask for heavy lifting yet. Third, impact. I would add brisk walking, stairs and small step ups first, then low-level hopping or jumping in small doses later in the plan, if the back and her blood count allow. I would not begin running now. Fourth, the back and her blood work. She has a sharp mid back pain after a heavy lift, so until a physician has reviewed it, I would avoid loaded forward bending, twisting, sit ups and impact, and use pain free movements only. I would also ask her physician to review her standing heart rate rise and dizziness along with her hemoglobin of 98 before I progress anything. Fifth, aerobic and flexibility work. Easy walking or cycling at a conversational pace, building toward 150 minutes a week over several weeks, and gentle mobility work. Sixth, practical details. I would plan sessions after meals when she is least urgent, near a washroom, bring water, and avoid exercise during a flare, replacing it with short gentle walks. Seventh, monitoring. I would track rate of perceived exertion, a fatigue scale, five repetition sit to stand time, grip strength and pain at each visit. I would ask her to check her heart rate and dizziness when she stands. I would reduce or pause if she has worsening back pain, cramping or diarrhea that interferes, dizziness, or a heart rate that stays high. I would share my plan with her gastroenterologist and a dietitian, because protein, calcium, vitamin D and iron are outside what I should prescribe, but are part of the same goal. I would reassess every four weeks and review the plan if she progresses or her medication changes.

scale.4: Gives a specific, individualized program with dose, progression, back precautions, monitoring and triggers, linking choices to steroids, low bone density, anemia and Crohn symptoms. The answer is organized, prioritizes safety and explains the reasoning clearly.
scale.3: Provides a sound program with dose and progression, but with limited individualization to her condition, thin monitoring, or few triggers to reduce or pause exercise.
scale.2: Lists general exercise ideas such as weights and walking, without dose, progression logic or case-specific precautions related to steroids, bone density and her recent back pain.
scale.1: Prescribes heavy lifting, running or spinal flexion loading despite low bone density, steroid use and new back pain, placing the client at risk of fracture.

questions.prompt: Ms. Okafor mentions what happened at work last week. Discuss how you would respond to this information today, including what you would assess, what you would do with her exercise plans and what you would tell her.

checklist.point: Recognizes that new focal back pain after lifting a 25 kg load in a person on prednisone with a lumbar Z-score of minus 2.3 needs fracture to be considered.
Takes a pain history including onset, location, night pain, neurological symptoms, bowel or bladder change and fever.
Examines posture, palpation for focal midline tenderness, neurological screen and movement tolerance gently.
Avoids spinal loading, manual pressure over the tender area and provocative testing until imaging or medical review.
Arranges prompt medical assessment and imaging by the physician, communicating findings with her consent.
Explains findings in plain language without giving a diagnosis, and without causing alarm.
Provides interim advice on activity modification, pain strategies within scope and signs needing emergency care.
Addresses the online advice about stopping prednisone, explaining that medication decisions belong to her physician.
Respects her choices and invites her questions about work and exercise.

questions.model_answer: I would treat this seriously but calmly. A sharp mid back pain after lifting a 25 kg load, in a 26 year old on prednisone with a lumbar Z-score of minus 2.3, could be a muscle strain, but it could also be a vertebral compression fracture. I cannot tell the difference by feel, so my job is to look for features that push me toward fracture, protect her spine, and get her to the right assessment quickly. First, I would take a focused history. When exactly did it start, what was she doing, where is the pain, does it wake her at night, does it catch with twisting, does it spread around the ribs or into her legs, and has she had any numbness, weakness, trouble passing urine or stool changes beyond her Crohn symptoms, fever or unexplained weight loss. Second, I would examine gently. I would look at posture and any new rounding, ask her to point to the spot with one finger, and palpate lightly for focal tenderness over a vertebra, which would raise my concern. I would do a neurological screen for strength, sensation and reflexes in the legs, and observe movement only within comfort. I would not push on the spine, do repeated end range movements, test for spinal loading or give manual therapy there. Third, the plan. I would hold all spinal loading, twisting and impact today, which means no lifting program or running, and keep her to walking and gentle movements that do not hurt. I would explain that we are pausing because her bones are more vulnerable while on steroids, and that this is temporary. Fourth, referral. With her permission, I would contact her gastroenterologist or family physician today to describe the findings and ask for assessment and imaging. If she had leg weakness, loss of bladder or bowel control, or severe uncontrolled pain, I would send her to emergency now. Fifth, communication. I would say that I do not know yet what this is, that most back pain after lifting is not serious, but with her medication and bone scan we check early. Sixth, the prednisone. I would tell her I understand the worry, because steroids do affect bone. But stopping prednisone suddenly can be dangerous and could trigger a flare, and I am not the person who can change it. I would encourage her to ask her gastroenterologist about bone protection options and offer to help her write her questions. Finally I would let her decide what she shares and when.

scale.4: Identifies possible vertebral fracture, assesses safely without provocative loading, holds spinal loading, arranges prompt medical review and addresses the steroid advice within scope of practice.
scale.3: Recognizes the concern and refers, but omits some assessment detail, interim safety advice, or the discussion about the online advice to stop the medication. The reasoning is mostly sound, but the answer lacks depth in one important area.
scale.2: Treats the pain as a simple muscle strain, continues the exercise plan, or refers without clear reasoning or safety precautions for her spine. The answer is partial, with limited reasoning and at least one significant gap.
scale.1: Applies manual pressure, loads the spine, or advises stopping or changing the medication, creating a risk of harm and operating outside scope. The answer misses the intent of the question or includes an unsafe element.

questions.prompt: Ms. Okafor asks you to write a note for her manager about her work limits and to help her keep her diagnosis private. Discuss your professional responsibilities in responding to her requests.

checklist.point: Obtains informed, documented consent before releasing any information and explains what will be shared.
Shares only minimum necessary information, such as functional limits, not her diagnosis or medications.
Bases work restrictions on objective findings and notes that they are temporary pending medical review.
Stays within scope: does not diagnose, set medical restrictions beyond physiotherapy findings or comment on drug dosing.
Supports her in making disclosure decisions and informs her about workplace accommodation processes.
Documents the request, consent, content of the note and communication with other providers.
Considers coordination with her physician for formal medical documentation and fitness to work forms.
Avoids discrimination, and acts with cultural safety and respect for her wishes.

questions.model_answer: I want to respect her privacy, help her with a real workplace need, and stay within what I am qualified to say. First, consent and purpose. Her health information belongs to her. Before I write anything for her employer, I would ask what she wants the manager to know and what she wants to keep private, then explain what I am proposing to share and why, and get her consent in writing. She can say no, change her mind, or limit it. I would also tell her that once I give a note to her, she controls who sees it. Second, the content. A work note should describe function, not diagnosis. I would write about what she can safely do for a defined time, for example, avoid lifting over a stated weight, avoid repetitive twisting and heavy carrying, allow short breaks and washroom access, with a review date. I would not include Crohn disease, her medications or her bone density results. The manager does not need them to arrange lighter duties. Third, basis and scope. My limits must come from my assessment and be honest about what they are. Because we are still waiting on a medical review for her back, I would call them temporary physiotherapy recommendations. I would not set long-term medical restrictions, declare her unfit to work, or comment on whether she should stay on prednisone. Those are decisions for her physician. If her employer needs a formal fitness-to-work or accommodation form, I would suggest her physician complete it and offer to send my functional findings to the physician with her consent. Fourth, supporting her choice. I would explain what disclosure can do and not do. Many workplaces provide accommodations based on functional needs alone, and she might talk with a human resources contact or union representative, and in Canada there are human rights protections against discrimination due to disability. I would not give legal advice, but I would let her know where she can get it. If she decides to disclose more, that would be her decision. Fifth, documentation. I would record her request, my explanation, her consent, what the note says, and the date. I would keep a copy of exactly what was released. Sixth, respect. She is young and anxious about her job, so I would make sure she does not feel her condition is something to hide in shame, only something she gets to manage on her terms.

scale.4: Obtains consent, limits the note to function, stays within scope, supports her disclosure choices, coordinates with the physician and documents the whole process. The answer is organized, prioritizes safety and explains the reasoning clearly.
scale.3: Addresses consent and minimal sharing, but is weaker on scope boundaries, coordination with the physician, or documentation of what was released. The reasoning is mostly sound, but the answer lacks depth in one important area.
scale.2: Writes a note without clear consent or minimum necessary content, or gives general privacy statements without applying them to her request. The answer is partial, with limited reasoning and at least one significant gap.
scale.1: Discloses the diagnosis or medications to the employer without consent, or oversteps scope with long-term medical restrictions or drug advice. The answer misses the intent of the question or includes an unsafe element.

safety_or_ethics_point: New focal mid back pain after a heavy lift in a young person on steroids with a low lumbar Z-score may be a vertebral compression fracture. A competent candidate withholds spinal loading and manual pressure, screens neurology, arranges prompt medical review, and declines to advise on stopping prednisone while respecting privacy.
common_errors: Candidates build a full lifting and running program without addressing the back pain, or focus on the fatigue and anemia and forget the injury. Others disclose the diagnosis in the employer note or give an opinion about the prednisone.
examiner_notes: A pass notices the new back pain as the priority and changes the plan before referring. Strong responses explain the consent and minimum necessary points in concrete terms. A fail prescribes impact or heavy spinal loading or gives medication advice.

title: Postpartum urinary leakage, pelvic health clinic
setting: Women's health physiotherapy clinic in a hospital outpatient department
client_profile: Ms. Priya Venkataraman is a 34 year old accountant who is 14 weeks postpartum after a first vaginal delivery with a second degree perineal tear, repaired with sutures. She leaks small to moderate amounts of urine with coughing, sneezing and when lifting her baby, about five times daily. She wears a pad. She has no burning with urination, no blood in the urine and no fever. Bowel movements are daily and without leakage. She has not returned to sex. She gets up once at night to void. The International Consultation on Incontinence Questionnaire short form score is 12 out of 21. Her abdomen shows a 3 finger-width diastasis above the umbilicus at rest. Perineal scar is healed and mildly tender. Pelvic floor muscle contraction on palpation, with her consent, is grade 2 out of 5 with a 3 second hold and weak endurance. She is breastfeeding. A friend told her to do 100 Kegels daily.
clinical_scenario: Her husband works away three weeks of each month and her mother lives in another province. The baby wakes four times nightly. At intake she completed the routine clinic questionnaires and tells you she has been "just getting through the days" and cries in the car after daycare drop off. She has not told her family doctor. She is hesitant about an internal examination because the delivery was traumatic, and she asked how long the visit will be because the baby is in the waiting room with a neighbour.

questions.prompt: Explain how you would organize your assessment and what clinical impression you would form from the information so far, including what else you would want to find out.

checklist.point: Forms an impression of stress urinary incontinence related to weak pelvic floor muscle function after vaginal delivery.
Screens for urgency, urge incontinence and mixed symptoms, voiding difficulty, bowel and prolapse symptoms using history.
Screens for red flags: infection, blood in urine, fistula, severe pain, fever, retention and neurological signs.
Explains the pelvic floor palpation, with consent, including strength, endurance, coordination and relaxation.
Considers contributors such as perineal tear, birth trauma, breastfeeding hormones, constipation, cough, lifting load and fatigue.
Notes the diastasis and decides whether it is a priority or a distractor in this context.
Uses an outcome measure and a bladder diary to quantify symptoms and plan reassessment.
Screens psychosocial factors and mood, including the low mood statements, and considers a validated screening tool.
Explains the findings and impression in plain language and agrees next steps with her.

questions.model_answer: I would begin with a clear impression, then show how I would test it. From what I have, the most likely picture is stress urinary incontinence after vaginal birth, with pelvic floor muscles that are weak and tire quickly. The pattern fits: leakage with cough, sneeze and lifting, no burning or blood, and a palpated grade 2 with a short hold. But I would not stop there, because other conditions can look similar. First, history. I would ask about urgency and urge leaks, because a mixed pattern changes the plan. I would ask how often she voids, whether she feels she empties, how the stream is, and whether she feels heaviness or a bulge, which would suggest prolapse. I would ask about bowel leakage and constipation, pain with the scar, and a bladder diary over three days would show her volume and fluid pattern. Second, red flags. I would ask about fever, pain on voiding, blood in the urine, constant dribbling that suggests a fistula, retention, severe perineal pain, foul discharge from the scar, and numbness or weakness in the legs. Any of these means medical review, not exercise. She has none now, but I would document that I asked. Third, the examination. With her clear consent, and an explanation of each step, and the option of a chaperone, to stop at any time, and a trauma-informed approach, I would palpate the pelvic floor externally or internally, whichever she prefers, and assess strength, endurance, repeated contractions, coordination with a cough and the ability to relax. The 100 Kegels a day her friend suggested could overwork the muscles, so I would assess for overactivity as well. I would also check the scar. Fourth, the diastasis. A three finger gap at 14 weeks is common and I would treat it as a secondary finding. Its function matters, so I would check whether she can control tension through the midline during a lift, but it is not the reason she leaks, and I would tell her that. Fifth, her wellbeing. She said she is just getting through the days and cries in the car. I would not skip over this. I would ask her directly and kindly about mood, sleep, support and any thoughts of harm. A validated screening tool such as the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, would help, and I would talk to her about it. Finally I would explain my impression in plain words, use the questionnaire score as a baseline, and agree what we do first.

scale.4: Forms a justified impression of stress incontinence, screens red flags and mixed symptoms, plans a consented examination, treats the diastasis as secondary and screens her mood.
scale.3: Forms the impression and plans a sound assessment, but misses mood screening, a full red flag screen, or the detail of consent for the examination.
scale.2: Lists assessment items without linking them to an impression, or over-focuses on the diastasis and exercise while skipping mood and red flags. The answer is partial, with limited reasoning and at least one significant gap.
scale.1: Misses red flags and the mood concern entirely, or proceeds with an internal examination without informed and ongoing consent. The answer misses the intent of the question or includes an unsafe element.

questions.prompt: Discuss how you would approach the next part of this visit so that it is safe and respectful for Ms. Venkataraman, including how you would respond to the things she has told you outside of her bladder symptoms.

checklist.point: Obtains informed, ongoing consent for any examination, offers choices, a chaperone and the right to stop.
Uses trauma-informed communication, privacy, and explains each step before touching.
Asks directly about her mood and any thoughts of self harm or harm to the baby, calmly and without judgement.
Responds to a positive screen or risk with same day contact to her physician or crisis resources as appropriate.
Provides information on supports such as the public health nurse, perinatal mental health services and crisis lines.
Adjusts the visit for the baby, time and fatigue, and uses short feasible home exercises.
Advises against overdoing 100 daily contractions and teaches a dosed program with rest.
Documents the discussion, the consent obtained and any referrals made, with the date and who was contacted.

questions.model_answer: My first priority is that she feels in control of what happens. I would pause before any examination and say, you decide what we do today, and you can stop me at any time. I would explain what the examination involves in plain words, offer a choice of external or internal assessment or doing it another day, offer a chaperone, and give her privacy to change. I would ask whether anything about the delivery would make this hard, and I would not ask her to describe the trauma unless she wants to. Her consent is not a one-time yes. I would check in during the exam, and if she hesitates, I would stop. Second, the baby. Her neighbour is watching the baby, and she is worried about time. I would ask her whether she would like a shorter visit today, or the baby in the room. We can do the history and teaching now and the examination at the next visit if she prefers. That is part of client-centred care. Third, what she told us about her mood. She said she is just getting through the days and cries in the car, and she has not told her family doctor. I would not wait for a later visit. I would say gently that many new mothers feel this way, that it is common and treatable, and that I would like to ask a few questions. I would ask about sleep when the baby sleeps, appetite, enjoyment, worry, and whether she has had thoughts of harming herself or the baby. If she says yes, or if the screening tool shows risk, I would stay with her, make sure she is not left alone, contact her physician or the local crisis service the same day, and ask her to agree to a plan, using a warm handoff. If she has no thoughts of harm but scores high, I would encourage her to see her family doctor within days, offer to help book it, and give her phone numbers for perinatal support lines, her public health nurse and the crisis line. I would ask permission before sharing anything with her husband or physician. Fourth, her exercise. The 100 Kegels a day idea could tire her muscles and does not suit a fatigued new mother, so I would teach a simple dose, such as 8 to 10 contractions of a few seconds, three times a day, linked to feeding, plus a brace with cough. Finally, I would document her consent, the mood discussion and my actions, and tell her what will happen next.

scale.4: Provides trauma-informed, consent-centred care, adapts to her time and baby, asks directly about mood and risk, acts on risk the same day and gives a realistic, dosed exercise plan.
scale.3: Handles consent and the mood discussion well, but lacks a clear same day action pathway, or practical adaptations to her time and fatigue. The reasoning is mostly sound, but the answer lacks depth in one important area.
scale.2: Mentions consent and referral in general terms, or notes the mood comment without exploring it or planning a response to it. The answer is partial, with limited reasoning and at least one significant gap.
scale.1: Examines without clear consent, or ignores the mood disclosure and possible risk, leaving the client unsupported. The answer misses the intent of the question or includes an unsafe element.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would work with other professionals and people in her life to support Ms. Venkataraman, including who you would involve, what you would share and how.

checklist.point: Gets her consent before sharing information with anyone and agrees on what is shared.
Contacts her family physician about mood symptoms, with a clear summary, and arranges follow up timing.
Identifies the midwife or obstetric provider and public health nurse as contacts for postpartum care.
Considers referral for medical assessment if red flags, prolapse or persistent leaks occur.
Involves her husband or support person only if she agrees, with practical roles such as night feeds.
Considers other supports: lactation consultant, community parent groups, a psychologist, a dietitian if relevant.
Communicates clearly who is responsible for what and the timelines for follow up.
Plans to monitor progress and reassess, including communicating changes to the team.

questions.model_answer: I would start with who, what, when and how, and I would start with her permission. I would ask Ms. Venkataraman who she wants involved and what she is comfortable with me sharing, and I would write her answer in the chart. First, her family doctor. She has low mood and has not told them. With her consent I would phone the clinic and then send a short written summary. I would state what she said, any screening score, that there are no thoughts of harm if that is the case, and the date I suggest she be seen, within the week. I would ask the doctor to confirm they received it. If she showed any risk to herself or the baby, the call would be urgent, the same day. Second, her birth team. The midwife or obstetric provider who delivered her knows about the tear and can check the healing, and the public health nurse often does postpartum home visits and screening. With consent, I would let them know that I am treating her urinary leakage and ask them to tell me about anything unusual they see. Third, if red flags appear, such as blood in the urine, fever, pain, a bulge or constant dribbling, I would stop exercise and ask her physician or a urogynecologist to assess her promptly. If she still leaks after a trial of well-dosed training, say six to twelve weeks, I would discuss with her whether to refer for further evaluation. Fourth, her partner and family. Her husband travels three weeks per month, so I would ask if she would like him to know about the plan, for example sharing night feeds so she can sleep. I would not tell him anything without her permission. I would ask about neighbours, friends or a parent group, and give her information on local supports. A lactation consultant could help if breastfeeding adds stress. Fifth, roles and timelines. I would tell her, and write in my letter, that I am responsible for the pelvic floor program and the review in two weeks, her family doctor for mood and medical care, and the public health nurse for baby and family support. I would also ask her to tell me what she hopes to get from each person. Finally, I would send brief updates after each major change, and I would check at the next visit whether she saw her doctor.

scale.4: Specifies who, what, when and how, grounds all sharing in her consent, urgently links the mood concern to her physician, and sets clear roles, timelines and monitoring.
scale.3: Identifies relevant team members and addresses consent, but lacks timelines, defined roles, or a plan for urgent contact about her mood. The reasoning is mostly sound, but the answer lacks depth in one important area.
scale.2: Names professionals in general terms without consent, content or timing, or focuses only on other physiotherapists and exercise. The answer is partial, with limited reasoning and at least one significant gap.
scale.1: Shares information without her consent, or fails to involve any physician about the mood concern, leaving her at possible risk. The answer misses the intent of the question or includes an unsafe element.

safety_or_ethics_point: The client describes crying in the car and just getting through the days, and has not told her doctor. This may signal postpartum depression. A competent candidate asks directly about mood and safety, screens with a validated tool, acts the same day if there is risk, and obtains consent before sharing information.
common_errors: Candidates focus on pelvic floor training and the diastasis and never return to the mood statement, or they share information with her husband or doctor without asking. Another common error is an internal examination without clear, ongoing consent.
examiner_notes: A pass catches the mood clue unprompted and handles it as a priority with consent and a clear pathway. Strong responses stay trauma-informed. A fail treats the case as a pure incontinence exercise prescription.

title: Cerebral palsy GMFCS III, school-based physiotherapy
setting: Elementary school, resource room and gym, community school physiotherapy service
client_profile: Kaito Nakamura is an 8 year old boy with bilateral spastic cerebral palsy, Gross Motor Function Classification System level III. He walks in the classroom with a forearm crutch walker and uses a manual wheelchair for distances. He lives with his parents and a younger sister. Passive hip abduction with the hips flexed is 25 degrees on the left and 40 degrees on the right. Hip flexion contracture is 15 degrees bilaterally. Hamstring popliteal angle is 60 degrees. Ankle dorsiflexion with the knee extended is minus 10 degrees on both sides. Gross Motor Function Measure 66 score is 52 on its 0 to 100 scale, unchanged from a year ago. Last hip radiograph was 18 months ago, with a left migration percentage of 32 percent and right 18 percent. He winces when his left hip is moved into abduction and has been avoiding the school standing frame, saying his leg hurts at night.
clinical_scenario: The teacher has asked you to extend his supported standing program to 90 minutes daily and to add stretching by the educational assistant before recess. The school board is reducing the physiotherapy caseload and has suggested discharge to a consult-only model. His parents work shifts and attend appointments infrequently. A form for annual follow up with the child's pediatric rehabilitation clinic is in the file, unsigned. The educational assistant has been told to stretch his hips "as far as they go" and Kaito has started saying he does not want to do physio.

questions.prompt: Explain how you would interpret Kaito's current findings and history, and describe what further information or assessment you would seek before you change any part of his school program.

checklist.point: Recognizes reduced left hip abduction with pain and prior migration percentage of 32 percent as a concern for progressive hip displacement.
Notes that surveillance is overdue since the last radiograph was 18 months ago in a child at GMFCS III risk.
Considers other sources of night pain such as spasticity, positioning, hip subluxation, fracture and constipation.
Interprets contractures and tightness as limiting standing, gait and positioning, and prioritizes them.
Notes that an unchanged GMFM-66 is within expectation for GMFCS III at age 8, and that migration over 30 percent warrants orthopedic referral through the physician.
Plans to take a pain history from Kaito using an age appropriate scale and to ask parents about sleep and behaviour.
Plans a focused exam: hip range, palpation, observation of pelvic obliquity, scoliosis screen and skin check.
Plans to request updated hip imaging and medical review through the responsible physician.
Considers goals from Kaito and family, such as school participation and mobility.

questions.model_answer: I would interpret Kaito's findings through the lens of his hips first, because that is the part with the highest stakes. Children with bilateral spastic cerebral palsy at GMFCS III are at real risk of hip displacement, and the risk rises with higher migration percentage and limited abduction. His left migration percentage was 32 percent 18 months ago, and the right 18. A migration over 30 percent is the usual point to ask the physician for an orthopedic referral, and he was already past it. Now his left hip abducts only 25 degrees against 40 on the right, it hurts to move into abduction, and he has night pain. That pattern makes me worry that the left hip may have progressed. I cannot tell from my hands, because only a radiograph can measure migration, so the key missing piece is a current hip X-ray and medical review. Surveillance is meant to be regular, so 18 months without it is overdue. Second, other causes of night pain. It could be spasticity, difficult positioning in bed, constipation, a growth related muscle problem, or a fracture. His bone density may be lower because of limited weight bearing. I would ask Kaito, using a faces scale or a body drawing, where and when it hurts and what helps, and ask his parents about sleep, mood, bowel habits, any fall, and what has changed in the last few months. Third, the other findings. Hip flexion contractures of 15 degrees, tight hamstrings and 10 degrees of lacking dorsiflexion explain the crouched stance and fatigue with walking, and they are important for standing and gait. But they are less urgent than the hip. His GMFM-66 score of 52 has not changed in a year, which is within what I would expect at this age for GMFCS III, so I would not read it as a failure of his effort or as a plateau to fix. Pain could still limit his participation, so I would ask what he wants to do at school and recess. Fourth, my examination. I would observe sitting and standing alignment for pelvic obliquity and windswept posture, screen the spine for scoliosis, check skin over the hips, and measure range gently, stopping at the first resistance or pain. I would not stretch the hip to its end range. I would also record a pain score and sleep pattern as a baseline. Fifth, communication. I would contact his parents and the child's pediatric rehabilitation clinic or physician for updated hip imaging. Until then, I would hold any change to the program that adds load or stretch around the left hip. In short, my interpretation is possible progressive left hip displacement until proven otherwise, with the other findings as contributors, and I would act on that before extending standing time.

scale.4: Identifies possible left hip displacement from the findings and overdue surveillance, considers other causes of pain, plans a focused assessment and requests imaging and review before changing the program.
scale.3: Recognizes the hip concern and requests imaging, but gives limited reasoning about other causes of pain or about what his unchanged function score means. The reasoning is mostly sound, but the answer lacks depth in one important area.
scale.2: Focuses on contractures and function without connecting the hip findings and pain to displacement risk or the need for updated imaging. The answer is partial, with limited reasoning and at least one significant gap.
scale.1: Dismisses the hip pain as behaviour or ordinary spasticity and proceeds to increase standing and stretching, placing the hip at risk. The answer misses the intent of the question or includes an unsafe element.

questions.prompt: Discuss how you would respond to the teacher's request and what you would put in place to keep Kaito safe while the questions about his program are answered.

checklist.point: Holds or reduces the extended standing and aggressive stretching until the hip has been reviewed.
Explains the reason to the teacher in plain language without breaching Kaito's privacy.
Changes the educational assistant's instructions: no forced stretching, stop if pain or resistance, use comfort based positioning.
Provides alternative active ways to stay mobile and participate, such as short supported standing and seating options.
Asks for Kaito's views, uses assent and listens to his refusal and pain as important information.
Teaches the assistant and family signs needing prompt review such as increasing pain, new refusal to bear weight, swelling or fever.
Plans night positioning and pain management discussion with parents and physician, within scope.
Documents instructions given, who received them and the date for review.

questions.model_answer: I would tell the teacher that I am glad she is thinking about how to help Kaito get more standing, and that I need to pause the plan for a short time because of what I found in his hip. I would not share details beyond what the school needs. I would say, Kaito's left hip is sore and I need his doctor to look at it before I ask him to stand longer or stretch more, so for now we should keep things comfortable. Second, the standing. Supported standing is useful for bone health and hip development when the hips are healthy, but if the hip is migrating or painful, long periods in an unsuitable position could add pressure. So until the hip is reviewed, I would reduce standing to short, comfortable periods, perhaps 20 to 30 minutes with his hips in a position that does not push the left into adduction, or I would pause it, depending on what I find. I would not push through pain. He has been avoiding the frame because his leg hurts, and I take that as information. Third, the educational assistant. She has been told to stretch his hips as far as they go. I would meet with her today, show her what is safe, and replace that instruction in writing: no stretching to end range, no forcing, stop at the first resistance or sign of pain on his face, and use slow, active movements and comfortable positions instead. I would tell her to report anything that worries her and who to call. Fourth, Kaito. He has started to say he does not want to do physio. I would sit with him, at his level, and ask what is hard and what he would like to be able to do. I would explain, in words an 8 year old understands, that we are going to look at his leg so it can feel better, and that he has a say in what we do. His assent matters, and if he says no or shows pain, we stop. Fifth, alternatives. I would suggest ways he can still take part, such as supported sitting in a good chair, short walks in his walker with a rest option, and recess games that do not stress the hip. Sixth, warning signs. I would give the teacher and parents a short list: new or worse pain, crying at night, refusing to bear weight, a swollen or hot hip, fever, or a fall. Any of these leads to a call to the parents and a same day medical visit. Finally I would document all instructions and set a review date for the week after the hip result.

scale.4: Holds the standing and stretching plan, retrains the assistant in writing, gains Kaito's assent, offers alternatives, and gives clear warning signs and a review date.
